en: *Prakaraṇāryavācāśāstra*, Fascicle One.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
To the Sugata who excellently taught the sublime three bodies, The fearless and untainted realization and doctrine,
And the sons of the Muni of the Supreme Vehicle who possess true reality— I now first pay homage with utmost sincerity.
I prostrate with my head in reverence to the Great Compassionate One, who is about to succeed to the throne of the Dharma King of All-Knowledge,
the refuge for the world without support, and the one who proclaims the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

In the past, I, Asaṅga, heard this from him; now, out of compassion for the holy teaching, I shall interweave the essentials of the stages (bhūmi) so that the text is concise, the meaning is complete, and it is easy to understand.
The skillful mastery in the meaning of the purification of the *saṃgrahavastu*, the realization (*abhisamaya*) of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness,
and the inconceivable yoga— these constitute the eleven chapters on the supreme determination (*viniścaya*).
The defilements of all realms, The truths, the bases, and the factors of enlightenment,
The person, the fruit, and all virtues— These are the nine topics.
The commentary says:
Regarding "all," there are five factors that comprehensively encompass the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. What are these five?
The verse says:
Mind, mental factors, matter, non-associated formations, and the unconditioned.
The treatise says:
"Mind" refers to the various designations for citta, manas, and vijñāna.
Question:
What is consciousness? Answer:
There are eight kinds of consciousness: namely, the ālayavijñāna; the visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses; the manas; and the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).

As for the ālayavijñāna, its substance consists of all-seed vipāka-consciousness, which arises with the karma and afflictions accumulated in previous lives as its conditions and the habitual tendencies of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) from beginningless time as its cause.

This consciousness is able to grasp and discern the material sense organs, the physical bases upon which those organs rely, and the habitual tendencies of conceptual proliferation; at all times, its arising and ceasing are of a single uniform nature and cannot be discerned.

Furthermore, it can maintain and discern the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), is associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*) and so forth, is consistently non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), serves as the causal basis for the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and so forth, arises simultaneously with the defiled and pure evolving consciousnesses and their sensations, and functions to increase the defiled evolving consciousnesses and so forth, as well as to diminish the pure evolving consciousnesses and so forth.
How is it known that this consciousness exists?
As the Blessed One has said:
"Enveloped by ignorance and bound by the fetters of craving, the fool brings about the acquisition of a body possessed of consciousness."
These words reveal that there exists the maturation-consciousness, the ālayavijñāna.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Like five types of seeds, this is called the consciousness with grasping (sopādāna-vijñāna)."
These words reveal the existence of the *ālayavijñāna* which contains all seeds.

Furthermore, it is said: "The *ādānavijñāna* is profound and subtle; containing all seeds like a violent torrent, I do not reveal it to the foolish and ignorant, lest they conceptualize and grasp it as a self."

Visual consciousness refers to that which is produced from seeds within the ālayavijñāna; it relies upon the eye faculty, operates simultaneously with it, takes visible forms as its objective sphere, and has the nature of discerning them.
As the Bhagavān said:
"When the internal eye-base is unimpaired, external visible forms appear, and the corresponding attention arises, then the visual consciousness produced thereby comes into being."
Furthermore, it is said that visual consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and visible forms.
One should understand this to apply likewise, up to and including tactile consciousness.
The distinction here is that each [consciousness] relies upon its own respective faculty, takes its own respective object as a condition, and performs its own distinct discernment.
All [characteristics] should be cited as in the two preceding sūtras.

"Mind" (*manas*) refers to that which arises from seeds within the *ālayavijñāna* and, in turn, takes that very consciousness as its object; it is associated with self-delusion, self-love, clinging to "mine," and self-pride—or the opposites thereof—and functions at all times with the mode of haughty elevation or equanimity, evolving simultaneously with those [afflictions], having the nature of discernment.
As the Bhagavān has said:

"When the internal sense-base of the mind is unimpaired, the external sense-base of phenomena is present, and the attention arising therefrom correctly arises, then the mental consciousness produced thereby comes into being."

Mental consciousness refers to that which arises from seeds within the ālayavijñāna, functions in conjunction with the mental faculty (manas), takes all common and uncommon phenomena as its objects, and has the nature of discernment.

Mental concomitants (caitta-dharma) refer to those phenomena that arise from seeds within the ālayavijñāna, which originate based upon the mind, evolve simultaneously with the mind, and are associated with it.
What, then, are they? They are the five omnipresent factors:
first, attention; second, contact; third, feeling; fourth, perception; and fifth, volition.
There are five object-specific mental factors:
first, desire; second, resolve; third, mindfulness; fourth, meditative concentration; and fifth, wisdom.
There are eleven wholesome mental factors:
1. Faith, 2. shame, 3. dread of blame, 4. non-attachment, 5. non-hatred, 6. non-delusion, 7. diligence, 8. pliancy, 9. heedfulness, 10. equanimity, and 11. non-harming.
There are six primary afflictions (*kleśa*):
first, greed; second, hatred; third, pride; fourth, ignorance; fifth, views; and sixth, doubt.
There are twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*):

1. Anger (krodha), 2. Resentment (upanāha), 3. Concealment (mrakṣa), 4. Affliction (pradāśa), 5. Envy (īrṣyā), 6. Avarice (mātsarya), 7. Deceit (māyā), 8. Sycophancy (śāṭhya), 9. Arrogance (mada), 10. Harmfulness (vihiṃsā), 11. Lack of shame (āhrīkya), 12. Lack of dread (anapatrāpya), 13. Torpor (styāna), 14. Agitation (auddhatya), 15. Lack of faith (āśraddhya), 16. Laziness (kausīdya), 17. Heedlessness (pramāda), 18. Loss of mindfulness (muṣitasmṛtitā), 19. Distraction of mind (cetaso vikṣepaḥ), 20. Lack of clear comprehension (asaṃprajanya).
There are four indeterminate factors:
first, remorse; second, sleep; third, vitarka; and fourth, vicāra.

Regarding attention (manasikāra): it arises from seeds within the ālayavijñāna, originates based upon the mind, functions in association with the mind, and has the movement of the mind as its essence.
Its function is to draw the mind [toward its object].
Because it causes the mind to share a single object of focus, it is said to be "conjoined" rather than "disjoined.
As it is stated in the Sūtra:
If there is attention toward something, there is discernment toward that very thing; if there is discernment toward something, there is attention toward that very thing.
Therefore, these two are always conjoined and never disjoined; it is impossible to designate these two phenomena as separate or distinct.
Furthermore, it is said in this way:
"The activities of the mind and mental factors are inconceivable.
It is also said:
When the mental attention (*manasikāra*) produced by that arises correctly, the visual consciousness and so forth produced in this manner arise.
Contact (*sparśa*) refers to the conjunction of the three factors, having discernment as its essence.
Its function is to serve as the basis for sensation.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"There are six groups of contact."
Furthermore, it is said:
with the eye and visible forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises.
Through the gathering and conjunction of these three factors, there is contact.
Furthermore, it is said:
contact is the condition for feeling.
Feeling has the nature of experiencing as its essence.
Its function is to serve as the condition for craving.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"There are six groups of feeling."
Furthermore, it is said:
sensation (*vedanā*) is the condition for craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
As for perception (*saṃjñā*), it refers to the sets of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*), which serve as conditions through their habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*).
It arises from seeds within the ālayavijñāna and originates based upon the mind.
It evolves simultaneously with the mind, taking the apprehension of characteristics as its essence,
and its function consists of initiating speech and deliberation.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"There are six groups of perception (ṣaḍ-saṃjñā-kāyāḥ).
It further states:
Discursive speech arises according to what is conceived.
"Conception" (vitarka) refers to that which causes the mind to engage in gain, loss, or that which is neither; it has mental action (*manas-karman*) as its essence.

It functions either to bring about union or separation, to grant or withhold, to produce craving or aversion, or to effect relinquishment. It gives rise to applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), or further produces the two actions of body and speech. Its activity consists of defilement or purification, and it functions as wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral.
As the Sūtra says:
"There are six groups of volition.
It further states:
It should be understood that what I have now called the six bases of contact are precisely the karmic results created by past volition.
"Desire" (chanda) has as its essence the longing for an object of one's preference.
Its function is to serve as the basis for diligence.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Desire is the root of all phenomena."
Resolve (*adhimokṣa*) has as its essence the act of determining and certifying an object as it is appropriate;
its function is to be unshakeable.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
We now give rise to a resolute conviction that these six internal bases are certainly devoid of a self.
"Mindfulness" (smṛti) has as its essence the clear recollection and non-forgetfulness of an object with which one has become familiar.
Its function is to serve as the basis for meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
As the Sūtra says:

"Various forms of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and recollection (*anusmṛti*), distinct thoughts, mindfulness, and memory; that which does not forget or lose the dharma, having the nature of the mind’s clear recording."
Samādhi (equipoise) has as its essence the one-pointed abiding of the mind upon the object of observation.
Its function is to serve as the basis for the wisdom that prevents the mind from scattering.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

The various states of mental abiding— namely, even abiding, settled abiding, close abiding, and fixed abiding— which consist of non-distraction, non-diffusion, gathering, tranquility, and meditative concentration,
are the state of the mind remaining upon a single object.
Wisdom (prajñā) has as its essence the discernment of the very object under investigation.

Its function is the realization of the objects of knowledge—whether they are in accordance with reality, contrary to reality, neither in accordance nor contrary to reality, or neither contrary nor non-contrary to reality.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"The discernment of phenomena, the supreme discernment, the thorough discernment of phenomena, complete understanding, close understanding, intelligent understanding, penetration, investigation, sagacity, clear awakening, the course of wisdom, and vipaśyanā."
Faith (*śraddhā*) has as its essence the mental clarity and acceptance toward that which possesses substance, qualities, and efficacy.

Its functions are: to eliminate the obstacle of lack of faith; to bring to fulfillment the provisions for awakening (*bodhisambhāra*); to benefit oneself and others; to lead toward the good realms of existence; and to increase pure faith.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"One gives rise to firm faith toward the Tathāgata.
Regarding *hrī* (moral shame): its essence consists of feeling ashamed of one's faults and evils, based upon oneself as the predominant factor (*adhipati*) and the Dharma as the predominant factor.
Its function is to sever the obstacle of lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), and as previously stated, its function extends up to the increase of shame (*hrī*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"One feels shame regarding that which should be shunned," and so forth, as explained at length.
*Hrī* (shame) refers to that which, based on the authority of the world, takes the nature of feeling shame for faults and evils.
Its function is to sever the obstacle of *anapatrāpya* (lack of shame), and as previously stated, its function extends up to the increase of *hrī*.
As the Sūtra says:
"To feel shame regarding what one should feel ashamed of," and so forth, as explained at length.
Non-attachment (*alobha*) has as its essence the state of being weary of existence and the requisites of existence, being without grasping, without concealment, without craving, and without clinging.
Its function is to sever the obstacle of greed, and as previously stated, its function extends up to the increase of non-greed.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The wholesome root of non-greed."
Non-hatred (*adveṣa*) means having a nature of compassion and sympathy that is free from the intent to harm sentient beings.
Its function is to sever the obstacle of hatred, and as previously stated, its function extends up to the increase of non-hatred.
As the Sūtra says:
"The root of goodness that is non-hatred.
Regarding "non-delusion," its essence is the correct realization of reality.
Its function is to sever the hindrance of delusion, and as previously stated, its function extends up to the increase of non-delusion.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The wholesome root of non-delusion."
Vigor (*vīrya*) has as its essence a courageous mind free from indolence and a lack of self-contempt.
Its function is to eliminate the obstacle of laziness, and as previously stated, its function extends up to the increase of vigor.
As the Sūtra says:
"Arousing diligence, one abides with power, exertion, valor, firmness, and courage, not relinquishing the noble yoke.
As for pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), its essence consists of being free from heaviness and rigidity (*dausthulya*) and the harmonious flexibility of body and mind.
Its function is to sever the obstacle of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), and as previously stated, its function extends up to the ability to increase pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
As the Sūtra says:
"The mind is satisfied, and body and mind are at peace."
Non-negligence (apramāda) has as its essence the synthesis of non-attachment, non-hatred, non-delusion, and diligence.

Its function is to enable the abandonment of unwholesome and evil states and the cultivation of their wholesome antidotes; it functions to eliminate the obstacles of negligence, and so forth, up to the increase of non-negligence itself, as previously described.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The arising of all immeasurable wholesome dharmas is entirely dependent upon the faculty of heedfulness (*apramāda*).
As for equanimity (*upekṣā*), its essence consists of the synthesis of non-attachment, non-hatred, non-delusion, and diligence.

By relying on this equanimity (*upekṣā*), one attains mental evenness and mental rectitude; the mind is free from agitation, and its function is to sever the obstacles to agitation, as previously described, up to its function of increasing equanimity.
Through heedfulness, one eliminates defiled phenomena; through that relinquishment, one dwells in the undefiled state once those phenomena have been eliminated.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"In order to eliminate greed and sorrow, the mind relies upon equanimity (*upekṣā*)."
Non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) means that because one does not afflict or injure sentient beings, its essence consists of compassion, sorrow, and sympathetic pity for all things.
Its function is to sever the obstacle of harming, and as previously stated, its function extends up to the increase of non-harming.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"By way of non-harming, one knows him to be wise," and so forth, as explained at length.
"Greed" (rāga) has as its essence the attachment to, concealment of, and clinging to the five aggregates of grasping (pañca-upādāna-skandha).

Whether arising simultaneously with birth (*sahaja*) or through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpita*), its functions are: to act as an obstacle to non-attachment; to act as an obstacle to the perfection of the provisions for awakening (*bodhisambhāra*); to cause harm to oneself and others; to lead toward the evil destinies (*durgati*); and to increase craving and desire.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"All those who possess craving are overcome and obscured by greed; so too are those who harbor hatred."
It is defined as having the nature of wishing to inflict harm upon sentient beings.

It may be either innate (*sahaja*) or conceptually arisen (*vikalpita*), and its function is to obstruct non-hatred (*adveṣa*); as previously stated, its function extends up to the increase of hatred (*dveṣa*).
As the Sūtra says:
"All those who possess hatred are overcome and obscured by hatred. Regarding pride (*māna*):
it refers to comparing oneself with others and conceiving of oneself as superior, equal, or inferior; its essential nature consists in causing the mind to become haughty and self-aggrandizing.

Whether arising simultaneously with birth (*sahaja*) or through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpita*), its function is to obstruct the absence of pride, and as previously stated, its function extends up to increasing pride.
As the Sūtra says:
there are three types of pride—the pride of "I am superior," the pride of "I am equal," and the pride of "I am inferior."
Ignorance (avidyā) has as its essence the failure to correctly comprehend reality.
It is either innate or conceptually constructed; its function is to obstruct correct comprehension, and as previously stated, its function extends up to the point of increasing ignorance.
As the Sūtra says:
"All those who are deluded are oppressed and obscured by ignorance.
"Views" refers to that which has the five views as its essence:

First is the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which consists of conceiving a self or what belongs to a self with respect to the five aggregates of clinging; its essence is defiled wisdom.

It is either innate or conceptually arisen, and its function is to obstruct the realization of non-self and non-perversion, as previously stated, up to its function of increasing the view of a personal identity.
As the Sūtra says:

"Thus knowing and seeing, one eternally abandons the three fetters, namely: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
The adherence to extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) consists of clinging to the five aggregates of clinging as being either annihilated or eternal; its essence is defiled wisdom."

Whether arising simultaneously with birth (*sahaja*) or through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpita*), its function is to obstruct the non-perverted understanding of impermanence; as previously stated, its function extends up to the increase of the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
As the Sūtra says:
"Kātyāyana, all the world relies upon two things: existence or non-existence. There are three types of false views:
namely, slandering the cause, slandering the fruit, or slandering the efficacy [of action], or else destroying the reality of things; their essence is defiled wisdom (*kliṣṭa-prajñā*).
It arises solely through conceptual discrimination, and its function is to obstruct right view; as previously stated, its function extends up to the increase of false views.
As the Sūtra says:
"Whatever is grasped by one who possesses false views is entirely inverted," and so forth, as explained at length.

The fourth is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which consists of regarding the aforementioned three views and the aggregates that serve as their basis as being supreme, superior, and foremost; its essence is afflicted wisdom (*kliṣṭaprajñā*).

It arises solely from conceptual construction; its function is to obstruct the non-erroneous understanding of suffering and impurity, and as previously stated, its function extends up to the increase of the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
As the Sūtra says:
"One firmly clings to and adheres to what one has seen for oneself," and so forth, as explained at length.

The grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) refers to the defiled wisdom that regards the aforementioned views and the aggregates upon which those views depend as being pure, liberating, and leading to transcendence; its essence is defiled wisdom.

It arises solely from conceptual construction; its function is to obstruct the non-erroneous understanding as previously described, and its function extends up to the augmentation of the adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), as stated in the Sūtra:
"One is bound by the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśasaṃyojana*)."
Doubt (*vicikitsā*) has as its essence indecisiveness regarding the various truths (*satya*).
It arises solely from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), and its function is to obstruct the absence of doubt; as previously stated, its function extends up to the point of increasing doubt.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Perplexity is doubt.
"Anger" has as its essence the provocation of the mind by way of adverse conditions in the present.
Its function is to obstruct non-aversion, and so on, up to its function of increasing anger (*krodha*).
Resentment (*upanāha*) has as its essence the failure to relinquish a grudge toward past adverse conditions.
Its function is to obstruct non-aversion, and so forth, up to its function of increasing resentment (*upanāha*).
Concealment (*mrakṣa*) has as its essence the hiding of one's own misdeeds, whether or not others offer admonition or instruction regarding those transgressions.
Its function is to obstruct the disclosure and repentance of transgressions, and its function extends to increasing concealment.

"Malice" (pradāsa) refers to the essence of uttering coarse words when others offer counsel regarding one's offenses, characterized by a violent and intolerant mind; its function is to obstruct virtuous friends, and its function extends to increasing malice.
Envy (*īrṣyā*) has as its essence a mind of resentment and displeasure toward the virtues, reputation, respect, and material gains belonging to others.
Its function is to obstruct loving-kindness and benevolence, and ultimately to increase envy itself.
Avarice (mātsarya) has the nature of accumulation and stingy attachment.
Its function is to obstruct non-attachment, and its further function is to increase avarice.
Deceit (māyā) has the nature of mental guile that manifests unreal things for the purpose of deluding others.
Its function is to obstruct affection and respect, and so forth, up to its function of increasing deception.
Deceit (*śāṭhya*) refers to the fraudulent display of deference and compliance for the sake of cheating others; its essential nature is mental crookedness.
Its function is to obstruct affection and respect, and so forth, up to its function of increasing deceit.
As the Sūtra says:
"Anger, enmity, concealment, vexation, envy, parsimony, deception, and deceit."
Pride (*mada*) has as its essence the mind’s haughty exaltation and lack of restraint upon the temporary acquisition of worldly prosperity and the like.
Its function is to obstruct disenchantment (*nirveda*), and its function extends to the further increase of pride itself.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"Fools who lack correct hearing, seeing that youth, freedom from illness, and lifespan abide only temporarily, give rise extensively to arrogance and negligence," and so forth, as explained at length.
Harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*) has as its essence the oppression and affliction of sentient beings, characterized by a lack of compassion, pity, sorrow, tenderness, and empathy.
Its function is to obstruct non-harmfulness (*avihiṃsā*), and furthermore, its function is to increase harmfulness.
As the Sūtra says:
"Those who harbor malice will inevitably cause harm and affliction to others.
Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) has as its essence the absence of remorse regarding one's own faults and transgressions, with respect to both oneself and the Dharma.
Its function is to obstruct a sense of shame (*hrī*), and its function extends to increasing the lack of shame (*āhrīkya*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"One feels no shame regarding what should be shunned; through this lack of shame, unwholesome and evil states arise," and so forth, as explained at length.
Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) has as its essence the absence of remorse for one's transgressions and evils with respect to the world.
Its function is to obstruct shame, and its function extends to the increase of lack of shame.
As the Sūtra says:
"Not feeling shame where one should feel shame; the arising of shamelessness gives rise to evil and unwholesome states," and so forth, as explained at length.
Torpor (*styāna*) has as its essence causing the mind to sink, due to relying on the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the body and taking pleasure in clinging to a lack of progress.
Its function is to obstruct vipaśyanā, and so forth, up to its function of increasing lethargy (styāna).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"In this person, there arises physical and mental lethargy."
Restlessness (auddhatya) has as its essence a lack of mental tranquility, resulting from improper seeking or from recollecting past experiences of play, pleasure, and the like.
Its function is to obstruct *śamatha*, and so on, up to its function of increasing restlessness (*auddhatya*).
As the Sūtra says:
"You are restless and moreover haughty," and so forth, as extensively explained.
Lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) has as its essence a lack of pure conviction regarding that which exists, possesses qualities, and possesses efficacy.
Its function is to obstruct faith, and furthermore, its function is to increase the lack of faith.
As the Sūtra says:
"If a person does not abide in impure faith, they will never lose any of their wholesome dharmas," and so forth, as explained at length.
Laziness (*kausīdya*) has as its essence a lack of mental exertion due to being addicted to the pleasure of sleep and reclining, and due to fear of progress and self-deprecation.
Its function is to obstruct the initiation of right effort, up to and including the function of increasing indolence.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"If one is indolent, one will certainly regress from right effort," and so forth, as explained at length.
Heedlessness (*pramāda*) has, in brief, greed, hatred, delusion, and laziness as its essence.

Because one relies upon these, the mind does not restrain unwholesome and evil states, nor does it cultivate their antidotes; its function is to obstruct heedfulness and even to increase heedlessness.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Heedlessness is the track of birth and death," and so forth, as explained at length.
"Loss of mindfulness" (muṣitasmṛtitā) has as its essence the defiled non-recollection of dharmas or meanings previously performed, spoken, or contemplated.
Its function is to obstruct non-forgetfulness, and its function extends to increasing forgetfulness.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"One who is forgetful is incapable of accomplishing anything," and so forth, as explained at length.

Mental distraction (*citta-vikṣepa*) refers to the state in which the mind does not find joy or delight in the wholesome qualities being cultivated; its essence consists in the scattering [of the mind] toward external objects.
Its function is to obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and furthermore, its function is to increase mental distraction.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"If one's mind is distracted by the five objects of desire and wanders without ceasing," and so forth, at length.

Lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*) refers to not dwelling with correct awareness regarding the activities of body, speech, and mind; its essential nature is defiled wisdom (*kliṣṭā prajñā*).
Its function is to obstruct right awareness (*saṃprajanya*), and so forth, up to its function of increasing wrong awareness (*asaṃprajanya*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"One who has lost mindfulness dwells in wrong awareness," and so on at length.
Regret (kaukṛtya) has as its essence the state of being dejected and remorseful regarding good or bad deeds already performed or not yet performed, whether they are defiled or undefiled.
Its function is to obstruct *śamatha*, and its further function is to increase the occurrence of regrettable actions.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"If one harbors regret, there will be no peace," and so forth, as explained at length.
Sleep (*middha*) has as its essence the contraction of the mind such that it functions without mastery.
Its function is to obstruct vipaśyanā, up to its function of increasing sleepiness.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"One who is greedily attached to the taste of sleep is like a great fish that has been swallowed."

Investigation (*vitarka*) refers to the essence of causing the mind to operate coarsely by engaging with external objects, whether at times through volition (*cetanā*) acting upon phenomena or at times through wisdom (*prajñā*) examining phenomena.
Its function is to obstruct internal clarity of mind, and so forth, up to its function of increasing discursive thought (*vitarka*).

Regarding *vicāra* (sustained thought): it arises from seeds within the *ālaya-vijñāna*, originates based upon the mind, and operates in association with it; its essence consists in the subtle engagement of the mind with external objects that have already been roughly examined by *vitarka*, causing the mind to turn toward them with subtlety.
The rest is as explained in the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*.
Up to the point that it functions to increase *vicāra*; because it takes the same object as the mind (*citta*), it is said to be associated (*samprayukta*) and not dissociated.
As the Bhagavān said:

"If one investigates this, one discerns this; if one discerns this, one investigates this. Therefore, these two are always conjoined and not unconjoined; these two dharmas cannot be established as separate or distinct."
Furthermore, it is said thus:
"The activity of mind and mental factors is inconceivable.
To realize these two, the *āgama* is as the Bhagavān has said:
Speech is initiated by relying upon vitarka and vicāra; it does not occur without vitarka and vicāra.
Regarding those mental factors that are mentioned only briefly here, they should be understood as explained in detail according to their respective applications.
Just as consciousness and mental factors are inconceivable, it should be understood that these various mental factors are likewise in relation to one another.

There are fifteen kinds of form (*rūpa*): namely, earth, water, fire, wind; the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; visible form, sound, odor, taste, and a portion of the tangible; and the form included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Earth is of two kinds:
first, internal; second, external.

Internal refers to that which is comprised of the five sense faculties, such as the eye and so forth, within each individual body, together with their respective bases and supports—characterized by solidity and being appropriated [by consciousness].

Furthermore, there is a further accumulation, namely: hair, body hair, nails, teeth, filth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, veins, and so forth—all these impure things constitute the internal physical form and its constituent parts.
Its function is to serve as the basis for experience.

"External" refers to the objects of the five sense-fields—form and so forth—which exist outside of one's respective body; it is that which is comprised by solidity and rigidity and is of a non-appropriated nature.
Furthermore, there is superior accumulation, namely gravel, stones, mounds, mountains, forests, bricks, and so forth.
When calamities such as water arise, these are subsequently destroyed; such is the external physical form of the earth element.
Its functions are: the function of enjoyment, the function of supporting enjoyment, the function of destroying enjoyment, and the function of providing nourishment as an antidote.
Water is also of two kinds:
first, internal; second, external.

The internal refers to the five sense faculties, such as the eye and so forth, within each individual body, along with their respective bases; it is characterized by moisture, is comprised of the moist, and is appropriated [by consciousness].

Furthermore, there is an accumulation of predominant elements, namely various impure substances such as mucus, tears, saliva, sweat, fat, marrow, phlegm, and so forth; these constitute the internal element of water.
Its function is to provide moisture, accumulation, and sustenance.
Externally, it refers to that which serves as the basis for the five objects—form and so forth—outside of individual bodies; it is comprised of moisture and is of a non-appropriated nature.
Furthermore, there is a superior accumulation, namely springs, streams, ponds, deep ravines, and great floods; when calamities such as fire arise, these are quickly consumed and dried up.
This is the external essence of water.
Its functions are to serve as a support for enjoyment, to undergo transformation through enjoyment, and to provide nourishment as an antidote.
Fire is also of two kinds:
first, internal; second, external.

The internal refers to the five sense faculties, such as the eye, within each individual body, along with their respective bases and locations; it is characterized by a nature that is appropriated and sustained by warmth.

Furthermore, there is a superior accumulation, which is to say, that which causes sentient beings to be thoroughly warmed and heated, and which also enables the digestion of whatever is consumed through drinking and eating.
All such things as these constitute the essence of internal fire;
its function is to mature, harmonize, and provide sustenance.
The external refers to that which serves as the basis for the five objects—form and so forth—outside of each individual body; it is comprised of warmth and heat, and is of a non-appropriated nature.

Furthermore, there is a superior accumulation, namely: blazing fires that spread through villages and cities, extending across islands and marshes, until they are extinguished due to reaching empty, remote, and supportless spaces; or fire sought through various means such as drilling wood or striking stones—once this fire has arisen, it soon turns to ashes. This is the nature of external fire.
Its functions are to cause transformation and decay through consumption, and to provide nourishment as an antidote.
Wind is also of two kinds:
first, internal; second, external.

The internal refers to the five faculties, such as the eye, within each individual body, along with their respective bases and supports; it is characterized by a nature that is appropriated and comprised of lightness and mobility.

Furthermore, there is a superior accumulation, namely the upward, downward, and horizontal movement of the inhalation and exhalation of breath; all such things constitute the substance of internal wind.
Its activity consists of initiating action and providing for experience.

Externally, it refers to that which serves as the basis for the five objects—form and so forth—distinct from one's own body; it is comprised of lightness and mobility, and is of a non-appropriated nature.

Furthermore, there is superior accumulation, namely the shattering of mountain cliffs and the prostration of forest trees; since these have been dispersed and destroyed, they are tranquil because they lack a basis.
If one seeks wind, it moves the clothes and shakes the fan; when it does not move or shake, it is stilled because it lacks the conditions [for its activity].
All such things as these constitute the external substance of wind;
their functions are to serve as a support for experience, to undergo transformation through experience, and to provide nourishment through counteraction.

The eye refers to that which is appropriated by the ālayavijñāna containing all seeds; it takes the matter derived from the four great elements as its object and serves as the basis for the consciousness that perceives the objective realm of form.
They have pure matter as their substance,
are included within the aggregate of form, and possess the nature of being invisible yet impinging.
As it is with the eye, so it is with the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
The distinction here is as follows: each serves as the basis for its own respective object and for the consciousness that takes that object as its condition.

"Form" refers to the objective domain traversed by the eye and the focal object of visual consciousness; its substance consists of derived matter from the four great elements, whether it be visible color, shape, or intimation.
Included within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), it is visible and possesses resistance (sapratigha).
This, moreover, is of three kinds: namely, the agreeable, the disagreeable, and that which is neither. What, then, are these?

That is to say, visible colors such as blue, yellow, red, and white; shapes such as long, short, square, round, coarse, fine, high, low, regular, and irregular; smoke, clouds, dust, mist, light, shadow, brightness, and darkness; the single visible color of space; and the color of reflected images—all these are called "form" (rūpa).
Sound refers to the object-domain of the ear and the focal object of auditory consciousness; its essence consists of audible tones produced by the four great elements.
It is subsumed within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) and is invisible yet resistant.
This, moreover, is of three kinds: namely, that which is agreeable, that which is disagreeable, and that which is neither.

It may arise from the striking together of hands and so forth; or from the plucking of strings or the beating of leather by means of vitarka and vicāra; or it may be initiated for worldly purposes, for the sake of maintaining one's livelihood, or for the purpose of expounding the meaning of the Dharma; or it may be the echo produced by relying upon cliffs and valleys.
Thus, whether it be the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*), or resonance (*pratiśrutkā-śabda*), these are called sound.

Fragrance refers to the objective sphere traversed by the nose and the object-condition (*ālambana*) of olfactory consciousness; its essence consists of odoriferous substances derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Included within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), it is invisible and possesses resistance (*sapratigha*).
This, moreover, is of three kinds: namely, pleasant fragrance, unpleasant fragrance, and that which is neither. What, then, are these?
That which is known as the fragrance of roots, stalks, bark, leaves, flowers, fruits, incense, and powders—whether innate, blended, or transformed—is called "odor."
Taste (rasa) refers to the objective sphere of the tongue and the focal object of tongue-consciousness; its essence consists of substances derived from the four great elements that can be tasted.
It is subsumed within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) and possesses the nature of being invisible yet impinging (anidarśana-sapratigha).
This, moreover, is of three kinds: namely, sweet, non-sweet, and that which is contrary to both. What are these?
They are the tastes of clarified butter, granulated sugar, rock honey, ripe fruits, and so forth—whether innate, compounded, or transformed; these are called taste.
A portion of tangibility refers to the objective sphere of the body and the focal object of body-consciousness; its essence consists of tangible objects derived from the four great elements.
It is subsumed within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) and possesses the quality of being invisible yet impinging (anidassana-sappaṭigha).
This, moreover, is of three kinds: namely, the pleasant, the unpleasant, and that which is neither. What are these? They are:

roughness, smoothness, lightness, heaviness, slackness, tension, warmth, cold, hunger, thirst, satiety, oppression, strength, weakness, itching, illness, old age, death, fatigue, rest, stickiness, and vigor; or that which is conditioned by luster or lack of luster, by solidity or lack of solidity, by binding or accumulation, by discord or harmony; whether innate, combined, or transformed—this is called a portion of contact (*spraṣṭavya*).

Matter included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) refers to that which is at all times the objective domain of the mind; it is subsumed under the aggregate of matter (*rūpaskandha*), and is invisible and non-obstructive.

This, moreover, is of three kinds: matter of restraint (*saṃvara-rūpa*), matter of non-restraint (*asaṃvara-rūpa*), and matter that is the objective domain of meditative concentration (*samādhi-gocara-rūpa*).
What is the matter of restraint (*saṃvara-rūpa*)?

It refers to the guarding of bodily and vocal actions; because the mind and mental factors perform their functions through its predominance, the nature of matter is established based on those factors that do not manifest.
What is the nature of non-restraint (asaṃvara-rūpa)?

It refers to those bodily and vocal actions that are not guarded; because they give rise to the primary mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta), the nature of matter (rūpa-dharmatā) is established based on their manifestation.
What is the form that is the object of the domain of samādhi?

It refers to the nature of the reflected image that arises as an object of focus, and the nature of the accomplished form produced by it, due to the mental states and mental factors associated with and functioning together with the three grades of samādhi—namely, inferior, middling, and superior. This is what is subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana).

Regarding "conditioned factors dissociated from matter and mind" (*rūpa-citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*): this refers to those conditioned factors that are dissociated from the mind; they are of a nature conventionally designated upon the states of mind, mental factors, and matter, yet cannot be designated as being either identical to or different from the mind and its associated factors.

Furthermore, these are distinguished into twenty-four types, namely: acquisition (*prāpti*), the attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the realm of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-deva*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneous character of a group (*nikāya-sabhāga*), birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), duration (*sthiti*), impermanence (*anityatā*), the body of names (*nāma-kāya*), the body of phrases (*pada-kāya*), the body of phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*), the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), transmigration (*pravṛtti*), determination (*pratiniyama*), association (*samyoga*), succession (*anukrama*), velocity (*java*), time (*kāla*), direction (*deśa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), conjunction (*sāmagrī*), and non-conjunction (*asāmagrī*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that there are other such distinctions of this kind.
As for "attainment" (*prāpti*), it is further of three types:

first, the nature of the distinction in the continuity comprised of the seeds of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the nature of the distinction in the continuity of sovereign arising; and third, the nature of the distinction in the continuity of the arising of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

The attainment of non-conception refers to one who has already become detached from the desire for the Sphere of Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna), but has not yet become detached from the desire for the higher stages; such a person contemplates perception as being like a disease, like an abscess, and like an arrow, [thinking] that only the Heaven of Non-conception is tranquil and sublime.

Because of the preliminary application of the mental attention directed toward the perception of renunciation regarding the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), there is the nature of the cessation of those mind and mental factors that do not constantly manifest.

As for the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*): it refers to one who has already become free from desire for the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and either enters the meditative absorption of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) or further advances beyond it.

Either one enters the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or further advances; because of the preliminary application consisting of the mental attention that conceives of a temporary cessation, there is the nature of the cessation of those mental states and mental factors that do not constantly manifest as objects of focus, as well as a portion of those mental states and mental factors that do constantly function.

The Heaven of Non-conception refers to those who previously attained the attainment of non-conception in this world, and by virtue of this, are subsequently reborn in the realm of the Non-conceptual Sentient Beings Heaven; it is the nature of the cessation of all minds and mental factors that do not constantly manifest.
The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) refers to the determinate nature of the duration of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), which is the maturation (*vipāka*) projected by prior karma.
The commonality of group (*nikāyasabhāga*) refers to the mutual similarity among sentient beings.
Regarding the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), there are two kinds:
first, the nature of an ignorant ordinary person; second, the nature of an unlearned ordinary person.
The nature of an ignorant ordinary person refers to the quality of ignorance within the bodies of sentient beings since beginningless time.
The nature of being an unlearned worldling refers to the nature of various false paths outside the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Birth refers to the nature of the arising of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Aging refers to the nature of the transformation of conditioned phenomena before and after their occurrence.
"Abiding" refers to the nature of the continuity of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) when they arise.
"Impermanence" refers to the nature of conditioned phenomena that, having arisen through their own characteristics, subsequently perish and disintegrate.
"Name-body" (*nāmakāya*) refers to the conventionally established designation that expresses the intrinsic nature of phenomena such as conditioned phenomena.
The "phrase-body" (*padakāya*) refers to the collection of names (*nāman*), which serves as the basis for verbal expression that reveals the meanings of defilement and purity.
The "syllable-body" (*vyañjanakāya*) refers to the nature of the phonemes (*akṣara*) that serve as the support for the former two.
"Flowing" (pravṛtti) refers to the nature of the uninterrupted continuity of the causes and effects of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
"Distinctness" (pratiniyama) refers to the nature of the distinctness between the causes and effects of conditioned phenomena.
"Correspondence" (yoga) refers to the nature of the mutual conformity between the causes and effects of conditioned phenomena.
"Velocity" refers to the nature of the rapid flow of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
"Succession" refers to the nature of conditioned phenomena flowing one after another in sequence.
"Time" refers to the nature of conditioned phenomena arising and ceasing anew as they pass from one to the next.
"Space" (方) refers to the nature of the pervasive boundaries of all material forms and formations.
"Number" (數) refers to the nature of the continuous flow of the individual, distinct bodies and characteristics of all formations.
"Conjunction" (和合) refers to the nature of the gathering of conditions for all formations.
"Non-concordant" refers to the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) having discordant conditions.

"Unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) consists of eight kinds: namely, space (*ākāśa*), cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the imperturbable (*āniñjya*), the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*), the suchness of wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma-tathatā*), the suchness of unwholesome phenomena (*akuśala-dharma-tathatā*), and the suchness of indeterminate phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma-tathatā*).
Space (*ākāśa*) refers to the nature of an objective sphere that serves as an antidote to the external forms perceived by the mind and mental factors.

Cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) refers to the non-arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) due to the non-encounter of causes and conditions; it is a cessation that is not of the nature of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*).

Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) refers to the ultimate non-arising of all contaminated conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) by means of the skillful application of wisdom; it is cessation that is of the nature of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*).

The unshakable (*āniñjya*) refers to the state of dissociation from suffering and pleasure attained during the interval between being free from desire for the "Universal Purity" (*śubhakṛtsna*) realm and the attainment of the fourth dhyāna.

The cessation of perception and feeling refers to the state of dissociation that occurs when one, having abandoned desire for the sphere of nothingness, enters the meditative attainment of cessation; therein, the mental states and mental factors that do not constantly manifest, as well as a portion of those mental states and mental factors that do constantly manifest, cease.
The suchness (*tathatā*) of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena refers to the nature of the pure objective sphere within wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena.

Furthermore, it should be understood that these five dharmas also possess three aspects: first, the aspect of superimposition; second, the aspect arising from superimposition; and third, the aspect of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The characteristic of superimposition refers to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) among all phenomena.

The characteristic arising from the superimposition of what is to be superimposed refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) among all phenomena, as it corresponds to its respective [basis].
Regarding the characteristic of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*), it refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) among all phenomena.
Having thus explained everything [regarding the characteristics], the elements (*dhātu*) shall now be explained.
The verse says:
"Realms refer to the desire realm, the form realm, and so forth, as well as the three-thousandfold world system.
The commentary states:
There are two kinds of realms: first, the three realms such as the desire realm; second, the three-thousandfold world system.

Regarding the three realms such as the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): first, the desire realm, which refers to the differentiation of the various aggregates (*skandha*) associated with the stage of not being free from desire and accompanied by manifold afflictions (*kleśa*).
Second, the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), which refers to the differentiation of the various aggregates associated with the stage already free from desire and accompanied by manifold afflictions.
The three formless realms refer to the distinctions among the aggregates of various afflictions in stages that are free from desire for form.

One should know that these three realms further possess five kinds of distinctions: first, the distinction of characteristics; second, the distinction of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*); third, the distinction of direction and location; fourth, the distinction of enjoyment; and fifth, the distinction of sustenance.

Regarding the distinctions among the characteristics of form (*rūpa*): in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), form possesses many characteristics, lacks clarity and purity, and consists of various diverse characteristics;
in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), form possesses few characteristics, is clear and pure, and is not of various diverse characteristics;
in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), although there is no form produced by karma, there exists form produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that is invisible and non-obstructive.

Furthermore, in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), there are characteristics associated with painful sensation (duḥkhavedanā), characteristics associated with ill-will (vyāpāda), and characteristics associated with many secondary afflictions (upakleśa);

in the form and formless realms (rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu), there are characteristics dissociated from painful sensation, characteristics dissociated from ill-will, and characteristics associated with few secondary afflictions.

Regarding the distinction of coarseness and heaviness (*dausthulya*): in the desire realm, coarseness and heaviness are coarse and harmful; in the form and formless realms, coarseness and heaviness are subtle and not harmful.

Regarding the distinction of location: the desire realm (kāmadhātu) resides in the lower region, the form realm (rūpadhātu) resides in the upper region, and the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) has no location.
Regarding the distinction of enjoyment: the desire realm enjoys external objects, while the form and formless realms enjoy internal objects.

Regarding the distinction of maintenance: the aggregates of the desire realm abide by means of the four nutriments (*āhāra*), while the aggregates of the form and formless realms abide by means of three nutriments.
As for the "trichiliocosm," it consists of one small thousand-world system, one medium thousand-world system, and one great thousand-world system.
That which is illuminated by one sun and moon is called a single world-system (*lokadhātu*).

Within such a thousandfold world-system, there are a thousand suns and moons, a thousand Sumeru kings of mountains, a thousand Jambudvīpas, a thousand Pūrvavidehas, a thousand Aparagodānīs, a thousand Uttarakurus, a thousand Cāturmahārājakāyika heavens, a thousand Trāyastriṃśa heavens, a thousand Yāma heavens, a thousand Tuṣita heavens, a thousand Nirmāṇarati heavens, a thousand Paranirmitavaśavartin heavens, and a thousand Brahmakāyika heavens; these taken together are termed the first small thousandfold world-system (*sāhasracūdikalokadhātu*).
Furthermore, one thousand small chiliocosms is called a second intermediate chiliocosm; furthermore, one thousand intermediate chiliocosms is called a third great trichiliocosm.
Question:
For what reason is a small thousandfold world system called "lowly and small"?
Answer:
It is just as a bull whose two horns have been cut off is called "lowly" or "small" because of its deficiency;
likewise, all that exists within the thousandfold world-systems below the Brahma-world is inferior to the higher realms, and is therefore called "lowly" or "small."
In this way, the three-thousandfold world system is destroyed by the three calamities, namely fire, water, and wind.
Furthermore, there are three types of these calamities.
The upper limits of these three calamities are the second, third, and fourth dhyānas respectively.
For those gods of the fourth dhyāna, it is the natural law that they arise and perish together with the palaces in which they dwell.
Furthermore, there arise three intermediate kalpas of destruction, namely: famine, pestilence, and warfare.

For twenty intermediate kalpas the world is in the process of dissolution; for twenty intermediate kalpas it remains dissolved; for twenty intermediate kalpas the world is in the process of formation; and for twenty intermediate kalpas it remains formed.
Thus, eighty intermediate kalpas combined are called a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*).

For example, just as rain falls from the sky in a continuous stream as thick as a chariot axle without interruption, so too in the eastern direction, infinite worlds appear without interruption—some forming, some being destroyed, some currently being destroyed, some having been destroyed and remaining, some currently forming, or having formed and remaining. This applies likewise to the worlds of the ten directions. Having thus explained the realms (*dhātu*), the defilements (*saṃkleśa*) shall now be discussed.
The verse says:
Afflictions, karma, and the nature of birth—these should be understood as the corresponding categories of defilement.
The commentary says:
The nature of affliction (*saṃkleśatva*) is threefold: first, the affliction of mental defilements (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*); second, the affliction of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*);

and third, the affliction of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*). Regarding the affliction of mental defilements: it refers to all primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), which together are termed the affliction of mental defilements.

Afflictions are briefly of ten kinds: first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); second, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); third, false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); fourth, the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); fifth, the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); sixth, attachment (*rāga*); seventh, aversion (*pratigha*); eighth, ignorance (*avidyā*); ninth, pride (*māna*); and tenth, doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Alternatively, there are two kinds: first, those abandoned through seeing; second, those abandoned through cultivation.
Alternatively, there are three kinds: first, those bound to the desire realm; second, those bound to the form realm; and third, those bound to the formless realm.

Furthermore, there are seven types of inverted conduct: first, conduct of false understanding; second, conduct of non-understanding; third, conduct that is neither understanding nor non-understanding; fourth, conduct of clinging to false understanding; fifth, conduct based on its causes and conditions; sixth, conduct arising from fear of it; and seventh, spontaneous conduct.

Mistaken practice refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), because they give rise to erroneous attachments regarding objects of knowledge.
Non-practice refers to ignorance (*avidyā*).
That which is neither understanding nor non-understanding is what is called doubt.

That which consists of adhering to false understanding is what is called the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and the greed and other afflictions arising from various views.
Those that function based on causes and conditions refer to those abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
Those that function out of fear refer to those abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).
Those that arise spontaneously refer to those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) and those abandoned through vision (*darśana-prahātavya*).

There are one hundred and twelve afflictions to be abandoned through insight, and sixteen afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation; thus, there are one hundred and twenty-eight afflictions in total to be abandoned through both insight and cultivation.

Thus, because of the various distinctions in meaning regarding these afflictions and defilements, various names are established, namely: fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), graspings (*upādāna*), ties (*gantha*), hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), stumps (*khila*), stains (*mala*), burns (*paridāha*), harms (*vihimsā*), arrows (*śalya*), possessions (*parigraha*), misconduct (*duścarita*), outflows (*āsava*), deprivations (*vaikalya*), fevers (*pariḷāha*), quarrels (*raṇa*), blazing fires (*santāpa*), fires (*agni*), dense forests (*gahana*), and obstructions (*vibandha*). Such are the distinctions among these meanings and their names.

Karmic defilement refers to bodily, vocal, and mental actions—comprised within the three realms as appropriate—which are either produced by afflictions or produced by wholesome dharmas assisted by the conditions of afflictions.
This, moreover, is of two kinds: first, volition; second, that which arises from volition.

This differentiation of karma is further manifold: that which is comprised within the desire realm is called merit and non-merit; that which is comprised within the form and formless realms is called the imperturbable.

Furthermore, there is projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*), which refers to both the performed and the accumulated [karma] that is capable of projecting the various results of the sentient world (*sattva-loka*) and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) as well as their maturation (*vipāka*).
Furthermore, there is productive karma (*janaka-karma*), which refers to that which assists what was previously projected by causing it to arise.
Regarding the defilement of birth: it means that birth occurs due to afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma;

because of birth, there is suffering. This suffering is of many kinds: the suffering of being constrained within the womb; the suffering of old age, sickness, and death; the suffering of association with the loathed; the suffering of separation from the beloved; the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; the suffering of growing up together with coarse and heavy formations (*dausthulya*); the suffering of repeated birth and death; and the suffering of being born into various unfavorable conditions (*akṣaṇa*). These are called "birth."

Chapter One, Part Two: The Compendium of Matters (*Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*). Having thus explained the defilements (*saṃkleśa*), the truths (*satya*) shall now be explained.
The verse says:
There are six kinds of truths.
The commentary says:

There are six kinds of truths: first, conventional truth; second, ultimate truth; third, the truth of suffering; fourth, the truth of origination; fifth, the truth of cessation; and sixth, the truth of the path.

The conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) refers to the collections of names, phrases, and syllables; all verbal expressions based on their meanings; the meanings understood through those verbal expressions;
and the previously attained worldly minds and mental factors, as well as the objects within their respective domains.
The ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) refers to noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), the objects experienced by that wisdom, and the mental states and mental factors associated with them.
As for the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), there are two types:
first, that which is subsumed under conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), and second, that which is subsumed under ultimate truth.
That which is subsumed under conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is as stated in the Sūtras:

the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of association with the disliked, the suffering of separation from the beloved, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
That which is subsumed under ultimate truth is as stated in the sūtras:
"Briefly summarized, all five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
As for the truth of origination, it has four types:
First, total inclusion; second, superior inclusion; third, inclusion by conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); and fourth, inclusion by ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Regarding total inclusion: all afflictions (*kleśa*) and karmas of the three realms are termed the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).

Regarding "superior inclusion": it refers to craving that arises with respect to one's own body—both already attained and not yet attained—as well as with respect to objects; craving for future existence, craving accompanied by delight, and craving for pleasure in various circumstances—all these are termed the Truth of Origination.
That which is subsumed under conventional truth refers to causes that can bring about the truth of suffering as subsumed under conventional truth.
That which is subsumed under ultimate truth refers to causes that can bring about the truth of suffering as subsumed under ultimate truth.
The truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) also has four aspects, as previously explained.

Regarding "complete inclusion," this refers to the complete inclusion of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), its abandonment without remainder, its total relinquishment, its exhaustion, its dispassion, its cessation, and its pacification.

Regarding "superior inclusion," this refers to the superior inclusion of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), which is abandoned and discarded without remainder; it is explained in detail in this manner.

Regarding "inclusion within conventional truth," this refers to the abandonment and discarding without remainder of the truth of origination as included within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); it is explained in detail in this manner.

Regarding that which is subsumed under ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*): it refers to the complete and remainderless abandonment and relinquishing of the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*) as it is subsumed within ultimate truth; this is explained in detail as follows.
As for the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*), there are likewise four kinds, as previously described.
Complete inclusion refers to all factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
Superior inclusion refers to the eight branches of the noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

Inclusion according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) refers to the truths of suffering, origin, and cessation as subsumed under conventional truth, for the sake of full knowledge, for the sake of permanent abandonment, and for the sake of realization.

Regarding all noble paths subsumed under the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*): this refers to the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the truths of suffering, origin, and cessation as they are subsumed within the ultimate truth; thus it is explained at length.

Regarding the meaning of the Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path: if, in a certain place, this is the domain of noble wisdom, then in that place suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are truths; because all noble ones unanimously declare these to be truths, they are therefore called "Noble Truths."
Having thus explained the Truths, the bases shall now be explained.
The verse says:
"The bases are eight and two."
The treatise says:
There are eight kinds of bases. What are these eight?
This refers to the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments.
Furthermore, there are two kinds. What are these two?
That is to say, the first dhyāna is of two kinds: mundane and supramundane; likewise up to the sphere of nothingness, which is of two kinds: mundane and supramundane;
whereas the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is exclusively mundane.

Regarding the mundane first dhyāna: having taken as its object either the predominant teaching on the transcendence of desire for the desire realm, or the predominant instruction on that transcendence, one attains a transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) through the application of attention (*manasikāra*) and the fervent cultivation of practice via the mundane path. However, because one does not penetrate deeply into the meaning of the objects of knowledge, one cannot permanently destroy the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) nor the locus of the afflictions of one's own stage; thus, it is a state subject to regression.

It is the basis for the mind and mental factors of the samādhi of its own level, just as in the case of the mundane first dhyāna; likewise, this extends up to the mundane sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, each taking as its object the superior teaching that is free from the desires of the lower levels, as explained in detail previously.

Regarding the supramundane first dhyāna: it refers to having previously entered the first dhyāna through mental attention characterized by such conduct, such aspects, and such signs; now, however, one does not employ mental attention characterized by such conduct, such aspects, and such signs. Rather, one contemplates all phenomena subsumed under form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as being like a disease, like an abscess, like an arrow, and as obstacles—impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; or alternatively, one contemplates that suffering is suffering, origination is origination, cessation is cessation, and the path is the path; or alternatively, one contemplates true suchness (*tathatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Having thus contemplated all phenomena as being like a disease, up to their ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi), his mind gives rise to weariness and fear toward such phenomena.

Having given rise to weariness and fear, he dwells with his mind concentrated upon the deathless realm (amṛtadhātu), or he dwells with his mind concentrated upon true suchness (tathatā), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi).

In this state, there is non-conceptual wisdom, its associated mind and mental factors, and the transformation of the basis upon which they rely; because one has deeply penetrated the objects of knowledge, one can eternally destroy the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), such that it is no longer a locus for any afflictions and is the dharma of non-retrogression.
This is called the supramundane first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness.
This should be explained in detail; furthermore, regarding the various dhyānas and formless attainments, four aspects should be known:
first, defilement; second, purity; third, establishment; and fourth, purification.
Regarding "affliction" (*saṃkleśa*): it refers to the arising of deep attachment to the taste (*āsvāda*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) within the higher dhyānas.
As for "attachment to the taste," there are ten types: 1. Attachment to the taste of innate attention (*sahaja-manasikāra*); 2.

Attachment to the taste of attention arising from conceptualization (*vikalpa-utpanna-manasikāra*); 3. Attachment to the taste of attention belonging to one's own level (*svabhūmi-manasikāra*); 4. Attachment to the taste of attention belonging to another level (*parabhūmi-manasikāra*); 5. Attachment to the taste of the past; 6. Attachment to the taste of the future; 7. Attachment to the taste of the present; 8. Attachment to the taste of the lower [levels]; 9. Attachment to the taste of the middle [levels]; 10. Attachment to the taste of the higher [levels].
"Purified" refers to the pure (*śuddha*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The pure, moreover, is of three kinds:

first, that which is produced by cultivation; second, that which is refined through higher stages; and third, that which is comprised of the capacity for functional fitness resulting from the removal of defilements.
Regarding the untainted (*anāsrava*), there are also three types:
first, supramundane untainted; second, untainted as its outflow (*niṣyanda*); and third, untainted as dissociation (*visamyoga*).
Regarding their establishment, there are further four types:

First, the establishment of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*); second, the establishment of the fundamental stage (*maula*); third, the establishment of meditative absorption (*samādhi*); and fourth, the establishment of rebirth (*upapatti*).
Regarding the establishment of the preparatory and fundamental stages, as it is said in the Sūtra:
"That this body is moistened, thoroughly moistened, thoroughly suffused, and thoroughly pervaded by the joy and bliss born of seclusion—this is called the preparatory stage of the first dhyāna."
As another sutra states:
"Within this very body, there is not even the slightest part that is not pervaded by the joy and bliss born of seclusion; this is called the fundamental first dhyāna."
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"That which, within this very body, is moistened, thoroughly moistened, thoroughly gratified, and thoroughly pervaded by the joy and bliss born of meditative concentration (samādhi)—this is called the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) of the second dhyāna."
As the Sūtra further states:
"Within this very body, there is not even the slightest part that is not pervaded by the joy and bliss born of samādhi; this is called the fundamental second dhyāna."
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"That which, within this very body, is moistened, thoroughly moistened, thoroughly gladdened, and thoroughly pervaded by the bliss that is free from joy—this is called the preparatory stage of the third dhyāna."
As another sutra states:
"Within this very body, there is not even the slightest part that is not pervaded by the bliss of detachment from joy; this is called the fundamental third dhyāna."
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"When one dwells pervading this very body with a pure mind and a cleansed mental state, fully accomplished and suffused, this is called the preparatory stage of the fourth dhyāna."
As another sutra states:
"Within this very body, there is not even the slightest part that is not pervaded by a pure mind and a stainless mind; this is called the fundamental stage of the fourth dhyāna."
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"Because all perceptions of form have been transcended, because all perceptions of resistance have ceased and vanished, and because one does not attend to any perceptions of diversity, one enters the sphere of infinite space; this is called the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space."
As another sutra states:
"Abiding in full possession" refers to the fundamental stage of the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
As it is said in the sutra:
Transcending all the sphere of infinite space and entering the sphere of infinite consciousness is called the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
As the Sūtra further states:
"Abiding fully" refers to the fundamental stage (*maula*) of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the sphere of nothingness, wherein there is not even the slightest thing"—this is called the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) of the sphere of nothingness.
As another sutra states:
"Abiding fully endowed" refers to the fundamental sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
As it is said in the sutra:

Transcending all spheres of nothingness and entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
As another sutra states:
"To dwell fully" refers to the fundamental stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding the establishment of meditative concentration, it is as explained in the sutra:

By being detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, one dwells having attained the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and characterized by the joy and happiness born of seclusion.

"Detached from sensual desires" means that, having either taken as an object the predominant teaching on detachment from the desires of the desire realm, or having taken those instructions as the cognitive object, one has abandoned the afflictive obscurations of the desire realm.
"Being free from evil and unwholesome dharmas" means severing the karma of the desire realm. Because these defiled dharmas can cause one to fall into the evil destinies, they are called "evil.
Because they can obstruct what is wholesome, they are called "unwholesome."
Vitarka refers to that which serves as the antidote to the two kinds of affliction: the thought of renunciation, the thought of non-ill will, and the thought of non-harm.
Vicāra refers to that which serves as the antidote to the two kinds of affliction: the investigation of renunciation, the investigation of non-ill will, and the investigation of non-harm.
"Detachment" refers to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) attained by severing the obstacles to be remedied through the cultivation of their antidotes.
"Arising" refers to that which is produced from this [transformation].

"Joy" refers to the experience subsumed under feeling (*vedanā*), consisting of mental gladness, mental vigor, mental fitness, and mental pliancy, belonging to one who has already undergone the transformation of the basis and who relies upon the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).

"Bliss" refers to that which, for one who has already undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), relies upon the *ālayavijñāna* to encompass its support, causing the body to be joyful, pleasant, and at ease—a state comprised within the category of feeling (*vedanā*).
"Initial" means that within the sequential meditative absorptions (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), this counting is the very first.

"Dhyāna" (meditative concentration) refers to having abandoned the defiled phenomena of the desire realm; it is the basis for applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*), and, by relying upon the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), the mind abides in one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*).
"Endowed with" means cultivation.
"Abiding in perfection" means having mastery and autonomy regarding entering, remaining, and emerging [from meditative absorption].
Furthermore, as it is said in a sutra:

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal clarity and the unification of the mind in one-pointed concentration, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is free from applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and bliss born of samādhi.

Regarding the stilling of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*): this means that after taking as an object either the authoritative teaching concerning the transcendence of desire for the first dhyāna, or the instructions regarding it, the applied and sustained thought belonging to the level of the first dhyāna become stilled and no longer manifest.
