"Internal serenity" (adhyātmasaṃprasāda) refers to the gathering of mindfulness and clear comprehension in order to counteract applied and sustained thought (vitarka-vicāra). Because the mind dwells in equanimity within its own internal substance, free from the turbid dharmas of applied and sustained thought, it is called "internal serenity."

"One whose mind is concentrated on a single object" means that when entering [this state], one dwells in a continuous succession for a long time, and various states of discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) do not manifest at all.
"Without discursive thought and without investigation" means having realized the state in which discursive thought and investigation have been abandoned.
Samādhi refers to the one-pointedness of mind of one who has already undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
As for "arising," it refers to the joy and bliss produced from samādhi, as previously explained.

The second dhyāna is defined as the subsiding of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), characterized by internal purity and being the basis for the joy and bliss born of samādhi; through reliance on the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parivṛtti*), the mind abides in one-pointedness.
The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, as stated in the Sūtra:

"By being detached from joy, one dwells in equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and the blissful experience of the body; the Noble Ones declare that one has attained the dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and bliss, and thus fully enters the third dhyāna."

Regarding "detachment from joy": this refers to either taking as an object the authoritative teaching concerning the transcendence of desire for the second dhyāna, or taking those instructions as one's objective domain, and thereby perceiving the faults and defects in the characteristics of joy within the second dhyāna.

Abiding in equanimity (*upekṣā*) refers to the state of dwelling in a mind that is impartial, upright, and unshakable—characterized by non-attachment and a sense of renunciation toward already arisen perceptions of joy and mental engagements, such that one does not find them acceptable. It is a nature of abiding that is undefiled.

"Mindfulness" (smṛti) refers to not forgetting and maintaining clarity regarding the aspect of non-arising joy that has already been examined, thereby causing joy to become certain and no longer manifest.
"Clear comprehension" (saṃprajanya) refers to when, due to a lapse in mindfulness, joy again manifests, one correctly discerns the aspect of that manifesting joy.

"Bliss" refers to that which is subsumed under the feeling of equanimity—free from joy and free from exertion—experienced by one who has undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

"Body" refers to the consciousnesses of the transformed basis, whether they be the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) or the ālayavijñāna; since there is no distinction in their mental nature, they are collectively termed the "body."

Regarding "right reception" (*samyaksamāpatti*): it refers to one who has already undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), being able to sustain the body and cause the body to be joyful; this is collectively termed the "right reception of the blissful body.
In this state, the experience of pleasure is profoundly tranquil, most excellent, and subtle, such as is not found in the higher or lower realms.
The "Noble Ones" refers to the Buddhas and their disciples.
"Proclaiming" means manifesting and establishing [the teaching].

Regarding "abiding in the bliss of equanimity and mindfulness," this is because there is no such sublime bliss in the stages above this, nor is there such superior bliss or the antidotes of equanimity and mindfulness in the lower stages.

The third dhyāna refers to that which, having transcended joy, is the basis for equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and bliss; based upon the transformation of the basis, the mind abides in one-pointedness.
The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, as stated in the Sūtra:

"By the abandoning of pleasure, and because suffering, joy, and grief have already been abandoned, one dwells having fully attained the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness."
The abandonment of pleasure refers to the time of entering the fourth dhyāna.
The prior abandonment of suffering refers to the time of entering the second dhyāna.
The prior abandonment of joy refers to the time of entering the third dhyāna.
"Having already abandoned sorrow" refers to the time of entering the first dhyāna.

"Neither-painful-nor-pleasant" refers to one who has undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*); it is neither ease nor unease, a feeling included within the category of feeling, which is the most supreme tranquility of the form realm, a most excellent sustenance that is free from fluctuation.

Purity of equanimity refers to the state of mental evenness, mental rectitude, and the state of abiding without mental fluctuation, because one has transcended all movement in the three stages of applied thought, sustained thought, and joy.

Purity of mindfulness refers to the clarity of mind that does not forget or lose its object, because it has transcended all movement associated with the three stages of applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*).
It is called "the fourth" because it is the fourth in the sequence of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).

Dhyāna refers to that which, because it delights in abandonment, is the basis for the purity of equanimity and mindfulness that is neither painful nor pleasant; based upon the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), the mind abides in one-pointedness.
The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, as the Sūtra says:

"By transcending all perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, one enters and dwells, having fully attained the sphere of infinite space, [perceiving] 'space is infinite.'"
"All" refers to the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
"Perception of form" refers to the perception of visible color (*varṇa-saṃjñā*).
"Transcending" means being free from desire for those [forms].

It should be understood that this is as in the sense of "transcending": the perception of resistance (*sapratigha-saṃjñā*) ceases and disappears, and one does not attend to perceptions of diversity (*nānātva-saṃjñā*).

Regarding "perception of resistance," this refers to the perception of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) which serve as its basis, as well as the perception of other derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).

"Various perceptions" refers to the various perceptions comprised within the category of derivative form (*upādāya-rūpa*), which occur in relation to the four great elements and their derivatives: such things as long and short, coarse and fine, square and round, high and low, regular and irregular, shadow and light, and brightness and darkness. These are the various perceptions included therein.

When one correctly enters the sphere of infinite space, the perception of resistance does not manifest and thus ceases; furthermore, by not directing the mind toward various perceptions, one thereby transcends all perceptions of form that serve as their basis.
"Boundless" refers to the fact that the various characteristics of the ten directions cannot be differentiated.
"Space" refers to the objective sphere that serves as the counteragent to form.
"The Sphere of Infinite Space" refers to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) and the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that depends upon it.
The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, as stated in the Sūtra:
"Transcending the sphere of infinite space entirely, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness and dwells fully possessed of the sphere of infinite consciousness."
"Transcending all the sphere of infinite space" means transcending both the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) and the fundamental stage (*maula*).
"Infinite consciousness" refers to the consciousness that takes infinite space as its object; now, this [consciousness] takes that [infinite consciousness] as its objective field.

Regarding the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), it refers to the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) in this state and the meditative concentration that relies upon it.
The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, as stated in the Sūtra:
Transcending the entire sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters and dwells in the full possession of the sphere of nothingness, wherein there is not even the slightest thing.
"Transcending the entire sphere of infinite consciousness" means transcending both its preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) and its fundamental stage (*maula*).

"Having nothing whatsoever" means that when one investigates the objective sphere beyond the station of infinite consciousness, not even the slightest thing is found; there is no distinct object other than non-existence itself, because one perceives only this state as being utterly tranquil.
The sphere of nothingness refers to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) in this state, as well as the meditative concentration that depends upon it.
The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, as the Sūtra says:
Transcending the sphere of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the fulfillment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
"Transcending the sphere of nothingness" means transcending both the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) and the fundamental stage (*maula*).
"Neither possessing perception" means having transcended the perception of nothingness.

"Nor lacking perception" means that when one investigates the sphere beyond the station of nothingness, one perceives only the extremely subtle mind and mental factors that take nothingness as their object; this is because one sees only this object as being utterly tranquil.

Regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*): this refers to the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) in this state and the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that depends upon it.
The rest is as previously explained.

As for the establishment of birth therein: those who have previously cultivated the lower, middle, and superior levels of the first dhyāna in this world are later born in that place and experience the fruits of three heavens, namely, the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, and the Mahābrahmā heavens.

If one has well cultivated the first dhyāna, which is without vitarka but with vicāra, the result is rebirth in the Great Brahmā Heaven (*Mahābrahmā*), for there is no other superior realm beyond that place.

If one has previously cultivated the second dhyāna in this world at the levels of inferior, medium, and superior, one will later be born in that realm and experience the fruits of three heavens, namely: the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*), the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (*Apramāṇābha*), and the Heaven of Utmost Pure Light (*Ābhāsvara*).

If one has previously cultivated the lower, middle, and upper levels of the third dhyāna in this world, one will later be born in those realms and experience the fruits of the three heavens, namely: the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parīttaśubha), the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (Apramāṇaśubha), and the Heaven of Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna).

If one has previously cultivated the lower, middle, and upper levels of the fourth dhyāna in this world, one will later be born in those realms and experience the fruits of the three heavens, namely: the Anabhraka Heaven, the Puṇyaprasava Heaven, and the Bṛhatphala Heaven.

From this point upward, because one is free from craving for form (*rūpa-rāga*), there are no distinctions of spatial location; although there are causes of inferior, middling, and superior cultivation, no distinctions in the arising of results are established.
If one cultivates the sphere of infinite space with inferior, middling, or superior intensity, one will experience the fruit of birth as a deva in the sphere of infinite space.
If one cultivates the sphere of infinite consciousness with inferior, middling, or superior intensity, one will experience the fruit of birth as a deva in the sphere of infinite consciousness.
If one cultivates the sphere of nothingness with inferior, middling, or superior degrees, one will experience the fruit of birth as a deva in the sphere of nothingness.

If one cultivates the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception with inferior, middling, or superior degrees, one will experience the fruit of birth as a deva in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
There are distinctions among them due to differences in the tranquility of their meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and due to whether or not they have completed their full lifespan.

Furthermore, because they dwell excessively in the relish (*āsvāda*) of the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), they meet with premature death before exhausting their life span.
If one practices the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna, both mundane and untainted, in its inferior degree, one receives the fruit of birth in the Śuddhāvāsa heaven of Avṛha.
If one practices it in its middling degree, one receives the fruit of birth in the Śuddhāvāsa heaven of Atapa.
If one practices the mixed cultivation of the superior grade, one receives the fruit of birth in the Heaven of Sublime Manifestation and Purity (*Sudṛśa-śuddhāvāsa*).
If one practices the mixed cultivation of the superior-superior grade, one receives the fruit of birth in the Heaven of Sublime Vision and Purity (*Sudarśana-śuddhāvāsa*).
If one practices the mixed cultivation of the highest grade, one receives the fruit of birth in the Heaven of Unobstructed Ultimate Purity (*Anāvaraṇa-viśuddha-śuddhāvāsa*).

If one has well-cultivated the fourth dhyāna within the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*), which is induced by the bodhisattva’s immeasurable and inconceivable samādhis, one receives the fruit of birth in the Mahāmaheśvara heaven, which transcends the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
"Purity" refers to the ultimate first dhyāna; based upon this, one brings forth all supreme qualities and swift supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Just as the characteristics of the purity of the first dhyāna are understood, so too should those of the remaining dhyānas and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) be known.
Regarding the absence of distinctions among the formless realms (*ārūpya*), it refers to the development of qualities such as the liberations (*vimokṣa*) of those stages.

In this way, one should understand that these various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) are established with distinctions of purity based on their being either defiled or immaculate.
The bases of reliance have already been explained; the factors of enlightenment shall now be discussed.
The verse says:
The factors of enlightenment are numerous, the primary being thirty-seven.
The treatise states:

The categories of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are manifold; those that are preeminent at the outset number thirty-seven, namely the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, as explained at length in the sūtras.

Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness: first is the foundation of mindfulness of the body. This means that having taken as an object either the body itself, or the teachings predominant regarding the body, or those instructions as their objective domain, one—by means of the wisdom born of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, whether consisting of a mere image or an actualized reality—well establishes mindfulness upon the objective sphere of the body, in order to achieve dissociation from the body.
Just as it is with the application of mindfulness to the body, so too should it be understood for the applications of mindfulness to sensation, mind, and phenomena.
The distinction here is that, respectively, each operates upon its own object as appropriate, up until the point of achieving dissociation from the phenomena.
Furthermore, in all instances, one should speak of the mind and mental factors associated with mindfulness (*smṛti*).

When such a mind of investigation is thus aroused, there are four kinds of objects of focus: first, the object grasped by the mind; second, the object experienced by the mind; third, the object discerned by the mind; and fourth, the object of the mind’s defilement and purification.
Regarding the four right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇa*), they are explained at length as in the sūtra.
First: for the sake of abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen, one generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses right effort, and applies mental exertion and mental sustenance.
"Those already arisen" refers to those subsumed under coarse entanglements (*paryavasthāna*).
"Evil and unwholesome dharmas" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) of the desire realm that give rise to evil conduct.
The meaning of "evil and unwholesome" has already been explained as before.
"In order to bring them to cessation" means that by cultivating their antidotes, one causes them to become attenuated.
"Generating desire" means giving rise to the aspiration to realize their cessation.
"Exerting oneself" means not tolerating evil and turning away from it.
"Arousing right effort" means cultivating various firm antidotes to that [evil].

These three preceding phrases reveal that within the non-concentrated states (*asamāhita-bhūmi*), the two types of wisdom—those derived from hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī* and *cintā-mayī*)—serve as weak antidotes.

"Exerting the mind" (*citta-pragraha*) refers to the actualization of the wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī*) as an antidote to those [defilements]; it means exerting the mind to uplift it when the mind has sunk or is defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding "exerting control over the mind" (*cittābhyutsāha*): this refers to when, during the manifestation of these very remedies, if the mind becomes agitated or is defiled by afflictions, one exerts control over the mind to cause it to descend [into stability].
Second, for the sake of not producing unarisen evil and unwholesome states, and so forth, as explained at length.

"Those that have not yet arisen" refers to the causes capable of giving rise to coarse entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), which are comprised within the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) in their state of intensification.
"For the sake of their non-arising" means to prevent these coarse entanglements from becoming manifest.
The arising of desire means the emergence of the wish to realize [the goal] so that it does not manifest.
The application of effort means dwelling in non-forgetfulness so that [the unwholesome state] does not manifest, by virtue of abiding well in mindfulness.
The arousal of right effort, the exertion of the mind, and the maintenance of the mind are all as previously explained.
Third, for the sake of causing unarisen wholesome dharmas to arise, and so forth, as extensively described.
"Those not yet arisen" refers to those not yet attained.
"Wholesome dharmas" refers to the three types of wisdom—arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation—which are called "wholesome" because they are free from fault.
"Causing [the aspiration] to arise" means that it arises because one causes that [attainment] to be obtained.
"Desire" refers to the arising of the desire for realization.
"Exertion" refers to seeking the correct means for its acquisition.
"Exerting right effort" means practicing for a long duration, with earnestness, and with great persistence.

These three preceding phrases clarify the attainment of wholesome dharmas—comprised of both the wisdoms of hearing and reflection—which serve as the antidotes to unwholesome and evil dharmas within the non-concentrated states (*asamāhita-bhūmi*).
"Exerting the mind and sustaining the mind" refers to [the exertion] for the sake of attaining wisdom through cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
The rest is as previously explained.

Fourth, in order to cause wholesome states that have already arisen to endure, not to be forgotten, to reach fulfillment through cultivation, to be cultivated further, to increase, and to expand, one generates desire and exerts effort, and so forth, as explained at length.
"Already arisen" means that it has already been attained.
"Causing it to abide" refers to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
"Causing it not to be forgotten" refers to the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
"Cultivating to fulfillment" refers to the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñābhāvanā*).
These three preceding phrases reveal that one merely guards what has already been attained as wholesome.
"Causing it to be practiced further, causing it to increase, and causing it to expand" follow their respective order because one does not merely become content with those [attainments].
The "desire for production" refers to the arising of the desire for realization.
The remainder is as previously explained.
The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are explained at length as in the Sūtra.
First, one attains samādhi through the predominance of desire (*chanda*).

For example, there may be a practitioner who, having cultivated superior roots of virtue in previous lives, gives rise to faith and desire toward a Great Teacher or among wise fellow-practitioners, and listens to the True Dharma.
Having thus desired to hear the true Dharma according to one's faith, one successively realizes the state of mind abiding in a single object.
Through this desire, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is accomplished.
For the purpose of abandoning arisen unwholesome states and preventing unarisen unwholesome states from arising, one generates desire and so forth, up to the stabilization of the mind.
If those wholesome dharmas that are antidotes have not yet arisen, he generates the desire for them to arise;

if they have already arisen, he generates the desire to maintain them, to prevent their loss, to bring them to fulfillment through cultivation, to cultivate them further, to increase them, and to expand them, even up to the stabilization of the mind.

In this way, the practitioner further cultivates the eight types of formative acts of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*): desire, exertion, faith, serenity, right mindfulness, right awareness, volition, and equanimity.
Through this desire, one achieves *samādhi*, which means attaining mastery therein.

"Unwholesome and unvirtuous states that have arisen or have not yet arisen" refers to those comprised by the minor fetters (*paryavasthāna*) and those comprised by the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) which are subtle, slight, and neither diminished nor destroyed.

"Causing them to be severed and causing them not to arise" means: for the purpose of abandoning the already arisen weak-grade fetters (*paryavasthāna*), and for the purpose of weakening the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The generation of desire up to the stabilization of the mind is as explained extensively before.
If those wholesome factors that serve as antidotes have not yet arisen, one generates the desire for them to arise;

if they have already arisen, one causes them to remain, prevents their forgetting, brings them to fulfillment through cultivation, practices them repeatedly, increases them, and expands them. One should understand that the process from generating the desire up to the stabilization of the mind is to be explained in detail as previously described.
"One who practices in this way" refers to one who dwells for a long time practicing in such a manner.
"Furthermore, cultivating desire" refers to the desire to realize that [defilements] no longer manifest and to bring about their impairment.
Exertion (*pragraha*) refers to the initiation of right effort toward *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, having desire as its cause.
Faith (*śraddhā*) refers to the cause for the arising of that desire, because it is the firm conviction regarding those [states] to be abandoned and those to be attained.
"Tranquility" refers to the state of making the body and mind serviceable by eliminating physical and mental heaviness through exertion.
"Right mindfulness" refers to ensuring that the mind does not forget within the context of guarding against the secondary afflictions of mental sinking and agitation.
"Right awareness" (saṃprajanya) refers to the analytical discernment that occurs at times when mindfulness is lost and secondary afflictions manifest.
"Volition" (cetanā) refers to the mental formation [of effort] within the context of tranquility (śamatha) and exertion (pragraha).
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) refers to dwelling in a mind that is undefiled, characterized by mental evenness, mental rectitude, and the quality of non-fluctuation.
Among all such bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), one should know that there are eight types of formative acts of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*).
The distinction here is as follows: second, through the predominance of diligence (*vīrya*), one attains *samādhi*.

For instance, a practitioner, relying on instructions and admonitions, whether in a secluded place, among forest trees, or in a quiet chamber, applies himself with long-term, courageous, thorough, and fervent right effort in such a location, thereby realizing the state of one-pointedness of mind.
Through right effort, samādhi is accomplished;
the rest is as previously explained.
Third, through mental predominance, one attains samādhi.

Suppose there is a practitioner who has previously cultivated the practice of śamatha; by virtue of this cause and condition, they contemplate internal phenomena and swiftly realizes the state of one-pointedness of mind.
Through the cultivation of the mind, samādhi is accomplished;
the rest is as previously explained.
Fourth, through the predominance of contemplation, one attains samādhi.

Suppose there is a practitioner who is learned and retains what he has heard; having accumulated that learning, he dwells alone in seclusion and quietude, and with wisdom he discriminates those teachings, discriminates them most subtly, and investigates them through universal awareness, thereby realizing the state of one-pointedness of mind.
Through observation, samādhi is accomplished;
the rest is as previously explained.
Regarding the five faculties, they are explained in detail as in the Sūtra.

1. The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*): By means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), it causes the mind to become pure, bright, and stainless; free from secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), one attains immovability (*aniñjya*).
Thereafter, for the sake of permanently severing the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), one seeks the direct realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) and practices the skillful means.
In order to attain their antidotes, one gives rise to superior faith.
Second is the faculty of right exertion, which refers to the advancement of courageous vigor based upon the faculty of faith, proceeding in conjunction with that faith.
3. The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*): this refers to clarity and non-forgetfulness based upon right effort (*samyakpradhāna*), which functions in conjunction with it.
4. The faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*): this refers to the mind abiding in a single object based upon the faculty of mindfulness, which functions in conjunction with it.
Fifth is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), which refers to the discernment of all phenomena based on the faculty of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), acting in conjunction with it.
Regarding the five powers (*pañca balāni*), they are explained at length as in the Sūtra;

that is, the faculty of faith and the others, because they have been well-cultivated and practiced extensively, are no longer disturbed by opposing factors such as lack of faith, and are further able to counteract those distracting phenomena.
The meaning of "unconquerable" is designated as "power.
Regarding the seven factors of complete awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*), they are explained at length as in the Sūtra.

First is the factor of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*): this refers to the manifestation of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) through the attainment of perfected virtuous power by means of the mundane path; having previously cultivated the mundane factor of mindfulness, one brings forth the supramundane, effortless, and non-conceptual [wisdom], which is clear regarding the Truths and does not forget the Truths.

Second, the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*): this refers to the effortless and non-conceptual state previously induced, which, relying upon mindfulness and proceeding together with it, results in the understanding of the truths and the awakening to the truths.

In this way, all these factors of universal awakening should be understood as follows: having been previously induced by that which is effortless and non-conceptual, they subsequently rely upon and proceed together with that very state.
Regarding the distinctions among these: the third, the factor of enlightenment of right effort, is mental vigor with respect to the truths;
the fourth, the factor of enlightenment of joy, is mental gladness with respect to the truths.
Fifth, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-sambodhyaṅga*), which renders the body and mind capable and resilient regarding the ultimate truth.
Sixth, the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-sambodhyaṅga*), wherein the mind dwells in one-pointedness regarding the ultimate truth.
Seventh is the enlightenment factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*), which consists of the mind being even toward the truth, the mind being upright, and the mind being free from fluctuation.
Furthermore, as it is said in the Sūtra:
"In this very state, one further skillfully cultivates the basis of tranquility," and so forth, as explained at length.
The basis for tranquility refers to its being the basis for tranquility within the desire realm.
The basis for freedom from desire refers to its being the basis for freedom from desire within the form and formless realms.
The cessation of the basis refers to the fact that one has attained the permanent and complete abandonment of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases without remainder.
The tendency toward relinquishment refers to the non-continuation of future aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Regarding the eight branches of the noble path, they are explained in detail as in the sūtras.

First is right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*): this refers to the purity of vision attained at the time of obtaining the branch of universal awakening (*abhisambodhi*) within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), as well as the purity of vision established through the subsequently attained branch of universal awakening within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); the synthesis of these two is termed right view.

2. Right Intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*): This refers to the intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, and the intention of non-harming that accompany right view; it consists of the continuous mental attention to the Truths during the path of cultivation, associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), causing the mind to enter and fully enter, to seek and fully seek, to manifest seeking, to awaken, to calculate, to observe, and to contemplate the nature of contemplation.

3. Right Speech (*samyag-vāc*): This refers to the attainment of four types of vocal karma within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), based on right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) and through the continuous mental attention (*manasikāra*) to the Truths by means of untainted (*anāsrava*) attention. It is subsumed under the precepts cherished by the Noble Ones (*ārya-kānta-śīla*). It consists of not delighting in [unwholesome speech], delighting in its cessation, and abandoning various forms of separation. It is characterized by clarity, protection, non-action, and non-separation; it is not practiced, not violated, and not transgressed. It is like a bridge or a raft for crossing over, remaining far removed from and not overstepping [the bounds of morality], and lacking any nature of various transgressions.

4. Right Action: This refers to the three types of bodily action attained within the path of cultivation by means of a continuous, untainted mental attention directed toward the Truths; these are subsumed under the precepts cherished by the Noble Ones (*āryakānta-śīla*), consist in the absence of delight in [unwholesome] separation and the removal of various forms of detachment, as explained in detail previously.

5. Right Livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*): This refers to the distancing oneself from unwholesome factors of wrong livelihood practiced during the cultivation of the path, up to the point of contemplating the Truths; it is comprised within the precepts cherished by the Noble Ones, as explained in detail previously.

Sixth, right exertion (*samyakpradhāna*) refers to the state of desire, right effort, exertion, vigor, endurance, invincibility, the mind’s right arousal, and the nature of continuous diligence, which occurs during the cultivation of the path through the contemplation of the truths, and within the practice of the foundations of mindfulness, the right abandonments, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, and the powers.

7. Right Mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*): This refers to mindfulness during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) up until the contemplation of the Truths (*satya*). Whether based on the path of calm (*śamatha*), the path of insight (*vipaśyanā*), or the path of both, it consists of mindfulness, right mindfulness, recollection, the non-forgetfulness of all mindfulness, and the clarity of mind regarding the factors of complete awakening (*bodhyaṅga*) that have been cultivated—namely, the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), right effort (*vīrya*), joy (*prīti*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). It is also the non-forgetfulness, the extreme non-forgetfulness, and the absolute non-forgetfulness of the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).

8. Right Concentration (*samyak-samādhi*): This refers to the one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*) within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), arising from the contemplation of the truths (*satya*) and, furthermore, from the gathering of right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) within the practice based on the three paths. It consists of the mind’s abiding, its steady abiding, its close abiding, its even abiding, its non-distraction and non-scattering, and its correct holding through *śamatha*.
It should be understood that these branches of the path arise in conjunction with one another, each subsequent one depending upon the preceding.
Furthermore, the verse says:
Wisdom and the doors of liberation, The tracks of practice, and serenity and insight.
The treatise states:
"Wisdom" refers to ten kinds of wisdom, as explained at length in the sūtras.
First is *dharmajñāna* (knowledge of phenomena), which is untainted wisdom regarding the objects of knowledge that are commonly understood and directly perceived.
2. Knowledge of types (*jñāna-prakāra-jñāna*): This refers to untainted knowledge regarding objects of knowledge that are not commonly understood and are not directly perceived.

3. Knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*): This refers to the knowledge produced through cultivation as the fruit of cultivation, which is able to know the minds and mental factors of others; it also refers to the sublime knowledge arising from the Tathāgatas’ instructions and exhortations directed toward sentient beings according to their inclinations and understandings, and according to their underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Fourth is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), which refers to mundane wisdom (*laukikaprajñā*); by relying upon this, the Tathāgata proclaims the sublime Dharma to all sentient beings according to their inclinations and understandings, and in accordance with their latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

5. Knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*): This refers to the nature of wisdom that clearly awakens through discernment, consisting of the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self regarding all contaminated conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), whether it be knowledge or vision.

Sixth, the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*): this refers to the wisdom or vision that contemplates the causes of all contaminated conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as cause, origination, production, and condition; the rest is as previously explained.

7. Knowledge of Cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*): This refers to the knowledge or vision consisting of the contemplation of cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation regarding the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) associated with outflows (*sāsrava*). The remainder is as previously explained.

8. Knowledge of the Path (mārgajñāna): This refers to the wisdom or vision consisting of the contemplation of the path, the reality, the practice, and the departure regarding the untainted path that is capable of severing all contaminated conditioned phenomena; the remainder is as previously explained.

9. Knowledge of Exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*): This refers to the knowledge that suffering has been known, its origin has been abandoned, its cessation has been realized, and the path has been cultivated; it either takes exhaustion as its object or constitutes exhaustion itself. Whether it is termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*) or "vision" (*darśana*), the rest is as previously explained.

10. Knowledge of Non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*): This refers to the knowledge that suffering has already been known and need not be known again; that its origin has already been abandoned and need not be abandoned again; that cessation has already been realized and need not be realized again; and that the path has already been cultivated and need not be cultivated again. It either takes non-arising as its object or constitutes non-arising itself. Whether it is termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*) or "vision" (*darśana*), the rest is as previously explained.
The gates of liberation refer to the three gates of liberation:
first, the gate of emptiness; second, the gate of signlessness; and third, the gate of wishlessness.
Emptiness is of two kinds:
first, the object of knowledge; second, wisdom.

Regarding the object of knowledge: it refers to the fact that within the objects grasped by the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of sentient beings, and within the objects grasped by the imagined nature of phenomena (*dharma*), both of these imagined natures are devoid of intrinsic nature, while the remaining aspect—the existence of selflessness—is present.
Within all phenomena, the absence of the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is itself the presence of selflessness (anātmatā);

within all phenomena, the presence of selflessness is itself the absence of the imagined nature. Thus, this state of both existence and non-existence is the non-conceptual object, free from the duality of being and non-being.
"Wisdom" refers to knowing that object as it truly is through mental engagement.
Signlessness also has two aspects:
first, the object of knowledge; second, wisdom.
The "object of knowledge" refers to the empty object that is itself the object of knowledge; because of this objective aspect, no phenomena whatsoever can operate upon it.
The "knower" refers to what was explained previously.
Aspirationlessness (*apraṇihita*) also has two aspects:
first, the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), and second, wisdom (*jñāna*).
The object of knowledge refers to the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that arise from perversion due to a lack of wisdom.
"Wisdom" refers to the thorough knowledge that arises from revulsion toward those objects.

"The practice of emptiness" refers to the non-apprehension of a self within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and the non-apprehension of conventionally discriminated phenomena among their various characteristics.

The practice of signlessness refers to the realization of the selflessness of sentient beings within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the realization of the selflessness of conventionally discriminated phenomena within all signs (*nimitta*), and the practice of cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation regarding extinction (*nirodha*).

The practice of wishlessness refers to [contemplating] impermanence, suffering, and impurity—as being like a disease, an abscess, or an arrow—as well as the practices of cause, origin, arising, and condition.
To take the knowledge of the emptiness of conditions as the path, as suchness, as practice, and as transcendence—this too is the practice of emptiness.
To take the knowledge of the signlessness of conditions as the path, as suchness, as practice, and as transcendence—this too is the practice of signlessness.
When the knowledge of conditions takes the path of wishlessness as its path, reality, practice, and departure, this too is the practice of wishlessness.

If these are designated collectively as "emptiness," "signlessness," and "wishlessness" without distinction, it should be understood that they encompass both mundane and supramundane wisdom arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

If they are termed the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one should know that these consist solely of the wisdom born of cultivation and pertain to both the mundane and the supramundane.
If they are termed the doors of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one should know that these pertain exclusively to the supramundane.
"Practice" refers to four kinds of practice, as explained at length in the sūtra.

First is "painful practice with sluggish superknowledge," which refers to the path or practice for the exhaustion of all outflows by one of dull faculties who has not yet attained dwelling in happiness in the present life.
2. The path of swift penetration with suffering (*duḥkhā pratipat kṣiprābhijñā*): this refers to those of sharp faculties; the rest is as previously explained. 3.

The path of slow penetration with ease (*sukhā pratipat dhandhābhijñā*): this refers to those of dull faculties who, having already attained abiding in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), practice the path or its cultivation for the sake of exhausting all outflows (*āsrava*).
Fourth, those who delight in swift penetration refers to those of sharp faculties; the rest is as previously explained.
"Tracks" refers to the four tracks of the Dharma, as explained at length in the Sūtra.

First, the track of non-attachment: because it is able to uphold the dharmas and meanings of the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), it is called a "track. For those who have not yet received [the precepts], it causes them to advance toward receiving them; for those who have already received them, it causes them to guard, increase, and expand them.
Just as with non-attachment, the second, non-hatred, is also like this.

Third, the path of right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti-vihāra*): it is called a "path" because it can maintain the factors of the aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhi-skandha*) and their meanings; thus, it causes those not yet arisen to arise, and those already arisen to increase and expand.

Fourth, the track of right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*): it is called a "track" because it can sustain the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*) and the aggregates of liberation (*vimukti*) and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*). It causes those [qualities] that have not yet arisen or been realized to arise and be realized, and causes those that have already arisen and been realized to increase and expand.

Calm abiding (*śamatha*) refers to the dwelling of the mind within during the time of correct practice upon the teachings as they have been heard and reflected upon; this occurs because one attends to the object that is the image of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and attains stable meditative concentration.

"Contemplation" refers to the discernment of all phenomena when one practices correctly according to the teachings as they have been heard and reflected upon; this occurs by means of mental attention directed toward the object that is the image of samādhi, and by attaining stable samādhi.
Furthermore, the verse says:
Abode and basis, The arousal of the mind and compassion,
The various practices, the nature of penetration, The stages, and the perfections (pāramitās).
The treatise states:
Regarding "abodes," there are four abodes, as explained at length in the sutras.

First is the "abode of wisdom," which refers to the mundane wisdom of skillful means through discerning contemplation; its purpose is to establish the meaning of supramundane knowledge that realizes the truths.

The dwelling place of the two truths refers to having attained the supramundane wisdom that contemplates the truths, for the purpose of establishing the meaning of abandoning the inversion regarding the existence of things.

Third, the dwelling place of relinquishment refers to the abandonment of the inversion regarding the existence of things, for the purpose of establishing the meaning of the cessation of all afflictions without remainder.
Fourth, the dwelling of tranquility refers to the tranquility of all remaining afflictions, for the purpose of establishing the non-arising of all suffering.
As for the basis, it refers to the four reliances, as explained at length in the sūtras.

First, rely on the Dharma and not on persons: this means that if a teaching is spoken by the Tathāgata or by his disciples as part of the twelvefold scripture (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), one should study and follow it accordingly; one should not study or follow it merely because it is practiced by ordinary persons.

2. Rely on the meaning, not on the letter: This means that regarding a teaching not composed of flowery words and phrases by those who employ ornamental rhetoric, but which can clearly manifest the uniquely complete, pure, and bright Brahma-faring—toward such a teaching one should have reverence, faith, and understanding, rather than toward flowery words and phrases composed by those who employ ornamental rhetoric to manifest perverted Brahma-faring or to fail to manifest Brahma-faring at all.

Third, rely on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and not on sūtras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). This means not falsely adhering to the various phenomena of dependent origination that accord with and conform to the profound emptiness taught by the Tathāgata; furthermore, do not dwell upon the literal or superficial meanings nor upon one's own internal views and attachments, but instead diligently investigate those sūtras that reveal the definitive meaning.

Fourth, rely on wisdom (*jñāna*) and not on consciousness (*vijñāna*). This means that one should not merely become satisfied with hearing and thus fail to advance in the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*); rather, in order to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*), one should diligently seek the wisdom of the inner realization of the true reality (*tattva-jñāna*).
Regarding the generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*): it refers to the bodhisattvas generating the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

When bodhisattvas abide in the *dharmatā* of bodhisattvas, desiring to benefit all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they rely upon those superior causal conditions and their modes of practice to generate a great vow for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. They receive the dharma of generating the mind, thinking: "I shall certainly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in order to deliver all sentient beings of the ten directions, so that they may be freed from all afflictions and freed from all suffering and hardship."
This arousal of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) is further of two kinds:
first, the conventional arousal of the mind; second, the arousal of the mind that realizes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Regarding the conventional arousal of the mind: it refers to someone who, standing with reverence before a wise person, gives rise to a superior intention and makes a vow, saying:
"Venerable sir, please remember," or "Noble one, please remember."
Or one may say:
"O Upādhyāya! I, who am named so-and-so, from this day forward shall generate the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, for the sake of bringing benefit to all sentient beings."

From this day forward, whatever I cultivate—whether it be generosity, ethical discipline, patience, right effort, meditative concentration, or wisdom—all of it is for the sake of realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
I now go forth from home in harmony with these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; may the Honored One bear witness that I am a bodhisattva.
A second and a third time he spoke thus.

Regarding the generation of the mind through realization of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*): it refers to one who has already passed the first incalculable aeon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), has realized the Bodhisattva’s first stage, the *Pramuditā* (Extremely Joyful), has entered the Bodhisattva’s state of certainty regarding non-arising (*anutpatti-dharmakṣānti*), has known as they truly are both unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*) and the skillful means for enlightenment, and has awakened to the fact that their own self is approaching and nearly reaching the fruit of great enlightenment. Because they have realized the equality of self and others, they attain the intention of the Great Self (*mahātman*). Because they have reached the Bodhisattva path that abides neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa, they attain the vast intention (*mahāśaya*).
Because of this, one does not retreat from the aspiration for great enlightenment; this is called the arousal of the mind through the realization of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Regarding "compassion": it refers to the bodhisattva who has thus aroused the mind, whose nature is non-harming, and who performs actions to bring about the cessation of suffering for sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions—whether they are sentient beings suffering from the three types of decline, those fixed in the suffering of the five destinies, those undergoing the four kinds of extreme suffering, those undergoing the six kinds of heavy suffering of suffering, or those undergoing the three aspects of the suffering of change.
"Various practices" refers to the ten types of Dharma-practice, as explained at length in the sūtras.
First, the practice of respectfully honoring, revering, copying, and upholding the teachings of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, whether they be many or few.
2. The practice of Dharma consisting of making offerings with various ritual implements, whether inferior or superior;
3. The practice of Dharma consisting of giving to others after having written it oneself, out of a heart of compassion.

4. If others generate the intention to revere and honor [the Dharma], proclaiming, expounding, and reading it with a sublime voice, one listens attentively to the practice of the Dharma out of veneration.
5. One generates pure faith and understanding, and with a mind of profound reverence, reads and recites the practice of the Dharma.
Sixth, desiring to cultivate practice in accordance with the Dharma, one receives the teachings from a teacher and recites them.
Seventh, having already recited them, one reviews the practice of the Dharma with a broad and sublime voice in order to maintain it firmly.
8. Out of compassion for others, one transmits them to them, expounding the practice of the Dharma according to its breadth or brevity.
9. Dwelling alone in a secluded and quiet place, one thoroughly investigates, examines in accordance with reason, and contemplates the practice of the Dharma.

Tenth: Practicing śamatha and vipaśyanā according to one's contemplation, for the purpose of entering [the path] and even for the sake of accomplishing the practice of the Dharma regarding all sought-after objectives.
*Exposition of the Holy Teachings* (Prakaraṇāryavācāśāstra), Fascicle Two.
*Exposition of the Holy Teachings*, Fascicle Three.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter One: Compendium of Matters (Vastusaṃgrahaṇī), Part Three. Regarding "thorough penetration," this refers to the seven kinds of thorough penetration, as explained at length in the Sūtra.

First, mastery of syllables (*akṣara-pratisaṃvit*): this refers to being free from conceptual discrimination regarding the thirty-two syllables; thus, one realizes the characteristics and meanings of what is practiced as they truly are, because one has previously well-cultivated the practice of the preeminent Dharma within the mind.

Second, mastery of the characteristics of syllables (*akṣara-lakṣaṇa-prativedha*): this refers to having discernment regarding the various characteristics of syllables within the form of a lion; it is the thorough realization, in accordance with reality, of the meanings of the characteristics of their activity. The rest is as previously explained.

Third, penetration of the grasper (*grāhaka*): this refers to the correct realization, in accordance with reality, that the mental factors associated with the object of focus are merely the aspect of discernment (*vijñapti*).

The remainder is as previously explained. Fourth, penetration of the grasped (*grāhya*): this refers to the correct realization, in accordance with reality, that all objects of the various consciousnesses are merely the reflected images of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). The remainder is as previously explained.
Fifth, penetration of bondage: this refers to the thorough realization, as it truly is, of the bondage of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*) and the bondage of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*);

the remainder is as previously explained. Sixth, penetration of liberation: this refers to the thorough realization, as it truly is, of liberation from the bondage of signs and liberation from the bondage of coarse heaviness; the remainder is as previously explained.

Seventh, the penetration of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which means the realization, in accordance with reality, of the true nature of phenomena—the dependent origination of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) from beginningless time regarding bondage and liberation, as well as their cessation, *tathatā*—because one has previously well-cultivated the practice of the superior dharma within the mind.
"Grounds" refers to the ten grounds of the bodhisattvas, as explained at length in the sūtras.

First is the Ground of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). This means that when bodhisattvas abide in this ground, because they have previously well-cultivated the practice of the Dharma through mental mastery, they transcend the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and attain the clear realization of the bodhisattvas. By virtue of correctly realizing the unsurpassed clear realization, the great bodhisattvas abide in a state of superior joy within this ground; therefore, it is named the Ground of Utmost Joy.

2. The Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*): This refers to the stage wherein Bodhisattvas, having previously well-cultivated the practices of the first ground, transcend all grounds of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas and realize the most pure and sublime aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*). Because it counteracts all subtle stains of transgressing the precepts, this ground is named "Freedom from Defilement."

Third is the Ground of Radiant Light (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*). This means that when Bodhisattvas dwell in this ground, because they have previously well-cultivated and purified the second ground, they transcend all grounds of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas and realize the aggregate of extremely pure samādhi, which is the basis for the light of great wisdom; therefore, this ground is named "Radiant Light."

Fourth is the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). This means that when Bodhisattvas dwell in this ground, because they have previously well-cultivated and purified the third ground, they transcend all grounds of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; they realize the extremely pure factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) and attain the aggregate of subtle wisdom that apprehends the objects of phenomena. They are able to manifest and burn away all afflictions; therefore, this ground is named "Blazing Wisdom."

Fifth, the Ground of Utmost Difficult Victory (*sudurjayā bhūmi*): This refers to the stage wherein Bodhisattvas, having previously well-cultivated the fourth ground, transcend all levels of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; they realize the aggregate of subtle wisdom regarding the objects of knowledge—the truths of dependent origination—and accomplish the noble path that is extremely difficult to achieve, which neither abides in saṃsāra nor remains in cessation. For this reason, this ground is named "Utmost Difficult Victory."

Sixth, the Ground of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*): This refers to the stage wherein Bodhisattvas, having previously well-cultivated the fifth ground, transcend all grounds of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas and realize the aggregate of sublime wisdom regarding the sphere of phenomena—the cessation of the flow of conditioned formations through the two types of activity consisting of the knowledge of extremely pure conditions and non-knowledge. For the most part, the wondrous wisdom that is spontaneous and continuous manifests before them; therefore, this ground is named "Presence."

7. The Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*): This refers to the stage wherein bodhisattvas, having previously well-cultivated the sixth ground, transcend all grounds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and realize the extremely pure and subtle aggregates of liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Because they have already far entered into liberation from all currently manifest signs (*nimitta*), this ground is named "Far-Going."

8. The Immovable Ground (*Acalā-bhūmi*): This refers to the stage wherein Bodhisattvas, having previously well-cultivated the seventh ground, transcend all grounds of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; they realize the most pure and subtle aggregates of liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation; because they are liberated from the obstacles to mastery over all signs (*nimitta*), they attain the basis for the effortless, spontaneous, and continuous path; therefore, this ground is called "The Immovable."

9. The Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*): This refers to the stage wherein Bodhisattvas, having previously well-cultivated the eighth ground, transcend all levels of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; they realize the most pure and subtle aggregates of liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation; and they become the basis for vast intelligence that is free from error and unimpeded by any obstacles to eloquence. For these reasons, this ground is named "Excellent Intelligence."

Tenth, the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*): This refers to the stage wherein bodhisattvas, having previously well-cultivated the ninth ground, transcend all grounds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; they realize the most pure and subtle aggregate of liberation and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; they are liberated from the cognitive obstructions that hinder the arousal of great supernormal powers; and they serve as the basis for the perfection of the dharma-body, which is like a cloud. For these reasons, this ground is named the Cloud of Dharma.
The *pāramitās* refer to the ten *pāramitās*, as explained at length in the sūtras.

First, the *dāna-pāramitā* (perfection of generosity) means that, based on the bodhicitta and led by compassion, one cultivates and refines it through the ten types of dharma-practice, with the seven types of penetration serving as its firm root. Whether through material wealth, the true Dharma, or fearlessness, it is characterized by the nature of being embraced by the five kinds of merit and the great self: first, giving because of non-attachment; second, giving because of non-contemplation; third, giving because of non-loss; fourth, giving because of non-discrimination; and fifth, giving because of dedication.

By means of these practices, bodhisattvas gather sentient beings through the provision of material necessities; furthermore, by means of close association and extensive cultivation, they cause those beings to perfect their provisions so that they shall attain the fruit of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Just as it is with the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*), so too should the perfections from ethical discipline (*śīla*) up to wisdom (*prajñā*) be understood.

The distinction here is that the second, the perfection of ethical discipline, consists in the nature of bodily, vocal, and mental actions subsumed under the ethics of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), whether for the sake of ceasing and abandoning unwholesome states, or for the sake of embracing wholesome dharmas, or for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
By means of this practice, bodhisattvas gather in all sentient beings through non-anger and non-affliction.

The third is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), which consists of: either the nature of non-anger through enduring the harm inflicted by others; or the nature of non-distraction through accepting various sufferings; or the nature of correct wisdom through the thorough investigation of all phenomena.
By means of this practice, bodhisattvas gather in sentient beings by enduring all manner of non-beneficial and harmful matters.

Fourth is the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), which refers to the nature of mental fortitude that is continuous and mature—whether due to the armor of generating the resolve for awakening, the application of skillful means, or the benefit of sentient beings—for the purpose of bringing forth all roots of virtue.
By virtue of this practice, although bodhisattvas have not yet subdued their afflictions, they are able to cultivate all forms of goodness with one-pointed dedication.

The fifth perfection, that of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), refers to the mind abiding in a single object of focus, whether for the purpose of counteracting afflictions, for the purpose of generating virtuous qualities, or for the purpose of benefiting sentient beings.
By means of these practices, bodhisattvas subdue their afflictions and cause them to abide in a state of non-manifestation.

The sixth is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), which refers to the discernment of the nature of all phenomena, whether for the purpose of applying antidotes to the afflictions, for the purpose of engendering virtuous qualities, or for the purpose of benefiting sentient beings.
By means of these practices, bodhisattvas permanently sever all seeds of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

The seventh is the perfection of skillful means (*upāyakauśalyapāramitā*); that is to say, by means of this skillful means, bodhisattvas—whether through conformity or opposition, through differing inclinations, through bestowing kindness or requiting it, through intimidation, or through purification—gather sentient beings through the three types of benefit, causing them to receive, to be disciplined, to abide, and to be established in various states of virtue.
The eighth is the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).

This refers to the fact that among bodhisattvas, whichever one may be their nature, because they possess much indolence and affliction, they consequently give rise to right aspirations and cultivate various virtues, thinking: "May I, in the future, attain a nature of courageous and correct diligence, with afflictions becoming thin and slight."

For this reason, in future lives, whatever aspirations they have set forth will all be fulfilled according to their wishes, and they will attain powerful strength in the cultivation of wholesome dharmas.

The ninth power is the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*); that is to say, because bodhisattvas have attained powerful strength through the wholesome dharmas they have cultivated, by relying on this power, they swiftly give rise to the perfection of meditative concentration.

The tenth is the perfection of wisdom (*jñānapāramitā*), which refers to the mundane discernment (*prajñā*) induced by the knowledge of the principles subsumed within the meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, as practiced by bodhisattvas.

By relying on this wisdom, bodhisattvas are able to swiftly give rise to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) that is supramundane, non-conceptual, and subsumed within the path of non-abiding nirvāṇa.
These ten pāramitās are all cultivated and practiced throughout all the stages (bhūmis).

As for those that predominate: it should be understood that the dāna-pāramitā exists primarily in the first stage, and so on in successive order until the jñāna-pāramitā exists primarily in the tenth stage.
Furthermore, the verse says:
The bodhisattva practices and the means of attraction,
As well as those gates of dhāraṇīs and samādhis, And the various immeasurable modes of attention.
The Treatise says:
Regarding the practice of a bodhisattva, there are four types of bodhisattva practices, as explained at length in the sūtras.

First is the practice of reaching the perfections (*pāramitā*), which refers to the ten *pāramitās*. These are collectively designated as the practice of reaching the perfections because they all constitute the meaning of transcendence within the Mahāyāna.

2. The branch of universal awakening (*sarvabodhipakṣyaprayoga*): This refers to the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*saptatriṃśadbodhipākṣikadharma*). They are collectively designated as the branch of universal awakening because they allow for the realization, in accordance with reality, of all objects of knowledge.

Third, the practice of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), which refers to the six supernormal faculties (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*). These are collectively designated as the practice of supernormal powers because they are all intended to attract and gather the realm of sentient beings to be converted, causing them to give rise to reverence and enter the meaning of the Noble Teaching.
Fourth, the practice of maturing sentient beings refers to the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); these are collectively explained as the practice of maturing sentient beings.

This is because they involve the twofold gathering—through material goods and through the Dharma—of those sentient beings who have already entered the sphere of those to be converted within the holy teaching.
Among these, "gathering by means of material goods" refers to the skillful means that assist in gathering [beings] so as to bring them to maturity.
"Gathering by means of the Dharma" refers to the correct gathering through the skillful means of transformation and subsequent transformation to bring them to maturity.
These four means of integration (saṃgrahavastu) are explained as means of integration based on five types of integrative practices.

The five integrative practices are: first, the practice of causing [beings] to attach themselves; second, the practice of causing them to accept the wholesome; third, the practice of causing them to arouse wholesome right effort; fourth, the practice of causing them to reach wholesome maturity; and fifth, the practice of causing them to attain wholesome liberation.
Regarding the "means of integration" (saṃgrahavastu), they refer to the four means of integration, as explained at length in the sūtras.
Their formal establishment should be understood in the same manner as the establishment of the practices for maturing sentient beings.
Regarding the "gateways of dhāraṇī," this refers to the immeasurable gateways of dhāraṇī of all bodhisattvas, as explained at length in the sūtras.

To explain the characteristics of dhāraṇī briefly: it means that bodhisattvas achieve mastery over the categories of syllables and attain unhindered sovereignty over the bodies of names, phrases, and phonemes, thereby obtaining the power of mindfulness and retention of such a kind.

By the power of mindfulness, one is able to manifest, differentiate, and expound all aspects of the meanings of defilement and purity within a single syllable; therefore, it is called a *dhāraṇī* gateway.
Regarding the gateways of samādhi, this refers to the immeasurable gateways of samādhi of all bodhisattvas, as explained at length in the sūtras.
To speak briefly, there are furthermore eight kinds, namely: from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Relying on each of these samādhi-gates, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to immeasurable samādhis, the names of which are not even reached by the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
These samādhis are all capable of establishing all the activities performed by the samādhis throughout the worlds of the ten directions; therefore, they are called "gates of samādhi."
Regarding the immeasurable mental orientations (*apramāṇa-manasikāra*), these refer to the five immeasurable mental orientations, as explained at length in the sūtras.

First is the immeasurable mental orientation toward sentient beings (*sattva-apramāṇa-manasikāra*). This refers to the subtle mental orientation, thoroughly cultivated through the superior practice of the Dharma by bodhisattvas, which contemplates the unspeakably diverse characteristics of the karmic retributions of all sentient beings included within the infinite worlds of the ten directions. These include those with one foot, two feet, four feet, or many feet; those with form or without form; those with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception; those belonging to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; those in the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, or gods; and those born from eggs, moisture, the womb, or by transformation.

Having reflected thus, one understands things as they truly are: how sentient beings proceed, how they return, how they are defiled, how they are purified, how they engage in wrong conduct, and how they engage in right conduct; and how, through such various distinctions in their conduct, such various types of karmic maturation arise.

2. Mental engagement with the immeasurability of worlds: This refers to how Bodhisattvas contemplate the characteristics of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions. Having contemplated them, they understand them as they truly are: that this world is defiled and this world is pure; they understand them all as being like illusions and transformations, merely images of false conceptualization, deceptive and unreal. They understand as they truly are their mastery over such matters as: their revolving according to characteristics, whether they are formed or destroyed; the establishment of various distinct forms and appearances; whether they are superior or inferior, coarse or subtle, distant or near; or when analyzed down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*); or regarding their expansion or contraction, their manifestation or transformation, their alteration, their distance or proximity, and their concealment or appearance. Thus, they attain mastery and understand these things as they truly are.
3. The mental attention to the immeasurability of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-apramāṇa-manasikāra*):
This refers to when bodhisattvas contemplate the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions;

having contemplated them, they understand them as they truly are, knowing that "this phenomenon is form (*rūpa*), this phenomenon is not form," and likewise regarding what is form and what is not form, as well as what is visible (*sanidarśana*).
...non-seeing; with resistance and without resistance; with outflows and without outflows; conditioned and unconditioned;
wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; faulty and faultless; bound to the realm of desire, bound to the realm of form, and bound to the formless realm;
that of the learner, that of the non-learner, and that which is neither of the learner nor the non-learner; views...
He understands, as they truly are, such dharmas as those to be abandoned, those to be cultivated, and those that are not to be abandoned;
dharmas of progression and dharmas of regression; defiled dharmas and pure dharmas; dharmas of saṃsāra and dharmas of cessation;
the dharmas of ordinary beings and the dharmas of noble ones; and the dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas.

Fourth, the mental attention to the immeasurable objects to be disciplined: this refers to bodhisattvas contemplating the various behaviors and various dispositions of the sentient beings to be converted throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions—whether they possess the disposition of śrāvakas, the disposition of pratyekabuddhas, or the disposition of tathāgatas—and all such dispositions of those to be disciplined.
Having reflected thus, he understands, as it truly is, those who are to be disciplined: "This one has dull faculties; this one has middling faculties;
this one has sharp faculties. This one has inferior resolve; this one has vast resolve. This one has a temperament of greed and a greedy disposition;
this one has a temperament of hatred and a hateful disposition; this one has a temperament of delusion and a deluded disposition."
...this is the mental disposition (*āśaya*) of those who practice with equal parts; this is the mental disposition of progress; this is the mental disposition of non-progress;
this is the noble and virtuous mental disposition in which the defilements (*rajas*) are slight; this is the proliferation of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
this is the attenuation of latent tendencies; this is the extreme subtlety of latent tendencies; this is the weakening of latent tendencies.
Sleep; this [person] has attenuated latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), while that one has them fully present;

this [person] understands through detailed exposition, while that one understands upon hearing only a brief summary; this [person] is disciplined by means of rejection, while that one is disciplined by means of acceptance;
this [person] is disciplined by what is mild, while that one is disciplined by what is coarse. This is coarse...
He understands as it truly is such cases as those who are subdued by being gentle and compliant, or those who are subdued only after having been set aside;
this is the fifth, the immeasurable mental engagements regarding the skillful means for subduing, which refers to the bodhisattvas’ contemplation up to the ten [powers].
Having reflected upon the skillful means for taming the sentient beings to be converted throughout immeasurable worlds, he understands them as they truly are:
that for some it is through the teaching of secret dharmas that they can be tamed, while for others it is through the teaching of explicit dharmas;
and that for some it is by means of gathering them in, while for others it is by means of subduing them.
This is the skillful means of transformation; this is the skillful means of conformity; this should be followed, and this should be opposed;
this is due to a discordant intention (*āśaya*); this is where one should bestow kindness and repay it;
this is where one should manifest majesty and exert power; this is due to purity; and this is due to manifesting extraordinary supernatural transformations.
This is because of manifesting extraordinary predictions; this is because of manifesting extraordinary instructions; this is because of manifesting various displays of majestic power;
this is because of skillfully inducing various teachings; this is because of coarse characteristics; this is because of subtle characteristics;
this is because of characteristics that are both coarse and subtle; this is because of setting aside; and this is because of brevity.

One must understand, as they truly are, such skillful means as these: that while some essential teachings on the Dharma are able to bring about subduing, others require the extensive exposition of those same essential teachings to achieve subduing.
Furthermore, the verse says:
The characteristics of mental attention to *tathatā*, the inconceivable faith and understanding,
and the vast *āśaya*— one should know these various categories.
The Commentary says:

Regarding the characteristics of the mental engagement with *tathatā* (suchness): it refers to the mental engagement that takes the seven kinds of all-pervading *tathatā* as its object, as explained at length in the sūtras.

First is the mental engagement with the *tathatā* of transmigration: this refers to those bodhisattvas who have already seen the truths, who, through the superior practice of the Dharma, thoroughly cultivate and purify their mental engagement when dealing with defiled and pure phenomena, contemplating the actual nature of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) as they have transmigrated from beginningless time.
Having reflected thus, one abandons the view of causelessness and the view of an unequal cause.

Second is the mental attention to the true nature and suchness (*tathatā*), which means, as previously explained, reflecting upon the causes of defiled and pure phenomena, up to the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena in all dharmas.
Having reflected thus, all views of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), as well as the mental engagements with the conceptualization of various signs, no longer manifest.

Third is the mental engagement with the suchness of representation-only (vijñaptimātratātathatā); that is to say, as previously explained, it consists of reflecting upon the nature of all phenomena as being representation-only, even regarding the basis for defiled and pure phenomena.

Having reflected thus, one understands it as it truly is: "It is solely because the mind is defiled that sentient beings are defiled; it is solely because the mind is pure that sentient beings are pure.
