Fourth is the mental attention to the establishment of *tathatā* (suchness), which means reflecting on the truth of suffering regarding the essence of defiled phenomena, as previously described.
Having reflected thus, one speaks for the sake of sentient beings so that they may understand.

Fifth is the mental attention to the suchness of wrong conduct; as previously stated, this involves reflecting upon the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) regarding the causes of defiled phenomena.
Having reflected thus, one preaches to sentient beings for the sake of bringing about their cessation.
Sixth is the mental attention to the *tathatā* of purity; as previously explained, this refers to reflecting upon the Truth of Cessation regarding the essence of pure phenomena.
Having reflected thus, one speaks for the sake of sentient beings in order to bring about realization.
Seventh is the mental attention to the *tathatā* of correct practice (*samyakpratipatti-tathatā*), which means, as previously stated, reflecting upon the Truth of the Path up to the pure practices.
Having reflected thus, he speaks for the sake of sentient beings so that they may practice.

Regarding those who have faith and understanding in the inconceivable: this refers to those bodhisattvas who have already attained faith and understanding regarding the points that are difficult to conceive, as explained at length in the sūtra.

To briefly describe the characteristics of this faith and understanding: it refers to giving rise to pure and straightforward faith in the most profound objects of knowledge—the sphere of activity of bodhisattvas who have entered the stages and of all Tathāgatas—as well as in the most vast majesty and power of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas; having realized that this is an inconceivable sphere beyond the reach of conjecture, one gives rise to faith and understanding.
Vast *āśaya* refers to the *āśaya* of the great self (*mahātman*) and the *āśaya* of universal pervasiveness.

The *āśaya* of the great self means that because bodhisattvas have attained the realization of the equality of self and others, they possess the pure faith and aspiration for all sentient beings to attain liberation.

Vast and universal *āśaya* refers to the pure faith and aspiration of bodhisattvas, who—having attained non-conceptual, equalizing understanding regarding both cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and cessation (*nirvāṇa*)—do not abide in either for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
One should know the individual enumerations of the various factors of enlightenment; that is, one should know their respective individual enumerations.
Having thus explained the factors of enlightenment, the persons [who possess them] shall now be discussed.
The verse says:

There are seven types, such as those who follow by faith; furthermore, one should know there are eight kinds, including those who will be reborn at most seven times and so forth; and there are six types, such as those of the nature of falling away.
The treatise states:
One should know that *pudgalas* (persons) are of many kinds.
Here, we shall first explain the seven types of noble beings (*ārya*), namely the seven beginning with those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), as explained at length in the Sūtra.

First, the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārī*): this refers to one who, by nature, possesses dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*), whose mental continuum has been thoroughly matured, and who from of old has always practiced with faith, understanding, and conduct. Due to these causes and conditions, they now, regarding the various truths (*satya*), proceed toward the contemplation of the truths through faith, understanding, and conduct.

2. Dharma-anusārin (follower by way of the Dharma): This refers to one who, by nature, possesses sharp faculties and a matured continuity; having from ancient times always practiced the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), by virtue of these causes and conditions, they now, regarding the various Truths (*satya*), proceed toward the contemplation of the Truths through the practice of discerning the Dharma.
3. Śraddhādhimukta (one resolved through faith), that is, one who follows by faith and has already seen the Noble Truths.
4. Dṛṣṭiprāpta (one attained through vision), that is, one who follows the Dharma and has already seen the Noble Truths.

Fifth, the body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*): this refers to one who has personally realized and dwells in the full possession of the eight liberations, yet has not yet attained the complete extinction of all outflows (*āsrava*) without remainder.

Sixth, the one liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*): this refers to one who has already attained the complete extinction of all outflows without remainder, yet has not yet personally realized and dwelt in the full possession of the eight liberations.

7. Both-liberated (ubhayatobhāga-vimukta): this refers to one who has already attained the complete extinction of all outflows without remainder, and who dwells having personally realized the eight liberations with full mastery.
Regarding the "eight types," these refer to the eight stages such as the fruit of stream-entry and its path, as explained at length in the Sūtra.

First, the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*): This refers to one who, with a thoroughly matured continuum, transcends all external stages of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*) and enters the state of rightness and freedom from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*). As long as they have not yet realized the first fruit of stream-entry, they will never meet an untimely death.

2. The fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*): if categorized according to its excellence, it consists in the permanent abandonment of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*); if categorized comprehensively, it consists in the permanent abandonment of all afflictions to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*). Because this noble one has already seen the truths, they have for the first time realized the fruit that flows against the current.

Third, the candidate for the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka*): this refers to one who, having either—by means of the mundane path—doubled the abandonment of desire for the realm of desire and entered into the state of rightness (*samyaktvaniyāma*), or who, being a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), cultivates the practice of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*) in order to abandon the superior and medium grades of afflictions of the realm of desire.

Fourth, the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin): it is either realized after one has already doubled the detachment from desire and entered the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma), or it is attained by a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) who further abandons the coarse and medium grades of afflictions of the desire realm.
Based on this very abandonment, it is said that desire, hatred, and delusion have become thin and faint. How is this known?

It is because when one observes an object through deliberate attention (*manasikāra*), the mind gives rise to equanimity (*upekṣā*); there is no mind that practices inclination, no mind that practices pursuit, and no mind that practices attachment. One should know that for such a person, the three poisons are thin and faint.

Fifth, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmipratipannaka*): this refers to one who, having previously abandoned attachment to the desire realm by means of the mundane path, enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktvaniyāma*), or who, being a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), advances to abandon the remaining afflictions of the desire realm and thus cultivates the practice of antidotes.

Sixth, the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala): it is either realized after one has previously abandoned desire and entered the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma), or it is attained by exhausting the remaining afflictions of the desire realm after having already attained the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala).

7. The candidate for arhatship (arhattva-pratipannaka): This refers to one who, having already studied and seen the tracks [of the path], cultivates the practice of counteractive measures in order to abandon the afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
8. The fruit of arhatship is attained by means of the permanent abandonment of all afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Regarding "at most seven returns" and so forth: this refers to the eight [categories] beginning with "at most seven returns," which are established based on rebirth, as explained at length in the sūtras.
1. The "seven-times-at-most" refers to the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).

Because they have well-cultivated the Noble Path, they will experience seven more births—either in the heavenly realms, or among humans, or in both heavenly and human realms—and thereafter attain the end of suffering.
2. *Kulaṃkula* (Family-to-family): This refers to those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).
Because they have well-cultivated the noble path, they are born either among the devas or among humans, proceeding from family to family until they reach the end of suffering.
Third, the "One-Interval" (ekāvacara), which refers to the fruit of the Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin).
Because they have well-cultivated the Noble Path, they will either be born in the heavens and attain nirvāṇa definitively in that very place,
or they will be born among humans and attain nirvāṇa definitively in this very world.
Fourth, attaining nirvana in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), which refers to the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

Having already severed the fetters pertaining to rebirth (*upapattisaṃyojana*) but not yet severed the fetters pertaining to the process of transition (*abhinirvṛttisaṃyojana*), by the power of having cultivated the Noble Path to a superior degree, one attains nirvana within the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*). Alternatively, there are those who attain nirvana without proceeding toward the place of birth; or there are those who proceed toward the place of birth but attain nirvana before reaching their original destination of rebirth.
Fifth, attaining nirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*), which refers to the fruit of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

Because they have cultivated the noble path to a middling degree, they have not yet severed the two types of fetters pertaining to rebirth; consequently, being born in one of the mind-made heavens (*manomaya-deva*), they realize nirvāṇa at the very moment of birth.

Sixth, the realization of cessation through non-exertion: this refers to those noble ones who, having practiced little and exerted little effort, realize cessation; all else is as previously described.
Seventh, there is the one who attains nirvana through practice (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin), which refers to the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmin).

Because they have cultivated the noble path only to a minor degree, they have not yet severed the two fetters; consequently, they are reborn in a single place among the mind-made devas (manomaya-deva), where, after performing many practices and exerting great diligence, they realize nirvana.
8. *Ūrdhvasrotas* (Upstreamer): This refers to the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).

Having been reborn in one of the various heavens of mind-born beings (*manomayakāya*), they are unable to attain the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) there; instead, they proceed further upward, attaining nirvana only within a subsequent body.
Regarding the six types of practitioners, such as those of the "nature of falling away" (*parihāṇadharman*), these refer to the six kinds of *aśaikṣa* fruits, as explained at length in the Sūtra.

First, the one of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) refers to one who possesses such dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*) that whether they contemplate self-harm or do not contemplate self-harm, whether they are heedless or not heedless, they are all capable of falling away from the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) as well as from mundane qualities (*laukikaguṇa*). Such a person is unable to refine their faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*) and is unable to give rise to superior qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*).

Second, those of the nature of contemplation (*cetanādharman*): this refers to those who possess such weak faculties that if they contemplate self-harm, they are able to avoid falling back, but if they do not contemplate self-harm, they may fall away.
This person reflects thus:
"May I rather be victorious over all the Māras than allow the Māras to be victorious over me.
Having reflected in this way, he then contemplates harming himself.
This [state] likewise cannot refine the faculties (*indriya*) nor can it give rise to superior qualities.

Third is the protection of the Dharma (*dharmarakṣā*): this refers to one who has attained such weak faculties; although they do not intentionally seek their own ruin, because they are not negligent, they are able to avoid falling back.
However, if the mind becomes negligent, they may fall back; they cannot refine the faculties nor can they give rise to superior qualities.

Fourth, abiding in immovability (*aniñjya-sthita*): this refers to one who has attained such dull faculties (*mṛdu-indriya*) that, although they do not intentionally harm themselves nor engage in negligence, they nonetheless do not regress; yet they are unable to refine their faculties (*indriya-saṃvaraṇa*) nor can they give rise to superior qualities (*viśeṣa-guṇa*).

Fifth, capability for thorough penetration: this refers to having accomplished such soft faculties that one is capable of non-retrogression, able to refine all faculties and able to give rise to superior qualities.

Sixth, the Immovable Dharma (akopyadharman): this refers to one who has possessed sharp faculties by their very nature since time immemorial. Such a person cannot be shaken from the wholesome roots already attained, nor can they be moved toward the arousal of superior qualities or the further refinement of faculties. For this reason, they are called those of the Immovable Dharma.
Furthermore, the verse says:
The seven types, beginning with those of dull faculties, Including both laity and renunciants,
And the three vehicles such as the Śrāvaka-yāna— These are those who can be saved and those who cannot.

Regarding the seven types beginning with those of dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*): first, those of dull faculties refers to those who possess the five faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*), yet whose faculties are either naturally dull or have not yet increased, resulting in sluggishness in their application (*prayoga*) when seeking higher progress.
Second, those of sharp faculties should be understood as the opposite of this.
Third, those of greedy temperament are those who, in previous lives, long practiced desire and failed to cultivate the antidotes to desire.

For this reason, even when encountering inferior yet attractive objects within this life, one gives rise to intense and continuous craving that is difficult to abandon and difficult to weary of; consequently, one’s application toward the cultivation of wholesome dharmas becomes sluggish.
As with the temperament of greed, so it is with the fourth, the temperament of hatred, and the fifth, the temperament of delusion.
The distinction here is that even when encountering a minor object of provocation, they give rise to fierce and continuous anger;
and even when encountering a coarse or superficial object of confusion, they give rise to fierce and continuous delusion.

Sixth, those of equal temperament (*samabhāga-carita*): this refers to those who, in previous lives, did not habituate themselves to superior degrees of greed, hatred, or delusion; or, even if they did so habituate themselves, they have subsequently cultivated the remedial methods for them.

For these reasons, within this present life, when encountering the three kinds of objects—desirable and so forth—one gives rise to the three types of entanglements and delusions, namely greed, hatred, and ignorance, according to the specific category of the object. These are neither difficult nor easy to abandon, neither difficult nor easy to weary of, and one’s progress in cultivating wholesome dharmas is neither slow nor swift.

Seventh, those of slight defilement: this refers to a person who, in past lives, did not habituate themselves for long to greed, hatred, and delusion, yet has already cultivated the remedial dharmas for them.

For this reason, although one encounters superior and desirable objects within this world, one is able to avoid the arising of intense and continuous fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion; even if inferior or middling degrees of these arise at times, they are easily abandoned and easily brought to disillusionment, such that one swiftly applies oneself to the cultivation of wholesome dharmas.
The "layperson" refers to one who dwells at home in white robes, enjoys the five objects of desire, and sustains their life by engaging in worldly occupations.

The "renunciant" refers to one who maintains the deportment and appearance of a renunciant, abandons worldly spheres, upholds the prohibitive precepts, and sustains themselves through pure alms-seeking in accordance with the Dharma.

Regarding the three vehicles, such as the Śrāvaka-yāna and others: first, the Śrāvaka-yāna refers to those who abide in the *dharmatā* of the śrāvakas; for the sake of personally realizing nirvāṇa, they generate the correct aspiration and then cultivate the practice of skillful means.

2. The Pratyekabuddha Vehicle refers to those who abide in the *dharmatā* of the pratyekabuddhas; for the sake of personally realizing cessation (*nirvāṇa*), they cultivate the practice of skillful means after having formed right aspirations, without relying on the instruction of a teacher.

Third, the Mahāyāna refers to abiding in the dharma-nature of the Mahāyāna; for the sake of enabling oneself and others to realize cessation, one generates right aspirations without relying on the instruction of a teacher and then cultivates the practice of skillful means.
Those who can be saved are those who possess the nature of quiescence of the three vehicles.
Those who cannot be saved are those who lack the nature of quiescence of the three vehicles.
Furthermore, the verse says:
There are nine types based on the entry into the means [of practice] and so forth; there are two based on the distinction of birth;
and furthermore, due to the distinctions among the various realms, one should know that there are thirteen kinds.
The treatise says:

Regarding the nine [stages] beginning with "entering the means" (*upāya*), the first is "having entered the means": this refers to having attained firm and pure faith in the Dharma and Vinaya as realized and taught by the Tathāgata himself; having already received the precepts (*śīla*); having already heard the true Dharma; having already increased renunciation (*tyāga*); and having already perfected right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Second, regarding those who have not yet entered the preparatory means (*upāya*), one should know that they are the opposite of this.
Third, there are obstructions; that is, there are three obstructions:

first, the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); second, the obstruction of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*); and third, the obstruction of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). These function as hindrances to the cultivation of wholesome dharmas.
Fourth, "unobstructed" should be understood as the opposite of this.

Fifth, "immature" refers to one who has not yet acquired the roots of goodness to nourish the mental continuum; such a person cannot realize the principle of the truths in the present life, nor can they attain the cessation realized through the lower, middle, or superior vehicles in the present life.
Sixth, those who have already matured should be understood as the opposite of this.
Seventh, those bound by all fetters, namely ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Eighth, those not bound by all fetters, namely the six kinds of noble learners (*śaikṣa*), from the fruit of stream-entry up to the sixth stage, the candidate for arhatship.
9. Unbound (*abaddha*), which refers to the fruit of the Arhatship of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Regarding the two types of birth-differences: first, the human realm (*manuṣyagati*), which means being born in the human realm and obtaining the human species.

2. Non-human realms (*amanuṣya-gati*): this refers to the various classes of beings born in other realms, namely those in the hells (*naraka*), animals (*tiryagyoni*), and the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), as well as gods (*deva*), nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.

Furthermore, it should be understood that there are thirteen types based on the distinctions among the realms (*dhātu*): 1. Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), meaning those born in the desire realm who have not yet seen the truths (*satya*).

2. Learners (*śaikṣa*) of the desire realm, meaning those born in the desire realm who have already seen the noble truths; these consist of six types of learners, ranging from the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*) up to the sixth, the candidate for arhatship (*arhattva-pratipannaka*).
3. Those in the desire realm who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), namely those born in the desire realm who have attained the fruit of arhatship.
4. Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the form realm, namely those born in the form realm who have not yet seen the truths (*satya*).

Fifth, those in training within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) refers to the two types of those in training who, having been born in the form realm, have already seen the noble truths: first, those in the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), and second, those progressing toward arhatship (*arhattvapratipannaka*).
Sixth, those in the form realm who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), namely those born in the form realm who have attained the fruit of arhatship.
Seventh, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the formless realm, namely those born in the formless realm who have not yet seen the truths.

8. Learners in the formless realm (*ārūpya-śaikṣa*): this refers to those who, having been born in the formless realm and having already seen the Noble Truths, are of two kinds of learners: first, those abiding in the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*), and second, those proceeding toward arhatship (*arhattvapratipannaka*).
9. Formless Non-learners (*ārūpya-aśaikṣa*): This refers to those who have attained the fruit of Arhatship while born in the formless realm.

10. Pratyekabuddhas of the Desire Realm: This refers to those who abide in the *dharmatā* of a Pratyekabuddha; whether they had not yet seen the Truths or had already seen them in previous lives, they are now born in the Desire Realm and, without relying on the instruction of a teacher, cultivate the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) through the power of prior causes, thereby realizing the permanent exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*).
This is further divided into two types: first, those who proceed alone like a *khaḍga* (rhinoceros); second, those who proceed as a superior leader of a group.

Eleventh, the Bodhisattvas of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) refers to those born in the Desire Realm who abide in the *dharmatā* of a Bodhisattva; for the sake of enabling themselves and others to realize *nirvāṇa*, they have already made the correct vow and practice all the skillful means for supreme enlightenment.

12. Bodhisattvas of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) refers to those born within the Form Realm who abide in the *dharmatā* of bodhisattvas; having distanced themselves from the Formless Realm, they cultivate the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) for the sake of enabling themselves and others to realize cessation (*nirvāṇa*). Having already made the correct vows, they practice all the skillful means (*upāya*) for supreme enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Thirteen: The inconceivable Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, by relying on the cultivation of the non-abiding path—which is free from both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa and is non-conceptual—realize the supreme transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) subsumed within the liberation-dharmakāya shared by all Buddhas; this transformation is all-pervasive, performing every kind of beneficial activity for all sentient beings throughout all worlds in the ten directions without end or exhaustion.
Thus, the *pudgalas* have already been explained; the fruits shall now be discussed.
The verse says:
The fruits consist of five kinds of abandonment, as well as thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) and purification (*viśuddhi*).
Purity, fruit, realm, and enlightenment—these are established by their own respective categories for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The commentary states:
"There are five kinds of abandonment regarding the fruits" means that among the various fruits, there are five types of abandonment.
First, the abandonment of the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*): this refers to being distanced from the active manifestation of various afflictive entanglements by means of four types of remedies.
The four remedies are: first, the remedy for distraction; second, the remedy of clear comprehension; third, the remedy of weakening; and fourth, the remedy of subjugation.

The remedy for distraction consists of skillfully practicing among the eight aforementioned practices of the sublime Dharma, or otherwise skillfully practicing other wholesome dharmas belonging to the stages of meditative concentration.
The antidote of manifestation refers to the cultivation of skillful means through the ninth stage of dharma-practice (*dharmacaryā*).
The antidote of weakness refers to the weakening of afflictions because the mind is supported by previously cultivated roots of virtue.
Subduing as an antidote refers to suppressing the seeds of afflictions according to one's capacity by means of the mundane path.
Second, the abandonment of latent tendencies refers to permanently severing the seeds of afflictions according to one's capacity by means of the supramundane path.
Third, the permanent exhaustion and abandonment of greed: this refers to the abandonment of the affliction of greed by means of permanently severing the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Just as there is the permanent exhaustion and abandonment of greed, so too should one understand the fourth, the permanent exhaustion and abandonment of hatred, and the fifth, the permanent exhaustion and abandonment of delusion; because all objective afflictions are ultimately severed through the power of the extremely pure and thorough penetration of insight, they are termed "permanent exhaustion and abandonment."

Regarding "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*), it refers to the nine thorough knowledges subsumed under the various fruits, which are explained in terms of the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).

First, there is the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the afflictions associated with the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin; this is because these two truths are comprised within the outflowing (*sāsrava*) category.

2. The thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin pertaining to the realms of form and formlessness, because these two realms are comprised within the stages of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

3. The thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of cessation pertaining to the desire realm, because this is comprised within untainted unconditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-asamskṛta*).

4. The thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the afflictions associated with the form and formless realms that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), because they are subsumed by the predominance of those specific meditative stages (*samāpatti-bhūmi*).

5. The thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the afflictions associated with the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*), because they are subsumed by the untainted conditioned (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*).

6. The thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the afflictions associated with the realms of form and formlessness that are to be abandoned by the path of vision, because they are governed by the predominance of those specific meditative stages.
7. The thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the five lower fetters, because of having transcended the lower realm.
8. The thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of desire for the realm of form (*rūparāga*), by virtue of transcending the intermediate realm (*madhyadhātu*).
9. The thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of desire for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*), by virtue of transcending the sublime realm (*praṇītadhātu*).
"Purity" refers to the nine kinds of purity, as explained at length in the sūtra.

First is purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*): this refers to one who is well-established in ethical discipline and properly guards the prātimokṣa vows; who is complete in lawful deportment and modes of conduct; who perceives great dread even in minor transgressions; and who undertakes and trains in the precepts.

Second, purity of mind: this refers to a certain person who, relying on purity of ethical discipline, dwells having fully attained the first dhyāna, as well as the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, by being secluded from sensual desires and unwholesome states, as previously described.

Third, purity of vision: This refers to a certain person who possesses a mind that is pure, bright, and stainless; being free from all afflictions, they abide in immovability. Desiring to realize the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*), they contemplate the truths and understand them as they truly are: "This is the noble truth of suffering; this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering; this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; this is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering."

4. Purity of the overcoming of doubt (*kāṅkṣāvitaraṇaviśuddhi*): This refers to a certain person who, relying on purity of view, has no confusion or doubt regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.

5. Purity of knowledge and vision regarding what is the path and what is not the path (*mārgāmārgajñānadarśanaviśuddhi*): This refers to a certain person who, relying on the purity of the overcoming of doubt, attains sublime knowledge and vision, [realizing] that only that which is taught by the Buddha and practiced by the Saṃgha can lead to liberation.
What, then, is this? It is that which can exhaust suffering and realize the limit of suffering.
As for the paths taught by various non-Buddhists, they cannot exhaust suffering nor realize the limit of suffering.

Sixth, the purification of the vision of knowledge regarding practice (*paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*): This refers to a certain person who, relying on the purification of the vision of knowledge regarding what is the path and what is not the path, attains sublime vision of knowledge and understands that the path to deliverance is of three grades—inferior, middling, and superior.
The inferior is comprised within the practice that is painful with slow progress;
the middling is comprised within the practice that is painful with quick progress and the practice that is pleasant with slow progress.
The superior [type] is comprised within the practice of swift penetration.

Seventh is the purification of conduct, knowledge, and vision regarding abandonment; that is to say, there is one who, relying on the purification of conduct, knowledge, and vision, attains sublime knowledge and vision, thinking: "I should abandon inferior and middling conduct, and I shall initiate superior and sublime noble conduct."

8. Purity through the cessation of the objectless (*anālambana-nirodha-viśuddhi*): This refers to a certain person who, relying on the purity of the knowledge and vision that abandons [defilements] through practice, realizes the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*) without remainder.

9. Purity of the Buddha-field: This refers to the supreme capacity shared by all Buddhas, which enables them to manifest the inconceivable adornments of a Buddha-field, including the most pure thoughts of a Buddha, the most pure thoughts of a Bodhisattva, and the dharmas associated with those thoughts.
"Purity" refers to the four types of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*), as explained at length in the sūtras.

First is verified confidence in the Buddha: this refers to the supramundane faith well-established in the Tathāgata by one who has already seen the truths, as well as the mundane faith well-established [in him] through subsequent attainment.
Just as with the verified confidence in the Buddha, so too should the second verified confidence in the Dharma and the third verified confidence in the Saṅgha be understood.

Fourth is the verified confidence in the morality beloved by the noble ones; this refers to the supramundane faith in which one who has already seen the truths is well-established in the morality of restraint from unwholesome action—attained through certainty—and the subsequently attained mundane faith in which one is likewise well-established.
The "fruits" refer to the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, as explained at length in the sūtras.

First is the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala): if categorized by its excellence, it is the permanent abandonment of the three fetters—namely, the view of a self-entity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), adherence to precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa), and doubt (vicikitsā);
if categorized by its completeness, it is the permanent abandonment of all afflictions to be abandoned through the path of vision (darśana-mārga).

Because those [defilements] have been abandoned, one attains the fruit of Stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), which is a state from which there is no falling back, characterized by either being reborn at most seven times (*saptakṛtparama*) or as a "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) practitioner.

Second, regarding the fruit of Once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*): if categorized according to its superior aspects, it consists of the permanent abandonment of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the attenuation of greed, hatred, and delusion;

if categorized in its entirety, it consists of the permanent abandonment of all afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), as well as the permanent abandonment of the superior and medium grades of afflictions bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that are to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Due to that abandonment, one attains the fruit of a Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), or alternatively, the state of being "one interval" away from liberation (*ekavīcika*).

Third is the fruit of a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*): if categorized according to its excellence, it consists of the permanent abandonment of the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*), namely: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), and ill-will (*vyāpāda*).

If categorized in its entirety, it consists of the permanent abandonment of all afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), as well as the permanent abandonment of the afflictions bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), or the permanent abandonment of the afflictions bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), or the permanent abandonment of a portion of the afflictions bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Due to that abandonment, one attains the fruit of non-returning, which may be cessation in the intermediate state, cessation upon rebirth, cessation without exertion, cessation with exertion, or else the upward-streamer.
4. Regarding the fruit of arhatship for śramaṇas: if categorized according to its preeminent aspects, it is the permanent and complete abandonment of desire, hatred, and delusion without remainder;
if categorized in its entirety, it is the permanent and complete abandonment of all afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation without remainder.
Because of that abandonment, one attains arhatship with all outflows forever exhausted; this is explained at length, including the six modes of constant abiding of an arhat.
As for the "realms" (dhātu), they refer to the three realms, as explained at length in the sūtra.
1. The realm of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*), which refers to the abandonment of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
2. The realm of detachment (*virāgadhātu*), which refers to the detachment from all conditioned phenomena to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
3. The realm of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*), which refers to the cessation of all conditioned phenomena subsumed under their bases (*āśraya*).
"Bodhi" refers to the three types of bodhi, as explained at length in the sūtras.

First is the bodhi of the śrāvakas, which refers to the nirvāṇa attained through the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) by means of the Śrāvakayāna, as well as the path leading to that nirvāṇa.

2. Pratyekabuddha-bodhi refers to the nirvāṇa attained through the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) by means of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, as well as the path leading to that nirvāṇa.

3. Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi refers to the nirvāṇa and the path leading to nirvāṇa attained through the transformation of the basis by means of the Mahāyāna, as well as the path that brings about the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings.
The "one beyond training" (aśaikṣa) refers to the ten qualities of one beyond training, as explained at length in the Sūtra.

First is the right view of one beyond training: this refers to an Arhat’s contemplation of suffering as suffering, up to the contemplation of the path as the path; it consists of the discernment of phenomena (dharmapravicaya), thorough investigation, and so forth, associated with untainted mental attention (anāsravamanasikāra), as explained at length previously.
Just as with the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), so it should be understood for all [factors] up to the eighth, right samādhi, as previously described.

Ninth, right liberation (*samyag-vimukti*) of one beyond training refers to the state of being free from the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of all afflictions; it is the quality of being pliant and capable on the mind of one beyond training, having become free from the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Tenth, the right knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagjñāna*), which refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) of an Arhat.
Regarding "by their own enumeration," it should be understood that each of the aforementioned fruits is distinguished by its own respective enumeration.
Furthermore, the verse says:

"Because many causes are severed, there is severance; The establishment of that from which severance proceeds, Arises through mental attention, reliance on cultivation, And the attainment of the sequence of severance."
The treatise says:

Regarding "abandonment through the severance of many causes," afflictions are abandoned because their fruits have many causes; that is to say, there are four kinds of causes for the abandonment of afflictions:
first, the extinction of the basis; second, the transformation of the basis; third, the knowledge of the object-condition; and fourth, the delighting in the object-condition.
Furthermore, there are five causes for severing all afflictions:
first, knowing their essence; second, knowing their objects; third, knowing their faults; fourth, avoiding their conditions; and fifth, cultivating the mental application of their antidotes.
Furthermore, there are four causes for the abandonment of afflictions:

first, by virtue of cessation without remainder; second, by virtue of transformation without remainder; third, by virtue of the cultivation of the antidote without remainder; and fourth, by virtue of the liberation of the mind without remainder.

Regarding the establishment of that from which abandonment proceeds: this refers to abandoning all afflictions by means of the objects of perception; once the afflictions have been abandoned with respect to those objects, because there is no longer any bondage, the associated mental factors are likewise abandoned in accordance therewith.
The afflictions of the future and present can be abandoned; the permanent destruction of their coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) is termed the abandonment of the afflictions.
Regarding "by means of attention" (*manasikāra*): it means that by means of the attention cultivated through the general contemplation of the truths, one abandons all afflictions.

Regarding "by means of reliance," this refers to abandoning all afflictions by relying upon the seven meditative absorptions, namely, from the first dhyāna up to the seventh, the sphere of nothingness.

Regarding "by means of cultivation," this refers to abandoning the afflictions by cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), up to and including the cultivation of the eight branches of the noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

Furthermore, regarding "attaining the sequence of abandonment," there are five types of sequential abandonment of the afflictions: (1) first abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); (2) subsequently abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); (3) first gradually subduing the manifest afflictions; (4) thereafter permanently severing all afflictions; and (5) finally transcending all afflictions.
Furthermore, the verse says:
One should know the distinctions of abandonment, As well as the characteristics and benefits of abandonment;
In this manner, according to what has been explained, One should further understand its many varieties.

The Commentary states: Regarding the statement that "the distinctions of abandonment should be known as manifold," the various distinctions in the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) are as follows: there is the abandonment of the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), the abandonment of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*); abandonment by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), abandonment by means of the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*); abandonment through the mental application of the Śrāvaka vehicle, abandonment through the mental application of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and abandonment through the mental application of the Bodhisattva vehicle; furthermore, there is temporary abandonment and ultimate abandonment. One should understand that the distinctions in the cessation of the afflictions include all such categories.

Regarding the statement, "One should further know that the benefits of the characteristic of abandonment are manifold," it should be understood that there are many kinds of beneficial characteristics associated with the abandonment of all afflictions, as explained at length in the Sūtra.

These are: being of a nature not to fall back; being destined for enlightenment; having reached the True Dharma; being on the verge of reaching the True Dharma; realizing and understanding the True Dharma; attaining realization of its fundamental source; attaining universal realization of its fundamental source; and the accomplishment of noble wisdom-vision. Through this, one can no longer conceive of phenomena such as suffering and pleasure as being created by oneself, created by another, created by both self and other, or created by neither self nor other through the combination of the two.

Furthermore, they no longer reckon that various sufferings and pleasures arise without cause; they no longer intentionally take the lives of animals and the like; they no longer intentionally transgress any of the precepts they have undertaken; they no longer commit the five deeds of immediate retribution; they no longer seek out teachers of external paths nor regard them as true fields of merit; they no longer look upon or observe the faces of other śramaṇas, brahmins, or members of heterodox groups; they no longer give rise to doubt or delusion regarding the phenomena of the three periods of time; and they no longer undergo the retribution of an eighth existence.
Thus having realized the fruit of arhatship, with all outflows forever exhausted, he has done what was to be done.
Having accomplished his task, he attains the six ever-present states of an arhat, as explained at length in the Sūtra; that is to say, he accomplishes the six modes of abiding in continuity.
If the eye sees forms, the mind is neither distressed nor elated, but remains in equanimity with mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Likewise, if the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mental consciousness perceives phenomena, the mind is neither distressed nor elated, but remains in equanimity with mindfulness and clear comprehension.

All the practices he undertakes are for his own benefit, for the benefit of others, for the welfare of sentient beings, for the happiness of sentient beings, out of compassion for the world, and so that gods and humans may attain meaningful benefit and joy.
One should know that there are many kinds of beneficial characteristics regarding the permanent abandonment of all such afflictions as these.
*Exposition of the Holy Teachings* (Xianyang shengjiao lun), Fascicle Three;
*Exposition of the Holy Teachings*, Fascicle Four.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter One, Part Four: Compendium of Matters (Vastusaṃgrahaṇī). Having thus explained the fruits, the various meritorious qualities shall now be explained.
The verse says:
The immeasurable liberations, the spheres of mastery, and the spheres of totality;
the absence of contention, the sublime knowledge of aspiration, the analytical knowledges, and the supernormal powers.
The Treatise says:
"Immeasurable" refers to the four immeasurables, as explained at length in the Sūtra.

First is the immeasurable of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which means being accompanied by a mind of loving-kindness—free from enmity, free from malice, and free from harm—vast, immeasurable, and thoroughly cultivated. One dwells having suffused one direction with this mental resolve, and so on in succession until all boundless worlds in the ten directions are fully pervaded.

That which is accompanied by loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the desire to bestow happiness upon sentient beings who experience neither suffering nor pleasure, because it is associated with the mental state of *āśaya*.
That which is "free from enmity" is its antidote, as it is the absence of hatred (*dveṣa*) that desires to inflict suffering.
Absence of aversion is its antidote, for aversion obstructs the requisites of happiness.
Absence of malice is its antidote, for malice desires what is unsuitable.
"Extensive" refers to mental attention directed toward the domain of vision;
"great" refers to mental attention directed toward the domain of hearing;
and "immeasurable" refers to mental attention directed toward the domain of realization.
"Thoroughly cultivated" means that through the application of repeated practice, one is free from all hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

"In one direction, and so forth in succession up to all infinite worlds in the ten directions" refers to taking as objects the entire vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*) and the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*).
"Resolution through mental engagement" refers to taking as an object the sphere of contemplation through resolution.
"Pervasive" refers to taking as an object the sphere of all sentient beings without exception.
"Abiding in fulfillment" is as explained previously regarding the dhyānas.
2. Immeasurable Compassion (*karuṇā-apramāṇa*): This refers to that which is accompanied by a compassionate mind, and so forth, as explained at length.

"Accompanied by a compassionate mind" means having the intention (*āśaya*) to extract suffering from sentient beings who are afflicted by it, due to its association with the mental state (*citta-samprayukta*).
Being without resentment is its antidote, because it does not inflict suffering or harm.
Being without malice is its antidote, because it prevents the infliction of suffering and harm.
That which is non-harming is its antidote, because one desires what is appropriate and rejoices in it.
The rest is as previously explained.
Third, the immeasurable of sympathetic joy (*muditā*) refers to that which is accompanied by a joyful mind, and so forth, as explained at length.
That which is associated with a joyful mind consists of rejoicing in the happiness of sentient beings who possess it, because it is conjoined with a mental disposition (*āśaya*) of sympathetic joy.
That which is free from enmity is its antidote, consisting of the lack of delight in providing the instruments of suffering to others.
Absence of malice is its antidote, because it does not take pleasure in obstructing the requisites for happiness.
Absence of harmful intent is its antidote, because it does not desire to inflict what is unsuitable and unpleasant.
The rest is as previously explained.
Fourth is the immeasurable of equanimity (*upekṣā-apramāṇa*), which refers to that which is accompanied by a mind of equanimity, and so forth, as explained at length.
"Accompanied by a mind of equanimity" means that it intends to bring about non-attachment, because it is associated with a mental disposition (*āśaya*) that is free from defilement.
Being without enmity is its antidote, for it prevents the arising of defiled greed and hatred.
Being without malice is its antidote, for it removes the obstacles that cause defiled greed and hatred.
That which is non-harming is its antidote, because it is untainted by the greed and hatred of perversion.
The rest is as previously explained.
What is the essential nature of these four immeasurables?

That is to say, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) has non-hatred as its essential nature; compassion (*karuṇā*) has non-harming as its essential nature; sympathetic joy (*muditā*) has non-envy as its essential nature; and equanimity (*upekṣā*) has both non-attachment and non-hatred as its essential nature, for all are dharmas that take pity on sentient beings.

Among these four, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is exclusively non-aversion (*adveṣa*); the next two immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are a portion of non-aversion; and equanimity (*upekṣā*) is a portion of both non-attachment (*alobha*) and non-aversion.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the mental states and mental factors, along with their attendants, associated with those [immeasurables] and their respective meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), constitute the essence of the four immeasurables.

First, one should thoroughly cultivate the mind through the practice of the superior Dharma; furthermore, by relying on pure meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one should know that the pure immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are then attained.
As for the "liberations," these refer to the eight liberations, as explained at length in the sūtras.
1. Liberation through the contemplation of forms while possessing form.
"Possessing form" refers to the mental engagement of reflective contemplation based on meditative concentration with form.
"Forms" refers to all forms, as extensively analyzed in the section on the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Regarding "contemplation": it is because one exercises mastery over transformations among all forms, and because one manifests those characteristics through mental resolve and reflection.
Second, the liberation of contemplating external forms while having no perception of form internally.
"Having no perception of internal form" refers to mental contemplation based on the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
"External" refers to mental contemplation of other forms, excluding the sense faculties such as the eye.
Regarding the contemplation of forms, it is as previously explained.
The third liberation is the liberation attained by realizing through bodily witness and dwelling in its fulfillment;
"pure" means that one exclusively contemplates pure and exquisite forms with mental resolve for the sake of attaining a superior state of abiding in peace and happiness.
Liberation means being liberated from the functional activity of pure and impure forms, because these obstruct the mind.
"Body" refers to the mental body (*manomaya-kāya*).
"Realization" means attaining realization through the abandonment [of defilements] by means of wisdom.
"Abiding in full possession" is as previously explained.
The formless liberations (*ārūpya-vimokṣa*) are as previously analyzed.

The distinction here is that, in order to realize mastery over all aspects of bodily action and to liberate oneself from its obstacles, one further sets aside the perception of light and color and performs the mental engagement of the conceptualization of infinite space; thus it is called the fourth liberation of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-vimokṣa*).

In order to give rise to the noble supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the absence of strife (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*), the unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and other such qualities; furthermore, in order to attain mastery over the mind that assists in giving rise to those qualities; and furthermore, in order to liberate oneself from their obstacles, one performs the mental engagement of infinite consciousness. This is called the fifth liberation: the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-vimokṣa*).

Once the practitioner has thus initiated the skillful means for generating merit, they cause the fourth dhyāna to arise and manifest so as to produce various meritorious qualities. This is for the sake of attaining the supreme, untainted dwelling of mastery, and furthermore, for the sake of liberating oneself from its obstacles; because one then performs the mental contemplation of the "nothingness" resolve, it is called the sixth liberation: the sphere of nothingness.

Because one desires to realize and attain mastery over the dwelling in the supreme existence, and furthermore, in order to liberate oneself from its obstacles, one performs the mental engagement of contemplation regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is called the seventh liberation, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

In order to realize the mastery of dwelling in the most supreme tranquility, and furthermore, in order to liberate oneself from its obstacles, one further causes the cessation of the mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation by withdrawing the mind from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is called the eighth liberation, the cessation of perception and feeling.
Regarding the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), they refer to the eight spheres of mastery, as explained at length in the Sūtra.

First: possessing the perception of internal forms, one contemplates external forms that are few—whether beautiful or ugly, inferior or superior—and having mastered the knowledge and vision of those forms, one attains such a perception; this is called the first sphere of mastery.
"Having the perception of internal forms" is as explained in the section on the liberations (*vimokṣa*).
"External" means that, excluding the sense faculties such as the eye, it manifests other forms.
"Contemplating all forms" is as previously described.
"Small" refers to matter comprised of physical requisites, because it is the object of conceptualization through mental resolve.
"Whether beautiful or ugly" refers to matter comprised of pure or impure forms, because it is the object of conceptualization through mental resolve.
Regarding "whether inferior or superior": this refers to forms comprised of pure or impure sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, which are mentally resolved and reflected upon.

Among those various forms, "superior" refers to the mental attention directed toward the antidotes and the objects to be remedied, because one is not troubled by the obstructive functions [of those objects].
"Knowing" refers to employing the path of śamatha;
"seeing" refers to employing the path of vipaśyanā.
To "attain such a perception" means that within the truly superior, one attains the truly superior, because there is no conceited perception.
Because one attains actual non-superiority amidst non-superiority and is free from conceited thoughts, this is the first base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Second, having the perception of internal forms while observing many external forms, up to this point, is called the second base of mastery.
The two types—observing the few and observing the many while internally perceiving no form—are likewise explained.
Regarding "internally perceiving form while observing external forms," it is as previously stated.
"Many" refers to the pervasive contemplation of the forms of both the sentient world (*sattvaloka*) and the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
The rest is as previously explained. Fifth,
one perceives external forms while being internally without the perception of form, observing them as blue—
blue in appearance, blue in manifestation, and blue in radiance— just like the *umakā* flower, or like the color of dyed blue cloth from Vārāṇasī.
In this same manner, the yellow, red, and white colors should all be explained in detail.
The distinction here is that the yellow is like the *karṇikāra* flower, or like the color of a saffron-dyed robe from Vārāṇasī.
The red color is like that of the bandhujīvaka flower, or like the color of cloth dyed crimson in Vārāṇasī.
The white color is like the star Uśanas, or like the color of fresh white cloth from Vārāṇasī.
"Blue" refers to the general term.
"Manifest blue" refers to innate blue.
"Visible blue" refers to blue produced through combination.
"Blue light" refers to the fresh, pure blue light emitted by those two.
Just as it is with blue, so too should it be understood through the detailed explanation that applies to yellow, red, and white.
The rest is as previously explained.
The reason two similes are given for a single location is to demonstrate the two types of form: that which is co-nascent (*sahaja*) and that which is composite (*saṃghāta*).

These eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) serve as the basis for the three kinds of liberation through the contemplation of forms as objects. Regarding the latter four bases of mastery, one contemplates with mental resolve the forms of the gods of the desire realm and the forms of the form realm.

Furthermore, it should be understood that these spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) function as antidotes to the mental engagement with the seeds of the lower stages that persist therein; they do not serve as antidotes to the mental engagement with the objects to be countered within their own stage.
Regarding the "totalities" (kṛtsnāyatana), they refer to the ten totalities, as explained at length in the sūtras.
These are: the earth totality, wherein one is able to comprehend [the perception of earth] above, below, and across, as non-dual and immeasurable.
In this same way, water, fire, and wind pervade.
Blue, yellow, red, white, space, and consciousness pervade above, below, and across—non-dual and immeasurable.
Regarding the "earth-kasiṇa" (pṛthivī-kṛtsnāyatana): because the basis of form is all-pervasive, the form that depends upon it is also all-pervasive, due to its increase.
"One who is capable of understanding" refers to the person (pudgala) who is able to realize this contemplation.
"Upward, downward, and across" means that it pervades all directions and the four intermediate points.
"Non-dual" means that it is free from other realms and is pervasive without being mixed with manifest colors (*varṇa*).
"Immeasurable" means that there are no boundaries, because its characteristics pervade everywhere.
Just as with the earth-totality (*pṛthivī-kṛtsnāyatana*), it is likewise with the other [totalities]—water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, and white—each according to what is appropriate.
The sphere of infinite space (*ākāśakṛtsnāyatana*) refers to the mental attention that contemplates the pervasiveness [of space] as an antidote to all forms; the rest is as previously explained.
The sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānakṛtsnāyatana*) refers to the mental attention that contemplates the pervasiveness of immeasurable consciousness; the rest is as previously explained.

In this context, mastery over superior form is attained by means of the three liberations; only after attaining them can one be said to possess mastery over superior form, because of their ultimate perfection.

Above the sphere of consciousness (vijñānāyatana), there is no further pervasiveness, because the objects of focus are immeasurable, lack distinct segments, and are free from the conceptualization of a basis.

One should know that the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) and the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) are the paths capable of purifying those liberations (vimokṣa). It should be understood that they bring about the purification of liberation because the spheres of mastery excel in their objects of focus, while the spheres of totality are pervasive in their objects.

"Non-contention" refers to the nature of non-deluded wisdom and vision, as well as the primary minds and mental factors associated with the meditative absorption (samādhi) that are subsumed under the ability to guard against the conduct of others' afflictions; this is because such conduct is extensively practiced.

The wisdom of sublime vows refers to the nature of non-deluded knowledge and vision, as well as the various primary minds and mental factors associated with meditative concentration (samādhi), which are induced by the thorough and accurate comprehension of all knowable phenomena—whether subsumed within the three times or beyond time—without exception; it is so called because one practices extensively through these modes of conduct.
The analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) refer to the four analytical knowledges, as explained at length in the sūtras.

First, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*): this refers to the nature of non-deluded wisdom and vision, as well as the associated meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and all mental states and mental factors, which are induced by and subsumed within the actual realization of the various names for all phenomena in all their aspects.

Second, the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) refers to the nature of non-deluded wisdom and vision, which is induced by and comprised within the real and correct awakening to the various characteristics of all phenomena in all their aspects; the rest is as previously explained.

Third, the analytical knowledge of etymological interpretation (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*): this refers to the nature of non-deluded wisdom and vision, encompassed by the realization of all things exactly as they are within the etymological explanations of all phenomena in every respect; the remainder is as previously stated.

Fourth, the analytical knowledge of unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) refers to the nature of non-deluded wisdom and vision, as well as the primary minds and mental factors associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which are induced by the realization of all aspects of all phenomena exactly as they are; this is because one traverses many such modes of conduct through it.
"Supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*) refers to the six supernormal powers, as explained at length in the sūtras.

First is the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge and vision of the basis of miraculous power (*ṛddhiviṣayajñānadarśanābhijñā*). This refers to the nature of knowledge and vision that is free from delusion regarding mastery over all types of bodily actions, as well as the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and the various mental states and mental factors associated with them; this is because one practices extensively within these determined spheres of activity.

2. The supernormal power of the realization through the wisdom and vision of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra-jñānadarśana-abhijñā*) refers to the nature of wisdom and vision that is free from delusion regarding all kinds of vocal actions as they are heard; the rest is as previously explained.

Third, the supernormal knowledge of realizing through wisdom and vision the distinctions among minds; that is, the nature of wisdom and vision free from delusion for entering into all modes of others' mental activities, the rest being as previously explained.

Fourth, the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the wisdom and vision that recollects past abodes: this refers to the nature of the wisdom and vision of non-delusion regarding all modes of conduct and destinies in the past; the remainder is as previously explained.

Fifth, the supernormal power of the realization through knowledge and vision of death and rebirth; that is to say, its nature is the knowledge and vision free from delusion regarding the modes of conduct leading to all types of existence and destinies, while the remainder is as previously explained.

Sixth, the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge and vision of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānadarśanābhijñā*). This refers to the nature of the knowledge and vision that is free from delusion regarding all afflictions and the remainderless cessation of suffering, as well as the various minds and mental factors associated with the corresponding meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because through these practices one frequently determines the objective sphere.
Furthermore, the verse says:
The primary marks and secondary signs, purity, As well as the powers, the fearlessnesses, The ways of non-protection,
the foundations of mindfulness, And the eternal severance of all habitual tendencies.
The Treatise says:
Regarding the "various marks," these refer to the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, as explained at length in the sūtras.
First is the mark of well-placed feet, which is attained because the Tathāgata’s provisions for enlightenment were perfectly fulfilled and because he fully maintained impartial conduct.
By virtue of these marks, those who see him even briefly immediately believe that the Tathāgata is a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
This refers to the mark of the feet—the insignia and the physical form of the feet.
Just as with the mark of the well-placed feet, all other marks of a Great Man should be understood in their entirety according to what is appropriate.
This means that regarding the hands, one should explain the hand-omens (*hasta-lakṣaṇa*), the hand-signs (*hasta-cihna*), and the hand-appearances (*hasta-saṃsthāna*).
Likewise, for the remaining limbs and joints, such as the crown of the head and so forth, one should explain them extensively according to their respective names.
The "excellent marks" (anuvyañjana) refer to the eighty secondary characteristics, as explained at length in the sutras.
Regarding these excellent marks, if they are categorized according to their complete inclusion within the primary marks, it is as described in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*;
if they are categorized according to what is appropriate for sentient beings or according to their predominant characteristics, it is as described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
If one wishes to analyze the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) in detail, they should be understood as explained in the detailed analysis of the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
As for "purity," it refers to the four kinds of purity in all aspects, as explained at length in the sūtra.

First, purity of the basis (*āśraya-viśuddhi*): this refers to the Tathāgata’s attainment of wisdom that is pure in all its aspects (*sarvākāra-viśuddha-jñāna*) and the abandonment that is pure in all its aspects; consequently, he possesses ultimate, unsurpassed mastery over the grasping, maintaining, and relinquishing of the basis.

Second, purity of the objective sphere (*viṣaya-viśuddhi*): this refers to the ultimate, unsurpassed mastery over the transformed objective spheres of all phenomena, resulting from the Tathāgata’s realization of the wisdom that is pure in all aspects (*sarvākāra-viśuddha-jñāna*) and his abandonment that is pure in all aspects.

Third, purity of mind: this refers to the ultimate, unsurpassed mastery over a mind in which all mundane and supramundane roots of virtue increase, due to the Tathāgata’s realization of the wisdom that is pure in all aspects and the abandonment that is pure in all aspects.

Fourth, purity of wisdom: this refers to the Tathāgata’s attainment of the wisdom that is pure in all aspects and the abandonment that is pure in all aspects; thus, regarding all objects of knowledge in all their aspects, his wisdom is ultimately unsurpassed, sovereign, and free from attachment and hindrance.
Regarding the powers (*bala*): these refer to the ten powers of the Tathāgata, as explained at length in the sūtras.

First is the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*). This refers to the nature of unimpeded wisdom that can provide accurate explanations and answers regarding all aspects of cause and effect, as well as the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) associated with it and the various mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).

2. The power of knowledge regarding one’s own karma (*karmasvakatājñānabala*): this refers to the nature of unimpeded knowledge regarding all types of actions performed in various locations and continuities, as well as the resulting retributions; the rest is as previously explained.

Third, the power of knowledge regarding the dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis: this refers to the nature of unimpeded knowledge regarding the skillful means for acquiring all worldly pure merits characterized by signs; the rest is as previously explained.

Fourth, the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties (*indriya-parāpara-jñānabala*): this refers to the nature of unimpeded knowledge regarding the distinctions among the faculties of sentient beings to be converted, which serve as the basis for supramundane merit; the remainder is as previously explained.

Fifth, the power of knowing the various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñānabala*): this refers to the nature of unimpeded knowledge regarding the differences in the mental dispositions (*āśaya*) of all sentient beings to be converted across all their aspects; the rest is as previously explained.

Sixth, the power of knowledge regarding the various elements (*nānādhātu-jñānabala*): this refers to the nature of unimpeded knowledge regarding the distinctions among the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of all sentient beings to be converted according to their various characteristics; the remainder is as previously explained.

Seventh is the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*). This refers to the nature of unimpeded knowledge regarding the distinctions among all vehicles and modes of transcendence (*nairyāṇika-viśeṣa*);

the rest is as previously explained. Eighth is the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-bala*). This refers to the nature of unimpeded knowledge regarding the distinctions among the various destinies of the past limit (*pūrvakoṭi-gati-viśeṣa*); the rest is as previously explained.

9. The power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñānabala*): This refers to the nature of unimpeded wisdom regarding the distinctions in the transitions toward the future limit among all phenomena; the rest is as previously explained. 10.

The power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*): This refers to the nature of unimpeded wisdom regarding the distinctions in the means of deliverance from the transitions toward and away from [saṃsāra] among all phenomena, as well as the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) associated with that, and all the primary minds and mental factors (*cittacaitta*).
Furthermore, among the various powers (*bala*), it should be stated that all are capable of answering questions according to reality.
As for the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), there are four; they are explained at length as in the Sūtra.
First, the Buddha makes this solemn declaration:
I am the Perfectly Awakened One.
If anyone should challenge me by saying that I have not attained perfect awakening regarding these dharmas, [then let them speak].
I have correctly seen that there is no basis for this objection; therefore, I am fearless.
This is because the Tathāgata has realized the sublime, excellent, and pure omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Second, the Buddha makes this solemn declaration:
My outflows are already exhausted.
If someone were to challenge me, saying,
"In such and such a way, your outflows are not yet exhausted," [I would know that to be so].
I see no grounds for this objection; therefore, I am fearless.
This is because the Tathāgata has realized the sublime, virtuous, and pure abandonment of all types [of afflictions].
These two forms of fearlessness rely upon the qualities of self-benefit.
3. The Buddha made this solemn declaration:
"I have taught my disciples the obstructive dharmas; that which is defiled will necessarily constitute an obstruction.
If someone were to raise an objection, saying:
The habitual tendencies of these defilements cannot act as an obstacle.
I perceive that this challenge lacks any basis; therefore, I am fearless.
That is to say, based on the Tathāgata, I have taught all types of dharmas that serve as antidotes for sentient beings who are to be converted.
Fourth, the Buddha made this solemn declaration:
"I have taught my disciples the path to liberation; through the cultivation of meditative concentration, one attains liberation.
Should anyone challenge this by saying:
"Although one may cultivate this path, it cannot lead to transcendence; it does not correctly bring an end to suffering nor realize the limit of suffering.
Regarding this difficulty, I see that there is no such cause; therefore, I am fearless."
This refers to the Tathāgata’s teaching of all types of remedial dharmas for the sake of sentient beings to be converted;
these two forms of fearlessness rely upon the virtue of benefiting others.
Regarding "non-guarding," this refers to the three non-guardings, as explained at length in the sūtras.

First, the Tathāgata’s current bodily actions are wondrously good and pure; there are no impure current bodily actions that need to be concealed, and for this reason, he does not maintain [the restraints].

This means that because the Tathāgata’s bodily actions (*kāyakarman*) are excellent, wholesome, and pure in every respect and at all times, when he teaches the Dharma correctly to sentient beings who are to be converted, he is able to subdue and gather all his followers through his supreme power.
Just as with the non-guarding of bodily action, one should know that the same applies to the second, non-guarding of vocal action, and the third, non-guarding of mental action.
As for the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), they refer to the three foundations of mindfulness, as explained at length in the sūtras.

This refers to abiding in the most excellent equanimity regarding the distinctions in conduct among the three types of disciples when gathering those to be converted—a state of mind that is neither attached nor resentful, and free from defilement.

The "permanent severance of all habitual tendencies" refers to the fact that all Tathāgatas have emerged from the birth and death of beginningless, immeasurable, and innumerable great eons; because they have realized their own nature so as not to follow after [delusions], they have attained the wondrous, pure wisdom and abandonment of a Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the verse says:
The sublime dharma of non-forgetfulness, as well as the great compassion of the Tathāgata,
the qualities of the Buddha’s unique attributes, and the sublime wisdom of all modes.
The treatise states:

"The sublime quality of non-forgetfulness" means that, in order to realize all aspects of all tasks to be performed for all sentient beings to be converted without missing the proper time, one realizes the sublime, pure wisdom and abandonment of a Tathāgata.
Regarding "the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata," it means that the compassion of the Tathāgata is designated as "Great Compassion" (mahākaruṇā) due to four causes and conditions.
First, because it is accomplished through the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) which is based upon all modes of sublime goodness and purity.
2. Because it is obtained through long-term cultivation;
3. because it is induced by sublime, pure wisdom;
4. because it takes as its object all aspects of suffering that are extremely profound, firm, and variously solid.
The qualities of the Buddha’s unique attributes (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) refer to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as explained at length in the sūtras.
It should be understood that these are established because they transcend all stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
First, the Tathāgata has no failure through error, meaning that he is free from any non-afflicted transgression or lapse.
Second, he has no abrupt or violent sounds, meaning that he is free from any non-afflicted loud laughter or harsh noise.
Third, there is no loss of mindfulness, meaning that he does not fail to recollect things done long ago or spoken long ago because they were not defiled.
Fourth, there is no unconcentrated mind, meaning that his attention and meditative absorption (samādhi) constantly accompany him throughout all modes of conduct, such as walking and standing.
Fifth, the absence of manifold perceptions, meaning that one realizes non-conceptual and undifferentiated wisdom regarding both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Sixth, the absence of relinquishing without discernment, meaning that one ultimately never abandons the welfare of sentient beings.
7. Non-retrogression in aspiration (*chanda*), which means attaining the purification of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
