As for the detailed classification of the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*): if a bhikṣu knows the noble truth of suffering as it truly is as suffering, knows the noble truth of the origin as it truly is as the origin, knows the noble truth of the cessation of suffering as it truly is as cessation, and knows the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is as the path, this is called the detailed classification of the training in higher wisdom.

Regarding the arising of discrimination: because of the accomplishment of ethical discipline (*śīla*), there is no regret; because of the absence of regret, joy arises; because of the arising of joy, the mind becomes glad; because the mind is glad, the body becomes tranquil; because the body is tranquil, one experiences happiness; because of experiencing happiness, the mind becomes concentrated; because the mind is concentrated, one contemplates reality as it truly is (*yathābhūtam*); because of contemplating reality as it truly is, revulsion arises; because revulsion arises, desire is abandoned; because desire is abandoned, there is liberation; because of liberation, one thinks to oneself, "I have realized liberation," and further gives rise to this knowledge and vision:
"Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."

Regarding the transformation of distinctions: there may be the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*), but no training in higher mind (*adhicitta*) and no training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
Or there may be the training in higher ethical discipline and the training in higher mind, but no training in higher wisdom.
If there is training in higher wisdom, there must necessarily be training in higher ethical discipline and higher concentration.

Regarding the distinction between the antidote and that which is to be countered: training in higher ethical discipline is the antidote for the cessation of active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*); training in higher concentration is the antidote for the subduing of active afflictions; and training in higher wisdom is the antidote for the permanent eradication of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Regarding "that which can induce superior birth and the certainty of superiority in discernment": this means that the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*) and the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*) can induce the pure stages and superior births characterized by purity, while the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*) can induce supramundane, definitive excellence.
The analysis of conformity to the Dharma refers to the ten types of factors that accord with the training:

first, prior causes; second, conformity to the teachings; third, skillful means according to principle; fourth, uninterrupted and earnest cultivation; fifth, intense aspiration; sixth, the power of sustained practice; seventh, the pacification of physical and mental heaviness; eighth, repeated investigation; ninth, freedom from timidity and fear; and tenth, freedom from overweening pride.
The prior cause refers to the maturation of the faculties and the fulfillment of the faculties in previous lives.
Teaching in accordance with the Dharma refers to the teaching of the unerring sequence.
Skillful means according to principle refers to practicing in accordance with the teaching; when one practices in this manner, one is able to give rise to right view.

"Practicing with uninterrupted and earnest diligence" means that during such application of skillful means, no time is wasted; one cultivates the categories of virtue and, with sincerity, swiftly brings them forth.
"One with intense aspiration" refers to one who gives rise to the aspiration for realization regarding supreme liberation, thinking:
"When shall I realize the state of dwelling in the perfection of the noble ones?"
Regarding the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*): it is said that one attains this power through two causes and conditions:
first, because of being naturally of sharp faculties; second, because of having practiced with purity for a long period.

Regarding the settling of physical and mental heaviness (*dausthulya*): if physical fatigue gives rise to physical and mental heaviness, then one's deportment (*īryāpatha*) is easily disrupted, and thus one attains rest.
If physical and mental heaviness arises due to excessive vitarka and vicāra, one should cultivate internal tranquility to attain rest.

If physical and mental heaviness arises due to excessive mental exertion and withdrawal of the mind, or due to the onset of the hindrances of dullness and drowsiness, one should cultivate insight and pure, sublime attention to attain rest.

If, by their very nature, the afflictions have not been abandoned and the physical and mental heaviness (dauṣṭhulya) concordant with the category of afflictions continues to follow and never depart, then one must correctly cultivate the Noble Path to attain tranquility.
"Repeatedly examining" means that, based upon ethical discipline (*śīla*), one repeatedly examines and understands, as they truly are, what has been poorly done and what has been well done.
If something was poorly done and should not have been abandoned, one does not abandon it; if something was well done and should have been abandoned, one abandons it.
If something was poorly done and should have been abandoned, one abandons it; if something was well done and should not have been abandoned, one does not abandon it.

By the predominant power of such contemplative attention (*manasikāra*), one repeatedly examines whether all afflictions have been abandoned or not; if one knows they have been abandoned, one should feel profound joy, and if one knows they have not been abandoned, one should repeatedly cultivate this path of antidotes.

Regarding "being without timidity or fear": this refers to the fact that from time to time one should know and contemplate the Dharma; because of not knowing, not contemplating, and not entering into realization, timidity and fear arise, resulting in a withered mind and a depleted mind.
When such thoughts arise repeatedly in this manner, one does not cling to them, but rather cuts them off, abandons them, and relinquishes them.

One who is free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*) means that regarding what has been attained, realized, and verified, one is devoid of overweening pride and free from inverted attachment; one forms the perception of having attained regarding what has been attained, the perception of having realized regarding what has been realized, and the perception of having verified regarding what has been verified.

These ten dharmas are called the "dharmas conducive to training" because they accord with the training precepts in their beginning, middle, and end for those who delight in correctly practicing the various bases of training.
Among these ten dharmas, the first one is preeminent for being conducive to the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*);
the remaining nine are preeminent for being conducive to the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*) and the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).

The classification of persons (*pudgala*) refers to how these three trainings apply to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those who have seen the truth (*dṛṣṭasatya*). The classification into inferior, middling, and superior grades refers to their practice (*caryā*) and their skillful means (*upāya*).

Regarding "by way of application": the practice characterized by difficulty and slow progress is termed inferior training; the practice characterized by difficulty and quick progress, as well as the practice characterized by ease and slow progress, are termed middling training; and the practice characterized by ease and quick progress is termed superior training.

Regarding "by way of skillful means": one who practices with neither earnest skillful means nor uninterrupted skillful means is said to be of inferior training; one who practices by means of either one of these is said to be of middling training; and one who practices possessing both skillful means is said to be of superior training.
The analysis of yoga refers to training correctly in the four types of yoga trainings:
first, faith; second, aspiration; third, right effort; and fourth, skillful means.
Faith consists of two aspects of practice and two bases. The two aspects of practice are:
first, the aspect of practice through patient acceptance; second, the aspect of purification. The two bases are:
first, the basis of contemplating the principles of the Dharma; second, the basis of resolving with faith in the majestic power of persons.
Regarding aspiration, there are four kinds of aspiration:

first, the aspiration for realization; second, the aspiration for inquiry and discussion; third, the aspiration for the provisions for realization; and fourth, the aspiration for the cultivation of skillful means.
Regarding the desire for realization: as when a practitioner gives rise to the desire to realize liberation regarding the higher [realms], as explained in detail previously.

Regarding the desire for inquiry: as when a practitioner, having already given rise to the desire for realization, goes into a monastery and approaches those who are knowledgeable, fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*), and those of right conduct and wisdom, in order to hear what has not yet been heard and to clarify and purify what has already been heard.

Regarding the desire for the provisions of realization: it is as when a practitioner gives rise to the aspiration for realization within the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), moderation in eating, the skillful means of wakefulness, dwelling in clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*), and in spiritual advancement.

Regarding "cultivating desire as a skillful means," this refers to generating a longing and a desire for realization within the context of uninterrupted application, earnest application, and the cultivation of the Noble Path.
Right effort refers to four kinds of right effort:
first, for the sake of hearing the Dharma; second, for the sake of reflection; third, for the sake of cultivation; and fourth, for the sake of purifying hindrances.

"Regarding 'for the sake of hearing the Dharma' means: for the sake of hearing what has not yet been heard, and for the sake of clarifying and purifying what has already been heard, one exerts the mind and skillfully practices those areas that have not yet been fully mastered."
"For the sake of reflection" means that, regarding the Dharma as it has been heard, one dwells alone in a quiet place to reflect upon, weigh, and examine its meaning.
"For the sake of cultivation" refers to repeatedly practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* while staying in a secluded chamber.

Regarding "for the sake of obstructing purity," this means that in order to purify the various hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), one exerts oneself day and night through walking meditation and sitting meditation, rousing the mind and skillfully practicing those areas in which one has not yet attained mastery.

Regarding skillful means, there are also four kinds: namely, by the superior power of guarding ethical discipline (*śīla*) and guarding the sense faculties, one brings about the purification of faculty-restraint (*indriya-saṃvara*) and abides well in mindfulness.
By virtue of being well-established in mindfulness, one attains non-negligence, guarding the mind and cultivating wholesome dharmas.
Through non-negligence, one causes the internal mind to correspond with *śamatha* (calm abiding) and attains superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) for the investigation of all phenomena.
These four types of yoga are divided into sixteen modes of practice.
Among these, by means of faith, one has conviction that the goal will be attained.
Because of this conviction that the goal will be attained, one gives rise to the desire for application toward all wholesome dharmas.
Because he cultivates the aspiration for practice, he exerts himself day and night, abiding in diligence, firmness, and heroic vigor.

Through right effort, he applies the means of cultivation in order to attain what has not yet been attained, to realize what has not yet been realized, and to manifest what has not yet been manifested.
Therefore, these four kinds of dharmas are called yoga.
Regarding "attention and discrimination," this refers to the seven kinds of attention, such as "attention that discerns characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*).

As for "attention that discerns characteristics," by means of this attention, one thoroughly understands the coarse characteristics of the desire realm and the tranquil characteristics of the first dhyāna.
How does one thoroughly comprehend the coarse characteristics of the desire realm?

It refers to the sixfold investigation of the faults of sensual desires: first, the object; second, the entity; third, the characteristic; fourth, the category; fifth, the time; and sixth, the principle.
Investigation of meaning refers to investigating that all sensual desires involve many faults and afflictions, many burdens and vexations, many epidemics, and many calamities and misfortunes.
Thus, these various desires possess many faults and afflictions, even up to many calamities and misfortunes; this is the coarse meaning.
As for the investigation of the object, it refers to either giving rise to desire for internal objects of desire, or giving rise to desire for external objects of desire.
Investigation of characteristics refers to investigating both specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Investigation of specific characteristics means discerning that "this is the desire for afflictions" and "this is the desire for objects."
Such sensual desires are either conducive to pleasure, conducive to suffering, or conducive to neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Those conducive to pleasure are the basis for the arising of craving and the basis for the inversion of perception and thought.
That which accords with suffering is the basis for ill-will (*vyāpāda*) and the basis for resentment (*krodha-upanāha*).

That which accords with neither-suffering-nor-pleasure is the basis for concealment (*mrakṣa*), vexation (*pradāsa*), deception (*māyā*), guile (*śāṭhya*), lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), and the inversion of views (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*).

Such sensual desires are either accompanied by violent and harsh feelings or accompanied by non-violent and non-harsh feelings; this is called the investigation into the specific characteristics of sensual desires.

Regarding common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*): this refers to the fact that when one investigates how all desires give rise to suffering, up to the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, [suffering] follows and binds them with complete equality.

One who enjoys desires, even if they possess desires in great abundance, should understand that these are phenomena characterized by the arising of suffering and so forth; these abundant desires will momentarily change and perish.
This is called investigating the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all sensual desires.

Regarding the investigation of their categories (*jāti*), it means investigating how all sensual desires belong to the dark category (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*): they are like a chain of dry bones, like a piece of putrid flesh, like a grass torch, like a fragment of glowing charcoal, like a venomous python, like what is seen in a dream, like borrowed ornaments, and like fruit gathered from the top of a tree.

Furthermore, he reflects that all sentient beings undergo the suffering caused by the pursuit of acquisitions, the suffering caused by separation from what is dear, the suffering caused by lack of contentment, the suffering caused by lack of mastery, and the suffering caused by unwholesome conduct.
Furthermore, the Bhagavān said: "I have taught that there are five faults in indulging in sensual desires: first, sensual desires offer little flavor;

second, those who indulge in desires experience much suffering and affliction, and many faults; third, those who indulge in desires are never satiated, never satisfied, never resting, and never ceasing; fourth, those who indulge in desires cause their fetters to increase; and fifth, those who indulge in desires commit no evil they will not do."

Furthermore, the wise and upright person, through immeasurable means, censures all sensual desires, saying: "These desires increase defilement and bring no satisfaction; they are common to all, unrighteous, and perverted; they are the cause of all evil conduct and increase craving for desire; therefore, the wise abandon them from afar, for they quickly disintegrate."

Relying upon the ground of heedlessness through various conditions, its nature is impermanent, empty, and void; it is a deceptive and ruinous phenomenon, like an illusion or a magical transformation that entices and deludes the foolish.

Whether it be desires of the present life or desires of future lives, whether they be the desires of the heavens or the desires of the human realm—all of these are the activities of Māra and the dwelling place of Māra.

Furthermore, based on that desire, it can cause the mind to give rise to immeasurable varieties of evil and unwholesome states—namely, the obstructive dharmas such as greed, hatred, and resentment—which act as obstacles when the noble disciples train in the precepts.
By means of such distinctions and faults, one predominantly investigates how all desires fall into the category of the dark side; this is called "investigating by way of category.

As for "investigating by way of time," it refers to constantly and continuously investigating, throughout the past, future, and present, that all desires involve much affliction, much calamity, and many disadvantages; this is called "investigating by way of time."

Regarding the investigation of principles: it means that these various desires are only fully accomplished, established, and increased by means of great resources, great seeking, great exhaustion, and furthermore, through various diverse spheres of activity.
Although external material resources may thus increase and reach fulfillment, by their very nature they quickly disperse and perish.
Furthermore, parents, wives, children, slaves, laborers, friends, officials, brothers, and kinsmen, though they gather for a time, will before long be scattered and destroyed.

Furthermore, the coarse physical body within is produced by the four great elements and nourished by rice and gruel; it constantly discards impurities and, though its resulting sufferings may be temporarily alleviated through bathing, massage, and the like, it is ultimately of a nature that is subject to dispersal and destruction.

One accepts various foods and drinks to remedy the suffering of hunger and thirst; one accepts and keeps clothing to remedy the afflictions of cold and heat, and to cover those parts of the body that should be concealed out of shame; one accepts various bedding and furniture to remedy the suffering of being oppressed by drowsiness and sleep, as well as to counteract the exhaustion of walking and standing; and one accepts various medicines and treatments to remedy the suffering of various diseases.
All such sensual desires serve only to treat suffering and should not be clung to with craving, except as medicine administered to treat a grave illness.

One may either investigate the coarse characteristics of these various desires according to the holy teachings; or else, give rise to them through one's own internal wisdom and vision; or further investigate them in accordance with logical principles; or further investigate that the intrinsic nature of desires has been established by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) since beginningless time, and that this inconceivable phenomenon should neither be conceptualized nor discriminated.
This is called investigating the principle.

Having thus understood the coarse characteristics (*audārikatva*) of the various desires through these six modes, one further understands the peaceful characteristic (*śāntalakṣaṇa*) of the first dhyāna. That is to say, within the first dhyāna there is no such extremely coarse and heavy characteristic as exists in the desire realm; because it is free from such coarse characteristics of desire, it is called the peaceful characteristic of the first dhyāna.

This is called the "mental application of discerning characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*), by which one discerns the coarse characteristics of the desire realm and the calm characteristics of the first dhyāna through mental attention belonging to the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*). It should be understood that at this stage, there is still an intermingling of hearing and reflection (*śrutacintā*).

Regarding attention through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*): it refers to the thorough investigation and penetration, as appropriate, of the coarse characteristics (*audārikatva*) of the desire realm and the calm characteristics (*śāntatva*) of the first dhyāna, without being interrupted by hearing or reflection, but purely giving rise to the resolute conviction of cultivation.

When one cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā by means of the signs of coarseness and tranquility, one repeatedly gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding those signs of coarseness and tranquility as they were previously investigated; therefore, this is called "attention consisting of resolute conviction" (*adhimokṣika-manasikāra*).

Regarding the mental application of detachment (*prāvivekya-manasikāra*): because one has extensively cultivated this type [of practice], in order to sever the afflictions of the initial stage, one gives rise to the path of antidotes; the mental application that arises simultaneously with the path of antidotes capable of severing those afflictions is called the mental application of detachment.

The mental application of "embracing joy" refers to having already abandoned the afflictions of the first portion of the desire realm and having already distanced oneself from the corresponding coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), thereby giving rise to joy and delight toward the subsequent superior stages of abandonment and distancing.

Furthermore, seeing the superior merit in abandonment, one realizes a limited degree of joy in detachment; from time to time, one rejoices within oneself through pure and sublime mental attention (*manasikāra*) in order to eliminate the fetters of lethargy, drowsiness, and restlessness. This is called the mental attention of "relishing" (*ratisaṃgrāhaka*).

Regarding the mental attention of observation (*pratyavekṣā-manasikāra*): it refers to when, having thus correctly cultivated delight in abandonment and delight in cultivation, one is supported by skillful means regarding virtuous qualities, such that the fetters of afflictions bound to the desire realm no longer manifest, whether one is walking or standing still.
The practitioner further reflects thus:
"Within this body of mine, is there desire or is there no desire?
Am I not grasping at or clinging to the objects of desire?"
For the sake of self-examination, he contemplates the marks of excellence, sublimity, and purity upon a single object.

However, because that practitioner has not yet completely abandoned the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), when contemplating such pure and sublime marks, he conforms to defilement, inclines toward defilement, and arrives at defilement; he does not abide in equanimity, nor does he feel revulsion, loathing, or restraint against it.
At that time, the practitioner knows for himself:
"I have not yet correctly distanced myself from sensual desires; my mind is not yet liberated. Therefore, the activities of sensual desire bind and constrain my mind."

"Just as water naturally subdues and gathers [impurities], I shall now certainly cultivate the path even more intensely so that the remaining latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) may be abandoned without remainder.
To further rejoice in superior abandonment and superior cultivation is called the mental attention of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*)."

The attention of the culmination of skillful means refers to the further cultivation of the factors of tranquility; because one delights in abandonment and delights in cultivation, one practices both tranquility and insight together, repeatedly observing.

In this way, the practitioner cultivates the remedies and periodically examines what has been abandoned and what remains unabandoned, causing the mind to distance itself from the fetters of the afflictions of the desire realm.
This is a temporary suppression and distancing, not the ultimate and permanent uprooting of the seeds.

At that time, the practitioner attains the path of preparation for the first dhyāna and brings to completion the mental attention that serves as the antidote to all afflictions; this is called the "mental attention of the culmination of preparation."

Regarding the mental attention to the fruit of the culmination of skillful means: it refers to the immediate entry into the fundamental first dhyāna concentration following that [mental attention], by virtue of the aforementioned causes and conditions.
This attention that arises simultaneously with the fundamental first dhyāna is called the "attention that is the fruit of the culmination of the means.

Just as there are seven types of attention in the first dhyāna, so too should one understand all the cases accordingly, from the second, third, and fourth dhyānas up to the meditative attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Furthermore, regarding the coarse characteristics (*audārika-lakṣaṇa*): it should be understood that within all lower stages, from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), there are briefly three types of phenomena belonging to those lower stages that ought to be reviled and abandoned. These are: first, the nature of dwelling in extreme suffering; second, the nature of dwelling in extreme lack of tranquility; and third, the nature of dwelling with extremely short lifespans.
Regarding the "inducing distinctions," there are four types of induction:
first, induction of the fruit; second, induction of detachment from desire; third, induction of the transformation of the faculties; and fourth, induction of superior qualities.
Regarding the analysis through questions and answers: this refers to the analysis through questions and answers by way of immeasurable doors, of which a small portion is now displayed.
Question:
In what way is the training in higher ethical discipline impure, and in what way is it pure?
Answer: There are ten causes by which ethical discipline is not pure. What are these ten?

First, receiving the śīla-vinaya restraint improperly at the outset; second, excessive sinking; third, excessive floating and distraction; fourth, being encompassed by negligence and indolence; fifth, giving rise to wrong aspirations; sixth, being encompassed by violations of proper conduct; seventh, being encompassed by violations of right livelihood; eighth, falling into the two extremes; ninth, being unable to achieve transcendence; and tenth, transgressing what has been received.

Regarding those who initially receive the śīla-vinaya in an improper manner: it is like a person who, perhaps to avoid the oppression of a king, or the oppression of powerful bandits, or the oppression of creditors, or due to the oppression of fear, or out of dread for the inability to survive, goes forth and receives the precepts—not for the sake of cultivating the Noble Path, not for the sake of pure brahmacarya, not for the sake of self-taming, not for the sake of self-peace, and not for the sake of one’s own nirvāṇa.
All such cases as these constitute the unrighteous reception of the śīla-vinaya. Regarding "extreme laxity":

it is like a person who lacks shame and dread of blame, whose sense of remorse is feeble and inferior, and whose nature is indolent; such a person practices the various training rules with indolence. This is called extreme laxity.

Regarding "extreme restlessness": suppose there is a person who perversely clings to what they have received and gives rise to regret where it is inappropriate; because they give rise to regret in a place where one should not regret, they harbor a mind of contempt and a mind of harm toward others in an improper manner, practicing this repeatedly without relinquishing it—this is called extreme restlessness.

Regarding those who are possessed by negligence and laziness: suppose there is a person who, having committed an offense in the past, failed to apply the appropriate remedy in accordance with the Dharma due to forgetfulness; and likewise, regarding offenses committed in the future or the present, fails to apply the appropriate remedy in accordance with the Dharma due to forgetfulness. Furthermore, they previously did not give rise to a vigorous aspiration to never violate the prohibitions of the precepts, thinking: "I shall act in such and such a way and abide in such and such a way; I shall act as I ought to act and abide as I ought to abide, so that no offense is committed."
Furthermore, regarding such conduct and such dwelling that ought not to be transgressed, there may be violations.
This person, throughout the past, present, and future, as well as during the time of their prior actions and while following [the path], is manifestly established in heedlessness.

Furthermore, they cling to sleep and reclining as their pleasure; being indolent and lazy, they take no delight in cultivation or exertion, and do not attend upon those who possess the knowledge of the holy life.
This is what is meant by being encompassed by heedlessness and laziness.

Regarding "one who initiates wrong aspirations": it is as if there is a person who initiates wrong aspirations while practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*), thinking, "May the celibate practice and ascetic observances I am now cultivating make me a lord of gods, or another deity," or else desiring gain and honor—meaning seeking various gains and honors from others—or simply wishing to realize gain and honor for oneself; this is called initiating wrong aspirations.

Regarding what is subsumed under the transgression of rules of conduct (*ācāra-vipatti*): for example, if there is a person who, in regard to the various modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*), or in regard to their activities, or in regard to the application of skillful means for cultivating the side of virtue as previously described, performs any action that contradicts worldly norms or violates the *vinaya*, this is called being subsumed under the transgression of rules of conduct.

Regarding the transgression subsumed under wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*): it is as when there is a person whose nature is characterized by great desire and lack of contentment, being difficult to support and difficult to satisfy; who seeks out all clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, medicinal requisites for illness, and other necessities through unrighteous means, rather than through righteous means.

For the sake of seeking clothing, food, drink, and other such things, and in order to manifest his own merits, this person falsely displays before others a demeanor that is contrary to his true nature and unaccustomed to him; furthermore, he manifests his sense faculties as tranquil and free from agitation, intending to lead others to believe he possesses virtue so that they will provide him with gifts and service—namely, clothing, food, drink, various seats and bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and other necessities, as well as physical service.

Furthermore, this person has a volatile and wicked appearance and speaks with coarse and harsh words without any sense of restraint. He adorns his body and proclaims his own name and lineage; or, being either learned or possessing extensive knowledge of the Dharma, for the sake of gain and honor, he preaches to others the teachings expounded by the Buddhas and their disciples, or he speaks of his own actual virtues, or slightly exaggerates them.
Or he causes others to proclaim his extraordinary marks in order to seek abundant and superior clothing, food and drink, and various other requisites for a śramaṇa.

Although he lacks nothing in terms of clothing, he nonetheless manifests the use of tattered and worn garments, intending that the laymen and householders who have faith in him will perceive his lack and thus bestow upon him many excellent and fine robes.
As it is with clothing, so it is with the other requisites for the livelihood of a śramaṇa.

Furthermore, when he does not obtain from faithful brāhmaṇas and householders the objects he desires—whether because they do not possess them or because they cannot give them away due to their own use—he then becomes pressing, reviling, and demanding.
Or, having received an inferior object, he treats it with contempt and returns it, speaking these words in the presence of the donor:

"Ho, noble son! There are other noble sons and daughters who, compared to you, are of low lineage and possess meager wealth; yet they are still able to give away such and such wonderful and pleasing objects. How much more so should you, who belong to a high and eminent lineage and are wealthy and prosperous, give such a base and loathsome object to me!"

All such cases as these—whether based on feigning dignified deportment, or based on improper speech, or based on proclaiming extraordinary marks, or based on pressing insults and rebukes, or based on drawing profit from profit—are instances of seeking clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, medicinal requisites for illness, and other necessities through unlawful means rather than through lawful means; this is called wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
This is called an offense subsumed under wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).

Regarding "falling into the two extremes": suppose there is a person who delights in and is attached to the enjoyment of the exquisite pleasures of the various desires; they obtain requisites such as clothing from others, whether by lawful or unlawful means, and they enjoy them without seeing their faults or knowing the way out—this is called one extreme.

Furthermore, suppose there is a person who practices self-mortification, afflicting his body with immeasurable varieties of painful matters, and undergoing various extreme ascetic observances: perhaps dwelling among thorns, or dwelling in ashes, or relying on a pestle, or a wooden board, or a skull; or remaining in a squatting posture, or practicing the squatting meditation (*utkuṭukāsana*); or serving fire up to three times a day, or staying in water up to three times a day; or standing on one leg while gazing at the sun as it revolves—all such practices and other forms of self-mortification constitute the second extreme.
This is what is called falling into the two extremes and being unable to achieve transcendence.

For example, there is a person who clings to the view of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and other ascetic observances (*vratas*), asserting that by practicing only ethical discipline and ascetic observances, one shall attain purity, liberation, and transcendence.
Furthermore, those who cling to views and firmly maintain the well-purified precepts of various non-Buddhist paths may think they will attain pure liberation and transcendence;
however, because these two types of purification are not ultimate, one cannot achieve true transcendence through them.
This is called being unable to transcend [suffering]. Regarding "transgressing what has been undertaken":

suppose there is a person who possesses no sense of shame whatsoever and never regards the decorum of a śramaṇa; he violates and destroys the prohibitions and precepts, practicing various unwholesome dharmas. Internally rotten and flowing downward, he is like a filthy snail, with the voice of a conch and the conduct of a dog. Though not a śramaṇa, he calls himself a śramaṇa; though lacking the brahma-faring life, he claims to be one who practices it. This is called transgressing what has been undertaken.
Due to these ten causes, the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*) is not pure;
if one reverses these, it is then pure.

Regarding the meaning of the purity and impurity of the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*), it is as explained in the "Chapter on Gathering Matters" (*Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*) within the section on pure meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that through this purification, the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*) is purified.
Such categories of questions and answers are immeasurable and boundless; they should be understood by applying the same principle.
The fivefold classification of bodhi consists of: first, lineage; second, skillful means; third, time; fourth, realization; and fifth, liberation. Regarding lineage:

śrāvaka-bodhi relies upon the lineage of dull faculties, pratyekabuddha-bodhi relies upon the lineage of middling faculties, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) relies upon the lineage of sharp faculties.

Regarding skillful means: the enlightenment of the śrāvakas is attained through skillful means in the practice of the six perfections; the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas is attained through skillful means in the predominant practice of profound dependent origination; and unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is attained through skillful means in the five fields of knowledge.

Regarding time: the enlightenment of a śrāvaka is attained by practicing for a minimum of three lifetimes; the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha is attained by practicing for one hundred great eons; and unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is attained by practicing for three great eons of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.

Regarding awakening: the awakening of a śrāvaka is realized through a teacher; the awakening of a pratyekabuddha is realized without a teacher by vowing solely for one's own benefit; and unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening is realized without a teacher for the benefit of both oneself and others.

Liberation refers to the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) realized through the enlightenment of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; it is comprised within the liberation from the afflictive obscurations (kleśāvaraṇa) and the liberation body (vimukti-kāya).

The transformation of the basis realized through unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) is comprised within both the liberation from all afflictive obscurations and cognitive obscurations (jñeyāvaraṇa), as well as the liberation body and the dharma body (dharma-kāya).
*Prakaraṇāryavācāśāstra*, Fascicle Seven;
*Prakaraṇāryavācāśāstra*, Fascicle Eight.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Two: Compendium on the Meaning of Purity, Part Four. Having thus analyzed hearing, taking refuge, and so forth, the verse says:
The noble conduct, the Supreme Vehicle, great enlightenment, and its qualities;
heterodox doctrines, the methods of debate, and their refutations—each of these should be known to have many varieties.
The treatise states:
"The various types of noble conduct" refers to the four noble conducts:
first, the conduct of the perfections; second, the conduct of the factors of enlightenment; third, the conduct of supernatural powers; and fourth, the conduct of maturing sentient beings.
The practice of reaching the other shore refers to the ten *pāramitās* as previously described; this is called the practice of reaching the other shore.

The practice of the factors of enlightenment refers to all thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, such as the four foundations of mindfulness as previously described, as well as the four types of thorough investigation and the four types of correct analytical knowledge; this is called the practice of the factors of enlightenment.
The practice of supernormal powers refers to the six kinds of supernormal powers as previously described; this is called the practice of supernormal powers.
The practice of maturing sentient beings refers to the two kinds of immeasurables as previously described:
first, the immeasurable of those to be disciplined, and second, the immeasurable of the means for disciplining them.

Furthermore, there are six kinds of maturation: first, the essence of maturation; second, the object of maturation; third, the distinctions of maturation; fourth, the means of maturation; fifth, the agent of maturation; and sixth, the characteristics of one who has already matured.
This is what should be understood as the practice for maturing sentient beings.
Regarding the various aspects of the Unsurpassed Vehicle, there are five types of Mahāyāna:
first, the seed; second, entry; third, the sequence; fourth, correct practice; and fifth, the fruit of correct practice.

It should be understood that, in their respective order, these are subsumed within the *Gotrabhūmi* (Chapter on Lineage), the *Cittotpādapaṭala* (Chapter on the Arising of the Resolve), the *Vihārapaṭala* (Chapter on the Dwellings), and the two chapters on the establishment of Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) found in the remaining sections of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.

Regarding the multiple aspects of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), they refer to five kinds of great enlightenment: first, essential nature (*svabhāva*); second, function (*karman*); third, skillful means (*upāya*); fourth, transformation (*parāvṛtti*); and fifth, cessation (*nirodha*).
Regarding "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*): it refers to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) that transcends all that is attained by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

This should be understood as having four aspects: first, the basis for arising; second, the basis for non-arising; third, the fruit of the thorough investigation of the knowable; and fourth, the pure characteristic of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Regarding the basis for arising: it refers to the supramundane path within the continuum of a Buddha; it is only by relying on this transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) that [the path] can arise, not otherwise.
If it were to arise even apart from this transformation of the basis, then it should have already arisen prior to the transformation of the basis.

Regarding "the non-arising of that which relies [upon it]": this refers to all afflictions and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), which, by relying on this transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), no longer arise.

If this were not the case, then prior to the transformation of the basis, when all conditions for the afflictions and their habitual tendencies were assembled, one should have already perceived them as never arising again.

Regarding "skillfully observing the fruit of the knowable": this refers to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), which is the skillful penetration of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) as the true fruit of the knowable.
Were it otherwise, the very essence of the Buddhas would still have further things to be known and further things to be abandoned.

Regarding the pure characteristic of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it means that this transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) is devoid of all marks and is manifested by the utterly pure dharma-realm.
Were it otherwise, it would necessarily be an impermanent and conceivable phenomenon.
However, this transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is of a permanent nature, inconceivable, and manifested as non-dual.

Furthermore, it should be understood that this inconceivable nature has five aspects: first, its intrinsic nature (svabhāva); second, its locus (sthāna); third, its abiding (sthiti); fourth, its identity and difference (ekatva-anyatva); and fifth, the accomplishment of its activity (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna).
Regarding self-nature: this nature of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is inconceivable whether it is identical to or distinct from form (rūpa).

Likewise, it is inconceivable whether it is identical to or distinct from sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna); inconceivable whether it is identical to or distinct from the earth element, water element, fire element, and wind element; inconceivable whether it is identical to or distinct from the sense bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and inconceivable whether it is existent or non-existent, and so forth.

Regarding its locus: this nature of the transformation of the basis is inconceivable whether it exists within the desire realm or apart from the desire realm; it is inconceivable whether it exists within the form or formless realms or apart from the form and formless realms; it is inconceivable whether it exists among humans or gods, or apart from them; and it is inconceivable whether it exists within the worlds of the ten directions or apart from them.

As for "abiding," it refers to abiding in such-and-such a manner in the blissful state of this transformation-basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), an inconceivable abiding; abiding in such-and-such a manner in the state of *śamatha*, an inconceivable abiding; abiding with mind, an inconceivable abiding; abiding without mind, an inconceivable abiding; abiding in such-and-such a manner in the noble state (*āryavihāra*), an inconceivable abiding; and abiding in such-and-such a manner in the celestial state (*devavihāra*) and the Brahma-state (*brahmavihāra*), which are inconceivable.

Regarding "identity and difference": all Buddhas abide together within a single untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*); their identity and difference are inconceivable. Regarding "the establishment of what is to be done":

this means that the nature of all Buddha-Tathāgatas is equal, and their wisdom, power, and majesty are equal. Abiding in the untainted realm and relying upon the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they establish such and such deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, which are inconceivable.

Furthermore, it should be understood that this is inconceivable for two reasons: first, because its meaning transcends verbal expression and lies beyond the path of language, it is inconceivable; second, because its meaning is supramundane and has no equal in the world, it is inconceivable.
Regarding "function" (*kāritra*): briefly stated, the ten kinds of mastery (*vaśitā*) are called function.

What are these ten? First, mastery over life; second, mastery over mind; third, mastery over requisites; fourth, mastery over karma; fifth, mastery over birth; sixth, mastery over vows; seventh, mastery over resolute conviction; eighth, mastery over miraculous transformations; ninth, mastery over knowledge; and tenth, mastery over phenomena.
Regarding skillful means (*upāya*), briefly stated, there are four kinds of transformations that are called skillful means:
first, in order to bring those who are not yet matured to maturity, one manifests the transformations of the various practices performed by bodhisattvas;
second, in order to liberate those who are already matured, one simultaneously manifests the transformations of the Tathāgata across a hundred *koṭis* of Jambudvīpas within a trichiliocosm.
Third, the manifestation of the transformations of śrāvakas through skillful means;
fourth, the manifestation of all the transformations of pratyekabuddhas for the sake of those sentient beings to be disciplined by them.
It should be understood that within these four kinds of transformative dharmas, the Buddha Bhagavān exercises unimpeded activity throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Regarding "transformation," two types should be understood: first, temporary transformation; second, ultimate transformation.
Temporary transformation refers to the fact that as long as sentient beings have not yet reached maturity or liberation, the transformations of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas continue without ceasing.

Regarding ultimate transformation: it is like the inexhaustible and inconceivable manifestation of the majestic power and brilliance of all Buddhas, which performs beneficial deeds for all sentient beings and flows on without ceasing.
Regarding cessation, two kinds should be known: first, temporary cessation; second, ultimate cessation.

As for temporary cessation, when sentient beings have already reached maturity and are already liberated, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, temporarily manifest entry into parinirvāṇa; this is not ultimate.
Ultimate cessation refers to the final and eternal exhaustion of all afflictions, their latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), and the suffering upon which they depend; this should be understood.
Regarding the various types of merit, the summary verse (*uddāna*) states:
Extraordinary and non-extraordinary, Equanimity and benefit.
Requital of Gratitude, Rejoicing and Praising, and Unfailing Skillful Means.
The Commentary says:

Regarding "extraordinary," it should be understood that when Bodhisattvas train in the vehicle of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there are five kinds of extraordinary qualities to be known.

What are these five? First, to give rise to affection for all sentient beings without any causal basis; second, to constantly remain within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) and endure great suffering solely for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings; third, to be skillfully able to understand and apply the means of subduing those sentient beings who are difficult to tame due to their many afflictions; fourth, to be able to progressively awaken to and enter into the most difficult-to-understand principles of ultimate reality; and fifth, to be endowed with inconceivable majestic power (*prabhāva*).
These five dharmas are not shared by other sentient beings; therefore, they are called "extraordinary.
Regarding those that are not extraordinary: when bodhisattvas train in the vehicle of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there are five kinds of non-extraordinary dharmas.
Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish these five kinds of dharmas, five kinds of extraordinary dharmas are accomplished and manifested. What are these five?

This means that because Bodhisattvas regard the suffering caused by benefiting others as their own joy, they constantly and universally undergo and practice the suffering that is the cause for benefiting others; this is called the first non-extraordinary quality.

Furthermore, although bodhisattvas clearly understand the faults of saṃsāra and the merits of nirvāṇa, they take delight in bringing sentient beings to ultimate purity as their own delight. Therefore, through the predominant power of purifying sentient beings, bodhisattvas constantly vow to undergo and practice the dharmas of saṃsāra; this is called the second non-distinctive dharma.

Furthermore, although bodhisattvas thoroughly understand the flavor of the joy of silence, they take the ultimate purification of sentient beings to be their own joy. Therefore, through the predominant power of purifying sentient beings, bodhisattvas constantly and diligently employ skillful means to preach the Dharma; this is called the third non-distinctive quality.

Furthermore, although bodhisattvas have already accumulated the roots of virtue of the six pāramitās, they take delight in bringing sentient beings to ultimate purity as their own delight. Therefore, for the sake of purifying sentient beings through the dominant influence [of that aspiration], they give with a pure intention and do not expect the maturation of the fruit of that giving; this is called the fourth non-distinctive dharma.

Furthermore, because Bodhisattvas regard the welfare of others as their own personal welfare, they constantly manifest and practice all deeds that benefit sentient beings; this is called the fifth non-distinctive quality.
It should be understood that because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish these five kinds of dharmas, five kinds of extraordinary dharmas are accomplished and manifested.
Regarding the "even-mindedness," it refers to the five kinds of even-mindedness that Bodhisattvas maintain toward all sentient beings.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva first generates the mind of enlightenment, just as they give rise to the great vow for the sake of attaining great bodhi, so too do they give rise to a mind of equanimity for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
Second, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to a mind of compassion toward all sentient beings that is accompanied by equanimity.
Third, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to a mind of love for all sentient beings like that for an only son, which is accompanied by equanimity.

The four bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arisen from various causes and conditions, having understood that these are the imagined entities of sentient beings, realize that the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) of one sentient being is the very same as the dharma-nature of all sentient beings; they thus give rise toward all sentient beings to a mind of equanimity conjoined with the wisdom of the equal dharma-nature.

Just as the five bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice acts of benefit toward a single sentient being, so too do they practice acts of benefit toward all sentient beings; therefore, they possess a mind of equanimity regarding all sentient beings, desiring to perform acts of benefit for them all.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s arising of five kinds of impartial mind toward all sentient beings.

Regarding "benefiting," it should be understood that there are five kinds of corresponding practices through which a bodhisattva mahāsattva performs all manner of beneficial deeds for sentient beings.
What are the five? First, regarding matters that are adverse or harmful, one attracts and gathers others by teaching the Dharma of right livelihood;
second, regarding matters that are not conducive but are beneficial, one attracts and gathers others by teaching the Dharma of what is conducive.
Third, they gather in those sentient beings who are destitute, unprotected, and afflicted by suffering by acting as their refuge;
fourth, they gather them in by proclaiming the path leading to the happy realms;
and fifth, they gather them in by proclaiming the paths of the three vehicles leading to nirvāṇa.

Regarding "repaying kindness," it refers to the five kinds of reciprocal beneficial actions that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva initiates toward sentient beings who have shown them kindness. What are these five?
First, to establish sentient beings in a state of well-being so that they may cultivate their own virtues;
second, to skillfully establish them so that they may cultivate the virtues of others;
third, to act as a refuge for those who are without support, without protection, and afflicted by suffering and poverty.
Fourth, to exhort others to make offerings to all Buddhas and Tathāgatas;
fifth, to cause them to personally transcribe the Dharma taught by the Buddha, as well as to receive, uphold, and make offerings to it.
There are five points regarding joyful praise that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should always joyfully praise.
What are these five? First, encountering the appearance of a Buddha in the world and being able to serve him;
second, constantly hearing from the Tathāgata the Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka associated with the six pāramitās.
Third, the capacity for the cultivation of practices that ripen all sentient beings;
fourth, the swift realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
and fifth, the harmonious assembly of the bodhisattva and śrāvaka congregations once enlightenment has been realized.
Regarding the practice of non-empty skillful means, it refers to the five kinds of superior practices of non-empty benefit for sentient beings by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
What are these five?
First, a bodhisattva mahāsattva prioritizes the intention to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
Second, a bodhisattva mahāsattva achieves non-erroneous awakening, understanding matters of benefit and happiness as they truly are.

Third, by teaching various dharmas through appropriate skillful means, he brings all sentient beings to full subdual according to their respective capacities; this alone is the ultimate capability of the Tathāgata.
Fourth, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are never weary in mind at any time.
Fifth, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas possess impartial great compassion, maintaining no partiality toward sentient beings whether they be inferior, middling, or superior.
Furthermore, the summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
Non-perverted skillful means, decline and superior progress,
similar and actual qualities, and the excellent taming of sentient beings.
The treatise states:
Regarding non-perverted skillful means, it should be understood that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess five kinds of skillful means which encompass all correct skillful means.
What are these five? First, the means of preservation;
second, the means of faultlessness; third, the means of the power of discernment; fourth, the means of purifying the superior intention; and fifth, the means of entering into certainty.

Regarding the skillful means of guarding: it refers to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s skillful protection of his own intelligence, whereby he swiftly assimilates the Dharma through innate wisdom (*sahaja-jñāna*).
Furthermore, he skillfully guards his mindfulness (*smṛti*); by virtue of this mindfulness, he maintains the assimilated Dharma without forgetting or losing it.

Furthermore, one skillfully guards wisdom; by means of wisdom, one thoroughly examines the meaning of the teachings one has received and penetrates them with right discernment. This is because one distances oneself from the causes for the decline of wisdom—namely, the lack of sagacity, mindfulness, and recollection—and because one draws near to and cultivates the causes for the maintenance and excellence of wisdom.
Furthermore, one well guards one’s own mind by virtue of properly protecting the doors of the sense faculties;
and one well guards the minds of others by virtue of protecting their minds through correct means.

Regarding the skillful means without fault: it refers to the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s unerring vigor toward all wholesome dharmas, dedicating them toward awakening immeasurably and without interruption.
The skillful means of the power of discernment should be understood as pertaining to all those abiding in the stage of conduct through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*).

The skillful means of the pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya*) should be understood as pertaining to those abiding in the stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśayabhūmi*) and the stage of correct practice (*caryāpratipattibhūmi*).
Regarding "entering the skillful means of certainty," it should be understood as abiding in the stage of certainty, the stage of certain practice, and reaching the ultimate stage.
It should be understood that these five kinds of skillful means collectively encompass all the correct skillful means of a bodhisattva.

Regarding "falling back," it should be understood that there are five factors conducive to regression for bodhisattvas: first, lack of respect for the true Dharma and those who teach it; second, negligence and indolence; third, associating with afflictions; fourth, associating with evil conduct; and fifth, giving rise to overweening pride by comparing oneself to other bodhisattvas to determine superiority or inferiority, as well as giving rise to overweening pride through misconceptions regarding the Dharma.

Regarding "excellence," it refers to the five superior factors of the bodhisattvas; these should be understood as being the opposites of the aforementioned five types of dark qualities (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), respectively.
Regarding "semblance virtues," it refers to the five kinds of semblance virtues of the bodhisattvas, which should be understood as being, in reality, faults.
First, they cause harm to sentient beings who are violent and transgress the precepts for that reason;
second, they falsely manifest themselves as being endowed with perfect dignified conduct;
third, regarding those dharmas corresponding to worldly artifice, refined rhetoric, and the treatises of non-Buddhists, they gain inclusion among the ranks of the wise and the intelligent.
Fourth, practicing virtuous deeds such as giving that are free from fault;
fifth, proclaiming and establishing the semblance of the true Dharma so that it may spread widely.
Regarding "actual merits," one should know that these refer to the five kinds of actual merits of all bodhisattvas.
First, through these causes and conditions, one gives rise to a superior compassion toward sentient beings who are violent and transgress the precepts;
second, one is naturally endowed with dignified deportment;
third, regarding the pure and true teachings and realizations spoken by the Tathāgata, one attains the status of being counted among the wise and the sagacious.
Fourth, practicing virtuous deeds such as blameless giving; fifth, teaching the true Dharma to prevent those that are similar [to it].

Regarding "skillfully taming sentient beings," this refers to how Bodhisattvas briefly and unerringly tame those to be converted in ten areas: first, in the area of abandoning misconduct; second, in the area of abandoning sensual desire; third, in the area of being free from transgressions or, having committed one, emerging from it; fourth, in the area of guarding all the doors of the sense faculties; fifth, in the area of abiding in correct awareness (*saṃprajanya*); sixth, in the area of avoiding clamor and bustle; seventh, in the area of distancing oneself from all evil discursive thoughts; eighth, in the area of being free from hindrances; ninth, in the area of being free from the entanglements of afflictions (*kleśa-paryavasthāna*); and tenth, in the area of being free from the heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) associated with the category of afflictions.
Furthermore, the summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
The prediction of the bodhisattvas, Their inclusion within the number of those destined for certainty,
What must definitely be done and what must always be done— These supreme dharmas should be known.
The Commentary states:
Regarding the prophecy of the bodhisattvas, it means that bodhisattvas receive the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment from all Tathāgatas at six stages.
First, those at the stage of the spiritual lineage who have not yet generated the bodhicitta;
second, those who have already generated the bodhicitta;
third, those currently abiding in the presence [of the goal].
Fourth, abiding without manifest presence;
fifth, having a temporal limit, meaning that one shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment within such a period of time;
sixth, having no temporal limit, meaning that no definite time limit is specified.

Regarding "falling into the state of certainty," this refers to the three kinds of falling into the state of certainty for bodhisattvas: first, falling into certainty by way of lineage; second, falling into certainty by way of generating the resolve; and third, falling into certainty by way of non-empty practice.

Regarding those of the lineage who have entered the state of certainty: this refers to bodhisattvas who, while abiding in the stage of the lineage, enter the number of those bodhisattvas destined for certainty.
Why is this? Because bodhisattvas who have accomplished the lineage are, upon encountering superior conditions, necessarily capable of realizing *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Regarding those whose resolve has entered the state of certainty: this refers to those bodhisattvas who have generated a resolute mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, such that until they realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, they never again regress.

Regarding "falling into certainty through non-empty practice," this refers to those bodhisattvas who have already attained mastery; thus, whatever bodhisattva practices they perform according to their wishes are never in vain.
Because they rely on this final stage of the state of certainty (*niyāma*), the Tathāgata bestows upon the bodhisattvas the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of their entry into certainty.

Regarding "that which must be done with certainty," it refers to the five matters that bodhisattvas must certainly perform; if they do not perform them, they will certainly be incapable of realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

What are these five? First, generating the bodhicitta; second, giving rise to compassion for all sentient beings; third, courageous and diligent effort; fourth, skillfully practicing in the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*); and fifth, having no weariness in mind.

Regarding "that which should be constantly practiced," this refers to the five areas in which bodhisattvas should constantly cultivate practice: first, they should constantly practice the conduct of heedfulness; second, they should act as a refuge for sentient beings who are without support or protection and are afflicted by suffering; third, they should constantly practice the conduct of making offerings to the Buddhas; fourth, they should constantly and fully understand errors and non-errors; and fifth, they should constantly practice within all mental engagements regarding every action, whether moving or staying, with the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*) as their guiding principle.
As for the most excellent dharmas, it means that all bodhisattvas, regarding these ten kinds of most excellent dharmas of concordant intention, should uphold them and establish them as supreme.

What are the ten? First, the bodhisattva lineage is the most excellent among all lineages; second, the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) is the most excellent among all right aspirations; third, right diligence in wisdom (*prajñā*) is the most excellent among all perfections (*pāramitā*); fourth, pleasant speech is the most excellent among all methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); fifth, the Tathāgata is the most excellent among all sentient beings; sixth, compassion is the most excellent among all immeasurables (*apramāṇa*); seventh, the fourth dhyāna is the most excellent among all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*); eighth, the emptiness samādhi is the most excellent among the three samādhis; ninth, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is the most excellent among the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*); and tenth, pure skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) is the most excellent among all skillful means.
Furthermore, the summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
The establishment of all designations, the investigation of all phenomena,
as well as thorough knowledge as it truly is, and also the various immeasurables.
The proclamation of the benefits of the fruit, the nature and inclusion of the Mahāyāna,
and the ten things a bodhisattva should know— the establishment of these various names.
The treatise says:
Regarding the establishment of designations: this refers to the four kinds of establishment of designations by Bodhisattvas.

Only Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas are able to correctly establish these designations; no others—whether devas or humans, śramaṇas or brahmins—are capable of establishing them, except for those who plagiarize the Buddha’s teachings and incorporate them into their own treatises.

What are the four? First, the establishment of the designation of phenomena; second, the establishment of the designation of truths; third, the establishment of the designation of principles; and fourth, the establishment of the designation of vehicles.

The establishment of the designation of the Dharma refers to the sequential compilation, sequential arrangement, and sequential production of the twelvefold division of the teachings, such as the sūtras; this is called the establishment of the designation of the Dharma.

Regarding the establishment of the designation of the truths (*satyavyavasthāna*): it refers either to the establishment of one truth, on the basis of the sense of being non-deceptive, wherein there is only this one and no second;
or to the establishment of two truths: first, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), and second, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Alternatively, three truths are established: first, the truth of characteristics; second, the truth of expression; and third, the truth of function.
Alternatively, four truths are established: first, the truth of suffering; second, the truth of origination; third, the truth of cessation; and fourth, the truth of the path.
Alternatively, five truths may be established: first, the truth of cause; second, the truth of effect; third, the truth of the knower; fourth, the truth of the known;

and fifth, the truth of non-duality. Alternatively, six truths may be established: first, the truth of reality; second, the truth of delusion; third, the truth of that which should be known; fourth, the truth of that which should be abandoned; fifth, the truth of that which should be realized; and sixth, the truth of that which should be cultivated.

Alternatively, seven truths may be established: first, the truth of gratification; second, the truth of disadvantage; third, the truth of renunciation; fourth, the truth of the nature of phenomena; fifth, the truth of resolute conviction; sixth, the noble truth; and seventh, the non-noble truth.

Alternatively, eight truths may be established: first, the truth of the suffering of conditioned existence; second, the truth of the suffering of change; third, the truth of the suffering of suffering; fourth, the truth of transmigration; fifth, the truth of the cessation of transmigration; sixth, the truth of defilement; seventh, the truth of purification; and eighth, the truth of correct means.

Alternatively, nine truths may be established: first, the truth of impermanence; second, the truth of suffering; third, the truth of emptiness; fourth, the truth of non-self; fifth, the truth of craving for existence; sixth, the truth of craving for non-existence; seventh, the truth of the means for their abandonment; eighth, the truth of nirvana with remainder; and ninth, the truth of nirvana without remainder.

Alternatively, ten truths may be established: first, the truth of oppressive suffering; second, the truth of suffering from the lack of necessary requisites; third, the truth of suffering from the discordance of the elements; fourth, the truth of suffering from the destruction of what is loved; fifth, the truth of suffering from coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*); sixth, the truth of karma; seventh, the truth of afflictions; eighth, the truth of hearing the true Dharma and proper mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*); ninth, the truth of right view; and tenth, the truth of the fruit of right view.
This is called the establishment of the designation of truths (*satya-prajñapti-vyavasthāna*); it should be understood that if analyzed in detail, it is immeasurable.

Regarding the establishment of the designation of principles (*yukti-prajñapti-vyavasthāna*), there are four kinds of principles: first, the principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*); second, the principle of efficacy (*kāritra-yukti*); third, the principle of logical proof (*upapatti-sādhana-yukti*); and fourth, the principle of natural law (*dharmatā-yukti*). These are to be known as the establishment of the designation of principles.

Regarding the establishment through the designation of vehicles: it should be understood that for the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Unsurpassed Mahāyāna vehicles respectively, there are seven types of designations and establishments.

Regarding the sevenfold establishment of designations for the Śrāvakayāna: first, the non-erroneous wisdom regarding the four noble truths; second, the basis of this wisdom; third, the object of focus of this wisdom; fourth, the companions of this wisdom; fifth, the activity performed by this wisdom; sixth, the provisions that assist this wisdom; and seventh, the fruit realized by this wisdom.
Just as there are seven kinds of designations and establishments for the Śrāvaka-yāna, so it is for the Pratyekabuddha-yāna.

Regarding the seven kinds of designations and establishments for the unsurpassed Mahāyāna: first, the wisdom of equanimous transcendence that is non-conceptual regarding the ineffable suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena; second, the basis of this wisdom; third, the object of this wisdom; fourth, the companions of this wisdom; fifth, the activity performed by this wisdom; sixth, the provisions that assist this wisdom; and seventh, the fruit realized by this wisdom.
These are known as the sevenfold designations and establishments of the three vehicles;

one should understand them thus. In this way, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time rely upon these four correct designations and correct establishments, which neither increase nor decrease.

Regarding the investigation of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-paryeṣaṇā*): it means that bodhisattvas, desiring to realize the thorough knowledge of reality as it is regarding all phenomena, give rise to the four investigations as previously explained.

Regarding "thorough knowledge of reality as it is," this refers to the four kinds of thorough knowledge of reality as it is that bodhisattvas generate with respect to all phenomena, as previously explained.
Regarding "the immeasurables," this refers to the five immeasurables upon which bodhisattvas rely to be able to initiate all skillful activities.

What are these five? First, the immeasurability of the realm of sentient beings; second, the immeasurability of the realm of worlds; third, the immeasurability of the realm of phenomena; fourth, the immeasurability of the realm of those to be disciplined; and fifth, the immeasurability of the realm of skillful means for disciplining them.
The immeasurable realm of sentient beings refers to sixty-four types of sentient beings:
first, hell-beings; second, animals; third, those in the realm of hungry ghosts; fourth, gods; fifth, humans; sixth, kṣatriyas;
seventh, brāhmaṇas; eighth, vaiśyas; ninth, śūdras; tenth, women; and eleventh, men. [Note: The list continues through sixty-four categories.]
12. neither male nor female; 13. inferior grade; 14. middling grade;
15. superior grade; 16. layperson; 17. renunciant; 18. ascetic practice; 19. restraint; 20.
non-restraint; 21. neither restraint nor non-restraint.
22. Those who have already abandoned desire; 23. Those who have not yet abandoned desire;
24. The group of those fixed in error; 25. The group of those fixed in correctness; 26.
The group of those who are undetermined; 27. Bhikṣus; 28. Bhikṣuṇīs; 29. Śikṣamāṇās; 30. Śrāmaṇeras.
1. The male novice (śrāmaṇera), 2. the female novice (śrāmaṇerī), 3. the male lay follower (upāsaka), 4.
the female lay follower (upāsikā), 5. one who practices meditative concentration (samādhi), 6.
one who recites the scriptures, 7. one who attends to the sick, 8. the senior elder (sthavira), 9. the middle-ranking elder.
1. Thirty-nine years of age; 2. Forty years of age; 3. Ācārya; 4. Upādhyāya; 5.
Co-resident (sahavāsin); 6. Neighboring resident (upavāsin); 7. Guest; 8.
Overseer of monastic affairs; 9. One who delights in gain and offerings; 10. Forty-seven.
48. Those who delight in reverence; 49. Those who delight in seclusion;
50. Those who are learned; 51. Those who possess wisdom; 52. Those who possess great merit; 53.
Those who practice in accordance with the Dharma; 54. Those who uphold the Sūtras; 55. Those who uphold the Vinaya.
Fifty-five: those who uphold the mātṛkā; fifty-six: ordinary beings (pṛthagjana); fifty-seven:
those who have seen the truth (dṛṣṭasatya); fifty-eight: those in training (śaikṣa); fifty-nine:
those beyond training (aśaikṣa); sixty: śrāvakas; sixty-one: pratyekabuddhas; sixty-two: bodhisattvas; sixty-three: the turning [of the wheel].
Regarding the wheel-turning sage-kings and the sixty-four Tathāgatas, if one considers the distinctions within the continuity of their physical bodies,
they are immeasurable and boundless. As for the "immeasurability of worlds," this refers to the immeasurable variety of names for the infinite worlds throughout the ten directions.
In this way, there is a world named Sahā, and the Brahmā king of this realm is named Sahāpati; one should know that there are such immeasurable distinctions.

Regarding the immeasurability of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it refers to wholesome dharmas, unwholesome dharmas, and indeterminate dharmas; one should know that there are immeasurable such doors of distinction.

Regarding the immeasurable realms of those to be disciplined (*vineya-dhātu*), one may establish a single type of realm of those to be disciplined; that is to say, because among all sentient beings, those who are capable of being disciplined constitute a single category.
Alternatively, two types are established: first, those bound by all fetters; second, those not bound by all fetters.
Alternatively, three types are established: first, those of dull faculties; second, those of middling faculties; third, those of sharp faculties.
Some establish four types: first, the kṣatriya; second, the brāhmaṇa; third, the vaiśya; and fourth, the śūdra. Others establish five types:
first, those of greedy temperament; second, those of hateful temperament; third, those of deluded temperament; fourth, those of proud temperament; and fifth, those of discursive temperament.
Alternatively, six types are established: first, the householder; second, the renunciant; third, the matured; fourth, the immature; fifth, the liberated; and sixth, the unliberated.
Alternatively, seven types are established: first, faith and respect;
second, contempt and disparagement;
third, neutrality.
Fourth, the detailed exposition;
fifth, the concise opening of wisdom;
sixth, that which is constantly disciplined.
The seventh [type] is that which is led by conditions; that is, it transforms in such and such a way whenever it encounters such and such conditions.
Alternatively, eight types may be established, namely the eight assemblies, from the assembly of kṣatriyas up to the assembly of brahmās.

Alternatively, nine types are established: first, those transformed by a Tathāgata; second, those transformed by a śrāvaka; third, those transformed by a pratyekabuddha; fourth, those transformed by a bodhisattva; fifth, those difficult to subdue; sixth, those easy to subdue; seventh, those subdued through gentle speech; eighth, those subdued through censure and expulsion; ninth, those subdued either from afar or nearby.
