Chapter Five: Establishing Suffering. Having thus established the characteristic of impermanence, [the following is established].
How is the characteristic of suffering established?
The verse says:
Birth is the cause for the desire to be free; the cessation of birth is the object of the desire for union.
Inversion, non-inversion, and revulsion—these causes constitute the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*).
The commentary states:
When a phenomenon arises, it serves as the cause for the distancing from desire; when a phenomenon ceases, it serves as the cause for the convergence of desire.

If one does not understand this cause of inversion, or if one does not skillfully penetrate this cause of non-inversion, one will give rise to a sense of weary detachment and desire for renunciation at all times.
Thus should the general characteristic of suffering be understood.
Furthermore, the verse says:
Based on the distinctions of the three types of feeling, The three characteristics of suffering are established;
Therefore, it is said that all feelings, In their essential nature, are suffering.
The treatise says:

Based on the distinctions among the characteristics of the three types of sensation, the three characteristics of suffering are established—namely, the characteristic of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the characteristic of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the characteristic of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
For this reason, the Buddha taught that all feelings are called suffering.
One should know that the first characteristic of suffering is established with respect to painful feelings and those phenomena conducive to painful feelings.
Regarding pleasant feelings and those phenomena conducive to pleasant feelings, one should know that the second characteristic of suffering is established therein.
Regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings and those phenomena conducive to such feelings, one should know that the third characteristic of suffering is established therein.
Because one does not understand this third characteristic, it serves as the cause for the arising of perversions such as permanence;
if one can understand it, it serves as the cause for the arising of non-perversions such as impermanence, and it can also give rise to the aspiration for nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, by understanding or failing to understand the third type of suffering, one should likewise know whether or not one understands the first two types of suffering.
Moreover, the characteristics of the first two types of suffering are established through worldly consensus, whereas the characteristics of the third type of suffering are not so established.
Now, it shall be established that the intrinsic nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
The verse says:
One should know that the nature of formations is suffering, Because they are all accompanied by coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
It is illogical for [the nature of] conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to be pleasure or equanimity; otherwise, there would be the fault of there being no liberation at all.
The treatise says:
It is not logical that the nature of conditioned phenomena is pleasure or that their nature is equanimity.
Why is this? Because in all states they are accompanied by coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), the intrinsic nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is suffering.

If it were not so, then according to their respective order, there would be no desire for pleasure or for that which is neither painful nor pleasant; there would be no perception of pain or of that which is neither painful nor pleasant; and there would be no perception of pleasure or pain.
Question:
You are in the same position; if there were only the nature of suffering in formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), there should be no sensations of pleasure or neither-suffering-nor-pleasure. Answer:
Because of non-comprehension, one says it exists.
Question:
It is the same for the self; because of non-comprehension, one says it exists.
Answer: Not so, for there would otherwise be the fault of there being no liberation.

If one thoroughly understands that even those formations which are pleasant by nature and those which are neither painful nor pleasant are suffering, this is called the clear realization of the Truth of Suffering; from this point on, one proceeds in succession until the attainment of ultimate liberation.
If one does not understand [this] and instead regards it as suffering, this is a perversion (viparyāsa), and one will be unable to realize ultimate quiescence (atyanta-śānti).
Furthermore, the verse says:
Obstacles such as gain and deep [attachment], Relying on diligence, abiding in the vehicle, and dwelling in emptiness.
Attachment is inferior, inverted, and defiled.
The commentary says:
Furthermore, the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is suffering; when even slight suffering is added to this, the characteristic of suffering becomes acute and intense.
Pleasure and the others are not like this.
Furthermore, the characteristic of suffering is profound and heavy, making it difficult to counteract;
pleasure and the others are not like this.
Furthermore, the characteristic of suffering is uniform and pervasive across all places; even those who have realized the vast Dharma are afflicted by it.
Moreover, clinging to permanence, bliss, self, and purity is termed "inversion," as it can obstruct the noble Dharma.
Furthermore, pleasure and so forth serve as the basis for the various afflictions, both great and small, such as craving;
moreover, the modes of suffering and so forth can induce superior progress toward the merits of higher stages.
Furthermore, remaining for a long time in such postures as sitting and so forth gives rise to great suffering that is unbearable.
Moreover, for one who clings to emptiness, great suffering likewise follows.
Furthermore, one who is attached to pleasure is of inferior nature.
Furthermore, to grasp at and conceive of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as pleasant is to be subsumed under perversion (*viparyāsa*).
Moreover, the desire for pleasure that arises based on worldly happiness is for the most part defiled (*kliṣṭa*).
Therefore, the intrinsic nature of all conditioned phenomena is suffering (*duḥkha*).
Furthermore, the verse says:
Just as with abscesses, scabies, leprosy, and the like, which serve as the bases for the three types of sensation,
so too do they give rise to the three kinds of contact, which subsequently follow upon the grasping of pleasure and the rest.
The treatise says:

One should know that the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is suffering, just like an abscess, scabies, or leprosy, as they serve as the basis for the three types of sensation. Why is this?

Because worldly ailments such as sores, scabs, and leprosy can give rise to the three kinds of contact—conducive to suffering, pleasure, and equanimity—sentient beings in the world, based upon these contacts, grasp them as suffering, pleasure, or neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
In this way, three types of contact arise with respect to all conditioned phenomena that are suffering by nature; from these contacts, feelings such as pleasure arise.
If these were absent, no feelings would arise.
Having thus demonstrated the characteristics of suffering by establishing the thesis, the reason, and the example,
for what further cause and condition are all conditioned phenomena established as having only three types of suffering— neither more nor less?
The verse says:
Their own characteristics, their own conceptualizations, and the nature of suffering as lack of peace—
these fifty-five should be known as being subsumed within the three types of suffering.
The treatise states:
Because the intrinsic nature of suffering consists of only three types:
first, by way of its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), namely the nature of suffering as suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

Second, it is due to one's own conceptualization; that is, the nature of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*). For if there were no conceptualization, although change and decay do occur, suffering would not arise for one who is already liberated.

Third, by way of being non-peaceful (*anairyāṇika*), namely the nature of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), because it is pursued by the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth.
These three distinctions of suffering should further be understood as consisting of fifty-five types.
What are the fifty-five kinds?
The verse says:
Realm, object-condition, body and so forth, destiny, species, truth, and the three periods of time.
Because there are differences in time, life-span, and category, they bring about the distinctions among the various sufferings.
The treatise says:

Because of the distinctions among the realms (*dhātu*), there are three types of suffering, namely: those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), those bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and those bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).

Due to the differentiation of conditions, there are six kinds of suffering: namely, the fundamental suffering of desire, the retributive suffering of ignorance, the suffering conditioned by past karma, the suffering conditioned by present causes, the suffering conditioned by pure karma, and the suffering conditioned by impure karma.

Due to the distinctions among the body and so forth, there are four kinds of suffering: namely, the suffering of bearing heavy burdens and the like, the suffering of the transformation of states, the suffering of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), and the suffering of birth and death.
There are five kinds of suffering due to the distinction of realms (*gati*), namely: the suffering of the hells up to the suffering of the heavenly realms.

There are five kinds of suffering due to the distinction of types, namely: the suffering of affliction, the suffering of deprivation, the suffering of great adversity, the suffering of the transformation of the beloved, and the suffering of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).

Due to the distinctions among the truths, there are eight kinds of suffering: namely, the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of association with the disliked, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.
Due to the distinctions among worldly conditions, there are nine kinds of suffering: namely, past suffering, which is produced by past, future, and present conditions;
likewise, future and present suffering are also thus.

Due to the distinction of time, there are four kinds of suffering: namely, the suffering of seasonal change, the suffering of hunger, the suffering of thirst, and the suffering induced by postures such as bending and stretching, inhalation and exhalation, and the closing and opening of the eyes.

Due to the distinctions in the sustenance of life, there are four kinds of suffering: namely, the suffering of insatiability regarding what is sought, the suffering of pursuit, the suffering of guarding, and the suffering of lack of autonomy.
Due to the distinction of categories, there are seven kinds of suffering:
first, the suffering of diminution, which refers to the category of householders;
second, the suffering of increase, which refers to the category of those who have gone forth.
Third, the suffering of affliction;
fourth, the suffering of separation from existence.
Furthermore, for one who has gone forth according to the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, there are three kinds of suffering:
First is the suffering of delusion, which refers to longing for the future and relishing the past;
second is the suffering of envy;
third is the suffering of being unable to overcome others.
Those who have left the household life by relying on a false teaching and discipline also experience three kinds of suffering:
first, the suffering of delusion, which refers to the inverted attachment to the dharmas that should be known;
second, the suffering of jealousy, which refers to the inability of the mind to tolerate the fame and profit obtained by the Buddha and his disciples.
Third is the suffering of being defeated by others, which refers to falling into a position of defeat when engaging in contentious debate for the sake of fame and profit.
The verse says:
It should be known that those who have not yet abandoned desire, form, and so forth, pertain to three types of stages.
All types [of suffering] exist in the desire realm; in the form and formless realms, two are excluded.
The commentary states:
These fifty-five kinds of suffering are subsumed within the three stages.
First, the stage not yet free from desire, which refers to that bound to the desire realm;
second, the stage already free from desire, which refers to that bound to the form realm;
third, the stage free from desire for form, which refers to that bound to the formless realm.
These three types [of suffering] are established as three kinds of suffering in their respective order: namely, superior, middling, and inferior.

Furthermore, within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all varieties of suffering are present; whereas in the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*), two kinds of suffering are absent—namely, the two comprised by the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*), as well as the two comprised by the fundamental suffering of desire and the retributive suffering of ignorance (*moha*). Nevertheless, other forms of suffering do exist there.
The verse says:
There are two kinds of conventional [truth], while the ultimate is said to be universal.
These two conditions extend to the higher stages; one should know that they lack present defilement.
The Treatise says:
Such sufferings are, in brief, of two kinds, distinguished as conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and ultimate (*paramārtha*).
Suffering subsumed under conventional truth is of two kinds: namely, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
There is one type subsumed under ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), namely, the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).
This is also called pervasive suffering (*sarvatraga-duḥkha*), because it extends throughout the three realms, such as the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

In the higher stages above the desire realm, there are two kinds of suffering produced by conditions: namely, suffering where there is prior karmic condition but no present causal condition, and suffering where there is pure condition but no impure condition.
The verse says:
They are not non-form, the heavy burden, The pervasive heaviness of the heavens, And the final limit of the truths;
The remaining seven are the secondary fetters of the upper realms.
The treatise says:

Within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is no suffering of the burden of the body; however, there is the suffering of the celestial realms (devagati), the suffering of coarse heaviness (dausthulya), and the suffering of the aggregates of grasping (upādānaskandha) at the ultimate limit of the truths.
This [suffering] pervades the three realms, including the desire realm, and is therefore called "pervasive suffering" (*sarvatraga-duḥkha*).

The other seven types of suffering, such as birth and so forth, are subsumed under the desire realm; although they may exist in the higher stages as latent attachments (*anuśaya*), they can still regress [from those stages], and thus they lack the intrinsic nature of suffering.
The verse says:
One should know that birth and the other [aspects of suffering] each have five kinds of distinctions;
they are associated with the heaviness of suffering (*duḥkha-dauṣṭhulya*) and serve as the basis for the three types of suffering.
The treatise states:

It should be understood that each of the seven types of suffering, such as birth and so forth, possesses five aspects: namely, because they are associated with suffering (*duḥkha*), because they are associated with coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), and because they serve as the basis for the three types of suffering.
Birth is the basis for the sufferings of old age and so forth, the basis for the afflictions, and the basis for the destruction of what is undesirable and unpleasing.
Old age is the basis for the decline of physical form and so forth.
Sickness is the basis for practicing what is undesired, the basis for not practicing what is desired, and the basis for the discordance of the great elements that accords with death.

Death is the basis for the separation from one's own body, the basis for the separation from wealth and treasures, and the basis for the suffering of being separated from what is loved and encountering what is hated.

The three types of suffering, such as association with the disliked and so forth, are the basis for physical oppression, the basis for mental oppression, and the basis for the resulting decline and loss.
The verse says:
"The last one and the last one, Each serve as the basis for four types of suffering."
"Birth, the root of birth, as well as the nature of suffering and transformation.
The commentary states:

Among the eight types of suffering, the suffering of the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*) subsumed within the last [suffering], and among the three types of suffering, the last, which is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*), are each "suffering" because they serve as the basis for the other four types of suffering.

First, the basis for the suffering of the life-process; second, the basis for the suffering that is the root of rebirth; third, the basis for the suffering of intrinsic nature; and fourth, the basis for the suffering of change.
The verse says:
Encompassed by the three times, Two conditions are suffering, not the latter.
The other various sufferings that have been described should be known as pertaining to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The treatise says:
Among the sufferings of the three periods of time in the stages above the desire realm, one should know that there is no suffering conditioned by the past or the future.

Why is this? Because in the higher stages, suffering does not arise from false conceptualization regarding the past or future; rather, there is only the presence of present conditions accompanied by coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Apart from what has been mentioned above, one should know that all remaining forms of suffering pertain exclusively to those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, for what reason and by what causal conditions does delusion (*moha*) arise with respect to the actual objects of suffering?
The verse says:
Through loss of mindfulness, lack of effort, distraction, improper reflection,
incorrect comprehension, delusion, and by means of heedlessness and so forth.
The treatise states:
Ignorance regarding suffering arises due to five causes, as well as from the previously mentioned factors such as negligence (*pramāda*).

The five causes are: first, the loss of mindfulness regarding past suffering; second, the failure to apply effort to investigate future suffering; third, the arising of the four perversions (*viparyāsa*) regarding present suffering; fourth, the conceiving of the suffering of *dauṣṭhulya* as a self due to improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*); and fifth, the lack of thorough understanding regarding the suffering inherent in all natures (*dharmatā*) due to incorrect comprehension.
Furthermore, mindfulness is lost due to four causes.
The verse says:
Because of dullness, because of weakness, And because of the arising of negligence.
Because the continuity is severed, one should know that forgetfulness arises.
The commentary states:
"Being dull-witted" refers to those of a deluded nature.
"Debilitated" refers to states such as that of death.
"Heedless" refers to attachment to sensory objects.
"The continuity is severed" refers to the severance of the continuity of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) prior to the arising of another birth.
Furthermore, it operates without effort due to four causes.
The verse says:
Because of dullness, because of negligence, and because of cherishing the present life.
Because one does not believe that there will be suffering, one proceeds without effort.
The commentary says:
"Obscurity" and "heedlessness" have already been explained as before.
"Cherishing the present life" means that because one cherishes present phenomena, one exerts no effort toward future suffering.
"Not believing in future suffering" means that because one does not believe in the existence of future suffering, one exerts no effort [to avoid it].
Furthermore, four types of inversion arise due to four causes.
The verse says:
Arising through similarity, continuity, transformation, And the false discrimination that opposes [the truth].
"Because of habitual practice and grasping as a whole, the four kinds of inversions arise.
The treatise says:
"Because one perceives a semblance of continuity as it evolves, the inversion of permanence arises."
The inversion of pleasure arises from the antidote to [the perception of] discrimination, because one falsely discriminates pleasure as the antidote to suffering.
The inversion of purity arises from habitual practice.
The inversion of self arises from grasping at a totality.
Furthermore, delusion regarding suffering arises due to a failure to discern five causes. What are these five?
The verse says: Distinctions of realm, distinctions of dependent origination, distinctions of stage, and distinctions of sequence,
as well as the distinctions of continuity— one should know that each of these has many varieties.
The treatise states:
There are three kinds of suffering based on the distinction of realms, namely the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Based on the distinction of conditions, there are seven kinds of suffering:
First, the condition of merit; second, the condition of non-merit—these two exist in the desire realm;
third, the condition of the imperturbable, which exists in the form and formless realms;
fourth, the condition of the envelopments and latent tendencies, which refers to ordinary worldlings.
Fifth is the condition of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), which refers to those who have seen the truths;
sixth is the condition of conditioned practice (*sābhisaṃskāra*), which refers to those who are not bodhisattvas;
seventh is the condition of wise practice (*jñānābhisamskāra*), which refers to all bodhisattvas.
Regarding the distinctions of states, there are twelve kinds of suffering:
first, that which is accompanied by pure pleasure, namely the various devas;
second, that which is accompanied by pure suffering, namely the denizens of hell, as well as a portion of hungry ghosts and animals.
Third, those accompanied by both suffering and pleasure, namely humans, hungry ghosts, and a portion of animals;
fourth, those accompanied by neither suffering nor pleasure, namely from the fourth dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*);
fifth, impure and pure places, namely birthplaces within the desire realm that are free from obstacles.

Sixth, the impure-impure state refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within the form and formless realms; seventh, the pure-pure state refers to those who have realized the truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*) within the form and formless realms;

eighth, the impure-impure state refers to the difficult birthplaces within the desire realm and the four types of suffering associated with entering the womb: first, entering the mother’s womb without clear comprehension, staying without clear comprehension, and exiting without clear comprehension; second, entering the mother’s womb with clear comprehension, staying without clear comprehension, and exiting without clear comprehension; third, entering the mother’s womb with clear comprehension, staying with clear comprehension, and exiting without clear comprehension; fourth, entering the mother’s womb with clear comprehension, staying with clear comprehension, and exiting with clear comprehension.

There are twelve types of suffering according to their sequential distinctions; that is to say, based on the sequential continuity of the twelve links of dependent origination, there are immeasurable varieties, because the continuities of sentient beings possess boundless distinctions.
Furthermore, it should be known that there are eighteen types of thorough and complete knowledge regarding all suffering. What are they?
The verse says:

Faith-understanding and analytical investigation, Non-distraction, mental weariness, and renunciation, The paths of seeing, cultivation, and the ultimate; Furthermore, as were the eleven previously mentioned.
The Commentary says:
First is the thorough knowledge of resolute belief, which refers to the wisdom born of hearing.
Second is the thorough knowledge of analytical discernment, which refers to the wisdom born of reflection.
Third is the thorough knowledge of non-distraction, which refers to the mundane wisdom born of cultivation.

Fourth is the comprehensive knowledge subsumed under the mind of revulsion, which refers to the knowledge of the levels conducive to penetration, such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth; because through this knowledge one contemplates the characteristics of one's own mind and turns away with total revulsion.
Fifth is the comprehensive knowledge of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), which refers to the knowledge based upon the path of seeing.
Sixth is the thorough knowledge of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-parijñā*), which refers to the wisdom based upon the path of cultivation.
Seventh is the thorough knowledge of the ultimate path (*niṣṭhāmārga-parijñā*), which refers to the wisdom subsumed within the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).

Furthermore, there are the eleven kinds of wisdom previously mentioned: (1) impure mundane wisdom; (2) pure mundane wisdom; (3) ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*); (4) wisdom with conceptualization regarding the characteristics of the impure; (5) wisdom with conceptualization regarding the characteristics of the pure; (6) non-conceptual wisdom regarding the characteristics of the pure; (7) wisdom prior to the accomplishment of what was to be done; (8) wisdom at the time of accomplishing what was to be done; (9) wisdom subsequent to the accomplishment of what was to be done; (10) the wisdom of the śrāvakas; and (11) the wisdom of the bodhisattvas.
Thus, there are eighteen kinds of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) that realize suffering as it truly is.
Furthermore, for the sake of exhausting all suffering through such thorough knowledge:
by what thorough knowledge is what kind of suffering exhausted?
The verse says:
Obsessions, doubt, and lack of delight in renunciation, Sinking, the miserable destinies, and other destinies— These arise from inferior conduct;
They are the pervasive and solitary exhaustion of all suffering.
The treatise states:
The pervasive wisdom of resolute belief can extinguish the suffering of entanglement;
the pervasive wisdom of analytical investigation can extinguish the suffering of doubt.
The pervasive wisdom of non-distraction can extinguish the suffering of not delighting in seclusion;
the pervasive wisdom of the mind’s aversion and withdrawal can extinguish the suffering of torpor;
and the pervasive wisdom of seeing the path can extinguish the suffering of the evil realms.
The pervasive knowledge of the path of cultivation can extinguish the suffering of other realms;
the pervasive knowledge of the ultimate path can extinguish the suffering arising from inferior practices, namely, excluding the path of swift and easy progress.
It should be understood that all remaining formations are termed inferior.

It should be understood that while the universal knowledge of a bodhisattva universally extinguishes all sufferings of both self and others, the universal knowledge of a śrāvaka extinguishes only his own suffering.
Chapter Six: Establishing Emptiness. Having thus established the characteristic of suffering, how is the characteristic of emptiness established?
One should know that the characteristics of emptiness are threefold:
first, the characteristic of self-nature; second, the characteristic of profundity; and third, the characteristic of differentiation.
What is the characteristic of self-nature?
The verse says:
If something does not exist here, And whatever else exists apart from it,
According to these two principles, The characteristic of emptiness is said to be non-dual.
The treatise states:
Regarding the self-characteristic of emptiness, it is neither definitively existent nor non-existent.
That it is not definitively existent means that within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the self-nature of sentient beings and the self-nature of phenomena are ultimately non-existent.
"It is not that they are definitely non-existent" means that within this [emptiness], there is the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena because their real nature exists.

"In accordance with two kinds of principles" means that within this very [emptiness], there is the principle of the absence of the two kinds of self and the principle of the presence of the two kinds of selflessness; in accordance with these two, it is said that emptiness has no dual characteristics.
First, it is not characterized by existence, because the self does not exist;
second, it is not characterized by non-existence, because the non-existence of the self exists. Why is this so?
The non-existence of these two selves is precisely the existence of the two kinds of selflessness;

the existence of this two-fold selflessness is precisely because these two selves do not exist. Therefore, emptiness possesses neither a definitively existent characteristic nor a definitively non-existent characteristic.
What is the characteristic of profundity?
The verse says:
The characteristic of profundity should be known as neither increasing nor decreasing in terms of what is taken up or abandoned.
The treatise states:
In accordance with the principle of non-duality previously explained, although all phenomena are relinquished, there is no decrease; although all phenomena are grasped, there is no increase.
Without grasping or abandoning, without increase or decrease—this is the characteristic of profound emptiness.
What are its differentiated characteristics?
The verse says:
Its distinctions are manifold, as they have been proclaimed in various ways.
The Commentary states:

This very emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is revealed by the Blessed One (*bhagavān*) in various sūtras through numerous distinctions, such as ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), and so forth.
Now, let us analyze this.
Ultimate emptiness (paramārtha-śūnyatā) is empty by virtue of being the ultimate; it is called ultimate emptiness because nothing exists therein.
This reveals four meanings.

What are the four? First, the sense of being devoid of a cause for a self; second, the sense of being devoid of the characteristics of a self; third, the sense of being devoid of no-cause; and fourth, the sense of being devoid of that which is not obtained through one's own karma.
When the six sense bases arise, they do not come from a self, nor do they aggregate or depend upon a self; this is what is meant by the meaning of being "devoid of a self as cause.
If one were to maintain that the six sense bases have a self as their cause, there would be no differentiation between the five destinies.

Furthermore, because the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) exist now where they previously did not, and having existed, disperse and perish, one is free from the notion of a self (*ātman*), for such characteristics do not belong to a self.

Moreover, because the ripening result (*vipāka*) arises with karma as its cause, there is no agent whatsoever, nor is there any sentient being who abandons or continues the aggregates (*skandha*); this is what is meant by being free from the notion of causelessness (*ahetuka*).

Furthermore, because sentient beings are conventionally designated based on the *bhavāṅga* (constituent of existence), and because this continuity flows as a single stream into the present maturation-dharmas rather than being a different continuity, it is therefore said to be "free from the meaning of obtaining what is not one's own karma."
Furthermore, how should one understand that the person (*pudgala*) has no self?

If there were a self, would it have the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), or would it reside within the aggregates, or would it reside elsewhere, or would it not have the characteristics of the aggregates?
The verse says:
Because of the fault that it would be merely conventional, because of the fault that the aggregates would be selfless,
and because of the fault that the self would be bodiless, the three types of self are not tenable.
The treatise states:

If the self as you conceive it were identical to the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), it would necessarily be merely a conventional designation (*prajñapti*). This contradicts your own tenet and thus constitutes a fault, because the self is conventionally established only in dependence upon the aggregates.
If the self were to abide elsewhere apart from the aggregates, it would follow that the self is without aggregates;
this too is a fault, because there is no self within the aggregates.
If, on the other hand, it does not have the characteristics of the aggregates, then the conceived self would be bodiless, and a bodiless self is illogical.
Therefore, these three [positions] are illogical.
Furthermore, if one maintains that a real self dwells within the aggregates, this too is not the case. Why is this so?
The verse says:
Like a master, fire, light, and space, There would be the faults of differing forms and dependence on others;
It would be impermanent and devoid of functional activity, Neither a cause nor possessing a self.
The treatise says:

Regarding the imagined real self that dwells within the aggregates, does it dwell like a master in a house, or like fire in fuel, or like light depending on a lamp, or like space amidst various objects?
All of this is unreasonable. Why?
Because there are five kinds of faults.
What are these five?
If [the self] were like a master dwelling in a house, its physical form would have to be distinct [from the body], because the master of the house and the house itself differ in appearance.
If it were like fire existing in fuel, there would be the fault of dependence on another, for fire depends on the power of the fuel and lacks independence.
If illumination were dependent upon a lamp, it would entail the fault of impermanence, because illumination arises and ceases according to the presence or absence of the lamp.

Furthermore, the first two types [of houses] also possess the fault of impermanence; for no house-owner is seen to be permanent, as even though the house may endure for a long time, its owner may go elsewhere or pass away.
Fire is likewise unstable in its presence or absence depending on the power of the fuel, due to its impermanent nature.
If it were like space, there would be the manifest fault of possessing functional activity (*karmakāritra*).
The functional activity of space is clearly observable, in that it provides no obstruction to activities such as coming and going;
the self, however, is not like this, and thus the fault is established.
Furthermore, the postulated self cannot be established as the cause of the fruit. Why is this?
Because external things such as seeds, which lack a self, can also be established as causes of the fruit.
Therefore, it is unreasonable to calculate that a self resides within the aggregates and acts as the cause for their fruits; furthermore, there is no real essence of a self to be calculated.
Question:
If there are only the aggregates and no separate self, who sees, who hears, and even who is capable of discerning?
Answer:

If one holds that seeing, hearing, and so forth are either the essence of the self, the activity of the self, or the instruments of the self, and thus clings to the self as being the seer, the hearer, and so on—all such views are unreasonable.
Why is this? The verse says:
"The self must be merely a designation; no analogy for it can be found."
The seven similes illustrate false discrimination; there is no "seer" and so forth—these three.
The treatise says:

If you maintain that the self is identical to seeing and the rest, and is further called the "seer" up to the "discerner," then the self you postulate must be merely conventional, for the self is only a provisional designation established upon the phenomena of seeing and so forth.
If one maintains that seeing and so forth are the action or the instrument, this is also not the case, because there is no supporting analogy.
Although one might falsely construct seven types of analogies, they entail many fallacies; therefore, all three [positions] are unreasonable.
What are the many faults?
The verse says:
If [the self] were impermanent like a seed, the agent would necessarily be merely conventional.
As one who has accomplished supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), one should exercise mastery over the mundane world.
The commentary states:

If you maintain that the self (*ātman*) functions in relation to actions such as seeing and hearing like a seed in relation to a sprout, then the self must be impermanent, because the seed is not permanent.

If you maintain that the self (ātman) acts in relation to the activities of seeing, hearing, and so forth, just as a potter acts in relation to a vessel, then the self must be merely conventional (prajñapti).
Why? Because in the world it is observed that a conventionally designated person (pudgala) performs the function of making a vessel, and no other [substantial entity] is seen to do so.

If you maintain that the self performs actions such as seeing just as those in the world who possess supernatural powers can produce transformations, then it must likewise incur the faults of being a mere conventional designation and of being subject to arbitrary will.
Why is this? Because apart from the conventional person (*pudgala*), no one else who has attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) perceives it.

Furthermore, we observe that those who have attained supernatural powers exercise mastery over transformative phenomena (*nirmāṇa*) according to their will; thus, I should likewise attain mastery over seeing and so forth without depending on external conditions.
Furthermore, the verse says:
The self is like the earth and like space; It should be impermanent and devoid of intrinsic nature.
Like those two, it should be without action, Yet karma can be clearly perceived.
The treatise states:
If you maintain that the self, in relation to actions such as seeing, is like the great earth which can support all things, then the self must be impermanent, because the earth is not permanent.

If you argue that just as space, being unobstructed, allows for the occurrence of actions, so too does the self allow for actions such as seeing, then the self must be without substantial reality; it would be like space, which is merely the absence of matter, because it is [by definition] space.

Furthermore, just as the great earth and space have no active function regarding support and so forth, so too the self should likewise have no active function regarding those [faculties] such as vision.
Since there is no such activity, it is unreasonable to maintain that there are "seers" and so forth.
Furthermore, the two functions of the great earth and space—supporting and non-obstruction—are clearly perceptible.
Since no distinct [self] can be found apart from seeing and other such activities, this is illogical.
Furthermore, if one maintains that seeing and so forth are the instruments of the self, this too is not the case.
Why is this? The verse says:
"That which can burn and that which can sever are produced solely by fire and so forth."
"The self, with respect to the instruments such as vision, is not like a knife, fire, or the like.
The commentary states:

If you maintain that the self grasps the instruments such as vision and is thus able to see, hear, and even cognize—just as a person grasping fire can burn or grasping a knife can cut—this is not logical.
Why is this? In the world, we observe that apart from a person who grasps, fire can burn by itself and a knife can cut by itself.

The same applies to seeing and other functions; although there is no self (*ātman*), seeing and its other activities should likewise exist inherently. Yet you do not admit this, and therefore it is not a valid analogy.

Furthermore, the world conventionally designates a "self," "person," or "sentient being" based on the composite of the various aggregates; it is this [composite] that grasps the sickle and so forth, capable of reaping and cutting. There is no separate, real self. Therefore, this is not a valid analogy.
Furthermore, the verse says:
Just as light has the function of illuminating, And there is no distinct entity apart from the light,
So too, regarding the internal and external, The meaning of emptiness and selflessness is established.
The treatise says:

We observe in the world that it is the luminous substance itself, possessing the function of illumination, that is called the "illuminator"; apart from the substance of light, there is no separate illuminator.

Likewise, it is the eye and so forth, possessing the functions of seeing and so on, that are called the "seer," and up to the "discerner," there is no separate seer and so forth. Therefore, all internal and external phenomena are equally devoid of a self.
Question:
If there truly is no self, how is it that the world undergoes defilement and purification? Answer:
All phenomena, whether defiled or pure, arise from causes and conditions; they do not depend upon a substantial self. Why is this?
The verse says:
Just as external objects in the world, though devoid of a self, can bring about benefit or harm, so too,
although there is no real self internally, the principles of defilement and purification should be established.
The treatise says:
Just as external objects, though devoid of a self, still possess various calamities, benefits, and the accomplishment of undertakings;
so too, although internal phenomena lack a self, the various meanings of defilement and purification are established. Therefore, there is no fault.
Furthermore, if there were no self, who would experience the retribution of results, who would be able to perform actions, and who would be liberated from all suffering?
The verse says:
The divisions of state, volition, and affliction, Because they are impermanent and subject to change.
The self is eternally without change; thus, experiencing, acting, and liberation would be impossible.
The commentary states:

According to your conception, the self remains eternally without variation throughout all times and circumstances—whether in states of pleasure or pain, in wholesome or unwholesome volitions, or amidst afflictions such as craving.
Because there is no transformation, it is illogical for there to be an experiencer, an agent, or one who is liberated.

As previously stated, although there is no real self, the conventional designations of a person undergo transformation across the three times; thus, the distinctions between the experiencer, the agent, the one who is liberated, and the temporal periods are all established.
Furthermore, if there were no self, who would transmigrate and who would return?
The verse says:
The nature of phenomena arises from conditions, Manifesting in a continuous succession.
That which possesses causes does not remain static; it is called "transformation" (pariṇāma) because of its alteration.
Just as the body, a sprout, a river, or a lamp possess various functions, if the self were eternal and unchanging, its transformation would be logically untenable.
The treatise says:
It is not because of the existence of a self that there is transmigration and return. Why is this?

That which is currently perceived as evolving necessarily possesses the characteristic of arising; it continues in a succession from prior to subsequent moments without interruption, constantly manifesting before one and being clearly visible.
That which has causes, does not remain static, and undergoes transformation is called "evolving" (*pravṛtti*); the cessation of this continuity is called "reversion" (*nivṛtti*).

Just as the body, a sprout, a river, or a lamp possess various functions such as coming and going, as well as arising and ceasing, so too does the self—contrary to what you conceive—possess the function of transmigrating, despite being permanent and unchanging.
If even the process of transmigration does not exist, how much less so its cessation?

Furthermore, if there were only conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and no self (*ātman*), then the various distinctions between sentient beings—whether in terms of their names or their conceptual designations—would not exist as they are perceived in the world.
The verse says:
Based on the notion of "self," names and concepts arise;
seeing these two kinds of faults, one realizes that throughout all things, the nature of a real self is entirely absent.
The treatise says:
A real self is not established by means of names and concepts. Why is this?
Because two kinds of faults are observed:

if worldly people were to give rise to various conceptual designations such as "the Buddha's savior" with respect to a real self, then their understanding of phenomena such as the body would necessarily be non-existent.
If one were to give rise to the conceptual designation (saṃjñā) of "self" with respect to the body and so forth, one should not say that the self possesses various functions. Why is this?
Because we observe in the world the arising of various conventional expressions, such as "the friend of the Buddha can see" or "the friend of virtue can hear," and so on.

Furthermore, regarding the observation of two kinds of faults: if one maintains that the intrinsic nature of the view of self is wholesome, it would be illogical for it to manifest spontaneously and give rise to defiled phenomena.
If that which is defiled could realize the self, it would be unreasonable.
Furthermore, when one who conceives of a self grasps at the self, is it the "I" that grasps, or is it the view that grasps?
If it were said that "I" grasp at a self, then those in the world who grasp at a self would not give rise to doubt as to whether it exists, does not exist, or what it is.
Why is this? Because the self is presently perceived.
If you say that one perceives by grasping at a self, then you should not now say that "I" am the grasper.
Due to such various faults as these, there is therefore no real self in the world.
Furthermore, if this is so, for what reason are various distinctions of names and concepts established within the True Dharma?
The verse says:
For the sake of ease of expression, for conformity with the world,
for the severance of fear, and to manifest both virtue and fault.
The Treatise says:
Although there is no real self (*ātman*), four reasons are given for establishing the designation and conceptualization of "sentient beings" (*sattva*):

first, to facilitate verbal communication; second, to conform with worldly convention; third, to cause beginners to be free from fear; and fourth, to manifest the distinctions between the merits and faults of oneself and others.

Furthermore, if there were no self, the world would not immediately give rise to the cognition of a "sentient being" upon merely seeing a physical form; nor would it be possible for various actions to be undertaken preceded by intentional thought.
The verse says:
Spontaneous awareness arises in a state of distraction, Which is clearly observable in the world;
If action were preceded by such awareness, There would be ten kinds of faults.
The treatise says:
A cognition that arises abruptly is not proof for the existence of a self.

Why is this? Because erroneous cognitions arise spontaneously as their very nature, as can be observed in experience; for example, the cognition of a man arising toward a woman’s body, the cognition of a woman arising toward a man’s body, the cognition of a person arising toward a tree stump, and the cognition of a tree stump arising toward a person.
Furthermore, there are ten faults in your calculation that the self initiates all actions preceded by volition and cognition. What are these ten?
The verse says:
Awakening, self, cause, effort, and sovereignty—each of these has two [types], including those with causes and those without causes; one should know that there are ten such fallacies.
The treatise says:
If you maintain that cognition (*buddhi*) is the cause from which various actions arise, then it is not the self (*ātman*) that initiates those actions.
If the self were the cause while volition (*cetanā*) and cognition were not causes, then there would be no initiation of various actions preceded by volition and cognition.
Furthermore, if you maintain that the self acts as the cause for initiating karmic actions, then all karmic actions should arise constantly.
If the self were not the cause, then the self would have no agency whatsoever.

Furthermore, if you maintain that there exists some other causal factor (*hetu-dharma*) which acts as a cause for the arising of various activities, then the "self" (*ātman*) you postulate would be devoid of agency.
Conversely, if there were no such cause, then all activities should arise constantly.
Furthermore, if you maintain that internal effort can produce effects, this too entails the two types of faults mentioned previously.
Moreover, if you maintain that the self possesses mastery over the performance of actions, it should constantly perform all that is desired and never perform what is undesired.
If there is no autonomy, it is not the characteristic of a self.
Thus, the characteristic of emptiness and its establishment have been explained.
Now, we shall demonstrate the distinctions of the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which is the object to be remedied by the true wisdom that contemplates emptiness.
The verse says: Lack of discernment, pervasive [delusion], superimposition, and that which is without basis,
as well as false views regarding fear toward objects— these five similes should be known.
The treatise says:
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) should be known to be of five kinds.
First is the view that does not examine the object, such as seeing a snake in a rope.

Second is the omnipresent view, which refers to the false view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) associated with the afflicted manas; because it constantly follows along at all times, it is like seeing what one experiences while dreaming.
Why is this so? It is just as a poor person might, within a dream, see themselves enjoying desirable objects.
In the same way, until a fool has given rise to the true awakening of suchness (tathatā), they constantly give rise to false conceptualizations and are pursued by the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi).
Third is the view of exaggerating things, which is like hoping for and being attached to another's wife.
Fourth is the view of unreal things, which is like a small child seeing a magical illusion.
Fifth is the perception of fear regarding objects, such as when a person fears a yakṣa they have drawn themselves.
Thus has the differentiation of the objects to be remedied been explained; now the differentiation of the remedies shall be demonstrated.
The verse says:
Non-substantiality and detachment, Through the three types of elimination,
Are the remedies for the various conceptions of bondage, With sixteen distinct varieties.
The treatise states:
Based upon the three types of self-nature—namely, the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita*) and so forth—three kinds of emptiness are established in their respective order:
first, the emptiness of non-existence; second, the emptiness of detachment; and third, the emptiness of elimination.
Furthermore, these three emptinesses serve as antidotes to the various distinctions among fetters and conceptualizations; there are sixteen such types.
It should be understood that among the fetters, there are fourteen types: the fetters of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*) and the fetters of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya-bandhana*).
First, the bond of the single sense-faculty;
second, the bond of mutual defilement among sentient beings;
third, the bond of the basis, which refers to the transmigration of the sense-faculties based upon the receptacle world.
Fourth, the bond of ignorance regarding knowledge;
fifth, the bond of false objects regarding objects;
sixth, the bond of craving for future existence.
Seventh, the bond of craving for non-existence;
eighth, the bond of clinging to causelessness and inequitable causes;
ninth, the bond of the pride of superiority.
10. The bondage of grasping at the self-nature of the thoroughly imagined;
11. The bondage of grasping at the self-nature of all phenomena;
12. The bondage of grasping at the self-nature of the thorough knowledge of all phenomena.
Thirteenth is the bondage of the self-substance of the thirteen types of persons;
fourteenth is the bondage of the thorough knowledge of the persons.
As for "all perceptions," this refers to the six kinds of perceptual bondages.
Because of weariness with these perceptions, the bodhisattva relies on emptiness and diligently cultivates the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) to liberate the mind.
What are called the six kinds of bondage through perception?
They are as follows: the internal perception arising in dependence upon the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena is called the first bondage of perception.
To give rise to external perceptions based on the body and so forth is called the second;
to give rise to internal-and-external perceptions based on the body and so forth is called the third;

and to give rise to the great vow and cultivate the foundations of mindfulness for the sake of liberating the infinite and incalculable realms of sentient beings throughout the ten directions—this conceptual perception is called the fourth.
The conceptualization that consists of dwelling in the correct observation of the body and so forth as being endowed with wisdom is called the fifth;
the conceptualization that consists of dwelling in the correct observation of the body and so forth as having a self or a person is called the sixth.
Furthermore, one should know that there are eleven distinct types of conceptual fetters (*saṃjñā-bandhana*) regarding the successive formation of the body and so forth.
What are these eleven? They are as follows:

first, the conceptual fetter consists of dwelling in the correct observation of the body and so forth according to their respective natures, as well as giving rise to discriminative conceptions regarding both the defiled and purified truths within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). This is called the first conceptual fetter.
To conceive the notion of "activity" regarding the ultimate truth of defilement is called the second;
to conceive the notion of "non-activity" regarding the ultimate truth of purity is called the third;
and to conceive the notion of "transmigration" regarding the ultimate truth of activity is called the fourth.
To conceive the notion of permanence regarding the unconditioned ultimate truth is called the fifth;
to conceive the notion of suffering regarding the process of saṃsāra because of its transformation through suffering is called the sixth;
and to conceive the notion of immutability regarding permanent phenomena is called the seventh.

Regarding the process of saṃsāra, the perception of intrinsic characteristics arises due to the specific characteristics of arising, ceasing, abiding, and changing, as well as due to the transformation of those intrinsic characteristics; this is called the eighth.
Regarding the ultimate reality of both the mutable and immutable, which are defiled and pure, the perception that encompasses all phenomena arises; this is called the ninth.
Regarding all phenomena—both defiled and pure—the perception of a "mine" (ātmiya) that is itself defiled or pure arises; this is called the tenth.
To give rise to the notion of an intrinsic nature and intrinsic characteristics regarding all defiled and purified phenomena is called the eleventh.

Having correctly observed these successive distinctions in the fetters of conceptualization and their respective objects, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva relies upon emptiness to cultivate the foundations of mindfulness so as to liberate the mind.
When one attains liberation from such bonds of conceptual construction, it should be known that one is liberated from all bonds of perception.

As for the sixteen kinds of emptiness, they are: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, great emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, emptiness of that which is indestructible and inexhaustible, emptiness of nature, emptiness of characteristics, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of non-existence, and emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence.
Furthermore, regarding this object of emptiness, there are six kinds of delusion through which one has wandered in saṃsāra since beginningless time. What are these six?
The verse says:
Intrinsic nature, attachment, lack of comprehension, loss of mindfulness,
omnipresence, partiality, and the differentiation of delusion constitute the process of saṃsāra.
The treatise states:
Ignorance of intrinsic nature refers to the essence of non-cognition that has characterized the continuous transmigration of all sentient beings since beginningless time.
Ignorance of attachment refers to the non-cognition arising from the erroneous views associated with various non-Buddhist outsiders.
Ignorance regarding lack of comprehension refers to the non-knowledge arising in unlearned ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Ignorance regarding loss of mindfulness refers to the non-knowledge arising in learned ordinary beings as well as in noble ones (*ārya*).
Universal delusion refers to the lack of wisdom regarding both the emptiness of sentient beings and the emptiness of phenomena that arises in ordinary worldlings.
Partial delusion refers to the lack of wisdom regarding only the emptiness of phenomena that arises in śrāvakas and others.
How is this principle of emptiness realized?
It is said to be by means of eight kinds of knowledge. What are these eight?
The verse says:
Abiding in the Dharma, seeking one’s own mind, Abiding in one’s own mind, and removing fetters;
fear, non-duality, defilement, and purity— One realizes the principle of true emptiness.
The treatise says:
First is the knowledge of the abiding of phenomena (*dharmasthitijñāna*), which refers to the knowledge that establishes the gateways of the Dharma based on the sūtras and other scriptures.
Second is the knowledge seeking the mind itself (*svacittaparyeṣaṇajñāna*), which refers to the investigation of one's own mind during the stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Third is the wisdom that abides in its own mind, which refers to the wisdom realizing *tathatā* at the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Fourth is the wisdom that removes the bonds of the mind, which refers to the wisdom that serves as the antidote to obstacles at the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Fifth is the wisdom associated with the practice of fearing [saṃsāra], which refers to the wisdom of the noble disciple (ārya-śrāvaka), because they fear the great suffering and affliction of transmigration.
Sixth is non-dual discriminative wisdom, which refers to the wisdom of the bodhisattva, because they do not discriminate between the faults of transmigration and the merits of quiescence.
Seventh is impure wisdom of non-virtue, which refers to the wisdom of those still in training (śaikṣa).
Eighth is pure wisdom of virtue, which refers to the wisdom of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
*Exposition of the Holy Teachings* (Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra), Fascicle Fifteen.

The Remainder of Chapter Six, "The Accomplishment of Emptiness": The commentary states:
Such a principle of emptiness is realized by relying upon cultivation.
What constitutes this cultivation?
The verse says:
There are eighteen distinctions in cultivation; they are either with poison or without poison, serving as antidotes to the five kinds of grasping. Briefly, two types should be known.
The Treatise says: There are eighteen types of cultivation distinguished by their characteristics.

First is the cultivation of mental attention associated with the Śrāvaka. This refers to one who is a Śrāvaka abiding in the *dharmatā* of a Śrāvaka—whether they have not yet entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) or have already entered it—who contemplates only self-benefit and not the benefit of others. Relying on the gateway of mental attention toward the established truths (*vyavasthāpita-satya*), they enter the principle of suchness (*tathatā*). Internally contemplating phenomena that are limited in scope, they give rise to the practice of renunciation, dispassion, and liberation. They cultivate this through mental attention for the sake of exhausting self-love; this is called the cultivation of mental attention associated with the Śrāvaka.

Second is the bodhisattva’s cultivation through mental attention (*manasikāra*). This refers to a certain bodhisattva who abides in the *dharmatā* of a bodhisattva—whether they have not yet entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) or have already entered it—who contemplates the benefit of both self and others. Relying on the gateway of mental attention toward the established and non-established truths, they enter the principle of *tathatā*. Internally perceiving the measureless Dharma, because great compassion is predominant, they initiate the practice of skillful means for the sake of benefiting and gathering others. Taking the tracks of the unsurpassed as their cause, they cultivate this mental attention in order to exhaust all attachment to self and others; this is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation through mental attention.

Third is the cultivation of mental attention on images (*nimitta-manasikāra-bhāvanā*). This refers to either contemplating an image that is concordant with the original object of experience within the samādhi belonging to the category of conceptual *vipaśyanā*, or alternatively, contemplating an image that is concordant with the original object of experience within the samādhi belonging to the category of non-conceptual *śamatha*. Cultivating in this manner is called the cultivation of mental attention on images.

The cultivation of mental attention through the culmination of objects (*vastuparyantamanasikārabhāvanā*) refers to reflecting upon all phenomena—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; distant or near—or further reflecting upon the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, exhausting all that exists and conforming to all that exists. Cultivating in this manner is called the cultivation of mental attention through the culmination of objects.

Cultivation through the accomplishment of five factors refers to having already realized the fundamental dhyānas as well as mundane and supramundane samāpattis; such practice is called cultivation through the accomplishment of factors.

Sixth is cultivation by acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*). This refers to when someone, relying on the first *dhyāna*, cultivates the perception of impermanence (*anitya-saṃjñā*), or even up to the perception of death (*maraṇa-saṃjñā*); at that time, all other wholesome perceptions not currently manifest—whether belonging to their own level or to lower levels—as well as all mundane and supramundane merits induced by them, are all cultivated so that they increase, become intense, pure, and arise; one attains mastery over those dharmas and achieves perfection. This is called cultivation by acquisition.

Seventh is cultivation through practice (*āsevanā-bhāvanā*): this refers to when someone, in the present, contemplates various phenomena and gives rise to wholesome perceptions such as impermanence regarding them, as well as practicing other wholesome dharmas in the present; such cultivation is called cultivation through practice.

The eighth is the cultivation of elimination (*vibhāvanā-bhāvanā*). This refers to a certain person who, by reflecting upon the characteristics of the images that are the objects of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), eliminates the fundamental nature and characteristics of all phenomena so that they no longer appear, following the principle of "using a wedge to extract a wedge."
It is just as when a person uses a fine wedge to remove a coarse wedge, or uses physical ease to dispel physical heaviness (*dausthulya*).
As previously explained, this is called the cultivation of removal (*vibhāvanā-bhāvanā*).

Ninth is cultivation by way of counteractives (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*), which refers to the cultivation through reflection on the counteractive of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇapratipakṣa*), the counteractive of abandonment (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*), the counteractive of maintenance (*dhāraṇāpratipakṣa*), and the counteractive of distancing (*dūribhāvapratipakṣa*); this is called cultivation by way of counteractives.

Among these, the path born of hearing and reflection is the antidote of revulsion; the supramundane path is the antidote of abandonment; its fruit, the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), is the antidote of maintenance; and the mundane path of wisdom born of cultivation is the antidote of distancing.

10. cultivation of the body, 11. cultivation of ethical discipline, 12. cultivation of the mind, and 13. cultivation of wisdom; one should know that these are called the nature of the cultivation of the body and so forth, practiced by relying on the faculties in their respective order to train in the three higher trainings.

The fourteenth is partial cultivation (*pradeśabhāvanā*), which refers to contemplating all phenomena to give rise to each of the various wholesome perceptions, such as impermanence, and cultivating other remaining partial wholesome dharmas; this is called partial cultivation.

Fifteenth is pervasive cultivation (*sarvatraga-bhāvanā*), which refers to contemplating all phenomena as having the single flavor of true suchness (*tathatā*); practicing in this manner is called pervasive cultivation.

Sixteenth is cultivation with movement (*saspanda-bhāvanā*), which refers to when one is diligently applying skillful means to cultivate the signless (*animitta*), yet in the interim gives rise to various cultivations involving signs; this is called cultivation with movement.

Seventeenth is cultivation through effortful practice (*abhisamskāra-bhāvanā*): this refers to when one cultivates the signless (*animitta*) through diligent means; because one gives rise to the cultivation of the signless through effortful practice without interruption or deficiency, it is called cultivation through effortful practice.

Eighteenth is the cultivation of fulfillment (*paripūri-bhāvanā*): that is to say, whether based on the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Mahāyāna, once one has attained mastery over all phenomena by means of any of these bases, such practice is called the cultivation of fulfillment.
These various cultivations are, in brief, of two kinds: cultivation with poison and cultivation without poison, due to being mixed or unmixed with the grasping at "I" and "mine.
Furthermore, it should be understood that these cultivations serve as the antidotes to five types of false attachments:

first, false attachment to sentient beings; second, false attachment to phenomena; third, the false attachment of negation; fourth, the false attachment of differentiation; and fifth, the false attachment of transformation.
"Wrong attachment regarding sentient beings" refers to the attachment to the aggregates as having a sentient being, an agent, or an experiencer.
"Wrong attachment regarding phenomena" refers to the attachment to the distinct intrinsic natures of form and so forth, just as they are expressed in words.
The erroneous attachment of negation refers to the clinging that all characteristics of phenomena do not exist.
The erroneous attachment of differentiation refers to the clinging that phenomena possess distinct intrinsic natures, such as the existence of a self or the non-existence of a self.
Regarding the misconception of transformation: this refers to the attachment that all phenomena initially possess a real self, which later becomes non-self.
Furthermore, these practices are briefly of two kinds: mundane practice and supramundane practice.
Furthermore, the verse says:
One should know that the fruit of cultivation consists of the merits of the three types of awakening;
it is based on the nature of the transformation of the basis, wherein the tasks to be accomplished are fulfilled.
The treatise says:

Because one cultivates emptiness, one realizes the sublime fruit; that is to say, by relying upon the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), one realizes the three types of enlightenment (*trividha-bodhi*) and attains immeasurable merits such as the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), and the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
And the fulfillment of the tasks to be accomplished, which refers to the ultimate perfection of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Chapter Seven: Establishing the Absence of Nature. In the *Śāsanodbhāvana-śāstra*, Chapter Seven, "Establishing the Absence of Nature," the treatise states:

In the "Chapter on Establishing Emptiness," it has already been established that sentient beings lack a self and that phenomena lack a self. Now, in order to establish the absence of a self in phenomena, the "establishment of the absence of nature" is explained.
The verse says:
One should know that there are three natures: first, the thoroughly imagined nature;
next, the dependent-arising nature; and finally, the perfected-reality nature.
The Commentary states:

One should know that the absence of nature (niḥsvabhāvatā) is not separate from intrinsic nature (svabhāva). Therefore, the meaning of the three intrinsic natures was explained first; it was spoken in this way because it reveals the underlying intention (saṃdhi) regarding the three kinds of absence of nature.
The three natures are: the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The imagined nature refers to the intrinsic essence of all phenomena as it is conceptually constructed based on verbal expressions.
The dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) refers to the intrinsic essence of all phenomena as produced in dependence upon various causes and conditions.
The perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) refers to the intrinsic essence of the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena.
The verse says:
One should know that the three natures of non-essence are not separate from the three self-natures,
by virtue of the non-essence of characteristics, the non-essence of arising, and the non-essence of the ultimate.
The treatise says:

Regarding these three kinds of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one should know that they are taught as the three absences of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) by virtue of three types of absence of intrinsic nature.

First is the absence of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*); this refers to the imagined intrinsic nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because the essence and characteristics of this intrinsic nature do not exist.

Second is the absence of nature in terms of arising (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*), which refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); this is because it arises through the power of conditions and does not arise spontaneously.

Third is the absence of nature in terms of the ultimate (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*), which refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); this is because the essence of this nature is the ultimate, and furthermore, because all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature.
Having already explained the three natures and the characteristics of the three absences of nature, we shall now demonstrate the principles that establish them.
How should one understand that the thoroughly imagined nature is entirely devoid of intrinsic character?
The verse says:
Not subsumed under the five categories, there is nothing further beyond these;
because names function toward objects, the two are mutually adventitious.
The treatise says:
The specifically characterized nature of that which is conceptually constructed is non-existent. Why is this so?
Because it is not subsumed under the five categories, there is nothing else apart from these five.
What are the five? First, characteristics; second, names; third, conceptualization; fourth, suchness; and fifth, correct cognition.
Question:
If the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) lacks intrinsic substance (svabhāva), how can it give rise to the act of imagining? Answer:
Because names operate upon objects;

that is to say, they circulate among objects in accordance with those conventional designations, while worldly fools cling to the notion that there is a real intrinsic nature in which name and object are definitively correspondent.
Question:
How should one know that this is a false attachment? Answer:
Because the two are mutually guests to one another. Why is this so?
Because names do not correspond to the essence of their referents, they are said to be "guests."
Meaning is also like the name; because it does not exist [inherently], it is said to be adventitious.
How is this known? The verse says:
Before the name, there is no cognition; there are many names and they are not fixed.
Regarding that which has meaning and that which lacks meaning, the application [of names] results in irrational meanings.
The Treatise says:
If the intrinsic nature of an object existed in the same manner as its name, then this cognition of the object should have already existed prior to the acquisition of the name.
Furthermore, because names are manifold, a single object would consequently possess multiple intrinsic natures.
Furthermore, because it is called "indefinite," the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of its meaning must also be indefinite. Why?
Because this very same name is also applied to other meanings.
Furthermore, does this name function with respect to an existent object or with respect to a non-existent object?
If it functions with respect to an existent object, that is not logical, for the three reasons previously stated.
If [the name] were to operate upon a non-existent object, then the principle previously stated—that the two are mutually adventitious—is established.
Furthermore, if one maintains that the object is substantially existent and is made manifest by the name, just as a lamp illuminates a form, this is not tenable.
Why is this? The verse says:
Because a name is established based on what has been grasped, others cannot then grasp it.
As sentient beings have false attachments, they superimpose [qualities] and thus fall into perversion.
The commentary says:
One first grasps the object and only then establishes its name; it is not possible to establish a name without having first grasped the object.
It is not logical that what has already been understood must be made manifest once again.
Furthermore, by means of this very name, those others who have not yet understood would fail to grasp the meaning.
The illumination of objects by a lamp is not like this; it is not the case that because of this lamp, other [cognitions] cannot apprehend the object being illuminated.
Furthermore, one should not maintain that the meaning differs while the name remains the same, because the apprehension of meaning arises solely in dependence upon the name.

For example, although there are only conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have flowed forth from beginningless time by their very nature as ordinary beings, through the power of repeated habituation, they give rise to the false attachment to a "sentient being" within the continuums of themselves and others.

Thus, because the mind has been habituated and cultivated by verbal expressions throughout the long night, one gives rise to false and pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) through these means, grasping at the existence of various phenomena (*dharma*).
This erroneous attachment to phenomena should be understood as a perversion (*viparyāsa*), for it is like the false superimposition (*samāropa*) made by sentient beings.
How do such inversions arise in mutual succession with the defiled phenomena?
The verse says:
"Through perfuming, the dependent [nature] arises; based on this, inversions are produced."
Thus, acting as mutual conditions, they arise in succession.
The treatise says:
By the power of this perfuming of inversion, the dependent nature of subsequent fruits arises.
Furthermore, based on this fruit, the inversion of grasping at phenomena arises again at a later time.
Thus, these two dharmas serve as mutual conditions for one another, such that birth and death continue in succession without interruption.
The principles for establishing [the nature of phenomena] have already been explained; now, the specific distinctions of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) shall be demonstrated.
The verse says:
"Nature and its distinctions, [Comprise] manifest awakening, latent tendencies (*anuśaya*),..."
The preparatory application (*prayoga*) is termed "universal imagination" (*parikalpa*); furthermore, it should be known that there are five kinds.
The treatise says:
Because there are six varieties of universal imagination, the nature of the imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) also has six kinds.
What are the six kinds of pervasive conceptualization?

First, conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-parikalpa*), which refers to the pervasive conceptualization that form and so forth possess a truly existent intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Second, conceptualization of distinctions (*viśeṣa-parikalpa*), which refers to the pervasive conceptualization of the various distinct characteristics of form and so forth—such as being determinately and truly existent, being with form or formless, being visible or invisible, and so on.
Third is the pervasive conceptualization of awakening, which refers to the pervasive conceptualization of those who are skilled in linguistic conventions.
