Fourth is the pervasive conceptualization of latent tendencies, which refers to the pervasive conceptualization of those who are unskilled in linguistic conventions.
Fifth, the pervasive conceptualization of preparatory application (*prayoga-parikalpa*), which is further divided into five types:

first, the preparatory application of craving; second, the preparatory application of aversion; third, the preparatory application of union; fourth, the preparatory application of separation; and fifth, the preparatory application of equanimity.
The sixth is called pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*), which is further divided into two types:
first, that arising from words and letters; second, that not arising from words and letters.
Regarding that which does not arise from words and letters, for example, there may be a conceptual attachment such as: "What is this thing?"
What is this thing? Of what nature is this thing? How is this thing?

That which arises from words refers to such conceptual attachments as: "this is this thing," or "this thing is thus"—whether it be form (*rūpa*) or up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), whether conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), whether permanent (*nitya*) or impermanent (*anitya*), or whether wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Such are these [attachments].
Furthermore, it should be understood that the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) is further characterized by five kinds of thorough imagination.

What are these five? First, the thorough imagination of the intrinsic nature of an object based on a name; second, the thorough imagination of the intrinsic nature of a name based on an object; third, the thorough imagination of the intrinsic nature of a name based on a name; fourth, the thorough imagination of the intrinsic nature of an object based on an object; and fifth, the thorough imagination of the two intrinsic natures based on both.

Regarding the nature of objects as imagined based on names: for example, there may be a conceptual attachment such that, because this thing is named "form" (*rūpa*), one must necessarily hold that the substance of form exists as a reality.

Since this entity is designated as feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, it must necessarily possess a truly existent essential nature (svabhāva) of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Regarding the imputation of a self-nature based on the meaning of these designations, for instance, one might conceive and cling to the question: "Is this entity called 'form' (rūpa), or is it not called 'form'?"
Is this thing called feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, or is it not so called?

Regarding those who conceptually construct the intrinsic nature based on names: as they cling to such notions, they fail to understand the actual substance of things but only know various conceptual distinctions of the name "form"; they fail to understand the actual substance of things but only know various conceptual distinctions of the names "feeling," "perception," "mental formations," and "consciousness."

Regarding the pervasive conceptualization of the intrinsic nature of objects based on objects: it is as when one, failing to understand the names for form (*rūpa*), engages in various conceptualizations regarding the essence of form itself; and failing to understand the names for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*), engages in various conceptualizations regarding the essential natures of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness themselves.

Regarding the two types of pervasive conceptualization of the two natures: as there is conceptual attachment, one thinks that this thing has the essential nature of form and thus names it "form," or that this thing has the essential nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and thus names it "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
The distinctions of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) have already been explained.
This imagined nature arises from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*); the distinctions of this conceptualization shall now be further explained.
The verse says:
There are eight kinds of conceptualization, which can produce three things;
one should know that the substance of conceptualization consists of the mind and mental factors of the two realms.
The treatise says:
Eight kinds of discrimination can produce three things.
What are these three?
First, the objective basis for the proliferation of conceptual discrimination; second, the objective basis for views and the conceit "I am"; third, the objective basis for craving and so forth.

As for the eight types of discrimination: first is intrinsic discrimination (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), which refers to discriminating the intrinsic nature of form and so forth within the objective entities that are the referents of the notion of form and so forth.

Second is the discrimination of differentiation (*viśeṣa-vikalpa*), which refers to the various conceptualizations that arise regarding the referents of names such as "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth—namely, "this is with form" and "this is without form," "this is visible" and "this is invisible," "this is resistant" and "this is non-resistant"—and so on. Because it takes the discrimination of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*) as its basis, it discriminates the meanings of these various differentiations.

Third is the conceptualization of total grasping (*saṃgrāhaka-vikalpa*), which refers to the conceptualization induced by the provisional designations of "self," "sentient being," "life-principle," "born being," and so forth, established upon the perceived objects of form and the rest; it functions as conceptualization because it takes the total grasping of many accumulated phenomena as its cause.

Furthermore, regarding the conceptual investigation induced by the provisional designations of "house" and so forth—which are established based on the objects of perception such as houses, armies, forests, food, drink, clothing, and vehicles—there are four types of self-discrimination (*ātma-vikalpa*).

These refer to false conceptualizations that arise conditioned by objects that are outflows (*sāsrava*), subject to grasping (*upādāna*), accumulated through long-term habituation to the notion of a self, and which serve as the basis for one's own views due to the repeated practice of erroneous attachments.

Fifth is the discrimination of "mine" (*mamakāra-vikalpa*): it refers to those things that are tainted (*sāsrava*) and subject to grasping (*upādāna*), which have been accumulated through long-term habitual clinging to "mine"; it is a false discrimination arising with conditions from objects that are the locus of one's own views due to the repeated practice of such erroneous attachments.
Sixth is the discrimination of the agreeable, which refers to discrimination based on objects that are pure, excellent, and pleasing.
Seventh is the discrimination of the disagreeable, which refers to discrimination based on objects that are impure, non-excellent, and displeasing.

Eighth is the discrimination of both the agreeable and the disagreeable, as well as that which is contrary to both; this refers to the discrimination of objects that are pure or impure, pleasant or unpleasant, or those that are free from both.
Thus, briefly stated, there are two kinds: namely, the essence of discrimination itself and the basis and object of discrimination.

Among these, the discrimination of intrinsic nature, the discrimination of distinctions, and the discrimination of grasping at a whole—these three types of discrimination produce the objective basis for the conceptual proliferation of discrimination.
The objects of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) are the entities that serve as the basis and conditions for perceptions, such as form (*rūpa*).

Conceptual proliferation—comprised of and manifested by names, perceptions, and verbal expressions—is the process of conceptualizing and deliberating upon these very entities in terms of immeasurable, diverse, and manifold distinctions.

In this context, the discrimination of "I" and the discrimination of "mine"—these two discriminations can give rise to the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), which is the root of other views and the root of pride, as well as the pride of "I am" (asmimāna), which is the root of other forms of pride.
Among these, the discrimination of the agreeable, the discrimination of the disagreeable, and the discrimination that is neither give rise, as appropriate, to greed, hatred, and delusion.
Therefore, these eight kinds of discrimination serve to produce these three types of phenomena.
If one wishes to briefly explain the essential nature of discrimination, it refers to all minds and mental factors within the three realms.
Furthermore, the verse says:
Bound by two fetters, One stubbornly clings to two intrinsic natures.
Therefore, regarding the liberation from the two bonds, there is truly neither attainment nor vision.
The Commentary says:

When the aforementioned various conceptual discriminations arise, one is immediately bound by the two bonds, namely, the bond of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*) and the bond of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*).
Due to these two fetters, one clings to two intrinsic natures, namely, clinging to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Therefore, once liberated from these two kinds of fetters, one correctly neither apprehends nor perceives these two intrinsic natures.
Why is this so? Because the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) is ultimately non-existent and thus cannot be apprehended.
Although the nature of the dependent origination (paratantra-svabhāva) does exist, because one does not grasp its characteristics, nothing is seen.
Having thus established the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva),
in order to establish the nature of the dependent (paratantra-svabhāva), the reasoning for its establishment shall now be explained.
The verse says:

If the basis and cause of the provisional were different from it, Or if they were destroyed, the two kinds of defilement could not be found; Therefore, one should know that the dependent nature exists.
The treatise says:
One should not proclaim that all phenomena exist merely as designations. Why is this?
Since conventional phenomena (prajñapti-dharma) necessarily have a basis and a cause upon which they depend, conventional phenomena cannot be established in the absence of real entities (dravya).
If it were otherwise, then because there would be no real entities, conventional phenomena would also be non-existent, which would result in the destruction of these two categories of phenomena.
Because these two factors would be destroyed, the phenomena of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) would be unobtainable.
Since the phenomena of affliction are indeed perceived in the present, one should know that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) must necessarily exist.
Furthermore, what are the characteristics of this dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)?
The verse says:
Its essence consists of the marks (*nimitta*) and the heavy residues (*dauṣthulya*); it arises through mutual conditioning.
It does not exist as something natural; therefore, it is said that arising has no intrinsic nature.
The Commentary states:
This dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*) has both characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and heavy latencies (*dauṣṭhulya*) as its essence.
Why is it called the *paratantra-svabhāva* (the dependent nature)?
Because these two arise by serving as mutual conditions for one another.
That is to say, with the *nimitta* (sign) as condition, the *dauṣṭhulya* (coarseness/heaviness) arises; and with the *dauṣṭhulya* as condition, it in turn gives rise to the *nimitta*.
If that is so, why is it called "the naturelessness of arising"?
It is because it is produced by the power of conditions and does not exist spontaneously.
Furthermore, is this other-dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) definitely existent or definitely non-existent?
The verse says:
Neither existence nor non-existence is fixed; all aspects are admitted.
Whether conventional or ultimate, when spoken of as existing, it is said to exist conventionally.
The treatise states:
The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) does not exist as determined by its designation, nor is it entirely non-existent; therefore, in every respect, it is neither existent nor non-existent.
However, it is admitted that all aspects can be expressed in speech—namely, as existent, as non-existent, as both existent and non-existent, or as neither existent nor non-existent.
Question:
Is this dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) substantially existent or nominally existent?
Answer: It should be understood that this nature applies to both the conventional and the substantially existent.
Question:
Is it existent by way of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) or is it existent by way of the ultimate (*paramārtha*)?
Answer: It should be understood that it is said to be existent by way of the conventional.
Furthermore, the verse says:
The proclamation of the self, phenomena, and their functions Is all termed the conventional;
One should know that the ultimate truth Consists of the seven kinds of suchness.
The treatise states:

Regarding conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one should know that it proclaims the self, phenomena, and their functions, as already explained in the "Chapter on Compendium of the Meaning of Purity" (*Śuddhārthasaṃgraha*).
Regarding ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it refers to the seven kinds of suchness (*tathatā*), as already explained in the "Chapter on Compendium of Bases" (*Vastusaṃgraha*).
Furthermore, the verse says:
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) Is the object of the two supreme knowledges;
It is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) And is devoid of identity or difference.
The treatise says:
This ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) should be understood as the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Question:
For what reason are the seven kinds of suchness called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)? Answer:

Because they are the objects of two most excellent types of wisdom, namely, supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*) and the mundane wisdom subsequently attained therefrom (*tat-pṛṣṭhalabdha-lokajñāna*).
Because this ultimate truth is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), it is not the object of any other cognition.
Furthermore, because this ultimate truth is free from conceptual proliferation, it is devoid of identity or difference with respect to phenomena that possess characteristics (*sanimitta-dharma*).
Why is this? Because this suchness cannot be said to be different from, nor not different from, phenomena that possess characteristics.
Furthermore, the verse says:
The objects of focus are pure, Ever without change;
The nature of goodness and the nature of bliss— All are fully accomplished.
The Commentary says:
Because the ultimate truth is free from identity and difference, it should be understood as the nature of the object of purification.
Why is this? Because by taking this object as a focus, one attains the purification of the mind.
One should know that it is also permanent, because its nature never undergoes change at any time.
Furthermore, one should know that it is wholesome because it is the object of purification.
Because it is permanent, one should know that it is blissful.
Furthermore, the verse says:

In reality, the ultimate lacks intrinsic nature; Because the self of conceptual proliferation does not exist, And because the dependent lacks those characteristics, This is the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature.
The treatise states:
The perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is said to be "without nature" because it is non-existent from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha). Why is this so?

Because this intrinsic nature is both the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and the absence of nature (*abhāva*), due to the fact that the nature of self and phenomena is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).

Therefore, it should be understood that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is called the "ultimate absence of nature" because it is the ultimate truth and because its nature is free from conceptual proliferation.

Regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it may also be established as being without nature in terms of the ultimate (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*) because of its distinct characteristics. Why?
Because it lacks the nature of the ultimate.

Furthermore, as previously stated, there are five kinds of characteristics: namely, the characteristic of the signifier, the characteristic of the signified, the characteristic of the relationship between these two, the characteristic of attachment, and the characteristic of non-attachment; moreover, there are three characteristics: namely, the characteristic of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-lakṣaṇa), the characteristic of the dependent nature (paratantra-lakṣaṇa), and the characteristic of the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa).
Do the five subsume the three, or do the three subsume the five?
The verse says:
Based on the three characteristics, one should know that the five types of characteristics are established.
According to what is appropriate for each, there are five distinct types of karma.
The treatise says:
It should be understood that these five characteristics are established based on the three specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Why is this so? The first and second rely on the three specific characteristics; the third relies on the characteristic of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*); the fourth relies on the characteristic of the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*); and the fifth relies on the characteristic of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, each of the three natures has five functions, as already explained in the "Chapter on Comprehending the Meaning of Purity.
Moreover, what was refuted in the preceding "Chapter on Establishing Emptiness" was the grasping at sentient beings, whereas what is refuted in this chapter is the grasping at phenomena.
Regarding these two types of grasping, which arises from which?
The verse says:
"Due to the grasping at phenomena, the deluded ordinary person gives rise to that grasping at a sentient being."
"He eliminates the nature of phenomena through awakening; by awakening to phenomena, his grasping at a self is severed.
The commentary says:
"Due to grasping at phenomena, the foolish worldlings give rise to grasping at sentient beings."
Because they eliminate the active fetters of grasping at sentient beings, they awaken to the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Because they awaken to the nature of phenomena, grasping at phenomena (*dharmanirgraha*) is forever severed.
When grasping at phenomena is severed, one should know that the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of grasping at sentient beings are likewise severed.
Furthermore, regarding what remains unsevered that constitutes defilement (*saṃkleśa*),
and regarding what, when severed, brings about purification (*vyavadāna*)?
The verse says:
Based on the dependent nature, when there is grasping, The habitual perfuming results in defilement;
When there is no grasping, the perfected nature, The habitual perfuming results in purity.
Defilement is of the nature of outflows (*sāsrava*); Purity is then without outflows (*anāsrava*).
One should know that this transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is of two kinds and inconceivable.
The treatise says:
Because of clinging to the first nature within the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), habitual tendencies (vāsanā) arise, whereby defilement (saṃkleśa) is established.
One should know that because the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is free from attachment, when it gives rise to perfuming (*vāsanā*), it becomes pure.

Defilement (*saṃkleśa*) is the nature of outflows (*sāsrava*), while purity (*vyavadāna*) is the nature without outflows (*anāsrava*). One should know that this nature without outflows is precisely the characteristic of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
Furthermore, this transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is inconceivable and is of two kinds.
What is meant by "inconceivable"?
The verse says:
Reality and essence, tranquility and qualities—
all these inconceivable aspects should be known through four paths.
The Commentary says:
This transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is inconceivable by virtue of four principles:
first, by way of its reality, meaning that it is eternal;
second, by way of its essential nature, meaning that it is neither material nor immaterial, and so forth.
Third, by way of tranquility, meaning it abides in tranquility;
fourth, by way of qualities, meaning this transformation of the basis possesses majestic power.

Furthermore, this transformation of the basis is inconceivable and is realized through four kinds of paths: namely, the four kinds of correct practice, the four kinds of thorough investigation, the four kinds of knowledge as-it-is, and the four kinds of objective entities.
What are the four? First, the pervasive object; second, the object of pure conduct; third, the object of skillfulness; and fourth, the object for purifying afflictions.
Among these, the pervasive object further comprises four types:
First, the image with conceptual differentiation; second, the image without conceptual differentiation; third, the culmination of the object; and fourth, the accomplishment of what was to be done.
Regarding the image with conceptual differentiation: it refers to the object of vipaśyanā that is practiced within samādhi and is concordant with the objects of knowledge.
Non-conceptual images refer to the object of samādhi that is concordant with the objects of knowledge, which is the culmination of śamatha.
The culmination of the object refers to the full extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and the mode of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
The accomplishment of what is to be done refers to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) and the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) that relies upon it.
There are five objects for the purification of conduct:

first, impurity; second, compassion; third, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); fourth, the differentiation of the elements (*dhātu-prabheda*); and fifth, mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation (*ānāpānasmṛti*).

There are five types of skillfulness regarding objects: namely, skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*), skillfulness regarding the elements (*dhātu-kauśalya*), skillfulness regarding the sense bases (*āyatana-kauśalya*), skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*), and skillfulness regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).

The objects for purifying afflictions refer to the two types of characteristics regarding the mundane path—the coarseness of the lower stages and the tranquility of the higher stages—and the four noble truths and so forth regarding the supramundane path.
Furthermore, as previously stated, there are two kinds of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). What are these two?
They are the distinction between the transformation of the basis of the Śrāvakas and that of the Bodhisattvas.
The verse says:
There are two kinds of śrāvakas: those who seek tranquility and those who seek enlightenment.
Relying upon the nirmāṇakāya, they proceed toward unsurpassed perfect awakening.
The transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) for all śrāvakas is attained through the cultivation of aversion and turning away;
the cultivation of the bodhisattvas through skillful means is based on non-dual wisdom,
because they do not abide in arising and ceasing.
The wisdom of all Buddhas is unsurpassed, bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; it is inconceivable and non-dual.
The commentary states:

It should be understood that the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) of the śrāvakas is of two kinds: first, that which tends toward quiescent extinction (*śama*), and second, that which tends toward enlightenment (*bodhi*).
Question:

Since the śrāvaka who has attained the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) has forever exhausted future existence (punarbhava), how can they realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi)? Answer:
One abides by means of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and is able to realize *bodhi*; it is not the *vipākakāya* (retribution body).
Furthermore, the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) of the *śrāvaka* is attained by practicing in opposition to the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
The transformation of the basis of the *bodhisattva* is attained by relying upon skillful means (*upāya*) and non-dual wisdom (*advaya-jñāna*).
How is it cultivated through skillful means? It is said:

by means of uninterrupted penetration into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); because the object of focus (*ālambana*) is vast; because of the arousal of supreme diligent effort (*vīrya*); out of regard for sentient beings; and through the thorough understanding of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
What is meant by relying on non-dual wisdom?
It means neither abiding in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa; it is because one does not look back toward saṃsāra, yet looks toward all sentient beings.
For this reason, one should know that the Buddha’s wisdom is most excellent and unsurpassed. Why is this?
Because the wisdom of other sentient beings either abides in saṃsāra or abides in nirvāṇa; therefore, it is not unsurpassed.

Furthermore, the wisdom of all Buddhas brings benefit, profit, and peace to all sentient beings; because it is perfectly capable of fulfilling the welfare of both self and others, it is supreme and unsurpassed.
The wisdom of other sentient beings, however, is either solely for their own benefit or benefits neither, and is therefore not unsurpassed.
For this reason, the wisdom of all Buddhas is inconceivable, for it does not abide in the two extremes and is able to perform deeds that benefit all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is no duality, such as parinirvāṇa and non-parinirvāṇa, because its nature is non-dual.
Chapter Eight: On the Accomplishment of Clear Observation (Abhisamaya), Part One. The Treatise says:
Having thus applied right effort to understand impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, what is it that one desires to observe?
The verse says:
One should know that what is currently being observed consists of inferior, middling, and superior matters;
whether they are with outflows or without outflows; and whether they have been previously seen or experienced, or are universal.
The Treatise says:
In order to manifest the observation of the objects of knowledge— whether inferior, medium, or superior— that are bound to the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness,
that which is "with outflows" (sāsrava) refers to what is subsumed under these very truths of suffering and its origin.
"Untainted" (*anāsrava*) refers to that which is subsumed under the truths of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and the path (*mārga-satya*).
"Not yet seen" refers to that which is subsumed under the [other] four truths.
"Not yet experienced" refers to that which is subsumed under cessation and the path.
"Universal" refers to the objective domain of the knowledge that perceives both manifest and non-manifest phenomena, as well as the knowledge of their categories.
Furthermore, by means of what is there realization?
The verse says:
Supramundane superior wisdom, which can eliminate what is to be abandoned by vision,
is realized through non-conceptualization and relies solely upon meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
The commentary states:
Supramundane wisdom can constitute direct realization (*abhisamaya*), whereas mundane wisdom cannot;
for the purpose of abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing, it is exclusively the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and not the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Question:
What, moreover, is their practice? Answer:
It is the realization through non-conceptualization;
that is, it is the realization of non-conceptual conduct as being present before one, not as something not yet realized.
Question:
Upon what does it rely? Answer:
It relies solely upon dhyāna, not upon the formless realms (ārūpya).
Furthermore, where does clear realization (abhisamaya) occur?
The verse says:
Extreme dejection does not exist in the miserable realms; extreme joy does not exist in the two higher realms.
Those dwelling among humans and devas in the desire realm [attain] the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) when a Buddha appears in the world.
The commentary states:

Direct realization does not arise within the miserable realms (*apāya*), because suffering is constantly present there and extreme dejection prevails, and because it is impossible to realize meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
In the form and formless realms, there is likewise no direct realization (*abhisamaya*), because of the predominance of longing and agitation and the weakness of aversion.

Therefore, direct realization does not arise in the two realms or the three destinies; it arises only in the two destinies of humans and gods within the single realm of desire, when a Buddha appears in the world.
Furthermore, who is able to realize [the truths]?
The verse says:
Those who have not yet abandoned desire, those who have partially abandoned it, and those who have already abandoned desire.
"Solitary, uniquely awakened to perfect enlightenment, the most supreme among those born from me.
The commentary says:
There are five types of *pudgalas* who can enter into clear realization (*abhisamaya*), or there may be none who enter it, because of the absence of a self (*anātman*).
What are these five?
First, those who have not yet abandoned desire; second, those who have partially abandoned desire; third, those who have already abandoned desire; fourth, pratyekabuddhas; and fifth, bodhisattvas.
How should one understand that it is only the mind (*citta*) that can enter into direct realization (*abhisamaya*), and not a self (*ātman*)?
The verse says:
The self is not the cause of cognition, Nor does it itself apprehend objects.
I do not personally realize [this] myself, because I cling to and cherish a self.
Since conditioned phenomena have objects that arise through dependence on conditions,
and because the three types of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and so forth are severed, one realizes it by relying on the mind.
The treatise says:
It is not reasonable to maintain that one can enter into clear realization by conceiving of a self. Why is this?
It is not logical for me to be the cause of cognition,
because if separated from cognition, it could not apprehend objects on its own. Why is this so?
If I were the cause of cognition, I would be impermanent, or else cognition would have to be eternal.
If I myself were able to apprehend objects, I should also be able to apprehend them before cognition has arisen.
Furthermore, if one conceives that "I" can enter into clear realization (*abhisamaya*), then this "I" should also be able to perceive its own nature.
If such were the case, there would be no liberation, because one would be grasping at a self as an object and giving rise to craving for it.
Why is this so? Because there is no one who, without grasping at a self, would fail to give rise to the conceit of "I" and craving for a self.
Therefore, it is logical to say that one can enter into clear realization by relying upon the mind.
Why is this? Because the mind is impermanent; it arises as cognition by depending on objects and conditions.
Furthermore, based upon the mind, both the heavy afflictions (*dausthulya*), the grasping at a self, and attachment to a self can all be completely severed.
Why is this? Because the mind is impermanent, it serves as the cause for the arising of wisdom;
because it possesses an object of perception, it apprehends the objective sphere simultaneously with wisdom.
Because it depends upon various conditions, wisdom does not exist at all times. Furthermore,
because the mind is the basis for the heavy burdens (dausthulya) and its nature is devoid of a self,
once one realizes omniscience, one is able to distance oneself from the heavy burdens and give rise [to wisdom], thereby forever eliminating the grasping at a self and attachment to a self.
How does one enter into clear realization (abhisamaya) through successive stages?
The verse says:
Having matured the mental continuum, or having heard the true Dharma...
Spontaneously and in accordance with ultimate reality, through the application of mental attention, one realizes clear observation;
by binding mindfulness to the object of focus and diligently cultivating tranquil concentration,
through the power of superior roots of goodness, one realizes the factors of the noble path to awakening.
The treatise states:
One who cultivates clear realization (*abhisamaya*) must first bring their own mental continuum to maturity.

Alternatively, they may do so by hearing the true Dharma—namely, the Śrāvaka vehicle—or spontaneously, as in the case of Bodhisattvas and Pratyekabuddhas, because they have applied thorough mental attention within their own inner minds; thus, they are able to enter clear realization.
Next, "binding the mindfulness to the object of focus" refers to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
"Diligent application" refers to the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
"Cultivating tranquil concentration" refers to the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
"Superior roots of goodness" refers to the roots of goodness such as faith and so forth, which constitute the superior provisions previously realized.
"Power" means that they cannot be mixed with the opposing obstacles, such as lack of faith.
The factors for realizing noble awakening refer to the realization of the branches of universal awakening by relying upon them.
The factors for realizing the noble path refer to the realization of the eight branches of the noble path.
In this manner, one successively attains entry into clear observation (*abhisamaya*).
Furthermore, at what point should one say that one has correctly entered into clear realization (*abhisamaya*)?
The verse says:
From this point, one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), And untainted right view (*anāsrava-samyagdṛṣṭi*) arises.
"One should know that through the permanent severance of the three fetters, one realizes clear observation (*abhisamaya*).
The treatise says:
Because of the previously cultivated appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), supramundane right view arises during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

By means of right view, the three fetters are permanently severed—namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*). One should know that up to this stage, one has entered into clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
However, since all phenomena pertaining to the afflictions of the evil destinies are entirely eliminated within this stage, why is it said that only the three fetters are permanently severed?
The verse states:
"Although the afflictions arising from the conception [of a self] are severed, [the elimination of] the evil destinies and the defilements [is implied]."
"Regarding the objects, views, and the Teacher, etc., they are subsumed under the three [fetters] as they arise.
The treatise says:

Because of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one is deluded regarding the objects; because of the adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), one is deluded regarding views; and because of that doubt, one gives rise to confusion regarding the True Dharma taught by the Teacher, the Buddha, and the Saṅgha of Right Practice. Therefore, it is said that only these three fetters are to be permanently severed, according to their predominance.
Furthermore, what are the characteristics of clear realization (*abhisamaya*)?
The verse says:
"By means of prior worldly knowledge, one discriminates the truths to their ultimate conclusion."
Regarding the truths, there is no preparatory application; it is characterized by the definitive arising [of certainty] and the aspect of the union of wisdom with its object.
One should know that the clear realization of the truths (satyābhisamaya) regarding the ultimate nature of the objects of knowledge consists of ten kinds of certainties.
The Treatise says:
"By means of prior mundane wisdom" refers to the wisdom arising from hearing up to the wisdom of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
"Thoroughly discerning the truths" means that one has already completed the thorough discernment of all the truths and no longer applies effort toward them.

The characteristic of definitive arising refers to the characteristic of definitive arising within the objects of the truths under investigation, occurring without the application of effortful exertion; this is the characteristic of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Furthermore, because this definitive wisdom (niścaya-jñāna) reaches the ultimate limit of the appearance of the union with its object,
and because there is no other distinct object to be sought beyond this, this contemplation is called "clear realization" (abhisamaya).
It should be known that these definitive characteristics further comprise ten types. What are the ten?
The verse says:
My nature has no three realms of existence; it is neither extinguished nor dualistic.
Without discrimination and without fear, it is definitively established within the cessation of self.
The commentary says:

Regarding the ten kinds of certainty: first, certainty regarding the non-existence of sentient beings; second, certainty regarding the non-existence of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); third, certainty regarding the existence of selflessness (*anātman*); fourth, certainty regarding the existence of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); and fifth, certainty regarding the existence of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*). These are the certainties therein.

Sixth is certainty regarding non-extinction, which means: either non-extinction because of non-existence, referring to the self of sentient beings and the self of phenomena; or non-extinction because of existence, referring to the two kinds of selflessness.
Seventh, the certainty regarding non-duality, meaning that there is no distinction between phenomena (*dharma*) and the emptiness of phenomena.

Eighth, the certainty regarding non-conceptualization within emptiness; ninth, the certainty regarding fearlessness toward the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). This means that while ordinary fools give rise to various fears regarding this nature, the wise have no fear therein; therefore, it is certain.
Tenth, regarding mastery, there is the certainty of being able to sever [the afflictions], meaning: "I shall no longer seek the means for severance from others," and thus it is certain.
Furthermore, how should one understand the sequence in which such clear realization (abhisamaya) is to be cultivated?
The verse says:
Initiation, realization, outflow, and fulfillment—these four occur in succession;
furthermore, one should know that the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*) and so forth follow in an eightfold sequence.
The treatise says:
The sequence of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) consists of either four, eight, or seven types. What are the four?
First is the initiatory [wisdom], which refers to everything from the wisdom born of hearing up to the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Second is the wisdom of realization, which refers to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Third is the wisdom of outflow, which refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The fourth is fulfillment, which refers to the path of culmination (*niṣṭhāmārga*). What are the eight?
They are the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthitijñāna*) up to the thoroughly purified knowledge (*suvyavadātajñāna*), as previously described.
What are the seven kinds?
The verse says:
Absence of regret regarding the object of focus, Seeing the sphere of experience as it truly is.
The path’s basis is free from delusion, And the pure, differentiated practice brings cessation.
The commentary states:

The sevenfold sequence refers to the purification of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*) up to the purification of knowledge and vision regarding the cessation of practice (*paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-viśuddhi*).
Because ethical discipline (*śīla*) is pure, there is no regret;
because there is no regret, the mind is settled upon its object;
because the mind is settled, one attains the vision of things as they truly are regarding the objects of knowledge.

Next, regarding the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha Jewels that serve as the basis for the path of seeing through knowledge of reality as it is, one attains the fourfold pure confidence (*śraddhā*) accompanied by innate wisdom;

next, one attains decisive wisdom regarding what has been realized and taught by the Sugata, namely: "Only within the Buddha's Dharma is there a purely immaculate path for deliverance from suffering, and not in other teachings";

next, one attains wisdom regarding the distinctions in practice within this path, namely: "The practice with difficulty and slow progress is of inferior quality; the practice with ease and quick progress is of superior quality; and the other two types of practice are of middling quality."
Next, based on superior correct practice, one gives rise to superior knowledge and vision regarding the remaining abandonments.

Furthermore, these seven purifications, beginning with ethical discipline (*śīla*), should be understood as being subsumed under the three trainings when explained briefly, and likewise subsumed under the three purifications.
What are the three purities?
The verse says:
One should know that the three purities comprise [the path]: purity of ethical discipline and purity of mind.
The path that relies upon the objective sphere is called the purification of wisdom.
The commentary states:

There are three kinds of purification, namely, the purification of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*), the purification of the mind (*citta-viśuddhi*), and the purification of wisdom (*prajñā-viśuddhi*).
Within the purification of wisdom, there are furthermore three kinds:
first, regarding the object; second, regarding the basis of the path; and third, regarding the essence of the path.
Within the essence of the path, it should be known that there are again three kinds: namely, by way of purity, by way of differentiation, and by way of abandonment.
Furthermore, within this sequence, by what order does one enter into clear realization (*abhisamaya*)?
The verse says:
Knowing the causes and conditions of the body and so forth, One skillfully penetrates the three periods of time.
Next, one should thoroughly understand the four kinds of suffering, and furthermore, the eight kinds of suffering should be known.
The treatise says:

First, in the stage of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one should skillfully understand the four types of causal conditions regarding body, feeling, mind, and phenomena (*dharma*). That is to say: through the accumulation of nutriment, the body accumulates; through the accumulation of contact (*sparśa*), feeling accumulates; through the accumulation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) accumulates; and through the accumulation of mental attention (*manasikāra*), phenomena accumulate.

Next, one should thoroughly understand this body as it pertains to the three periods of time: that is, observing the arising of phenomena in the future, observing the cessation of phenomena in the past, and observing both the arising and cessation of phenomena in the present.

Next, one should understand that this very body and so forth are afflicted by four types of suffering: namely, the suffering of bearing a heavy burden, the suffering of the transformation of states, the suffering of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*), and the suffering of birth and death.

Since wholesome and unwholesome phenomena act as causes that bring about the suffering of death and rebirth within saṃsāra, to fully understand these two sufferings of death and birth is itself to fully understand the suffering of phenomena.

Immediately following this, one will contemplate the Truths; therefore, one first understands the eight modes of suffering, namely, the suffering of birth up to, in brief, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.
Furthermore, the verse says:
From this correct contemplation of the truths, the wisdom of the sixteen aspects arises;
it serves as the remedy for the four inversions and acts as the basis for each subsequent stage.
The Commentary states:

After knowing the eight types of suffering, one next correctly contemplates the principles of the four truths, giving rise to the wisdom of the sixteen aspects; the former serves as the basis for each subsequent stage.

This means that, in order to counteract the four perversions, the four aspects of the Truth of Suffering are established: first, the aspect of impermanence is established to counteract the perversion of permanence; second, the aspect of suffering is established to counteract the perversions of pleasure and purity; third, the aspect of emptiness is established to counteract the perversion of self; and fourth, the aspect of non-self is established to counteract these [preceding three].
Why is this so? Because the self is empty apart from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and because the very essence of these conditioned phenomena lacks the nature of a self.

Next, regarding the four aspects of the origin—the cause, the arising, the production, and the condition—of the four cravings for permanence, bliss, purity, and self, which constitute the Truth of Origin (*samudaya-satya*): [the practitioner contemplates them as] impermanence, suffering, impurity, and non-self.
Next, regarding this truth of cessation, one gives rise to the four modes of contemplation: cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation.
Next, regarding this truth of the path that realizes it, one gives rise to the four modes of contemplation: path, correctness, practice, and deliverance.
Furthermore, the verse says:
From this point, through further cultivation, there arise in the mind total disenchantment,
discernment of the truths, certainty, and ultimate awakening.
The treatise states:
Following the knowledge of the sixteen aspects, one further cultivates practice; first, there arises a mind that universally feels revulsion toward its own mind, which is called "Heat" (ūṣmagata).
From this point upward, the knowledge that discriminates the Truths (satya) arises, which is called "Summit" (mūrdhan).
From this point upward, the wisdom of definitive awakening arises; this is called "patience" (*kṣānti*).
Furthermore, from this point upward, the wisdom of ultimate awakening arises; this is called the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
*Prakaraṇāryavācāśāstra*, Fascicle Sixteen;
*Prakaraṇāryavācāśāstra*, Fascicle Seventeen.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Eight: The Section on the Culmination of Clear Realization (Abhisamaya), Part Two. The Treatise states:
Having thus attained the roots of goodness such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, one should know that from this point one enters into clear realization.
The verse says:
From this point, there are three moments of liberation-knowledge without further application;
these one hundred and twelve [moments] encompass the abandonment of the ten categories of afflictions.
The Commentary states:

Immediately following this, without further application of effort, three mental cognitions arise that liberate one from the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*):

first, the cognition that internally dispels the conventional designation of sentient beings; second, the cognition that internally dispels the conventional designations of all phenomena (*dharma*); and third, the cognition that universally dispels the conventional designations of both sentient beings and all phenomena.
Among these, the first two are dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), and the third is subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
These three knowledges can sever one hundred and twelve afflictions (*kleśa*), which are subsumed under ten categories.

Regarding the one hundred and twelve afflictions: there are ten types each to be abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and so forth in the desire realm; there are nine types each to be abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering and so forth in the form and formless realms, as anger (*pratigha*) is excluded from each of those.
These are called the one hundred and twelve afflictions (*kleśa*).
Which ten afflictions do they subsume?
They are the five whose nature is view (*dṛṣṭi*) and the five whose nature is not view, as previously explained.
Furthermore, the verse says:
These are the factors of enlightenment; They are the six aspects of purified wisdom.
Because their activity is non-conceptual, They are established according to their functions.
The Treatise says:

It should be known that this wisdom is the true realization of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) and not a stage of expedient means; it also possesses six kinds of characteristics of pure wisdom, namely: the characteristic of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).

Because this wisdom is non-conceptual, the characteristics of the six types of wisdom are established merely according to their respective functions; it should be understood that these six kinds are not established by way of differences in their modes of activity.
Furthermore, the verse says:
When a bodhisattva abides in this stage, having first cultivated the power of superior causes,
they give rise to a mind of equanimity regarding the suffering of their own body and that of others.
The treatise states:

Within this stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), because bodhisattvas have previously cultivated the power of superior provisions, they give rise to five kinds of equanimous minds regarding the suffering within their own and others' continuums. These are: the equanimous mind of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*), the equanimous mind of selflessness, the equanimous mind of the exertion of abandonment, the equanimous mind of the exertion of non-attachment to flavors, and the equanimous mind of the clear realization of all bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, the verse says:
This is the intention of the Great Self; In its intrinsic nature, nothing is attained.
One should know that the vast intention Is non-differentiation regarding the two natures.
The Commentary states:

It should be understood that this nature of the mind of equality is itself the *āśaya* of the Great Self (*mahātman*) and the vast *āśaya*, because nothing is apprehended within the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

One also finds nothing to be grasped regarding the faults of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the virtues of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), because of the absence of conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*).
Furthermore, the verse says:
Next, sixteen lines above, Is the pure mundane knowledge (*śuddha-laukika-jñāna*).
"Because it counteracts the realms and stages, the ultimate task is accomplished.
The commentary states:

From this point onward, following the clear observation of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), there are sixteen aspects within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in which mundane and supramundane pure wisdoms arise.

This refers to the arising of two types of knowledge regarding the truth of suffering associated with the desire realm: first, the knowledge of analytical investigation through clear observation (*abhisamaya-parīkṣā-jñāna*), and second, the knowledge of certainty through clear observation (*abhisamaya-niścaya-jñāna*);
there are likewise these two types of knowledge regarding the truth of suffering associated with the form and formless realms.

Just as there are four kinds of knowledge regarding the truth of suffering, so too there are four kinds of knowledge for each of the truths of origin, cessation, and the path; thus, in total, there are sixteen kinds of knowledge.

Furthermore, regarding such wisdom of clear realization (*abhisamaya*): if it is that attained by Śrāvakas and others, it serves as the antidote to the afflictions (*saṃkleśa*) of the three realms—desire, form, and formlessness;
if it is that attained by Bodhisattvas, it serves as the antidote to the ten obstacles to the stages (*bhūmi*).

In this way, one should know that all tasks to be accomplished reach their ultimate fulfillment; that is to say, the ultimate fulfillment of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), which is also the ultimate fulfillment of the wisdom of clear realization (*abhisamaya-jñāna*), and is termed the "ultimate clear realization" (*paryanta-abhisamaya*).
Furthermore, the verse says:
These distinctions of clear realization (abhisamaya) are either six or eighteen;
their characteristics, benefits, and varieties are numerous, as explained in the sūtras and śāstras.

The treatise states: It should be known that there are further six types of differentiation in clear realization (*abhisamaya*): first, the clear realization of reflection; second, the clear realization of faith; third, the clear realization of ethical discipline; fourth, the clear realization of the truths through the knowledge of clear realization; fifth, the clear realization of the truths through the knowledge at the limit of clear realization; and sixth, the ultimate clear realization.
Question:
What constitutes the essence of the clear realization through reflection? Answer:
It has as its essence the wisdom produced by superior reflection, or the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) that accompany it.
Question:
What is the essence of the clear realization through faith (śraddhābhisamaya)?
Answer:

Its essence consists of the pure faith in the Three Jewels based on superior mundane and supramundane conditions, or it consists of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) that accompany them.
Question:
What constitutes the essence of the clear observation of ethical discipline (*śīla-abhisamaya*)? Answer:
Its essence consists of the bodily and vocal actions beloved by the noble ones (*ārya-kānta*), or alternatively, the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) that accompany them.
Question:
What constitutes the essence of the clear realization of the truths through the wisdom of clear realization? Answer:

It has as its essence the noble wisdom that takes the non-established truths (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*) as its object, or alternatively, the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) that accompany it.
Question:
What constitutes the essence of the realization of the truths through the knowledge at the conclusion of clear observation (*abhisamayāntika-jñāna-satyābhisamaya*)?

Answer: Its essence consists of the noble wisdom that takes the established truths (*prajñaptisatya*) as its object, or it consists of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) that accompany it.
Question:
What constitutes the essence of ultimate realization (*abhisamaya*)? Answer:

Its essence consists of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and so forth; or alternatively, it consists of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) that accompany them.
Furthermore, there are eighteen varieties of this clear realization (*abhisamaya*): namely, the clear realization of the wisdom born of hearing,

the clear realization of the wisdom born of reflection, the clear realization of the wisdom born of cultivation, the clear realization of the wisdom of the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*),

the clear realization of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the clear realization of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the clear realization of the ultimate path (*niṣṭhāmārga*), and the purification of the unwholesome...
The clear mundane knowledge realization; the well-purified mundane knowledge realization; the ultimate knowledge realization;
the impurely purified knowledge with conceptualization regarding practice realization; the purely purified knowledge with conceptualization regarding practice realization;
the purely purified knowledge without conceptualization regarding practice realization; and that which precedes the accomplishment of what is to be done.

The clear realization of the wisdom of practice, the clear realization of the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done, the clear realization of the subsequent wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done,
the clear realization of the wisdom of śrāvakas and others, and the clear realization of the wisdom of bodhisattvas and others.
Furthermore, the characteristics and benefits of such clear realization (*abhisamaya*) should be understood as manifold according to various sūtras and śāstras.
Question:
What are the characteristics of the clear realization through reflection (*cintā-abhisamaya*)?
Answer:

If there is one who accomplishes the contemplation of reflection, they are able to correctly understand that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all conditioned phenomena are suffering, all dharmas are without self, and nirvāṇa is tranquil.
Although he dwells in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), he is already able to understand all this with such certainty that no śramaṇa,
brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world can rightfully lead him astray or cause him to relinquish it.
Question:
What are the characteristics of the clear realization of faith? Answer:

If there is one who has accomplished the clear realization of faith—whether abiding in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or not abiding in that stage—they will, in this present life or in future lives, never proclaim among a different assembly that there is another great teacher, another well-spoken Dharma, or another Sangha of right practice.
Question:
What are the characteristics of the clear observation of ethical discipline (*śīla-abhisamaya*)? Answer:

If there are those who have accomplished the clear observation of ethical discipline (*śīla-abhisamaya*), they will never intentionally take the life of even an animal, nor engage in taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, lying with full knowledge, or drinking *sura*, *maireya*, and *madana*—alcoholic liquors that cause heedlessness.
Question:
What are the characteristics of the clear realization of the truths through the wisdom of clear realization? Answer:

If there is one who has achieved the realization of wisdom and the realization of the truths, they will never rely upon heterodox views to initiate karmic actions, nor will they harbor doubt or delusion regarding their own realization, nor will they seek purification by being attached to the signs of auspiciousness in all places of birth, nor will they slander the Three Vehicles or create karma for the evil realms; how much less could they commit the various immediate transgressions (*ānantarya-karma*) such as harming one's father or mother, and they shall ultimately not undergo an eighth existence.
Question:
What are the characteristics of the clear realization of the truths through the knowledge at the conclusion of the clear realization? Answer:

If there is one who has accomplished the realization of the truths through the knowledge at the conclusion of clear observation (*abhisamayāntika-jñāna-satyābhisamaya*), they will never feel timid or afraid when others pose difficult questions regarding their own realization.
Question:
What are the characteristics of ultimate realization (*paryavasānābhisamaya*)?
Answer:

If one has attained ultimate realization (*niṣṭhā-abhisamaya*), they will never fall into the five bases of transgression; they will never intentionally take the life of a sentient being, nor take what is not given, nor engage in sexual misconduct—that is, the practice of non-celibacy; they will never speak falsehoods, hoard wealth, or indulge in sensual desires. Furthermore, they will never fear matters that cannot be definitively explained (*avyākṛta-vastu*), and they will never cling to the views that suffering and pleasure are produced by oneself, produced by another, produced by both self and another, or produced neither by self nor another but arising without cause.
All such instances as these are termed the characteristics (*nimitta*) of clear realization (*abhisamaya*); one should know that this is itself the benefit (*anuśaṃsa*) of clear realization.
If one follows the sūtras and the śāstras, it is as explained extensively above.
Chapter Nine: On the Accomplishment of Yoga. The *Śāsanodbhāvana-śāstra* states:
The preceding section explained that within this stage, the bodhisattva first cultivates the power of causes and so forth.
What is called the power of prior causes?
The verse says:
The yoga of the perfection of wisdom, And meditative equipoise free from conceptual construction.
"In every respect and in all ways, there is no conceptual differentiation.
The commentary states:

Relying upon *samāpatti* (meditative attainment), one initiates the superior practice of the yoga of *prajñāpāramitā*. This very right wisdom (*samyak-prajñā*) is able to reach the other shore; as it is the most supreme skillful means for great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), it is therefore called "yoga."

This meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) upon which one relies is without conceptual differentiation (*avikalpa*), because it is without conceptual differentiation regarding all phenomena (*dharma*) and in every respect (*sarvākāra*).
What is meant by "all" and "in every respect"?
The verse says:
All things in all their aspects, the three characteristics and the three wheels—
namely, names, characteristics, defilement and purity, as well as that which is neither of these two.
The treatise states:
"All" refers to the three spheres:
first, the objects of knowledge; second, the wisdom that knows; and third, the knower.
"All aspects" refers to three characteristics: first, the characteristic of names;
second, the characteristic of defilement and purity; and third, the characteristic of neither.
"Names" refers to the twelve kinds, such as provisional designations and so forth.
"Name and mark" refers to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
"Defiled" refers to afflicted phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*).
"Pure" refers to all wholesome phenomena (*kuśaladharma*).
That which is neither is the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena.
Furthermore, regarding that which has been described as "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*), with respect to what kind of phenomena is it said to be non-conceptual?
The verse says:
Regarding phenomena and the emptiness of phenomena, there are no two kinds of conceptual proliferation;
they are non-conceptual and infinite, for anything beyond this is not reasonable.
The treatise says:
Since both phenomena and the emptiness of phenomena are devoid of these two kinds of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), they are called "non-conceptual. What are these two?
That is to say, there is both existence and non-existence. Why is this?
Form is not existent, because the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is non-existent.
Nor is it non-existent, because the entities that serve as the basis for those designations do exist.
The emptiness of form is also not existent, because it is manifested through the absence of the imagined nature;
nor is it non-existent, because it is manifested through the selflessness of all phenomena.

Just as it is with form and the emptiness of form, so too should one know that it is the same for all other phenomena and the emptiness of all phenomena. Apart from these phenomena and their emptiness, no other object can be apprehended; therefore, only two kinds of non-conceptuality are taught.
It is not that non-conceptualization itself becomes further conceptualized, for that would entail the fault of infinite regress, as there would be no further object of knowledge beyond this.
Furthermore, the verse says:
If there were absolutely nothing apprehended, There would be neither wisdom nor liberation.
Both establish the grasping of that which is beyond words, in order to conform to [the truth] that it is not without function.
The treatise says:
If these two kinds of conceptualization did not exist, then there would be no grasping.
Because there is no grasping whatsoever, even the essence of wisdom does not exist, let alone reaching the other shore.
Therefore, there must necessarily be a departure from verbal signs and grasping.
By virtue of this [absence of] grasping, both wisdom and the reaching of the other shore are fully accomplished.

Why is this so? Because by means of this noble wisdom, although one does not apprehend the nature of characteristics as they are expressed in words, one nevertheless apprehends the nature of characteristics that transcends words.
Question:
If this noble wisdom did not apprehend the characteristics and nature [of phenomena] as they are expressed in words, the proclamation of the True Dharma would be useless.
Answer: Not so;
it is for the sake of conformity.
Why is this so? It is because the Tathāgata proclaims the True Dharma in order to conform to the relinquishing of the grasping at verbal signs.
Chapter Ten: On the Accomplishment of the Inconceivable. From the *Śāsanodbhāvana-śāstra*, Chapter Ten: On the Accomplishment of the Inconceivable. The Treatise says:

One must first engage in contemplation before entering into direct realization (*abhisamaya*); therefore, one should employ skillful means to contemplate while remaining detached from that which is inconceivable.
What is meant by "that which is inconceivable"?
The verse says:
Nine matters are inconceivable because they rely upon five bases;
there are five kinds of causes, and both virtues and faults each have three types.

The treatise states: There are nine kinds of things that are inconceivable: first, the self; second, sentient beings; third, the world; fourth, karmic retribution; fifth, the sphere of those in meditative concentration; sixth, the sphere of the Buddhas; seventh, the fourteen undeclared points; eighth, that which is not the true Dharma; and ninth, all that is induced and subsumed by the afflictions.
If one contemplates these nine matters, such contemplation will necessarily depend upon five bases before it arises:
first, views; second, patience; third, investigation; fourth, gain; and fifth, distraction.
Relying on views, one conceives of a self and sentient beings;
relying on acceptance, one conceives of the world;

and relying on investigation, one conceives of karmic retribution, the spheres of those in meditative concentration, the spheres of the Buddhas, and the fourteen points of things that are set aside as indeterminate.
Relying on thoughts of gain and honor is not the true Dharma;
relying on thoughts of distraction is that which is drawn in and encompassed by all afflictions.
Question:
For what reasons and conditions should these nine matters not be contemplated? Answer:
For five reasons and conditions.
First, because the self and sentient beings lack intrinsic characteristics, they should not be subject to conceptualization.
Second, because the world manifests as a conditioned formation, it should not be subject to conceptualization.
Third, because the karmic retributions and the two types of objects possess a profoundly deep character, they should not be subject to conceptual deliberation.
Fourth, because indeterminate matters do not possess a fixed character, they should not be subject to conceptual deliberation.
Fifth, because it is not subsumed by the true Dharma or by the various afflictions, and because it leads to characteristics that result in what is meaningless, it should not be contemplated.
If one were to contemplate such matters, know that it would lead to three kinds of faults:
first, the fault of mental distraction; second, the fault of generating non-merit; and third, the fault of failing to attain the wholesome.
If it is inconceivable, it can induce three kinds of merit; the opposite should be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, the verse says:
It should not be thought of nor recorded, One should know this is due to four causes.
"Not fixed as one, yet profound; it leads to dwelling in signs that are meaningless.
The commentary says:
Furthermore, to state it briefly, due to four kinds of causes, one should not personally contemplate inconceivable matters, nor should one provide explanations for others regarding them.
First, because it is not certain whether the self and sentient beings exist or do not exist, they are inconceivable and cannot be definitively declared.
Second, because both karmic retribution and its two objective spheres are profoundly deep, they are inconceivable and cannot be definitively declared.

Third, matters concerning the world that are indeterminate are not the true Dharma; they are drawn in and encompassed by all afflictions and lead to what is meaningless. Therefore, they are not to be contemplated and are not to be declared.

Fourth, True Suchness is neither identical to nor separate from phenomena such as conditioned activities; because its nature is established by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), it cannot be conceptualized and cannot be definitively described.
Furthermore, the verse says:
One should not contemplate whether the self exists or does not exist, For this results in two faults;
regarding others as well, there are likewise two faults. Thus, one should not contemplate [the self] as being either identical to or different from [the aggregates].
The treatise says:
One should not contemplate whether the self exists or does not exist. Why is this?
Because it would result in two faults:
if one conceives of [the object] as existing, one falls into the fault of the superimposition (*samāropa*) of existence upon that which is not truly existent;
if one conceives of it as non-existent, one falls into the fault of the denial (*apavāda*) of existence regarding that which exists conventionally.
If one maintains that [the self] is either identical to or different from other sentient beings, two faults likewise ensue.
If one maintains they are identical, there is the fault that there would be many sentient beings;
if one maintains they are different, there is the fault that it would not be the six sense bases.
Furthermore, the verse says:
Although the two do not depend on views, They should not be conceptualized because they are established;
Such arising occurs without conceptualization, Because it is accompanied by three faults.
The treatise says:
Although these two—the world of sentient beings and the receptacle world—do not depend on views, they likewise should not be conceptualized. Why is this?
Because it is commonly understood by the world as having the characteristic of being presently manifest.
Question:
Why does one not reflect on whether this thing arises in such a manner or not?
Answer:
If one reflects in this manner, one might think that it is exactly thus, or different from thus, or that it is not thus; for these three types of faults would follow accordingly.
Furthermore, the verse says:
The happy realms and the miserable realms— The two agents are not fixed;
Past wholesome and unwholesome karma, Their locations, objects, and so forth, are inconceivable.
The treatise states:

Regarding karmic retribution, one should not speculate that those who practice the cultivation of merit will certainly go to a happy realm, nor that those who commit evil deeds will certainly go to an evil realm, because these outcomes are not fixed.
Furthermore, the pure and impure karma of past lives—whether in terms of their location, their specific events, their causes, or their retributions—is inconceivable.
Moreover, the verse says:
The nature of true thusness and the outflow-free state, The purposeful accomplishment of beneficial deeds.
The Tathāgata is one who dwells in meditative concentration (*dhyāyin*), because he possesses incomparable mastery.
The commentary states:

Within the two types of spheres—the sphere of those who dwell in meditative concentration and the sphere of the Buddha—both *tathatā* (suchness) and the nature of the untainted (*anāsrava*) are inconceivable.
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the "accomplished activities" of the Buddhas and others: the deeds performed for the benefit of sentient beings are likewise inconceivable. Why is this?
Because there are no analogies;
within all the worlds, there is not even the slightest matter that can serve as an analogy for these two kinds of profound realms.

Furthermore, because they possess mastery, the Tathāgatas and others perform their activities by virtue of having attained mastery over the mind through internal realization; for all worldly functions are not observed to occur apart from the conjunction of causes and conditions.
Furthermore, the verse says:
What is proclaimed by the non-Buddhists Can lead only to what is meaningless;
It is irrational, far removed from the four [noble] states, And being indeterminate, it is not to be contemplated.
The Treatise says:
All matters that should not be recorded and should not be contemplated are so because they are what is taught by various heterodox outsiders;
furthermore, they lead to all manner of lack of benefit.
Because it does not accord with correct principle;

and because it is far removed from the four bases of right reflection, namely: the basis of reflection on causes, the basis of reflection on results, the basis of reflection on affliction, and the basis of reflection on purification.
Furthermore, as previously stated, if one contemplates that [the self], there are three kinds of faults.
How do they come to be?
The verse says:
Exerting effort in what is improper, slandering the Great Self,
and failing to cultivate pure virtue— therefore, these three faults are formed.
The commentary says:

Because one exerts effort in what is improper, there arises the fault of mental distraction; because one slanders the supreme qualities of those who have attained meditative concentration and of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, there arises the fault of non-merit; and because one does not initiate pure and wholesome dharmas, there is the fault of failing to attain the wholesome.
Furthermore, the verse says:
One should remain far removed from the inconceivable, And contemplate that which is within the sphere of the conceivable;
Possessing eight kinds of merit, Therefore, one should contemplate in accordance with reality.
The treatise says:
Because there are such faults for one who forcibly attempts to conceptualize that which is inconceivable, one should remain far removed from it.
One should reflect according to reality upon that which is conceivable; if one reflects in this manner, it possesses eight meritorious qualities.

What are these eight? They are as follows: being able to thoroughly understand the cryptic teachings and the profound teachings; contemplating based on the meaning rather than the literal words; possessing a small measure of pure faith and conviction; possessing a small measure of wisdom and analytical observation; firm contemplation; precise contemplation; constant and diligent contemplation; and being well-able to bring one's contemplations to completion without becoming weary or regressing along the way.
Furthermore, the verse says:
That which is taught by all Buddhas, Is not contradicted by the Omniscient One;
Because of five causes and two causes, One should not entertain doubts regarding this.
The treatise says:

For five reasons, one should not take pleasure in contemplating that which is inconceivable: because it was spoken by the Buddhas; and because it is not in contradiction with thorough knowledge, abandonment, realization, and cultivation within the Four Noble Truths.
Furthermore, it is briefly established by two causes: namely, scripture (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*).
Scripture refers to that which has been spoken by the Buddhas; realization refers to the thorough knowledge of suffering and so forth.
Chapter Eleven: Compendium of the Sublime Determination (*Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*). Part One of the Eleventh Chapter of the *Śāsanodbhāvana-śāstra*. The Treatise says:

Having thus reflected upon the skillful means for distancing oneself from inconceivable states, one should initiate various forms of supreme discernment regarding nine matters by means of ten aspects.
What are these ten?
The verse says:
Number, characteristics, distinctions, existence, location, limits, and origination;
"Perception, skillfulness, inclusion, and so forth—these are the superior determinations of various matters.

The treatise states: "The ten kinds of characteristics are: first, number; second, characteristic; third, differentiation; fourth, existence; fifth, location; sixth, limit; seventh, origination; eighth, perception; ninth, skillfulness; and tenth, inclusion, etc."
In this context, "number" refers to the fifteen categories of form (*rūpa*), and so forth.

"Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the conventionally established characteristic (*prajñapti-lakṣaṇa*), the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
In this context, the "thing" (vastu) is also called a "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa), because it is that which is characterized.

The "name" (nāman) is also called a characteristic, as is the "correspondence" (yoga), because both are the complete set of characteristics; it is like how the correspondence with the color of fire indicates the presence of heat.
Sentient beings such as these are also called "characteristics" (*nimitta*), because they possess characteristics.
Grasping (*upādāna*) is also called a "characteristic," because it is the essence of that which characterizes.
As for their distinctions, they refer to the differentiations such as having form or being formless, being visible or being invisible, and so forth.
"Existence" refers to existence as designation (*prajñaptisat*), existence as substance (*dravyasat*), and ultimate existence (*paramārthasat*).
