"Location" refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) abiding together with their derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), or form and mind abiding in the same location, or the mind of the form realm and so forth abiding successively in dependence upon a body belonging to the desire realm.
"Limit" (paryanta) refers to such things as form reaching its limit at the Form Realm and at the ultimate atom; likewise, pleasant feeling reaches its limit up to the Third Dhyāna, and so forth.
Arising refers to the production of phenomena through such causes and conditions, such as the arising from the force of a projection and so forth.
Perception refers to the delusion regarding phrases and the like.
"Skillfulness" refers to skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*) and so forth.
"Inclusion and so forth" refers to inclusion, association, basis, object-condition, or formal inquiry.

There are many such types of questions and discussions, namely: the single-phrase question, the question following the preceding phrase, the question following the subsequent phrase, the four-phrase question, and the question regarding non-existent things.
One who can thoroughly understand these in this manner is said to be skilled in answering questions.
Furthermore, regarding all matters, one should give rise to various forms of supreme discernment (*viniścaya*). Among these, the discernment of mind and mental factors shall now be explained first.
The verse says:
The nature of mind is of two kinds: Maturation (*vipāka*) and transformation (*pravṛtti*).
First is the ālayavijñāna; second, the seeds—these two should be known.
The treatise says:
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of mind-nature: first, the maturation mind (vipākacitta); second, the evolving mind (pravṛtticitta).
Regarding the ripening consciousness (*vipākacitta*), it is precisely the ālayavijñāna, also termed the "consciousness of all seeds" (*sarvabījaka-vijñāna*).
This, moreover, should be understood as being of two kinds: first, its establishment through proof (*siddhi*), and second, its formal definition (*vyavasthāna*).
How is this established?
The verse says:
Appropriation, the beginning, clarity, seeds, karma, and bodily sensation.
The mindless attainments and the end of life—these would all be irrational [if it did not exist].
The treatise says:
The ālayavijñāna is proven to definitely exist by means of eight kinds of evidence.

That is to say, if the ālayavijñāna did not exist, the appropriation of the basis would be impossible; the initial arising [of consciousness] would certainly be impossible; clear arising would be impossible; the seeds of all phenomena would be impossible; the four types of karmic functions would be impossible; various bodily sensations would be impossible; the two mindless meditative attainments would be impossible; and the consciousness at the time of death would be impossible.
Question:
Why is it that, if the ālayavijñāna did not exist, the appropriation of the basis (āśrayopādāna) could not be established? Answer:
It is due to five causes. What are these five?
Namely, the ālayavijñāna arises from the cause of prior formations, while the evolving consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, arise from present conditions.
As the Sūtra says:
"The various evolving consciousnesses arise by the power of the sense faculties, their objects, and attention," and so forth at length.
This is called the first cause.
Furthermore, the six groups of consciousness can be found to be either wholesome or unwholesome; this is called the second reason.
Moreover, the six groups of consciousness cannot possibly be found to be comprised solely within the category of uniform, indeterminate maturation (*vipāka*); this is called the third reason.

Furthermore, the six groups of consciousness each arise based on their respective supports; if each consciousness were to arise based on its own specific support, then those specific supports would have to be appropriated while the others would not, which is logically untenable.
Even if one grants that there is a grasper, it is still illogical because consciousness is detached [from the body].
This is called the fourth reason.
Furthermore, there would be the fault that the basis [of consciousness] would have to undergo repeated appropriation (*upādāna*).
Why is this so? Because visual consciousness sometimes arises and sometimes does not arise; the same is true for the other consciousnesses.
This is called the fifth reason.

It is not logical [to claim that the self exists], because it is produced by causes consisting of prior karma and present conditions; because it is either wholesome or unwholesome; because it cannot be apprehended as a single entity; because it has distinct bases; and because it would entail the fault of being repeatedly appropriated.
Question:
Why is it that an initial arising cannot be apprehended? Answer:
Should there be an objection stating:
"If the ālayavijñāna exists, then two consciousnesses would arise simultaneously," one should reply to them as follows:
You falsely conceive of a fault where there is none, for it is possible for two consciousnesses to arise simultaneously.

Why is this so? It is because if someone were to desire to see, and so forth, up to desiring to cognize, at one and the same time, it would be illogical for only one specific consciousness to arise first.

Why is this? At that time, there is no distinction in the mental attention (*manasikāra*), and the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) appear without impairment; for what cause and condition would consciousness not arise simultaneously?
Question:
Why is it that the arising of clarity cannot be apprehended? Answer:

If one were to dogmatically maintain that consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously, then a clear and distinct mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) operating in the same object as the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and others would be impossible. Why is this so?

When mindfulness arises taking a past object as its condition, at that time the non-lucid mental consciousness (manovijñāna) proceeds in the present; it is not the case that the mental consciousness is currently active with respect to a present object.
Since there exists such a lack of clarity [in the mental consciousness], one must therefore admit that the various consciousnesses arise simultaneously;
otherwise, one must admit that the sixth mental consciousness lacks the nature of clarity, which would constitute a logical error.
Question:
For what reason is the seed not obtainable? Answer:
Because the six groups of evolving consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ vijñānakāyāḥ*) are each distinct from one another.

Why is this so? These six evolving consciousnesses arise as unwholesome immediately after wholesome states; wholesome states arise again immediately after unwholesome states; neutral (*avyākṛta*) states arise immediately after both; inferior realms arise immediately after middling realms; and sublime realms arise immediately after middling realms.

In this way, it is not logically tenable that a superior realm arises immediately after an inferior realm, that the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) arises immediately after the outflowing (*sāsrava*), that the outflowing arises immediately after the outflow-free, that the supramundane arises immediately after the mundane, or that the mundane arises immediately after the supramundane; such characteristics cannot constitute the essence of the seed.

Furthermore, since those various consciousnesses are interrupted for long periods, yet their continuity flows on without ceasing for a long duration, it is therefore not logical that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) can maintain the seeds.
Question:
For what reason are all karmas unapprehendable? Answer:
If the various consciousnesses did not arise simultaneously and their respective karmas did not proceed together, it would not be logical. Why is this?
To speak briefly, there are four kinds of karma:
First, the function of discerning the vessel-world; second, the function of discerning the basis; third, the function of discerning the self;

and fourth, the function of discerning objects. These four types of discerning functions are simultaneously observable in every moment; they do not exist as such distinct functional operations within a single consciousness in a single moment. Therefore, there must necessarily be the simultaneous arising of multiple consciousnesses.
Question:
For what reason is bodily sensation impossible to obtain if the ālayavijñāna does not exist? Answer:

That is to say, there is someone who, whether through correct reflection or incorrect reflection, engages in investigation; whether the mind is in meditative concentration or not, various and manifold bodily sensations arise. If this consciousness did not exist, such bodily sensations could not be experienced;
since they are indeed presently experienced, the ālayavijñāna must certainly exist.
Question:
Why is it that, if the ālayavijñāna did not exist, the various mindless meditative attainments could not be obtained? Answer:
As the Bhagavat said:
"One should know that when entering the attainment of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), consciousness does not depart from the body.
If this consciousness were absent, then at those times, consciousness would have departed from the body."
If consciousness were to depart from the body, one would necessarily lose life; it cannot be said that [consciousness] remains in meditative absorption.
Question:
For what reason is consciousness unobtainable at the time of death if the ālayavijñāna does not exist?

Answer: It is as when someone is approaching the end of life; either from the upper part of the body, consciousness gradually departs and the sensation of cold gradually arises, or from the lower part of the body. It is not that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does not function at such times; therefore, we know that only the *ālayavijñāna* is capable of sustaining the body.
If this consciousness were abandoned, one would perceive a sensation of coldness in those parts of the body, and the body would lack tactile perception;
however, this is not the case for the mental consciousness. Therefore, it is illogical that this consciousness should be absent.
Thus has been explained the reasoning for the establishment of the ālayavijñāna.
How is it established?
The verse says:
The objective referent and association are mutually the nature of two causes;
consciousness and the rest flow together, [characterized by] defilement and cessation.
The commentary says:
Briefly stated, the establishment of this consciousness is by way of five aspects:

first, the aspect of the objective referent; second, the aspect of association; third, the aspect of mutual causality; fourth, the aspect of simultaneous occurrence; and fifth, the aspect of defilement and its cessation.

It should be understood that the first four types of characteristics establish the process of arising (pravṛtti), while the latter one type of characteristic establishes the process of cessation (nivṛtti).
Question:
How are the characteristics of the objective referent (ālambana-nimitta) established?

Answer: Briefly stated, this consciousness functions by discerning two kinds of objects: first, by discerning internal appropriation; second, by discerning the external, non-conceptual phenomenal world as its vessel.

Regarding the discernment of internal appropriation (*ādāna*): this refers to the discernment of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of false attachment to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), as well as the various material sense-faculties (*indriya*) and their bases. That is to say, in the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) or the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), there is only the appropriation of the habitual tendencies of false attachment.

Regarding the discernment of the external, non-conceptual vessel-world: this refers to the discernment of the ālayavijñāna—which serves as the basis for internal appropriation—such that at all times, without interruption, there appears the appearance of the vessel-world.
For example, when a lamp flame arises, it internally grasps the wick and oil, while externally emitting light.

In the same way, one should understand that the principle by which the ālayavijñāna arises is likewise: it internally conditions and grasps the objects of appropriation, and externally conditions the objects of the vessel-world.
Furthermore, this very consciousness is subtle in its engagement with objects, such that it is difficult for even the wise of the world to comprehend.
Moreover, this very consciousness engages its objects without interruption and without change; from the initial moment of appropriation until the end of life, it flows as a single-taste discernment.
Furthermore, this very consciousness arises and ceases moment by moment with respect to its objects; one should know that its continuity through moments flows on as neither permanent nor unitary.

Moreover, this very consciousness, within the desire realm, takes as its object a limited sphere of appropriation; within the form realm, it takes as its object an extensive sphere of appropriation; within the formless realm, in the spheres of Infinite Space and Infinite Consciousness, it takes as its object an immeasurable sphere of appropriation; in the sphere of Nothingness, it takes as its object a subtle sphere of appropriation; and in the sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, it takes as its object an extremely subtle sphere of appropriation.

Thus, because it discriminates two kinds of objective supports (*ālambana*), because it discriminates objective supports subtly, because it discriminates through similarity, because it discriminates moment by moment, because it discriminates limited appropriated objective supports, because it discriminates vast appropriated objective supports, because it discriminates immeasurable appropriated objective supports, because it discriminates subtle appropriated objective supports, and because it discriminates extremely subtle appropriated objective supports—this is called the establishment of the characteristics of the objective support of the *ālayavijñāna*.
Question:
How is the establishment of the characteristics of associated transformation defined? Answer:

This ālayavijñāna is constantly associated with five universal mental factors (*cittasamprayukta-dharma*), namely: attention (*manaskāra*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*).
These five factors are also comprised within the category of maturation (*vipāka*); they are extremely subtle, and thus difficult to discern even for those of great wisdom in the world.
In this way, the mental factors associated with this mind also constantly and uniformly engage their objects.
Furthermore, the feeling associated with this very consciousness is exclusively of a neutral nature, being neither painful nor pleasant.
It should be understood that the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the other mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) are likewise.

Thus, because they are associated with the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), because they are associated with a single type of maturation (*vipāka*), because they are associated with the most subtle [consciousness], because they arise in association with an object that is constantly of a single type, because they are associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*), and because they are associated exclusively with the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), this is called the establishment of the mode of activity of the *ālaya-vijñāna* as it functions through association.
Question:
How are they established as mutual causes? Answer:
The ālayavijñāna and those evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñānas) serve as two kinds of causes for one another: first, it is the generative cause as seeds; second, it is the causal basis.

Regarding the generative cause as seeds: this means that whenever any evolving consciousness—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—arises, all of them arise solely due to the seeds within the ālayavijñāna.

Regarding the cause of the basis: it means that because the five groups of consciousness arise by depending upon the material sense organs (rūpīndriya) grasped by the ālayavijñāna, they do not occur without such appropriation.
Furthermore, because this consciousness exists, the mental faculty (manas-indriya) comes to be; based upon this mental faculty as its support, mental consciousness arises.

Just as the five groups of sensory consciousnesses proceed by depending on the five types of material faculties such as the eye, and these five faculties are not non-existent, so too it is with mental consciousness: the mental faculty is not non-existent.

Furthermore, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and the ālayavijñāna function as two kinds of causes: first, because they nourish their seeds within the present life; and second, because they gather and plant those seeds so that they may arise in future lives.

Regarding the nourishment of those seeds within the present life: this refers to how, in accordance with the ālayavijñāna as its basis, whenever wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arise, they do so by arising and ceasing simultaneously with that single basis, thereby perfuming (*vāsana*) this consciousness in such and such a manner.

Due to these causes and conditions, the subsequent evolving consciousnesses proceed as wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate; they proceed with increasing intensity, proceed with blazing vigor, and arise with full clarity.

Regarding the phrase "planting those seeds within the subsequent dharma," this refers to the category of perfumation (*vāsanā*) that is capable of drawing forth and sustaining the future; it is precisely this resultant *ālaya-vijñāna*.

Thus, by virtue of being the seed-cause, the support-cause, the cause for nurturing seeds, and the cause for gathering and planting seeds, this is called the establishment of the mutual causality between the ālayavijñāna and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
Question:
How are the characteristics of the simultaneous arising of the various consciousnesses established? Answer:
The ālayavijñāna may at times arise together with only one evolving consciousness (pravṛttivijñāna), namely, with the manas. Why is this?

Because this manas is always associated with the characteristics of arrogance, such as the view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the conceit of "I" (asmimāna); whether in states with mind or states without mind, it always arises simultaneously with this [ālaya]vijñāna.

Furthermore, this mind-faculty (*manas*) constantly takes the ālayavijñāna as its object, arising with the modes of activity consisting of the grasping of a self and the manifestation of pride and arrogance.
Moreover, at certain times, this very consciousness arises simultaneously with two evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), namely, the mind-faculty and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

At one time, it may arise simultaneously with three evolving consciousnesses; that is, when any one of the five groups of sensory consciousnesses arises, there are the two preceding ones and this one.
At one time, it may arise simultaneously with four evolving consciousnesses; that is, when any two of the five groups of sensory consciousnesses arise, there are the two preceding ones and these two.

In this manner, at one time it may even arise simultaneously with up to seven evolving consciousnesses; that is to say, when the five groups of sensory consciousness arise in combination, there are the first two [the storehouse consciousness and the manas] along with these five.

Furthermore, it was previously stated that the mental consciousness arises dependent upon the afflicted manas; as long as the manas has not ceased, one remains bound by the discernment of signs and cannot attain liberation.
Once the manas has ceased, one is liberated from the bondage of signs.
Furthermore, this mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) can take both external objects and its own object as its cognitive domain.
Taking external objects refers to taking the objects of the five groups of sensory consciousness either collectively or individually.
Taking its own object refers to taking the dharma-object (*dharmaviṣaya*) as its cognitive domain.
Furthermore, at certain times, the ālayavijñāna functions simultaneously with painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
These feelings are associated with the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna), arise based upon the evolving consciousnesses, and are produced from the seeds of this [ālaya] consciousness.

Furthermore, within the human realm, among the gods of the desire realm, and within a portion of the realms of hungry ghosts and animals, there arises simultaneously with them a feeling of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure that is innate; this co-exists at one time with the various feelings associated with the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna), which include suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, as they continue in a mixed succession.

If, within the realm of hell-beings, one's experience is eclipsed by others, the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant—which is associated with the evolving consciousness—occurs simultaneously with a continuous stream of feelings consisting purely of suffering, unmixed with anything else.
One should know that because this feeling is eclipsed, its characteristics are difficult to discern.

Just as in the hells it invariably arises together with painful feeling, so too in the three lower dhyāna stages it invariably arises together with pleasant feeling, and from the fourth dhyāna stage up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), it invariably arises together with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Furthermore, at one time, the ālayavijñāna may arise simultaneously with various mental factors—wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—that are associated with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).

In this way, while the ālayavijñāna arises simultaneously with the various evolving consciousnesses, it also arises simultaneously with adventitious sensations and adventitious wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate mental factors.
However, one should not say that it is associated with them.
Why? Because it does not function with the same object as they do.
Just as visual consciousness and the eye, though they arise together, are not associated, so it is with this case as well;
because it shares a slight resemblance to that phenomenon, it serves as an analogy. One should understand the principle of the analogy in this way.

Furthermore, just as with the various mental factors (*caitta*), although there is no difference in the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of these mental factors, they nevertheless function simultaneously within a single body without mutual contradiction because their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are distinct.
In the same way, it should be understood that this [ālayavijñāna] and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) also function simultaneously without mutual contradiction.
Furthermore, it is like how, based upon a violent torrent, many waves arise simultaneously in various ways without contradicting one another;
or like how, based upon the surface of a clear mirror, various reflections arise simultaneously without contradicting one another.
In this way, one should know that it is not contradictory for many evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) to arise simultaneously based upon the *ālaya-vijñāna*.

Furthermore, just as a single visual consciousness, at a single moment and with respect to a single objective sphere, may apprehend only one type of color-form without distinguishing marks, or may, at a single moment, suddenly apprehend various types of color-forms.

Just as visual consciousness [perceives] forms, so it is for the others up to tactile consciousness [perceiving] tangibles; regarding a single moment or a single objective sphere, it may grasp a single characteristic, or it may simultaneously grasp multiple objective characteristics.

In this way, one should know that it is not contradictory for the discriminating mental consciousness, at a single moment, to either apprehend a single object or simultaneously apprehend many objects.

Furthermore, as previously stated, the mental faculty (manas) always functions in conjunction with this consciousness; at all times, until it is severed, one should know that it is constantly associated with four types of spontaneously arising afflictions, namely: the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the conceit "I am" (asmimāna), self-love (ātmasneha), and ignorance (avidyā).

These four afflictions, whether in the state of meditative concentration or in the non-concentrated state, should be known as constantly active; they are not incompatible with wholesome states and so forth, and are of the nature of obscured-neutral.

Thus, because it evolves simultaneously with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), because it evolves simultaneously with all feelings (*vedanā*), and because it evolves simultaneously with the wholesome and so forth, this is called the establishment of the characteristic of the simultaneous evolution of the *ālayavijñāna*.
Question:
How is the establishment of the characteristics of the cessation of the defilements of the ālayavijñāna defined? Answer:
To speak briefly, one should know that the ālayavijñāna is the root of all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa*). Why is this?

This ālayavijñāna is also the root for the arising of the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*), because it can produce the sense faculties, the bases upon which the faculties depend, and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
It is also the fundamental basis for the arising of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), because it is capable of producing the receptacle world.

Furthermore, this very consciousness is also the fundamental basis for the mutual arising of all sentient beings, because all sentient beings serve as reciprocal dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for one another.

Why is this so? Because there is no sentient being who, at the time of seeing, hearing, or otherwise perceiving another sentient being, does not experience feelings such as suffering or pleasure arising from that interaction.
For this reason, it should be understood that the realms of sentient beings act as mutual dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for one another.

Furthermore, because the ālayavijñāna possesses all seeds, it constitutes the essence of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) in the present life; it is the cause for the arising of the truth of suffering in future lives, and it is also the cause for the arising of the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*) in the present life.

Because it is the root of the arising of the sentient world, the root of the arising of the receptacle world, the essence of the truth of suffering in the present life, that which can give rise to the truth of suffering in the future, and that which can give rise to the truth of origination in the present, one should know that the ālayavijñāna is the root of all defilements.

Furthermore, the seeds of wholesome roots such as the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) that are maintained within the ālayavijñāna are not causes for the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*), because these wholesome roots conducive to liberation and so forth are contrary to the process of cyclic existence (*pravṛtti*).
Because all other roots of goodness existing in the world arise from this, they become increasingly bright and pure. Why is this?
By virtue of these conditions, the seeds of their own kind that they have grasped become increasingly functional and increasingly powerful, such that the seeds increase and reach full development.
Due to these seeds, those various wholesome dharmas arise with increasing clarity and purity.
Furthermore, they are able to induce superior, desirable maturation (*vipāka*) in future lives.
Moreover, based upon this *ālayavijñāna* containing all seeds, the Blessed One said:
The eye-element, the form-element, and the eye-consciousness-element, up to the mind-element, the mental-object-element, and the mind-consciousness-element;
this is because there are various elements within the ālayavijñāna.
Furthermore, as the sūtras state regarding the simile of the akṣa-fruit cluster, this is because there are multiple realms within the ālayavijñāna.
Therefore, one should know that this very root of affliction, the ālayavijñāna, is transformed and extinguished through the cultivation of wholesome dharmas.

Furthermore, regarding the cultivation of these wholesome dharmas: if ordinary beings, by means of mental attention directed toward the evolving consciousnesses as their object, employ skillful means to abide in the mind for the purpose of entering the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the first truth.
It is not that one who has not yet seen the truths and has not yet attained the Dharma-eye regarding those truths can penetrate the *ālayavijñāna* of all seeds.

Once such a person who has not yet seen the truths has cultivated this practice, they will either enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) of a Śrāvaka or enter the state of right determination of a Bodhisattva.

Having thoroughly penetrated all dharma-spheres, one is also able to penetrate the ālayavijñāna; at that time, one contemplates in their entirety all the various defilements within each individual's own internal continuum.
Furthermore, he understands that his own body is externally bound by the bondage of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*) and internally bound by the bondage of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*).

Moreover, this practitioner [understands this] because the ālayavijñāna is the source-element (*dhātu*) of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) comprised within all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
Having condensed all those formations within the ālayavijñāna into a single mass,
a single accumulation, and a single heap; and having formed them into one heap—
Because one has cultivated and repeatedly practiced the wisdom that takes true suchness as its object,
the basis upon which it relies undergoes a transformation; immediately following this transformation of the basis,
one should know that the ālayavijñāna has been severed.
Because of this abandonment,
it should be known that all defilements have been abandoned.
Furthermore, because this transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is its opposite, it should be known that it can counteract the ālayavijñāna.

Furthermore, the essence of the ālayavijñāna is impermanent and characterized by grasping; the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is permanent and devoid of grasping, because the noble path that takes true suchness as its object is able to effect this transformation.
Furthermore, the ālayavijñāna is accompanied by coarse heaviness (dausthulya), whereas the ultimate transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti) is completely free from all coarse heaviness.

Moreover, the ālayavijñāna is the cause for the arising of afflictions and the non-arising of the noble path, while the transformation of the basis is the cause for the non-arising of afflictions and the arising of the noble path.
This establishes the nature of the sustaining cause (*pratiṣṭhā-hetu*), not the nature of the generative cause (*janana-hetu*).

Furthermore, the ālayavijñāna renders one powerless with respect to wholesome, pure, and indeterminate phenomena; whereas the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) grants great mastery over all wholesome, pure, and indeterminate phenomena.

Furthermore, regarding the characteristic of the cessation of this ālayavijñāna: it means that because this ālayavijñāna is directly severed and ceases, one abandons the two kinds of grasping; although the body remains, it is like a magical transformation (nirmāṇa).
Why is this so? Because the causes for future existence have been severed, one abandons the grasping for future existence;

because the causes for all afflictions in the present life have been severed, one abandons the grasping that serves as the basis for all defilements in the present life. Since all heavy burdens (*dauṣṭhulya*) have been removed, only the conditions for life remain for a temporary stay.
Because this exists, it is said in the Buddha’s sūtras:

"At that time, one experiences only the sensation of the limit of the body and the sensation of the limit of life," and so on at length, until: "all sensations experienced in this very life are completely extinguished."

Because it establishes the root of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), because it establishes the entry into, the penetration of, and the cultivation of mental attention (*manasikāra*), and because it establishes the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), this is called the establishment of the characteristics of the cessation of affliction within the ālayavijñāna.

Thus, having established mind, thought, and consciousness according to the principle of ultimate truth, one should accordingly clarify all principles regarding the defilement and purification of all mind, thought, and consciousness within the three realms, in accordance with the principles thus explained.

If the principles of mind, mentation, and consciousness are elucidated in other contexts, it is because those instances were taught solely for the sake of those disciples possessing the intelligence of ordinary worldlings, as a skillful means to facilitate their easy entry into the Dharma.
Question:
If one accomplishes the ālayavijñāna, does one also accomplish the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna)?
Conversely, if one accomplishes the evolving consciousnesses, does one also accomplish the ālayavijñāna?

Answer: This should be explained by way of four propositions (catuṣkoṭi). That is to say: there are those who possess the ālayavijñāna but not the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna), namely: those in mindless sleep, those in mindless fainting, those who have entered the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñisamāpatti), those who have entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), and those born in the Heaven of Non-conception (asaṃjñideva).

There are those who have attained the transformation of consciousness but not the ālayavijñāna; namely, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas while abiding in the state of having a mind.
There are those who achieve both, namely those remaining in other states of existence while possessing mind.

There are those who achieve neither, namely Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas who have entered the meditative attainment of cessation, or who abide in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
*Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, Fascicle Seventeen;
*Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, Fascicle Eighteen.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Eleven, Part Two: Determination of the Superior [Teachings], Section on the Establishment of the Differentiated Characteristics of the Mind. Furthermore, one should understand the establishment of the differentiated characteristics of the mind.
The verse says:
Through the power of the basis and the object, the distinctions of the mind are established;
furthermore, by means of seven modes of activity, these associated factors should be known as difficult to comprehend.
The treatise says:
It should be understood that the differentiation of mental states is established by the power of both the basis (*āśraya*) and the object (*ālambana*).
Regarding the power of the basis, this refers to the establishment of visual consciousness up to and including mental consciousness.

Regarding the power of the object (*ālambana-bala*): this refers to the establishment of consciousnesses of form (*rūpa-vijñāna*) up to consciousnesses of phenomena (*dharma-vijñāna*), and consciousnesses of blue, yellow, up to consciousnesses of suffering and pleasure.

Furthermore, such [consciousnesses] are understood through seven types of modes of activity (*ākāra*) that discern the difficult-to-know distinctions among various minds: (1) the distinction of the vessel-like aspect of the unknowable continuity that abides for a long time; (2) the distinction of the aspect of the objects of many kinds; (3) the distinction of simultaneous occurrence (*sahabhū*); (4) the distinction of the rapid transition between the antidote and that which is to be countered; (5) the distinction of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); (6) the distinction of rebirth; and (7) the distinction of the mind of liberation.
Furthermore, the verse says:
Lacking mastery over its objects, Abiding in a base support,
And turning according to the power of conditions— One should know that the mind is thus bound.
The treatise states:

The mind is said to be bound for three reasons: first, because it lacks mastery over its objects of perception; second, because it dwells within a defiled basis; and third, because it undergoes transformation through the power of various conditions.

In this context, "lack of mastery over the object of focus" refers to the inability to abide as one desires with mastery over the object regarding the suppression of signs, transformation, modification, and so forth.
Furthermore, the verse says:
Distraction and abiding, The six types and the fifteen types;
With objects such as the six [senses] and so forth, The remedial minds are not one.
The treatise says:

One should know that there are six types of mental distraction, fifteen types of mental abiding, and six types of mental engagement with objects, among many other such distinctions; it should also be understood that the minds which serve as their respective antidotes are likewise not of a single kind.

Regarding the six types of mental distraction: first is the distraction of attention (*manasikāra-vikṣepa*), which refers to bodhisattvas abandoning the attention associated with the Mahāyāna and regressing to the practice of inferior attention associated with the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

Second is external mental distraction, which refers to allowing the mind to flow and scatter toward the five excellent sensual desires, toward the signs of bustle and commotion, and toward external objects associated with discursive thoughts and secondary afflictions.
Third is internal mental distraction, which occurs either due to lethargy, sleep, or inferiority;
or due to attachment to the flavors of meditative absorption;
or due to the afflictions associated with various states of concentration that disturb the mind.
Fourth is distraction of the mind due to signs (*nimitta-vikṣepa*), which refers to relying on external signs while mentally attending to the characteristics of internal objects.

Fifth is distraction of the mind due to heaviness and rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya-vikṣepa*), which refers to the arising of various sensations conditioned by internal mental attention, whereby one conceives of "I" and "mine" due to the body of heaviness and rigidity.
The six types of natural mental distraction refer to the five groups of sensory consciousnesses.
Regarding the fifteen ways in which the mind abides: first is the initial development of the abiding mind, which refers to the practice of the skillful means for *samādhi*.
Second is the mind that has attained and abides [in concentration], which refers to having already attained the *anāgamya* (preliminary) samādhi.
Third is the mind that perfectly abides, which refers to having already attained the fundamental dhyāna samādhi.
Fourth is the mind dwelling in mastery, which means attaining whatever one desires with respect to this very state.
Fifth is the mind dwelling in movement, which refers to the three lower dhyānas.
Sixth is the mind abiding in immovability, which refers to the fourth dhyāna.
Seventh is the mind abiding in tranquility beyond this, which refers to the liberations of the tranquil formless realms.
Eighth is the mind abiding in supreme tranquility, which refers to the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha-vimokṣa*).
Ninth is the mind abiding in resolute faith (*adhimukti*), which refers to the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamaya-jñāna*).
Tenth is the mind abiding in certainty, which refers to the wisdom arising from reflection.
Eleventh is the mind abiding in images, which refers to the wisdom arising from mundane cultivation.
12. The mind abiding in the perfection of reality refers to the supramundane wisdom produced through cultivation.
13. The mind abiding in renunciation with overweening pride refers to the mundane meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and formless attainments (*ārūpya*).

Fourteenth is the mind dwelling in renunciation free from overweening pride (*anabhimāna*), which refers to the renunciation of worldly meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and formless attainments (*ārūpya*).

Fifteenth is the mind dwelling in the defilement of the three modes of activity (*trividha-saṃskāra*), which means that consciousness dwells following form, dwells taking form as its object, and dwells dependent upon form; and so on, up to dwelling following formations (*saṃskāra*), dwelling taking formations as its object, and dwelling dependent upon formations.
In this context, "abiding in accordance with form" means because it is the basis for appropriation (*upādāna*).
"Abiding by taking form as an object" means because it grasps the objective field (*viṣaya*).
"Abiding dependent on form" means because of its coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*).

In this manner, up to and including the three [stations] beginning with "following," one should know that consciousness is not a station of consciousness, because it can exhaust craving by taking its own mind as an object.

Furthermore, regarding the six types of objects of focus, these are: constant objects of focus, non-constant objects of focus, pervasive objects of focus, objects of focus for pure conduct, objects of focus for skillfulness, and objects of focus for purifying the defilements.

With this as a preliminary, there are furthermore many other conditions and objects: namely, a mind bound to the desire realm takes as its object realms belonging to the desire, form, and formless realms, as well as the unbound realm; likewise, minds bound to the form and formless realms, as well as unbound minds, each take four kinds of objects.

Furthermore, based on a mind bound to the desire realm, there arise minds bound to the desire, form, and formless realms, as well as unbound minds; based on a mind bound to the form realm, there arise minds bound to the form and formless realms, as well as unbound minds; and based on a mind bound to the formless realm, there arise minds bound to the formless realm, as well as unbound minds.
Furthermore, a past mind takes as its object the past, future, and present; likewise, future and present minds each take all three time periods as their objects.
Moreover, a wholesome mind takes as its object the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate; likewise, unwholesome and indeterminate minds each take all three types as their objects.

Furthermore, a mind accompanied by pleasure takes as its objects three kinds of spheres, including those accompanied by pleasure; likewise, a mind accompanied by suffering and a mind accompanied by neither-suffering-nor-pleasure each take three kinds of objects.
Furthermore, minds associated with greed, hatred, and delusion each take as their objects three types of spheres that correspond to those very afflictions.

Moreover, regarding the fact that the minds to be remedied are not of a single kind: this refers to the five types of minds bound to the desire realm, namely, the mind to be abandoned through the vision of suffering up to the mind to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.
In this way, the minds associated with the form and formless realms each have five types, and together with the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), they constitute sixteen types of mind.
Furthermore, there are twenty types of mind; that is to say, the minds associated with the desire realm consist of eight types:

(1) innate wholesome mind, (2) acquired wholesome mind, (3) unwholesome mind, and (4) obscured-neutral mind; and the non-obscured-neutral mind is divided into four types, namely: (5) resultant mind, (6) deportment mind, (7) craftsmanship mind, and (8) transformation mind.
There are six types of mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), excluding the unwholesome mind and the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika-citta*).

There are four types of mind associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), namely, excluding the unwholesome mind, the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika-citta*), the mind of craftsmanship, and the mind of transformation (*nairmāṇika-citta*).
There are two types of non-bound minds: namely, the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*) and the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, the superior determination of the activities of mental factors (*caitasika*) shall now be explained.
The verse says:
Based on the discernment of multiple objects, each arises according to its own function;
one should not deliberate upon mental factors (*caitasika*), for they operate in accordance with their corresponding objects.
The treatise says:

Because the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) rely upon the eight types of consciousness that are capable of cognizing multiple objects, they each perform their own specific functions and arise; since they exist in dependence upon the mind (*citta*), they are called "mental factors."
One should not further contemplate that object of perception, because it functions as a condition equal to consciousness and its other conditions.
As the Sūtra says:
"If one feels this sensation, one wills this very same thing."
If there is volition (*cetanā*) regarding this, there is likewise perception (*saṃjñā*) regarding this;
if there is perception regarding this, there is likewise discernment (*vijñapti*) regarding this.

Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the functions of the five universal mental factors—attention (*manasikāra*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*).
The verse says:
Drawing forth the mind, the threefold discrimination, experiencing the locus, and discerning characteristics;
engaging with qualities and faults and so forth—these are called the functions of attention and the rest.

The treatise states: The activity of mental attention (*manasikāra*) consists in directing the mind; the activity of contact (*sparśa*) consists in the discernment of the threefold harmony; the activity of sensation (*vedanā*) consists in experiencing states that are disagreeable, agreeable, or neutral; the activity of perception (*saṃjñā*) consists in the thorough discernment of the characteristics of objects; and the activity of volition (*cetanā*) consists in performing meritorious deeds, non-meritorious deeds, or those that are neither.
The remaining mental factors and karma have been explained in detail as before.
Furthermore, the determination of material phenomena shall now be discussed.
The verse says:
In the higher realms there is no odor or flavor; The great elements and their derivatives may be found accordingly.
An atom has no intrinsic substance; The seven things do not exist as real entities.
The Commentary says:
Regarding the absence of odor and flavor in the upper realms: this is because odor and flavor do not exist above the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

As for "the great elements and derived matter being present according to what is obtainable": among the aggregates, those great elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) that are currently perceivable exist as their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); those that are not obtainable are simply absent therein.
That atoms lack intrinsic nature means that all atoms are merely established through conceptual construction; they have no real intrinsic nature.

That the seven types of entities are not substantially existent means that these seven kinds of things lack substantial reality: first, manifest color; second, shape; third, reflected images; fourth, sounds; fifth, derived matter of the sphere of tangibles; sixth, matter of restraint; and seventh, matter of non-restraint.
Furthermore, the verse says:
Subtle atoms combine yet are not separate; Good and evil have no inherent nature.
The three marks and perception exist nowhere outside [of them]; The sphere of phenomena consists of twelve types of form.
The treatise says:

"Subtle conjunction without separation" refers to the fact that at the location of the great atoms (*paramāṇu*), the derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) which depends upon them is not separate from them; furthermore, other matter in different locations, whether in a state of aggregation (*saṃghāta*) or conjunction (*saṃyoga*), is likewise not separate.

There is nothing in the nature of good or evil that exists spontaneously; form does not possess the nature of good or evil by virtue of its own essence, for it is only conventionally designated as good or evil in accordance with the mind that gives rise to it.

Regarding the statement that there is nothing external to the three marks of perception: apart from the three marks of form, there is no separate form, namely, visible and resistant form, invisible and resistant form, and invisible and non-resistant form.

Regarding the three types of perception (*saṃjñā*), there is no separate form outside of the forms that are their objects of activity—namely, the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), the perception of resistance (*sapratigha-saṃjñā*), and the perception of various distinctions.

As for the twelve types of form included in the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*), these refer to the forms subsumed under the *dharmāyatana*, which briefly stated have twelve characteristics:

(1) the characteristic of an image; (2) the characteristic of the accomplishment of what is to be done; (3) the characteristic of being invisible; (4) the characteristic of being non-resistant; (5) the characteristic of not being produced from real primary elements (*mahābhūta*); (6) the characteristic of belonging to the mind; (7) the characteristic of being mundane; (8) the characteristic of being inconceivable; (9) the characteristic of being the fruit of mundane meditative concentration (*samādhi*); (10) the characteristic of being the fruit of supramundane meditative concentration; (11) the characteristic of being the object of one's own or lower stages; and (12) the inconceivable characteristic of the transformations performed by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas through mastery over the mind.
Furthermore, the superior discernment of the formations dissociated from mind shall now be explained.
The verse says:
One should know that those dissociated [from mind] Are all existents established by designation.
The nature of provisional existence is of six kinds, for all of them involve two faults.
The treatise says:
One should know that all formations dissociated from mind are provisionally existent; briefly stated, there are six kinds of the nature of provisional existence.
What are the six? They are those matters that can give rise to six kinds of discourse.
What are the names of these six kinds of discourse?

1. Discourse associated with a master; 2. Discourse that transcends "this" and "that"; 3. Discourse of conventional designation by the multitude; 4. Discourse on the collection of various phenomena; 5. Discourse that does not pervade all things; 6. Discourse on impermanence.

Regarding discourse concerning the relation to a possessor (*svāmisaṃbandha-vāda*): this refers to discourse that is understood only when attributed to a possessor, and not when it is not so attributed.
For example, when one says "at the time of arising," one asks, "Whose arising is this?"
One observes that this discourse arises in dependence upon its respective subject: namely, the arising of form, and the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
When speaking of form, whose form is it?
One should observe that this discourse arises with respect to its respective subject.

Just as it is with "arising," so too should all other categories of formations dissociated from mind—such as "abiding," "alteration," and "impermanence"—be understood in their entirety according to what is appropriate.
This is called discourse associated with the possessor of attributes (*svāmisaṃyukta-vāda*).
If a thing can give rise to such discourse, one should know that this is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*).

Regarding "discourse that is free from 'this' and 'that'": it means that various discourses do not manifest this by means of this, nor do they manifest that by means of that; this is what is called discourse free from "this" and "that."

If a discourse expresses something by means of this [factor], that discourse arises both with respect to the characteristic of substantial existence and with respect to the characteristic of conventional designation.

If a discourse expresses something by means of that [factor], that discourse likewise arises both with respect to the characteristic of substantial existence and with respect to the characteristic of conventional designation.

If it is not by means of this that this is manifested, nor by means of that, then those discourses and these discourses would arise solely with respect to conventional characteristics (*prajñapti-lakṣaṇa*).
How, then, could discourse that manifests this by means of this arise with respect to real characteristics (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*)?
Just as one speaks of "the hardness of the earth," how could this [hardness] further arise in relation to a conventional characteristic (*prajñapti-lakṣaṇa*)?
It is like speaking of "the roundness of a stone."

Just as the earth is solid and a stone is round, so too should one know that water is moist, oil is slippery, fire is warm, a flame is burning, wind is moving, and a gust is blowing; it is exactly thus.
How does discourse that reveals something by means of another arise with respect to the characteristic of the real (dravya-lakṣaṇa)?
For example, such expressions as "the consciousness of the eye" or "the touch of the body.
How, then, does this same discourse arise with respect to the characteristic of the conventional (prajñapti-lakṣaṇa)?
For example, as when it is said that the Buddha rescued Guṇamitra’s food, drink, clothing, ornaments, and so forth.
What is this kind of discourse—neither revealing this by means of this, nor revealing that by means of that—which arises solely with respect to the characteristics of the conventional (prajñapti)?

For example, the door of a house, the wall of a house, the mouth of a jar, the belly of a jar, the chariot of an army, the trees of a forest, ten of a hundred, three of ten—such as these are called discourses that distance "this" and "that."
The discourse established by common consensus refers to the discourse that establishes the intrinsic nature of speech through six types of characteristics. These six types of characteristics are:

the characteristic of the objective entity (*vastu-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of what should be cognized (*vijñeya-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of beauty and so forth (*śubhādi-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of benefit and so forth (*hitādi-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of the mode of expression (*abhilāpa-ākāra-lakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of misconduct and so forth (*mithyā-pratipatti-ādi-lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*): the characteristic that is the object-apprehended by consciousness refers to those characteristics which are apprehended by consciousness. The characteristic that should be known by consciousness refers to those characteristics which are able to give rise to consciousness through mental attention (*manasikāra*).
The characteristic of "pleasant" and so forth refers to those characteristics which are the objects-apprehended by contact (*sparśa*).
The characteristics of benefit and so forth refer to those characteristics apprehended by sensation (*vedanā*).
The characteristics of verbal expression and appearance refer to those characteristics apprehended by perception (*saṃjñā*).
The characteristics of misconduct and so forth refer to those characteristics apprehended by volition (*cetanā*).

Discourse concerning the aggregation of multiple phenomena refers to discourse that establishes a self-entity through the combination of many factors; for example, discourse such as "I" regarding internal form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, or discourse that establishes distinctions regarding external form, odor, taste, and tangibility, such as "house," "jar," "army," or "forest."

Regarding discourse that is not universal: this refers to discourse that proceeds in some instances but recedes in others. For example, the term "house" proceeds only with respect to a house and recedes when applied to villages, pavilions, and the like;
the term "jar" recedes when applied to other vessels such as pots;
and the term "army" recedes when applied to individual men, women, and so forth.
Āraḍa spoke of the retreat [of consciousness] from the roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth of distinct trees.

Regarding the discourse on impermanence, one should know that it has four kinds of causes: namely, by way of destruction, by way of non-destruction, by way of application, and by way of transformation.
Regarding "due to destruction": for example, once a jar has been destroyed, the designation "jar" ceases and the designations "potsherds," etc., arise.

Regarding "due to non-destruction": for example, when various medicinal ingredients are combined together to form either a pill or a powder, the designations for the "various medicines" cease and the designations for the "medicinal pill" or "powder," etc., arise.

Regarding "due to application" (*prayoga*): it is like applying various efforts to a piece of gold to fashion diverse ornaments such as bracelets and earrings; at that time, the designation "piece of gold" is abandoned, and the designations for the distinct objects, such as "bracelet" or "earring," arise.
Regarding "due to transformation": for example, when food, drink, and so forth undergo transformation, the designation "food and drink" is abandoned and the designation "excrement and filth" arises.

One should understand that such categories as these involve discourse on non-eternality; wherever such six types of discourse arise with respect to various things, one should know that those things are all conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*).
Question:
It is said that all formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) are conventionally existent (prajñapti-sat).
How is this to be understood?
Answer: Due to two kinds of faults: first, the fault of the cause; second, the fault of the essence. Regarding the fault of the cause:

if one says that "arising" is the cause of arising because it can produce arising, and thus is called "arising," then no distinct arising as a result could be obtained. For what purpose would this [cause] be designated as "arising," since it is the cause capable of producing [it]?
If one says that "arising" (jāti) is the very essence of arising, then because it would arise from something else, it should not be described as that which causes arising.
The same should be understood, according to reason, for the other formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra).
Furthermore, because those factors from the mind and so forth, up to the formations dissociated from the mind— all conditioned phenomena— are of the nature of causes,
the determination of these causes shall now be explained.
The verse says:
Three faults; the cause is not fivefold; the characteristics of the cause are briefly combined with the fetters;
based on the distinctions of dependence and location, there are many ways of establishing [the categories].
The Treatise says:

There are those who, based on the theories of identity and difference, establish six kinds of causes: namely, the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), and the maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
The efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
These six types [of causes], excluding the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), are logically untenable as causal natures for the remaining five causes, because they entail three kinds of faults.
What are the three? For instance, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) has three faults.
If one says that a cause which is homogeneous is called a "homogeneous cause," there is the fault of [the definition being] already established (*prasiddha*).
Why is this? If dharmas such as the wholesome already possess the essential nature of being wholesome and so forth prior to their arising, what need would they have for a cause?
If one were to say that the similar type itself is the cause—calling it a "similar-type cause" (sabhāga-hetu)—then there would be no fruit, resulting in the fallacy of uncertainty (anaikāntika).
Why is this? If its fruit is not shown, what could be its cause?
Furthermore, it is not a determinate cause, because even dissimilar phenomena can serve as causes.

If one says that what is not of the same class is not a cause of the same class, then the designation itself would incur the fault of being a hollow convention; for the term "cause of the same class" would have no objective referent and would be established in vain.
In this same manner, the three kinds of faults regarding the other four types of reasons should also be explained extensively according to reason.
Furthermore, having refuted the illogical reasons, we shall now establish the characteristics of logical reasons.
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of causes:
first, the cause characterized by bondage; second, the cause characterized by conjunction.

The cause characterized by bondage refers to the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*); this is explained in terms of their capacity to give rise to future existence (*punarbhava*).

Regarding "the causal condition of conjunction" (*sāmagrī-hetu*), this refers to the arising of various phenomena through the conjunction of causes and conditions; this is explained in terms of that which is capable of producing [an effect] at the present time.
Furthermore, it should be understood that there are many other types of classifications for the characteristics of causes and their bases as briefly described here.

Regarding "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*): it should be understood that when, by virtue of something being prior, something being established, or something being conjoined, various phenomena arise, are obtained, are established, are accomplished, or perform their functions, that [prior factor] is said to be their cause.
Question:
With what as the precursor, by what is it established, through the conjunction of what, and by means of what dharma does [another] dharma arise? Answer:

With their own seeds as the precursor, with the exception of the seeds of the support itself, the remaining supports—whether material or non-material—as well as karma, serve as the foundation; through the conjunction of these with their attendants and objective conditions, the various phenomena belonging to the realm of desire, the realm of form, the formless realm, or those that are unconditioned arise, as is appropriate for each.
Question:
By what as a precursor, by what as a foundation, and through the conjunction of what, does one obtain what dharma?
Answer:

Having the lineage of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and tathāgatas as their precursor, they realize nirvāṇa—the dissociation from afflictions—by establishing themselves through internal causal power and by harmonizing with external causal power.
Among these, the power of internal causes refers to internal wholesome dharmas such as appropriate mental attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), having few desires, and being content with little.

Furthermore, it includes being born as a human being in a noble land, having no deficiency in the sense faculties, being free from karmic obstructions, and possessing pure faith toward the Tathāgata. Such dharmas as these are called the power of internal causes.

As for external causal power, it refers to the appearance of Buddhas in the world to proclaim the sublime Dharma, those who abide in the True Dharma acting as companions, and those endowed with compassion and faith serving as patrons; such factors as these are termed external causal power.
Question:
By what as the precursor, by what as the foundation, and through the conjunction of what, is what phenomenon established?
Answer:

Preceded by a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) and a desire for the objects of knowledge, and established by means of propositions (*pakṣa*), reasons (*hetu*), and examples (*dṛṣṭānta*), the intended thesis (*sādhya-artha*) is only then successfully established through the reconciliation of a non-contentious assembly and the opponent.
Question:
With what as the precursor, by what is it established, through the conjunction of what, and by what dharma is it accomplished?
Answer:

Preceded by skillful knowledge (*śilpasthānika-jñāna*), it is established according to one's diligent application; because the various implements for the spheres of craft (*śilpasthāna*) are brought into harmony, those respective spheres of craft are accomplished.

Furthermore, with craving as the precursor, that which dwells by means of nutriment is established upon its basis; because the four nutriments provide cohesion, sentient beings who have already been born are sustained and able to persist.
Question:
What serves as the precursor, what serves as the foundation, through the conjunction of what, and what is the function of which dharma?
Answer:

With one's own seeds as the primary factor, those very seeds from a previous life serve as the basis for establishment, and because they serve as the conditions for arising, the actions performed by oneself are accomplished through one's own agency.
Regarding "the action performed by itself," it is like the function of seeing belonging to the eye.
In this way, one should know that the remaining sense faculties each perform their own distinct functions.
Furthermore, just as the earth can support, water can moisten, fire can burn, and wind can dry—such categories as these are called the distinct functions of external phenomena.
Regarding the bases (*āśraya*), there are fifteen kinds of causal bases:

first, speech; second, reception; third, habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); fourth, moistened seeds; fifth, that which has ceased without interval; sixth, the object-field (*viṣaya*); seventh, the faculties (*indriya*); eighth, activity; ninth, human effort (*puruṣakāra*); tenth, seeing reality; eleventh, conformity; twelfth, differentiated capacity; thirteenth, conjunction; fourteenth, obstruction; fifteenth, non-obstruction.
As for the distinctions, they consist of ten causes, four conditions, and five fruits. The ten causes are:

the cause of conventional designation (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*), the cause of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*), the cause of attraction (*ākṣepa-hetu*), the cause of origination (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*), the cause of sustenance (*parigraha-hetu*), the cause of production (*āvāhaka-hetu*), the cause of specific determination (*pratiniyama-hetu*), the cause of cooperation (*sahakāri-hetu*), the cause of opposition (*virodha-hetu*), and the cause of non-opposition (*avirodha-hetu*).

The four conditions are: the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

The five fruits are: the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*), the concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), the fruit of disentanglement (*visamyoga-phala*), the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).

In this context, that which conforms to all phenomena is called the "preceding designation" (*pūrvaka-saṃjñā*); because it is preceded by designation, it is spoken of—this is what is meant by the "cause of conventional expression" (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*) for those phenomena.
That which is depended upon, or that by reason of which, one seeks or grasps at various objects, is called the "condition of dependence" (*apekṣā-hetu*).
Just as, in dependence upon the hand and with the hand as cause, the activity of grasping arises;
and in dependence upon the feet and with the feet as cause, the activities of coming and going arise.
In dependence upon the joints and with the joints as cause, the actions of bending and extending arise.
In dependence upon hunger and thirst and with hunger and thirst as cause, one seeks out food and drink.
According to such immeasurable principles as these, one should know that all are termed the "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*).
If a seed is, with respect to its own final fruit, the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
This very seed is the productive cause (*janana-hetu*) for its own fruit.
All other conditions (*pratyaya*) besides the seed are the supportive causes (*parigraha-hetu*).
The fruit produced by this very seed is the drawing-forth cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) for the fruit subsequently drawn forth by the later seed.
That which can act as various distinct causes for different categories is called the "cause of specific determination" (*pratiniyamahetu*).

Whether it be the "contingent cause" (*apekṣāhetu*), the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepahetu*), the "generative cause" (*abhinirvṛttihetu*), the "supportive cause" (*parigrahahetu*), the "inducing cause" (*āvāhakahetu*), or the "cause of specific determination," the collective inclusion of such causes is termed the "cause of common function" (*sahakārihetu*).
If something acts as an obstacle to that which is to arise, it is called a contrary cause (*virodha-hetu*).
If it is free from such obstacles, it is called a non-contrary cause (*avirodha-hetu*).

Regarding the seeds of all phenomena as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*): if, immediately following this consciousness, various cognitions necessarily arise, then this [consciousness] is the immediately preceding condition for those [subsequent cognitions].
Whatever objects are apprehended by the various minds and mental factors constitute the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

As for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it consists of all supports other than the seeds, such as the eye and its concomitant factors in relation to visual consciousness, and likewise the remaining sense faculties in relation to their respective consciousnesses.
Furthermore, wholesome and unwholesome dharmas that appropriate desirable and undesirable fruits—categories such as these—are dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

The retribution in the evil realms brought about by unwholesome dharmas, and the retribution in the good realms brought about by contaminated wholesome dharmas, is called the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
If, through the habituation of unwholesome states, one delights in dwelling in unwholesomeness, unwholesome states will increase;
if, through the cultivation of wholesome states, one delights in dwelling in wholesomeness, wholesome dharmas will increase.
Furthermore, when a subsequent result arises in accordance with its preceding karma, it is called a result of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*).
If the various afflictions are extinguished by means of the Noble Eightfold Path, this is the result of dissociation (*visamyogaphala*).

If ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) eliminate various afflictions (*kleśa*) by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), because this is not a definitive transformation, it is not the fruit of dissociation (*visamyogaphala*).

As for worldly persons who, in the present life, exercise human effort (*puruṣakāra*) based on any one of the various arts and crafts (*śilpasthāna*), such as agriculture, commerce, service to a king, writing, arithmetic, accounting, and seal-making.
Because it relies upon this, crops reach full maturity and the accomplishment of results such as commercial profit is attained; this is called the result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Visual consciousness is the dominant result (*adhipati-phala*) of the eye faculty, and so on, up to mental consciousness being the dominant result of the mind faculty.
Furthermore, the fact that the bodies of sentient beings do not disintegrate is the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Moreover, because each of the twenty-two faculties exerts its own distinct dominant power, their respective fruits arise; one should know that all such fruits are termed dominant fruits.
Question:
How is it established? Answer:
The cause of conventional expression (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*) is established based on the basis of speech. Why is this?

Because, based upon the establishment of phenomena associated with the desire realm, phenomena associated with the form and formless realms, and unconditioned phenomena, there first arises conceptualization (*saṃjñā*); because conceptualization precedes it, speech is produced; and because of speech, one gives rise to various verbal expressions according to what is seen, heard, sensed, and known. Therefore, the cause of conventional expression is established based on the basis of speech.
The dependence cause (*apekṣā-hetu*) is established based on the basis of the cause of experience (*anubhava-nimitta-adhiṣṭhāna*). Why is this?
Because those who desire the pleasure associated with the realm of desire, by depending upon this [basis], seek to acquire, accumulate, or enjoy the various objects of desire.
Those who desire to seek the pleasure bound to the realms of form and formlessness, because they contemplate this, will either seek to acquire those various conditions or seek to enjoy them.
Those who seek the pleasure that is unconditioned, because they contemplate this, either seek to acquire those conditions or seek to utilize them.

Those who do not desire suffering, because they contemplate this, either seek to distance themselves from or seek to utilize the acquisition of those conditions or the abandonment of those conditions.
Therefore, the causal condition of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*) is established based on the basis of experience (*anubhava-adhiṣṭhāna*),
and the causal condition of projection (*ākṣepa-hetu*) is established based on the basis of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-hetu*). Why is this so?

Through the perfuming of pure and impure karma, the various formations (*saṃskāra*) of the three realms bring about the attainment of desirable or undesirable personal bodies within desirable or undesirable destinies.
Furthermore, by the predominant power of this very [karma], external requisites either come to fulfillment or undergo diminution.
Therefore, based on the locus of the habitual tendencies of pure and impure karma among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) is established;
based on the locus of the moistened seed-cause, the producing cause (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*) is established.
Why is this? All phenomena bound by desire, as well as those bound by form and the formless, each arise from their own respective seeds.
"Craving" is named the moisture, and the "seeds" are that which is moistened; because of these moistened seeds, the distinct individual bodies previously projected now attain arising.
As the Sūtra says:
"Karma is the cause that brings about birth; craving is the cause that gives rise to birth.
Therefore, based on the locus of the moistened seed, the cause for the arising of birth is established.

Based on the causal basis of immediate cessation, as well as the object, the faculties, the activity, and the human effort, one establishes the grasping cause by means of the causal basis of seeing reality.

Why is this? Because those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) proceed by way of the appropriation of the immediate cessation of all phenomena bound to desire, the appropriation of their objects, the appropriation of the faculties, the appropriation of their functions, and the appropriation of human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
Just as it is with the formations bound by desire, so it is with the formations bound by form and the formless.
Because they are embraced by the vision of reality, other unbound formations proceed.
Therefore, based on the locus of the true seeing of the function of the sense faculties regarding objects that have ceased without interval, the appropriating cause (*parigraha-hetu*) is established;
based on the locus of the concordant cause, the productive cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) is established.

Why is this? Because wholesome dharmas bound to the desire realm can induce all superior wholesome dharmas bound to the desire realm; likewise, these wholesome dharmas bound to the desire realm can induce all superior wholesome dharmas bound to the form and formless realms, as they are in conformity with them.

Just as wholesome phenomena bound to the desire realm [produce results], so too do wholesome phenomena bound to the form realm induce superior wholesome phenomena bound to the form realm, as well as superior wholesome phenomena bound to the formless realm or those that are unbound.

Just as wholesome dharmas bound to the form realm [lead to further results], so too do wholesome dharmas bound to the formless realm lead to the attainment of various superior wholesome dharmas bound to the formless realm and to those wholesome dharmas that are unbound.

Just as with wholesome dharmas bound to the formless realm, so too do wholesome dharmas that are unbound lead to the attainment of various superior wholesome dharmas that are unbound, as well as leading to the realization of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, unwholesome dharmas can induce superior unwholesome dharmas; that is to say, for example, sensual desire can induce hatred, delusion, pride, views, doubt, bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct.
Just as it is with sensual desire, so it should be understood in full for hatred, delusion, pride, views, and doubt, each according to its respective application.

Likewise, indeterminate dharmas can induce wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas; that is to say, the ālayavijñāna which maintains the seeds of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
