Furthermore, indeterminate dharmas can induce similar and superior indeterminate dharmas; that is to say, various types of edible food can induce already-born sentient beings to remain without perishing, and can induce the power of their satisfaction to increase, because they are concordant with them.
Therefore, based on the locus of the cause of conformity, the cause of production is established;
based on the locus of the cause of differentiated function, the cause of specific determination is established. Why is this so?

Because the intrinsic functional capacity (*svabhāva-śakti*) of phenomena bound by desire (*kāma-pratisaṃyukta*) possesses differentiation, they are able to produce various phenomena with differentiated natures.

As it is with phenomena bound by desire, so it is with phenomena bound by form (*rūpa-pratisaṃyukta*), phenomena bound by the formless (*ārūpya-pratisaṃyukta*), and unbound phenomena (*apratisaṃyukta*).
Therefore, based on the locus of differentiated functional capacity, the specific cause (*pratiniyamahetu*) is established;
based on the locus of the combined cause (*sāmagrīhetu*), the cooperative cause (*sahakārihetu*) is established. Why is this so?
It is by virtue of obtaining the conjunction of its own arising that phenomena bound to the desire realm arise.
As it is with phenomena bound to the desire realm, so it is with those bound to the form realm, those bound to the formless realm, and those that are unbound.
Just as with the conjunction of arising, so too it is with the conjunction of attainment, the conjunction of establishment, the conjunction of accomplishment, and the conjunction of activity.
Therefore, based on the locus of conjunction, the cause of common purpose (*sahabhāga-hetu*) is established.
The opposing cause (*virodha-hetu*) is established based on the locus of the obstructive cause. Why is this?
When a phenomenon bound by desire (*kāma-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*) is about to arise, if an obstruction is present, it cannot come into being.
As it is with phenomena bound by desire, so it is with phenomena bound by form, phenomena bound by the formless, and phenomena that are unbound.
As it is for the sake of arising through desire, so it is for the sake of obtaining, for the sake of establishing, for the sake of accomplishing, and for the sake of functioning through desire.
Therefore, the contradictory cause (*virodha-hetu*) is established based on the basis of obstruction (*āvaraṇa-adhiṣṭhāna*),
while the non-contradictory cause (*avirodha-hetu*) is established based on the basis of non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa-hetu*). Why is this so?
When a phenomenon bound by desire is about to arise, it arises provided that no obstructing conditions are present.
As it is with phenomena bound by desire, so it is with those bound by form, those bound by the formless, and those that are unbound.
As it is with arising, so it is with obtaining, establishment, accomplishment, and activity.
Therefore, based on the locus of non-obstruction, the non-contradictory cause is established.

Furthermore, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is established based on the basis of the seed-condition; the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is established based on the basis of the immediately ceased condition; the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is established based on the basis of the objective-condition; and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is established based on the basis of the remaining conditions.

Furthermore, based on the basis of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and the basis of concordant causes and conditions, the fruition of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and the fruition of natural outflow (*niṣyandaphala*) are established; based on the basis of the cause of seeing reality (*tattvadarśana*) and the basis of causes and conditions, the fruition of disconnection (*visamyogaphala*) is established; based on the basis of the cause of human effort (*puruṣakārahetu*) and the basis of causes and conditions, the fruition of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) is established; and based on the basis of the remaining causes and the basis of causes and conditions, the dominant fruition (*adhipatiphala*) is established.

Furthermore, the meaning of "conducive benefit" is the meaning of cause (*hetu*); the meaning of "establishment" is the meaning of condition (*pratyaya*); and the meaning of "accomplishment" is the meaning of fruit (*phala*).

Furthermore, there are five aspects of the establishment of causes: namely, the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), the instrumental cause (*upāya-hetu*), the coexistent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the immediately preceding cause (*anantara-niruddha-hetu*), and the long-past cause (*dūra-niruddha-hetu*).
The productive cause refers to the cause of origination.
The instrumental cause refers to the remaining causes.
The co-existent cause refers to a portion of the sustaining cause, such as the eye in relation to visual consciousness, and likewise the ear and so forth in relation to the remaining consciousnesses.
The cause of immediate cessation refers to the cause of arising.
The cause of long-term cessation refers to the cause of projection.

Furthermore, there are five characteristics of establishing causes: namely, the agreeable cause, the disagreeable cause, the cause of increase, the cause of transmigration, and the cause of cessation.
Furthermore, there are seven characteristics for establishing a cause: namely, that impermanent phenomena are the characteristics of a cause.

No permanent phenomenon can be designated as a cause; these are: the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), the acquisitive cause (*prāpaka-hetu*), the demonstrative cause (*sādhaka-hetu*), the accomplishing cause (*nirvartaka-hetu*), and the functional cause (*kāritra-hetu*).

Furthermore, when an impermanent dharma acts as a cause for another impermanent dharma, it serves as a cause for the nature of another and not for its own nature; yet it also serves as a cause for its own subsequent nature, rather than being identical to that very moment.

Furthermore, when acting as a cause for another nature and subsequently as a cause for its own nature, it must have already arisen and not yet ceased; it is not the case that it has not yet arisen or has already ceased.
Moreover, when acting as a cause while having already arisen and not yet ceased, it necessarily obtains other conditions; it is not the case that it does not obtain them.
Furthermore, when other conditions are encountered, it necessarily undergoes transformation; it does not remain untransformed.
Moreover, at the time of transformation, it must possess corresponding functional capacity; its functional capacity does not diminish or disappear.
Furthermore, when functional capacities correspond, they must be mutually commensurate and concordant; they are not non-commensurate or discordant.
Thus, these seven types of causal characteristics should be understood as being established according to their respective applications.
Furthermore, the determination of the unconditioned shall now be explained.
The verse says:
Because of the mind’s objects and so forth, and because of the objects of purification.
Due to four kinds of dissociation (*visamyoga*), eight unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are established.
The treatise says:
The eight kinds of unconditioned phenomena have already been explained in the "Chapter on the Compendium of Bases" (*Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*).

Regarding unconditioned space (*ākāśa-asamskṛta*), it is established as permanent because the objective aspect (*ālambana-nimitta*) that serves as the object of the mind is similar [to itself]; this is not because the mind that takes it as its object or the objective realm it perceives undergoes change at any time.
Suchness is established by virtue of being the object of purification; for when this suchness is purified, its essential nature as the object of cognition remains eternally as it is.

Based on four kinds of dissociation (*visamyoga*), the other four unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are established, namely: non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and the other three.

"Dissociation" refers to: ultimate dissociation through the departure from conditions; ultimate dissociation from afflictions through analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*); temporary dissociation from suffering and pleasure; and temporary dissociation of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Having thus explained all the definitive analyses (*viniścaya*), the definitive analysis of the elements (*dhātu*) and their entities (*vastu*) shall now be explained.
The verse says:
One should know that the three realms (*dhātu*) Are distinguished by twelve aspects.
The objects to be remedied and the remedies themselves / Can only suppress and subdue the seeds.
The Commentary says:
It should be understood that within the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness, there are twelve distinct types of characteristics.

Regarding the various distinctions, these should further be understood as being of six kinds: namely, multiple bases, multiple appearances, multiple locations, multiple objects, multiple afflictions, and multiple activities.
Second, the distinction between the two realms of rebirth;
third, the distinction between being accompanied by suffering, pleasure, or neither-suffering-nor-pleasure;

fourth, the distinction between having obstacles and being without obstacles—meaning that in the desire realm there may be either obstacles or their absence, whereas in the two upper realms there are only obstacles because their functional capacity is diminished.

Regarding the distinctions between the five impure places and the impure body and so forth: there may be a place that is impure while the body is pure, namely, being born in a realm of desire where there are no obstacles.
There are cases where the environment is pure but the body is not pure; this refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the realms of form and formlessness.
There are cases where the environment is impure and the body is also impure; this refers to those born in difficult circumstances (*durgati*) within the desire realm.
There are cases where both the locus and the body are pure, namely those who have already seen the truths within the form and formless realms.

There are six distinctions of enjoyment: that is, the enjoyment of external-sphere objects and the four kinds of nutriment in the desire realm, and the enjoyment of internal-sphere objects and three kinds of nutriment in the two higher realms.
1. The distinction between the superiority and inferiority of the seven roots of goodness;
2. The distinction between the roots of goodness associated with mixed unwholesome conduct and those not associated with mixed unwholesome conduct;
3. The distinction between the thickness and thinness of the heavy residues (*dausthulya*).
Tenth, the distinction of birth.

Eleventh, the distinction of obtaining a self-body (*ātmabhāva-pratilambha*): that is to say, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one obtains four kinds of self-bodies; in the two higher realms, there is only one kind, because those [other] realms lack [the conditions for] such [deaths], and because there is neither self-harm nor harm by others.

There are twelve distinctions of verbal expression; that is to say, the desire realm possesses all four types of verbal expression, while the form realm lacks them because it is devoid of initial mental application (*vitarka*) and sustained investigation (*vicāra*), and in the formless realm, none of them exist at all.

Furthermore, one should understand the distinction between the remedial and the remediable within these three realms: that is, the desire realm is the remediable, while the form realm is the remedial;
the form realm is the remediable, while the formless realm is the remedial.
Furthermore, the lower stages are that which is to be remedied, while the higher stages are the remedy.
Such remediation merely suppresses the seeds, rendering them weak and inferior; it does not constitute permanent destruction, because [the afflictions] will arise again.
Furthermore, the verse says:
The Dharma King, the saltiness of the ocean, Long life in the evil destinies due to desire,
And multiple worlds sharing a single [kalpa]— Each has two kinds of causes and conditions.
The treatise says:
For what reason and by what conditions is the Yama King, the Lord of Ghosts, called the Dharma King?
It is because he gathers and benefits those sentient beings.
They are able to provide benefit through two kinds of causes:
first, by causing them to remember the deeds committed in previous lives, so that they may reproach and loathe their own past unwholesome karma;
second, by causing them not to commit further unwholesome karma in the presence of the hell-wardens, so that they may swiftly attain liberation from those hells.
For what reason do the waters of all great oceans have a bitter-salty taste?
It is due to two causes:
first, because the power of the merit of aquatic sentient beings is predominant, it prevents other sentient beings from entering therein.
Second, because the non-merit (*apuṇya*) of beings born on land is predominant, it prevents them from entering to take the precious treasures.
For what reason is the lifespan of a portion of beings in the realms of hell and animals so long, whereas it is not so for those included within the happy destinies (*sugati*) of the desire realm?

This means that long lifespans in the miserable realms result from two causes: first, because wholesome dharmas of the desire realm can only arise through the power of discernment and strenuous effort; second, because unwholesome dharmas arise spontaneously without the need for discernment.

For what reason, within this trichiliocosm, are there many worlds extending up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, yet they are collectively referred to as a single world reaching only as far as the Brahma-world?
That is to say, it is also due to two causes: first, because they are identical in their formation and destruction;
second, because they establish the assemblies. *Exposition of the Holy Teachings* (Xianyang shengjiao lun), Scroll 18 and Scroll 19.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Eleven, Part Three: The Compendium on the Determination of the Superior. The Treatise says:
Thus has been explained the determination of the entities of the elements (*dhātu*).
Now, within the superior determination of the entities of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), the superior determination of the afflictions of mental defilement (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*) shall first be explained.
The verse says:
The four afflictions associated with the mind arise universally and simultaneously;
they are indeterminate and cease last; their nature corresponds to that of the state in which they arise.
The treatise says:

It should be understood that the afflictions associated with the mental faculty (*manas*) are omnipresent across all states; they manifest simultaneously with all contaminated wholesome minds and so forth, because they are not mutually contradictory.
Furthermore, these afflictions are all innate (*sahaja*), not arising from discrimination (*vikalpita*);
they are of the nature of obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), not unwholesome (*akuśala*), and are suddenly severed by the final diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*).
Furthermore, these afflictions are of four kinds, namely: ignorance (*avidyā*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*), and self-love (*ātmasneha*).
It should be understood that for a person (*pudgala*) born within this realm, the afflictions associated with this mind are subsumed under the essential nature of this very realm.
Furthermore, the verse says:
The continuity of all births, Manifestation and conditions,
Latent tendencies, objects, and coarse heaviness— Each is differentiated into twenty [types].
The Treatise says:
If one is born in this realm and on this stage, then all afflictions of that realm and stage cause the continuity of existence to arise.

Furthermore, regarding these afflictive defilements—whether as active manifestations (*samudācāra*), conditions (*ālambana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), objective referents (*ālambanaviṣaya*), or dysfunctional states (*dausthulya*)—it should be known that each possesses twenty aspects of affliction.
There are twenty types of active manifestation (*samudācāra*): first, the manifestation of the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) according to one's desires, referring to householders;
second, the manifestation of the fetters not according to one's desires, referring to those who have gone forth;
third, the absence of discernment (*avijñapti*), referring to those who dwell in a poorly taught Dharma.
Fourth is that which is discerned, namely those who preach the Dharma well;
fifth is mutual predominance, namely those whose conduct is dominated by craving and so forth;
sixth is universal equality, namely those whose [defilements] are practiced in equal measure.
Seventh, those with attenuated [defilements], namely those who practice with attenuated passions;
eighth, the manifestation of external-door fetters, namely those who have not yet abandoned desire;
ninth, the manifestation of internal-door fetters, namely those who have abandoned desire by means of the mundane path.
10. The manifestation of the fetter of excessive dominance refers to ordinary worldlings;
11. the manifestation of the fetter of loss of mindfulness refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*);
12. the manifestation of the fetter of conceptualization refers to those who are firmly attached.
Thirteen: the manifestation of innate entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), which refers to those who do not firmly adhere [to their faults];
fourteen: the manifestation of investigation (*anveṣaṇa*), which refers to those who delight in investigation;
fifteen: the manifestation of lack of mastery (*asvatantra*), which refers to those who are asleep.
16. The manifestation of the sixteen masteries, which refers to those who have attained awakening;
17. The manifestation of the irremediable, which refers to those lacking the nature for nirvāṇa;
18. The manifestation of the remediable, which refers to those possessing the nature for nirvāṇa.
19. The manifestation of grasping at signs (*nimittagrahaṇapravṛtti*), which refers to those who, through discursive investigation (*vitarka*), grasp at the characteristics of phenomena;
20. The manifestation of not grasping at signs (*animittagrahaṇapravṛtti*), which refers to those who do not, through discursive investigation, grasp at the characteristics of phenomena.

There are twenty conditions for afflictions: first, pleasure; second, suffering; third, neither-suffering-nor-pleasure; fourth, desire; fifth, vitarka (discursive thought); sixth, contact; seventh, prior habituation; eighth, latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); ninth, not associating with virtuous friends; tenth, not hearing the true Dharma; eleventh, improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*); twelfth, lack of faith; thirteenth, laziness; fourteenth, loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*); fifteenth, distraction (*vikṣepa*); sixteenth, lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*); seventeenth, the affliction of heedlessness (*pramāda*); eighteenth, the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*); nineteenth, due to the departure from desire; and twentieth, due to rebirth.

There are twenty types of latent afflictions (*anuśaya*): first, the latent afflictions of the non-concentrated states; second, the latent afflictions of the concentrated states; third, those that follow their own objects; fourth, those that follow other objects; fifth, those that have been impaired; sixth, those that have not yet been impaired; seventh, those that are concordant; eighth, those that are discordant; ninth, those that are complete; tenth, those that are deficient; eleventh, those that are susceptible to destruction; twelfth, those that are not susceptible to destruction; thirteenth, predominant latent afflictions; fourteenth, equal latent afflictions; fifteenth, subtle latent afflictions; sixteenth, latent afflictions accompanied by discursive thought (*vitarka*); seventeenth, latent afflictions without discursive thought; eighteenth, latent afflictions that produce much suffering; nineteenth, latent afflictions that produce little suffering; and twentieth, latent afflictions that do not produce suffering.

Regarding the twenty kinds of objects of the afflictions (*kleśa*): first, objects that possess substantial reality; second, objects lacking substantial reality; third, objects with specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); fourth, objects with general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); fifth, objects perceived directly; sixth, objects not perceived directly; seventh, objects of the external gate; eighth, objects of the internal gate; ninth, objects of one’s own category of affliction; tenth, objects of another category of affliction; eleventh, objects of oneself; twelfth, objects of others; thirteenth, non-existent objects; fourteenth, objects associated with outflows (*sāsrava*); fifteenth, objects free from outflows (*anāsrava*); sixteenth, conditioned objects (*saṃskṛta*); seventeenth, unconditioned objects (*asaṃskṛta*); eighteenth, objects of one’s own mental conceptualization; nineteenth, objects of recollective conceptualization; twentieth, objects of phenomenal characteristics (*vastu-nimitta*).

There are twenty kinds of *dauṣṭhulya* (coarseness/heaviness): first, the *dauṣṭhulya* of nature and retribution; second, the *dauṣṭhulya* of nature and afflictions (*kleśa*); third, the *dauṣṭhulya* of nature and karma; fourth, the *dauṣṭhulya* of the affliction-obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*); fifth, the *dauṣṭhulya* of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); sixth, the *dauṣṭhulya* of meditative concentration-obscuration; seventh, the *dauṣṭhulya* of karma-obscuration; eighth, the *dauṣṭhulya* of retribution-obscuration; ninth, the *dauṣṭhulya* of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); tenth, the *dauṣṭhulya* of improper reflection (*ayoniśomanasikāra*); eleventh, the *dauṣṭhulya* of sorrow and distress; twelfth, the *dauṣṭhulya* of fear; thirteenth, the *dauṣṭhulya* of fatigue and exhaustion; fourteenth, the *dauṣṭhulya* of food; fifteenth, the *dauṣṭhulya* of sleep and dreams; sixteenth, the *dauṣṭhulya* of sexual desire; seventeenth, the *dauṣṭhulya* of the discordance of the great elements (*mahābhūta*); eighteenth, the *dauṣṭhulya* of the transformation of time-periods; nineteenth, the *dauṣṭhulya* of death; and twentieth, the *dauṣṭhulya* that is omnipresent.

Furthermore, to speak briefly, afflictions are understood through five aspects: namely, their essential characteristic (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), their causal characteristic (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*), their classificatory characteristic (*prakāra-lakṣaṇa*), their characteristic of mental distraction regarding objects (*viṣaya-citta-vikṣepa-lakṣaṇa*), and their resultant characteristic (*phala-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, to what extent should one speak of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the afflictions and their unwholesomeness?
The verse says:
Because they conform to and give rise to themselves, Because they are seeds, and because they are entities.
Because they give rise to four faults, and because of three causes of impurity.
The treatise says:

They are called *anuśaya* (latent dispositions) due to four kinds of causes. First, because they accord with their own arising; that is to say, if an object of affliction accords with this affliction;
Second, because of the persistence of the seeds;
third, because of their predominance;
and fourth, because they give rise to four faults.
The four faults are: first, the fault of non-quiescence; second, the fault of differentiation; third, the fault of initiating activity; and fourth, the fault of grasping causes.
Among these, the former is manifested by two [factors], while the three types are manifested by four.
Question:
To what extent should one understand the characteristics of unwholesome afflictions?
Answer: It is due to three causes: namely, because it is violent and intense, because it afflicts sentient beings, and because it can obstruct the wholesome.
Furthermore, the definitive analysis of the preeminence of karmic defilement shall now be explained.
The verse says:
Karmic volition and that which follows volition are distinguished into thirteen types;
their results consist of six and three stages, and karma is determined in five ways.
The treatise says:
If karma is explained briefly, there are two types, namely volition (*cetanā*) and that which follows volition (*cetayitvā*).
This karma further has thirteen distinctions:

1. Physical action; 2. verbal action; 3. mental action; 4. action subsumed under discipline (*saṃvara*); 5. action subsumed under non-discipline (*asaṃvara*); 6. action subsumed under neither; 7. meritorious action; 8. non-meritorious action; 9. immovable action; 10. black action with black ripening; 11. white action with white ripening; 12. black-and-white action with black-and-white ripening; 13. action that is neither black nor white and has no ripening, which is able to exhaust all actions.
It should be understood that such karma has six kinds of fruits and three kinds of stages.
The six kinds of fruits are: desirable fruit, undesirable fruit, pure fruit, ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*), concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*), and dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
The "three stages" refer to the stage of active function, the stage of habitual tendencies, and the stage of fruition.

Furthermore, such karma has five kinds of determinations: first, determination regarding experience in the present life; second, determination regarding experience in the next birth; third, determination regarding experience in subsequent lives; fourth, determination regarding the manner of experiencing retribution; and fifth, determination regarding the performance of the action itself.
Furthermore, the verse says:
The four types, such as karma of one's own making, And their prior maturation are likewise four;
One should know that there are further nine types, Which are simply distinctions between these two.
The treatise states:
As the Blessed One said:
"Māṇava, you should know that all sentient beings are the products of their own karma; karma is the root of contention, born from karma, and karma is their refuge."
Thus, this karma performed by oneself should be understood as being of four kinds:

because it can yield its fruit within one's own continuum; because the antidote and the counteracted appear before one; because it arises from the past into the present; and because it serves as the cause for future existence.
Because it is for the sake of exhausting karma, it is called the "basis of karma.

Furthermore, one should know that there are four ways in which the maturation of this karmic retribution occurs, according to priority: namely, first, the maturation of the most serious karma; second, the most recent; third, that which was habitually practiced; and lastly, that which was performed earlier.
Furthermore, one should know that karma which is subject to definite maturation cannot be severed;
however, karma whose retribution is indefinite cannot act as an obstacle to the severance [of defilements] upon the attainment of detachment from desire.
Moreover, various non-Buddhists give rise to such views and propound such doctrines:
In accordance with the various karmas created by sentient beings—whether accompanied by pleasure or accompanied by suffering—the ripening they receive is likewise so.
All those non-Buddhists are merely possessed of false attachments.
Why is this? Because they possess two types of experience.
That is to say, wholesome karmas result in both the retribution of suffering and the retribution of pleasure; unwholesome karmas are likewise the same.

Furthermore, one should know that karma becomes wholesome or unwholesome by depending on two types of roots: namely, wholesome karma arises by depending on the wholesome roots, and unwholesome karma arises by depending on the unwholesome roots.
Furthermore, one should know that the distinctions between wholesome and unwholesome karma arise from nine causes.
First, they arise by way of the cause and the field; that is to say, there are distinctions based on the wholesome or unwholesome roots as well as the fields such as those who are worthy of respect.
Second, by way of the object (*vastu*), meaning by way of objects that are complete or incomplete;
third, by way of the means (*upāya*), meaning by way of uninterrupted and earnest means;
fourth, by way of the basis (*niśraya*), meaning by way of a basis that is either pure or impure.
Fifth, by way of mental attention (*manasikāra*), that is, by means of intense pure faith (*śraddhā*) and predominant entanglements (*paryavasthāna*).
Sixth, by way of aspiration and resolve (*chanda-adhimokṣa*), that is, by means of dedicating [the roots of virtue] toward the pursuit of superior or inferior fruits of maturation (*vipāka*).
Seventh, by way of its accompaniment, meaning it is embraced by other remaining wholesome or unwholesome dharmas.

Eighth, by way of frequent cultivation, meaning one practices it oneself and teaches others to do so, praises it, rejoices in it, and feels joy in one's heart upon seeing those who share the same dharma.
Ninth, it is by way of many people, meaning that one performs this karma in common with many others.
Furthermore, the superior discernment regarding the defilements of birth shall now be explained.
The verse says:
Death at the end of one's lifespan may be certain or uncertain; premature death occurs due to six causes.
At the stage of clear comprehension, there are three moments of mind; the intermediate state (antarābhava) may or may not exist.
The treatise says:
There are two kinds of death at the end of life: first, that which is certain, namely in the northern continent of Uttarakuru;

second, that which is uncertain, namely in other places. Furthermore, premature death occurs due to six causes: first, by not avoiding what is uneven; second, by loss of mindfulness; third, by mental anger and resentment; fourth, by the exhaustion of the lifespan; fifth, by the exhaustion of karma; and sixth, by the exhaustion of merit.
Furthermore, at the time of death, there are three types of consciousness: wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral. These occur when the mind is in a state of clarity;
however, if one reaches a state of lack of clarity, it is necessarily and exclusively neutral.
Furthermore, after the end of life, there may be an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for those who are about to be born into the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*);
or there may be no intermediate state for those who are about to be born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Furthermore, the verse says:
Depending on others and having an object of perception, Defiled minds arise;
Within the four modes of birth, And throughout the three realms and five destinies.
The treatise says:
Relying upon another intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one takes the place of birth as an object; a defiled mind arises, causing the continuity of the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*).

Furthermore, among the four modes of birth, one undergoes various births and deaths, namely: birth from an egg (*aṇḍaja*), birth from a womb (*jarāyuja*), birth from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*), and birth by transformation (*aupapāduka*).
Furthermore, one undergoes various births and deaths within the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness, as well as within the five destinies beginning with the hells.
Thus, regarding death, birth, and the respective locations, the determination of the excellence of the defilement of birth has been revealed.
The determination of the objects of the truths shall now be explained.
The verse says:
One should know that conventional truth consists of conceptual understanding, meaning, and expression.
The nature of that purified object of focus is called the ultimate by way of skillful means.
The commentary states:
All verbal expressions and the meanings obtained through the conceptual understanding derived from them are termed conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Whether it be the object of purification, the nature of purification, or the means thereto, all are termed the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Regarding the object of purification, this refers to the four noble truths and suchness (*tathatā*).
Purity refers to the purity of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
The means refers to the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Furthermore, the verse says:
One should know that these four kinds are comprised of both defilement and purification;
they are like not yet seeing [the disease] and not yet having experienced it, and like the cause for the cessation of the disease.
The treatise says:
One should know that the Four Noble Truths are subsumed under two categories of phenomena: those that are defiled and those that are pure.
Defiled phenomena are of two kinds: either results or causes.
Purity is likewise so.

Regarding these Four Noble Truths, since beginningless time, all sentient beings have not yet perceived the two truths of cessation and the path as they truly are, nor have they ever experienced them.
Furthermore, just as there is illness, the cessation of illness, and their two causes, the four truths are established.

The truth of suffering is like illness; the truth of origination is like the cause of illness; the truth of cessation is like the cessation of illness; and the truth of the path is like the cause for the cessation of illness.
Furthermore, the verse says:
One should know that these Four Noble Truths each possess four characteristics and four aspects;
The four types, such as thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), Are distinguished by their nature as cause and effect.
The Treatise says:
It should be known that each of the Four Noble Truths has four aspects.

Regarding the Truth of Suffering, its four aspects are: first, the suffering of arising; second, the suffering of internal conditions; third, the suffering of external conditions; and fourth, the suffering of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*).

The first refers to the suffering of birth; the second refers to the sufferings of old age, illness, and death; the third refers to the suffering of association with the disliked, the suffering of separation from the beloved, and the suffering of not obtaining what one desires; the fourth refers to the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*).

The Truth of Origination has four characteristics: first, craving in general; second, craving for future existence; third, craving accompanied by delight and greed; and fourth, craving for various specific objects.
The truth of cessation has four characteristics: first, the exhaustion of craving; second, detachment from desire; third, cessation; and fourth, nirvana.
The truth of the path has four characteristics, namely the four types of practice such as the sluggish and painful progress, which have already been explained.
Furthermore, it should be understood that each individual truth has four aspects, as already explained in the "Chapter on the Manifestation of Clear Realization" (*Abhisamayālaṃkāra*).

Moreover, regarding these truths, one should understand the essential nature of their causes and effects in terms of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), permanent abandonment (*prahāṇa*), realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), and the cultivation of the path (*mārgabhāvanā*).

The first three are the fruits, and the cultivation of the path is the cause—namely, the thorough knowledge of the cause of suffering, the permanent abandonment of the cause of origination, and the realization of the cause of cessation.
Why are these called "truths" (satya) according to the conventional [perspective] and so forth?
The verse says:
That cognition is without conflict; so too are its nature and its realization.
The truths are of three kinds and are exclusively wholesome; furthermore, two kinds should be known.
The Commentary says:

Regarding "their cognition is free from conflict because it is the nature of things (*dharmatā*)," this means that because it is the nature of things, worldly fools and others have a cognition of those phenomena that is free from conflict; this is called the conventional truth as the nature of things (*saṃvṛtisatya-dharmatā*).

"Realization is likewise" means that for those who have already seen the truths, their realization of the dharma-nature is free from contradiction; this is why it is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) by way of this principle.
The Bhagavān said:
"All noble ones (ārya) regard these as truths; therefore, they are called Noble Truths (āryasatya).

Furthermore, regarding the four truths such as suffering and so forth, one should know that the first two pertain to all three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral—while the remaining two are exclusively wholesome."
Furthermore, there are two kinds of the wholesome: namely, the mundane and the supramundane.
These, in turn, are of two kinds: namely, those comprised within abandonment and those comprised within the path.
Having thus explained the determination of the entities of the truths, the determination of the bases shall now be explained.
The verse says:
One should know that there are seven bases, which are of three kinds of supporting natures;
skillfulness regarding them is twofold, as extensively explained in fourfold sets and so forth.
The treatise says:
It should be understood that because there are three kinds of bases, the Bhagavān taught seven types of reliance.
What are these three kinds of bases?
First, the basis for the exhaustion of outflows; second, the basis for the arousal of qualities; third, the basis for dwelling in happiness in the present life.
Furthermore, it should be understood that there are two kinds of skillfulness regarding this basis:
first, skillfulness in samādhi; [and second, skillfulness in the dharma].
2. Skillfulness in *samāpatti*.
This is analyzed in detail through four propositions, as the Blessed One stated in a summary verse (*uddāna-gāthā*):
"Some practitioners of dhyāna Are skillful in samādhi;..."
"Or samāpatti, or both together, or neither, and so forth.
What is skill in *samādhi* but not skill in *samāpatti*?

This means being skilled in the three samādhis, such as emptiness and so forth, but not being skilled in the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and so on.
What is skill in meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) but not skill in samādhi?

This refers to being skilled in entering and emerging from the *abhibhvāyatana*, the *kṛtsnāyatana*, the *asaṃjñisamāpatti*, and other such *samāpattis*, rather than merely being skilled in the three *samādhis*.
What is skillfulness in both?
It refers to being skillful in both the distinctions of the samādhis and the samāpattis as they have been explained.
What is lack of skillfulness in both?
This refers to being unskilled in both the distinctions between the samādhis and the samāpattis as they have been explained.

Furthermore, one who is skilled in samādhi but not skilled in samāpatti is one who thoroughly understands the distinctions of the names, phrases, and syllables of the samādhis entered, yet does not thoroughly understand the various modes, characteristics, and signs of the practices that lead into those samādhis.

One who is skilled in *samāpatti* but not skilled in *samādhi* refers to someone who, being well-versed in the modes, characteristics, and signs of the *samādhis* they enter, enters those meditative absorptions; yet, they do not well understand the distinctions among the names, phrases, and syllables of these *samādhis*, such as thinking, "I am now entering this or that named *samādhi*."

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who are able to enter a hundred or a thousand *samādhis*, yet they are unable to discern the distinctions among the sets of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*) of those concentrations, such as thinking, "I am now entering this or that named *samādhi*," until they have heard from the Buddhas or from Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have attained the ultimate consummation, or until they themselves have attained the ultimate consummation.
Question:
How does one abide in meditative concentration? Answer:

That is to say, there is someone who is well able to discern and grasp the characteristics and signs of the various formations for entering meditative concentration; because they have well discerned and grasped them, they abide in whatever concentration they wish to enter.
Furthermore, there is no falling away from the various samādhis entered.
Thus, there are two kinds of abiding:
first, it is called abiding because one dwells securely in meditative concentration; second, it is called abiding because one is able not to fall away.
Question:
How does one emerge from meditative absorption? Answer:

That is to say, there is a person who no longer reflects upon the characteristics and signs of the formations that enable entry into meditative concentration; rather, because they attend to phenomena with a mental attention belonging to the same category as the state of concentration, yet which is subsumed under the conceptual signs of the non-concentrated stage, they arise from this samādhi;
or they arise due to following what has been done, or due to the determination of what must be done, or due to the fulfillment of a prior vow.
"Actions according to circumstances" refers to activities concerning robes, alms bowls, and various requisites.
"Decisive actions" refers to such practices as answering the calls of nature, serving one's teachers and elders, and going for alms.

Regarding "that which is performed through a formal vow": this refers to a case where someone has pledged to perform some service for another, or rises from meditative concentration in order to enter yet another state of concentration.
Question:
What is "volitional formation" (*saṃskāra*)? Answer:
One enters meditative absorption by means of practicing upon an object of focus; therefore, it is called "practice" (*saṃskāra*).
This refers to the practices of coarseness, tranquility, sickness, an abscess, an arrow, impermanence, and so forth, which arise based on samādhi.
Question:
What is meant by "characteristics"? Answer:
If there is one who is about to enter meditative absorption, at that time the signs of absorption (samādhi-nimitta) will necessarily arise.
By means of these signs, the practitioner knows for himself: "I shall soon enter such-and-such a state of absorption," or "I have already entered it."
Furthermore, the instructor also knows that for this practitioner, such-and-such signs arise, and that before long they shall enter such-and-such a meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Question:
What is meant by "signs" (*nimitta*)?
Answer: There are two kinds of signs: first, the sign of the object (*ālambana-nimitta*), and second, the sign of the cause (*hetu-nimitta*).
As for the sign of the object, it refers to the sign of conceptualization (*vikalpa-nimitta*); by taking this as an object of focus, one enters meditative concentration.

The causal characteristic refers to all the provisions for entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*). These include: following the instructions of the teacher; accumulating the requisites for concentration; cultivating a mind of joy and desire for practice along with a sense of renunciation; thoroughly discerning the signs of distraction and non-distraction; and not being disturbed by others—whether humans, non-humans, sounds, or physical actions.
Question:
What is meant by "being well-tamed"? Answer:

If samādhi is constrained by the signs of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), it is like water that is naturally held back; it is not tranquil, not sublime, and not a path of security, and one cannot realize the single-pointed concentration of the mind.
It should be understood that at that time, this samādhi is not called "pliant" (dama) and does not abide according to one's will.
That which is the opposite of this is called "pliant.
Question:
What is meant by "the sphere of activity"? Answer:
It refers to the objective domain of samādhi; beyond this domain, one certainly cannot know.

Just as one who has entered the first dhyāna cannot know or see the matters of the second dhyāna and so forth, likewise, one cannot know or see the degrees of faculties (*indriya*) or the degrees of individuals (*pudgala*).
Question:
How is it induced? Answer:
It refers to that which can concisely encompass the meaning of extensive textual passages and can give rise to all supreme qualities.
Question:
What kind of samādhi is called "lovely"?

Answer: It refers to possessing shame (*hrī*), dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), affectionate respect (*gaurava*), and pure faith (*śraddhā*); applying attention in accordance with reality (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), mindfulness, and clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*); guarding the sense faculties; maintaining ethical discipline without regret, and so forth, up to delighting in entering *samādhi* at the very end, just as one desires.
One should know that the opposite of this is called "unpleasant.
Question:
What is meant by "pleasant" and "unpleasant"?

This refers to being partially accomplished and partially unaccomplished in such qualities as shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*); that is, possessing shame and dread of blame, yet not being associated with affection and respect (*gaurava*), and so forth, as explained at length.
Question:
What is increase? Answer:
This refers to the fact that samādhi has already attained increase.
Question:
What constitutes decrease?
Answer: It refers to having attained samādhi and then losing it.
Question:
What is the skillful means?
Answer: It refers to the path leading to the two [goals].
Question: What is śamatha? Answer:
This refers to the characteristic of mental attention toward non-conceptual images.
Question:
What is "appropriation" (upādāna)?
Answer:
It refers to the arising of a grasping sign by means of any one of either a pure sign or a luminous sign.
Question:
How is it relinquished? Answer:
It refers to the attainment of the characteristic of equanimity that is superior within the category of wholesome qualities.
Furthermore, the superior discernment based on the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) shall now be explained.
The verse says:
"The enumerations, obstacles, and divisions of the meditative absorptions, as well as their extensive establishment."
"Far removed from suffering and movement, / Each subsequent stage is increasingly superior.
The commentary asks:
Regarding the four types of dhyāna described above, why are there exactly four—neither more nor less?
This is because the matters of suffering and pleasure have been brought to their ultimate end. Why is this so?
Because, proceeding gradually up to the fourth dhyāna, one attains transcendence over sorrow, suffering, joy, and pleasure.
Question:
What are the obstacles to be overcome by the first dhyāna? Answer:
There are five things to be known: first, discursive thoughts of desire, ill-will, and harm; second, suffering; third, grief; fourth, transgression of the precepts; and fifth, distraction. Question:
What are the obstacles to be overcome in the second dhyāna?

Answer: There are also five kinds that should be known: first, craving for the first dhyāna; second, vitarka and vicāra; third, suffering; fourth, restlessness; and fifth, inferiority of concentration.
Question:
What are the obstacles to be overcome by the third dhyāna? Answer:
There are four kinds that should be known: first, craving for the second dhyāna; second, joy (*prīti*); third, exultation (*praharṣa*); and fourth, inferiority of concentration (*samādhi-hīnatva*).
Question:
What are the obstacles to be remedied by the fourth dhyāna?

Answer: There are also five kinds to be known: first, inhalation and exhalation; second, craving for the third dhyāna; third, pleasure; fourth, mental attention to pleasure; and fifth, inferiority of concentration.
Question:
How many factors (aṅga) are there in the various dhyānas? Answer:
Initially, there are five factors. What are these five?
They are vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), prīti (joy), sukha (bliss), and citta-ekāgratā (one-pointedness of mind).
The second dhyāna has four factors, namely: internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
Question:
What is the essential nature of internal serenity?
Answer: It has mindfulness, clear comprehension, and equanimity as its essence.
The third dhyāna has five factors, namely: mindfulness, clear comprehension, equanimity, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.

The fourth dhyāna has four factors: purity of equanimity (*upekṣā-pariśuddhi*), purity of mindfulness (*smṛti-pariśuddhi*), neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
Question:
Since mindfulness, clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*), and equanimity exist in all stages, why are they not mentioned in the first dhyāna and the others?
Answer: In the first dhyāna, because it is induced by way of vitarka and vicāra, they exist but are not mentioned;

in the second dhyāna, because there is the activity of the essential nature of *prīti* (joyful exultation) and because it is enveloped and obscured by a portion of the mental factors of affliction (*kleśa*), it is designated collectively by the name "inner serenity" (*adhyātmasamprasāda*).

Because all minor afflictions associated with that mind are abandoned within the third dhyāna, and in order to manifest its specific characteristic, the Sūtra states that one is "distant from joy and greed."
In the first dhyāna, although one is free from the craving for sensual desire, one is not yet free from the craving for joy;
in the second dhyāna, although one is free from the craving for applied and sustained thought, one is not yet free from the craving for joy;
in the fourth dhyāna, this very equanimity and mindfulness are extremely pure and clearly manifest.
Therefore, one should understand their specific distinctions as they apply to each of the dhyānas respectively.
Question:
For what reason are four factors established for the first dhyāna and five factors for the others?
Answer: Because it is the basis for abiding, because it is conducive to the benefit of abiding, and because it is the essence of abiding.
Furthermore, because it involves reflecting upon objects, because it involves experiencing objects, and because it is non-distracted regarding objects.

Furthermore, it is because it serves as a basis for what is conducive and beneficial, because it is the basis for higher mind (*adhicitta*), and because it is the basis for higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of counteracting the three types of disturbances that obstruct abiding.
The three types of afflicted abidings are the afflicted abiding, the painful abiding, and the delusory abiding.

Furthermore, for one who enjoys the five sensory desires, there are three kinds of primary activities that manifest that enjoyment of desires: first, seeking what is to be enjoyed through correct means; second, correctly enjoying it once it has been obtained; and third, acting with mastery and spontaneity.

It should be understood that for one who thus cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the factors (*aṅga*) are established according to their respective requirements based on three types of correct activities.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the factors are established for one who cultivates meditative concentration as an antidote to self-mortification.
This, moreover, consists of three types of remedies:
first, the remedy for detachment from desire; second, the remedy for ceasing the affliction of body and mind; and third, the remedy for pacifying external mental distraction.
Question:
Why, after stating that one has become free from desire within the first dhyāna, does it further state that one is "distant from evil and unwholesome states"? Answer:
This is for the purpose of revealing the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the various desires and revealing their characteristic of defects (*ādīnava-lakṣaṇa*).
As for the characteristic of defects: because those desires give rise to unwholesome conduct and cause one to fall into the most debased states, they are called "evil" (*pāpa*);
because they arise in opposition to wholesome dharmas, they are called "unwholesome" (*akuśala*).

Furthermore, it is to manifest the ability to sever the afflictive defilements (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), and to manifest the ability to sever the previously accumulated karmic defilements (*karma-saṃkleśa*).

Furthermore, it is to manifest the severing of the desires arising from the sphere of sensory enjoyment for those in the household life, and to manifest the severing of the phenomena arising from the sphere of discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) for those who have gone forth.

Furthermore, it is to manifest the abandonment of sensual thought (*kāma-vitarka*), as well as to manifest the abandonment of ill-will thought (*vyāpāda-vitarka*) and harmful thought (*vihiṃsā-vitarka*).

Furthermore, it is to manifest that [the practitioner] attains the same characteristics as those external seers (*bāhiraka-ṛṣi*), and to manifest the abandonment of the evil spells (*abhicāra-mantra*) that arise after their [attainments] have degenerated.
Question:
For what reason is it said that the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is not abandoned within the first dhyāna? Answer:
Because that category of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) has not yet been abandoned.

If the category of coarse heaviness associated with the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) were already severed in the first dhyāna, there would be no difference between it and abiding in the second dhyāna; therefore, one should know that within the first dhyāna, the category of coarse heaviness associated with suffering has not been severed.
Question:

Since mental applications (*vitarka*) and discursive thoughts (*vicāra*), among other factors, can provide benefit and support within the first dhyāna and so forth, causing their respective stages to attain purity, for what reason did the Tathāgata designate them as "movement"?
Answer: It is said to be "moving" in relation to other stages, not in relation to its own stage.
Question:
For what reason are the successive factors established within the desire realm and the first dhyāna, etc.?

Answer: Briefly, there are three reasons: namely, because of the relationship between the antidote and the object to be countered; because of the realization of benefit; and because of the realization of the essential nature.
These three causes are comprised within the five factors (*pañcāṅga*) of the four dhyānas; they should be understood according to their respective applications.
Question:
What is the distinction of the second dhyāna compared to the first dhyāna?
Answer: It is the excellence of the perfection of samādhi.
Question:
What is the superior distinction of the third dhyāna compared to the second dhyāna?
Answer: It is the superior distinction of being conducive to benefit and complete perfection.
Question:
What is the superior distinction of the fourth dhyāna compared to the third dhyāna? Answer:
It is pure, complete, and superior.
Furthermore, the verse says:
The joy of the preparatory stages is subject to movement; Only the first [dhyāna] can exhaust the outflows.
There are also two kinds of conditions for sound; [one] abandons eight through the eight attainments (*samāpatti*).
The treatise says:
In the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna, joy (*prīti*) is subject to movement, unlike the joy of the fundamental dhyāna.
Furthermore, it is only the concentration included within the initial access concentration (*anāgamya*) that can exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*), and no other.
Moreover, there are two kinds of initial access concentration: namely, the mundane (*laukika*) and the supramundane (*lokottara*).

The remaining access concentrations (sāmantaka) are exclusively mundane; because one has already attained the first fundamental untainted (anāsrava) dhyāna, the untainted access concentrations of the higher stages do not manifest.
Furthermore, when one perceives external sounds while remaining in meditative concentration, it should be understood that this perception occurs through two types of apprehension:

first, by means of the mental consciousness that discerns the object of the concentration as well as various other objects; and second, by means of the ear-consciousness that arises simultaneously with it.
Regarding "the eight attainments abandon eight things," this means that the eight kinds of *samāpatti* (attainments) are able to abandon eight matters.
What are these eight?
They are the four dhyāna *samāpattis*, which are realized by abandoning speech, vitarka (applied thought), prīti (joy), and sukha (bliss).
By relinquishing the perceptions of form, space, consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness, one realizes the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Dwelling in happiness in the present life, One is able to enter into clear realization (*abhisamaya*)."
The praise of the liberation through perception should be understood as having four causes.
The commentary states:
Only the dhyānas constitute the nature of dwelling in happiness in the present life, because they possess both types of peace—those of body and mind.
It is not the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), because they lack bodily tranquility.

Furthermore, one enters into clear realization (*abhisamaya*) by relying on the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), not the formless attainments, because insight (*vipaśyanā*) is most intense within the various meditative concentrations.

Furthermore, those who cultivate dhyāna and various meditative absorptions repeatedly enter and emerge from the formless liberations (*ārūpya-vimokṣa*), praising their characteristics because they are utterly tranquil.
Moreover, the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) repeatedly praise them because they conceive the notion of liberation regarding the formless attainments.

Furthermore, it is by relying on the samādhi of perception (*saṃjñā-samādhi*) that one is liberated and able to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*), up to the point where the samādhi of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is most intense and powerful.
Therefore, the Bhagavān said:
"It is only by relying on the meditative attainment of perception (*saṃjñā-samāpatti*) that one realizes and penetrates [the truth], and not in any other stage."

Regarding the four kinds of causes: it should be understood that the various *samāpattis* serve as the four types of supporting causes for dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) and so forth, respectively.
Furthermore, the verse says:
One should know that the relishing of flavor and so forth Are of ten kinds, six kinds, and three kinds;
The signs of decline, the continuity, the obstacles, and the remedies Each have many varieties of distinction.
The treatise says:

It should be understood that the three types of dhyāna—those associated with relishing (*āsvādana*), those that are pure (*śuddha*), and those that are untainted (*anāsrava*)—consist of ten, six, and three kinds respectively, in their proper order.
What are the ten kinds?
They are as already explained in the Chapter on the Compendium of Bases (Vastusaṃgrahaṇī). What are the six kinds?
That is to say, there are six kinds of purity:

first, the purity of elicitation; second, the purity of superior refinement; third, the purity of subsequent attainment; fourth, the purity of the removal of defilements; fifth, the purity of integration; and sixth, the purity of capability.
What are the three types? They are:
supramundane untainted [wisdom], untainted [wisdom] of dissociation from fetters, and subsequently attained untainted [wisdom].
Furthermore, regarding the continuum that has regressed from the state of freedom from desire, one should know that there are many varieties of both those obstacles and their remedies.

That is to say, one may regress due to an imbalance in the physical basis (*āśraya*). For example, there is one who, having encountered a severe illness, regresses and loses meditative concentration (*samādhi*). As the Venerable Vakkali said:
"I am currently unable to enter this samādhi; could it be that I have regressed from this samādhi because of excessive heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*)?"

Furthermore, there is another case: someone whose nature is characterized by a great deal of *dausthulya* (coarseness and heaviness) due to past habituation; because of this excessive *dausthulya*, they fall away from *samādhi*.

Or, they may fall away because the object is exceptionally sublime; that is to say, there is someone who, upon encountering a sublime object appearing before them, loses their concentration—just as it is heard that certain non-Buddhist sages, having attained the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, fell away from that concentration upon touching the body of a beautiful young maiden.

Or, one may fall away due to receiving honor and offerings; that is to say, there are some who, upon encountering excellent and sublime honor and offerings before them, lose their meditative concentration, as was the case with Devadatta and others.

Or, one may fall away due to contempt and disparagement; that is to say, there are some who, when reviled and rebuked by others with anger, lose their meditative concentration, just as the various non-Buddhist seers, having fallen away through wrathful resentment, cast various evil spells.

Or one may fall away due to pride (*māna*); that is to say, there is someone who, because of the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) they have attained, becomes self-exalting and treats others with contempt, thereby falling away from that concentration.

Or one may fall away due to overweening pride (*abhimāna*); that is to say, there is someone who, having given rise to overweening pride regarding a concentration not yet attained, falls away from the concentration they had previously attained.

Alternatively, one may regress due to a lack of mental attention (*amanasikāra*). That is to say, there is someone who previously entered various meditative absorptions by means of such modes, aspects, and characteristics; later, because they no longer reflect upon these modes, aspects, and characteristics, they fall away from that absorption.
Or, one may regress due to a lack of full maturity; that is to say, there is someone who, having begun practicing their initial tasks and newly giving rise to wholesome qualities, regresses.

Or, one may lose meditative concentration because many of one's own afflictions manifest; that is to say, there is someone who, due to craving for higher dhyānas or even doubt regarding higher dhyānas, loses meditative concentration.

Or one may fall away due to the exhaustion of lifespan, the exhaustion of merit, or the exhaustion of karma; that is to say, as when someone, having passed away from a place of birth in a higher realm, falls and is reborn in a lower realm.

Furthermore, if a person (pudgala) possesses weak afflictions and weak roots of virtue, they will only fall away after exerting effort over many moments, and they will only enter meditative absorption after exerting effort over many moments.

If a person possesses weak afflictions and superior roots of virtue, they will only fall back after exerting effort over many moments, yet they will swiftly attain meditative absorption in a single moment.

If a person (pudgala) possesses superior-grade afflictions and inferior-grade roots of virtue, they will quickly lose their meditative concentration in a single moment, and only after exerting effort over many moments can they enter concentration.

If a person possesses both superior afflictions and superior roots of goodness, they may rapidly fall away from meditative concentration in a single moment, yet they can also rapidly enter meditative concentration in a single moment.
Furthermore, the verse says:
Those of sharp faculties and those who have undergone a change of birth, one should know that they do not fall away;
because they produce meditative absorption based on a lower stage, and because they are born after having already abandoned desire.
The Treatise says:
Such falling away from meditative concentration does not occur for those of sharp faculties.
Even if one undergoes a change of birth, there is likewise no falling away for those of dull faculties.

Furthermore, meditative absorptions such as the dhyānas must first be initiated based on a lower stage, because one enters meditative absorption in this [lower] realm and only subsequently is born there.
Why is this? Because it is only those who have first become detached from desire that are later able to be born there.
Having thus explained the determination of the bases (*āśraya-viniścaya*), the determination of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya-viniścaya*) shall now be explained.
The verse says:
Based on the two vehicles and the Great Vehicle, By means of twenty-seven aspects,
"One should know that right effort establishes the factors of enlightenment.
The commentary says:

One should know that the factors of enlightenment are established based on the two vehicles of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha, as well as the Mahāyāna, by means of twenty-seven kinds of characteristics of right effort.
What are the twenty-seven kinds of right application? They are:
the application of right contemplation connected with the object of focus; the application of abandoning defilement and embracing purity;
the application of cultivating the internal mind to make it pliant and compliant; the application of bringing forth the supramundane true Dharma; and that which is uninterrupted [by them].
The method of lacking skillful means; the method of realizing awakening through truth; the method of realizing other forms of tranquility;
the method of entering into that which is to be known; the method of entering into abandonment; the method of penetrating the impurity, lack of bliss, and presence of suffering;
the method of the perfection of training; the method of observing objects without distraction; and the method of the non-destruction of the noble teachings.
Furthermore, it includes the skillful means of knowing that which is to be known through wisdom and its fruits; the skillful means of aspiration; the skillful means of compassion for sentient beings;

the skillful means of cultivating and purifying wisdom; the skillful means of the clear realization of phenomena (*dharmābhisamaya*); the skillful means of advancing toward the remedies and that which is to be remedied;
the skillful means of accumulating the provisions of merit; the skillful means of maturing sentient beings; and the skillful means of gathering [them].
The skillful means of all bodhisattva paths; the skillful means of manifesting majestic power; the skillful means of eliciting verbal teachings;
the skillful means of accumulating vast and profound mental cultivation; the skillful means of distancing oneself from the karma of lacking the Dharma;
and the skillful means of establishing sentient beings in the two realms of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the verse says:

The three distinctions of the body and so forth, And the observation of their reflected images, Arise through the three types of knowledge—learning and the rest; Thus, one remains mindful of the Dharma without delusion.
The treatise says:
It should be known that the body and so forth each have three kinds of distinctions.
Regarding the three types of the body: there are those whose nature is impure by its own essence, such as the internal parts of the body;
Some parts of the body are similar to being pure, such as the skin;
some parts of the body are transformed and impure, such as the livid discoloration and other states of the body after death.
There are three kinds of feeling: namely, suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
There are three kinds of mind: namely, the pleasant and so forth.
There are three kinds of phenomena associated with feeling: namely, black, white, and mixed.
Regarding the contemplation of those images, it is as stated in the *Sūtra on Investigation*:
"Because one contemplates those images of the body and so forth as being of the same category as the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-vastu*), they are called 'images' (*pratibimba*)."
What is called "conformity" (anuvartana) has the meaning of "similarity.

Furthermore, this contemplation of conformity consists of three types of knowledge: namely, the knowledge born of hearing (śrutamaya-jñāna), the knowledge born of reflection (cintāmaya-jñāna), and the knowledge born of cultivation (bhāvanāmaya-jñāna).

These three types of knowledge, through the power of mindfulness, are free from confusion regarding the *sūtras* and other teachings that serve as their predominant conditions; therefore, they are called "mindfulness-abidings" (*smṛtyupasthāna*) with respect to the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, because they abide by means of the power of mindfulness.
Furthermore, the verse says:
Those [factors] to be countered are of nine kinds; one should know that mental attention is twofold;
the distinctions in cultivation are threefold; and two kinds are without loss or destruction.

The treatise states: It should be understood that there are nine kinds of counteractive obstacles to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): first, lack of revulsion; second, lack of mental attention (*amanasikāra*); third, the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) associated with calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*); fourth, sinking; fifth, inability to endure; sixth, contentment with what is meager or inferior; seventh, forgetting the instructions; eighth, transgressing ethical conduct (*śīla*); and ninth, abandoning the yoke of desire, delight, and the exceedingly intense, sublime roots of goodness.

Furthermore, there are two kinds of mental attention (*manasikāra*) in the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): namely, non-lax mental attention and non-defiled mental attention.
The Sūtra states:
"The 'blazing' refers to the first; 'with right knowledge and mindfulness, removing worldly greed and sorrow' refers to the second."
Furthermore, this second [factor] can eliminate three kinds of defilements.
What are these three kinds of defilements?
First, the mind gives rise to regret due to the causes and conditions of violating precepts; because of this hindrance, the mind cannot attain concentration at the initial stage.
Second is mental dullness and lethargy within; due to this hindrance, although one has attained meditative concentration, the mind forgets the object of focus and sinks into torpor.

Third is outward mental distraction; due to this hindrance, although one has realized sublime dharmas, one becomes attached to worldly fame and gain, or, failing to realize further progressive dharmas, the mind gives rise to distress.

Regarding the threefold distinction in cultivation: each of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) has three modes of cultivation, namely, observing the body internally, externally, or both.
Furthermore, regarding the body, one may observe only its reflected image, or use the reflected image as an analogy for the body, or observe them combined as a whole.
Just as it is with respect to the three aspects of the body, so it is likewise for the dharmas up to that point.
Furthermore, there are two ways in which the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are not lost or destroyed:
first, being undestroyed from the outset, which means non-distraction; by the power of this, one is able to skillfully initiate [the practice].
Second, there is no subsequent loss or destruction, meaning that one is free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*); by the power of this, one thoroughly cultivates the ultimate.
Furthermore, the verse says:
To sever sinking and agitation, The two kinds of corresponding paths [are employed].
"Observe the relinquishing of afflictions, and act to exhaust the three types of craving.
The commentary states:

Within the stage of cultivating the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one should cultivate the two types of associated paths in order to sever lethargy (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*).
As it is stated in the *Bhikṣuṇī-sūtra* and the *Svayaṃcittanimitta-grahaṇa-sūtra*.
How does the *Bhikṣuṇī-sūtra* speak? As that sūtra says:
In order to sever dullness and lethargy, one should contemplate a small portion of a pleasing and pure mental image.
In order to sever agitation and restlessness, one should again briefly withdraw the mind.
What does the *Sūtra on Grasping the Characteristics of One’s Own Mind* say? As that sūtra states:

"Because one does not grasp the characteristics of one's own mind, the mind becomes sunken; because one grasps a small portion of external attractive characteristics, the sinking secondary afflictions are temporarily suspended."

However, as the mind has not yet attained concentration, one further briefly collects it; seeing the fault of sinking, one again takes up external signs, and seeing the fault of agitation, one again takes up the sign of one's own internal mind. At that time, one is able to sever the secondary afflictions of sinking and agitation so that the mind attains right concentration, because by briefly collecting the mind and taking up the sign of one's own internal mind, one becomes free from sinking and agitation.
Furthermore, it should be understood that by means of observing through the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*), one is able to abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*), as stated in the *Śyena-sūtra*.
Thus, that sūtra says:
"That which is called 'the hawk' (*śyena*) is a metaphor for the mental activity (*citta-carita*) of the practitioner."
"Not within one's sphere of activity" is a metaphor for that practitioner contemplating an attractive object.
"Being seized by a hawk" is a metaphor for that practitioner being seized by the entanglement of greed.
The quail’s grievance and complaint is a metaphor for the practitioner’s mind giving rise to regret and remorse.
The temporary letting go is a metaphor for the practitioner’s entanglement with craving momentarily subsiding.
The clod of earth is a metaphor for the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
The large field and mound are metaphors for the contemplation of impermanence (*anityatā*).
The cave and hollow are metaphors for the contemplation that penetrates true suchness (*tathatā*).
Calling out to the hawk is a metaphor for the mental engagement of observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-manasikāra*).
The hawk swiftly approaching is a metaphor for the afflictions of greed about to manifest.
Entering the cave is a metaphor for the contemplation of *tathatā*.
The hawk suffering harm from itself is a metaphor for the severance of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that this path of union is capable of exhausting the three types of craving—namely, craving for companionship, craving for gain and honor, and craving for future existence.
To counteract these, it is revealed that there is no distinction between the self and phenomena (*dharma*).
Furthermore, the verse says:
To sever overweening pride, The perversions based on attachment to flavors,
And for the three types of mental engagement, One cultivates the foundations of mindfulness.
The treatise states:

One cultivates the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) in order to counteract overweening pride (adhimāna), to counteract the meditative concentration that serves as a basis for relishing (āsvāda), and to counteract the four inversions (viparyāsa).
To counteract those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), as the Sūtra says:
"One should dwell in mindfulness only upon this body, sensation, mind, and phenomena; or even possess only wisdom, or only vision, or only focused mindfulness."

This overweening pride is of two kinds: that which arises regarding the coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) of the body and so forth that has not yet been abandoned, and that which arises regarding the remedial factors for the classes of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) that have not yet been perfected.
To counteract the meditative concentration that serves as a basis for attachment to flavor, as the Sūtra says:
"Because there is no basis.
To counteract perversion, as the Sūtra says:

Having no slight grasping toward any worldly phenomena because of the abandonment of perversions, one no longer grasps even the slightest five aggregates of clinging as permanent, pleasant, self, or pure.

Furthermore, it should be understood that there are three ways the mind inclines toward the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): namely, when wandering through a village, the mind inclines toward renunciation; when staying amidst the bustle of crowds, the mind inclines toward seclusion; and when dwelling in a quiet room, the mind inclines toward *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, because it tends toward transcending the realms of birth and death, toward the departure from afflictions, and toward the joy of cessation (*śānti*), the mind tends toward *nirvāṇa*.
