Chapter Eleven, Part Four: The Determination of the Superior [Factors]. Thus has been explained the determination of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
The supreme discernment regarding persons (pudgala) shall now be explained.
The verse says:
Based on the distinctions of faculties and so forth, Five [types] are established, yet only two [exist].
"Assuming five [categories] to be known, the three matters are brought to completion.
The Commentary says:
It should be understood that based on the distinctions of the faculties (*indriya*) and so forth, the fivefold classification is established as being ultimately twofold.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Because they take only two faculties as their objects, only two types of attention can be known;
because they take only two types of attention as their objects, only two types of cultivation can be known."
Because there are only two types of cultivation as conditions, only two types of practice can be known;
because there are only two types of practice as conditions, only two types of *pudgala* (persons) can be known.
"Practice" refers to the latencies (*vāsanā*) induced by cultivation.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the designation of a *pudgala* (person) is established by way of five causes:
first, by way of spiritual lineage (*gotra*), namely, those who are deliverable and those who are not;
second, by way of entry (*avatāra*), namely, the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth.
Third, by way of training (*śaikṣa*), namely those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Fourth, by way of attainment, namely those abiding in the four fruits and the three paths of approach (*pratipannaka*).
Fifth, by way of faults and virtues, namely those with obstructions and those without obstructions, and those bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) and those not bound by all fetters.
Furthermore, three fulfillments (sampad) are established based on three factors:
first, fulfillment of the faculties (indriya-sampad), which refers to those of immovable dharma (akopya-dharman);
second, fulfillment of meditative concentration (samādhi-sampad), which refers to attaining the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
The fulfillment of the three fruits refers to the arhat.
Thus has been explained the determination of the person (pudgala-viniścaya).
Now, the determination of the matter of the fruits (phala-vastu-viniścaya) shall be explained.
The verse says:
Realizing the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) and non-arising; The two causes and effects being without retrogression;
Because of three causes, there is neither annihilation nor permanence; Three fruits and three causes are thus predicted.
The treatise states:

Because one realizes the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), the various afflictions (*kleśa*) do not arise; it should be understood that this transformation of the basis is what is called "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*).

Furthermore, for two reasons, there is no regression from the fruit: namely, because it would be unreasonable [to claim] that one has realized arhatship without having permanently destroyed the seeds of the afflictions.
If the seeds of the afflictions have already been permanently destroyed, then the afflictions must necessarily not arise again, as their causal seeds no longer exist.
Furthermore, this permanence is established through three causes and conditions:
first, because it is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); for it is observed that conceptual proliferation is impermanent by nature.
Second, because it is manifested by the *tathatā* of twofold purity, it is like the malleable nature of refined gold;
third, because it is the nature wherein afflictions do not arise, being without distinction between before and after.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of fruits which the Tathāgata prophesies by means of three causes:

first, the prophecy of the verified purities (*avetyaprasāda*), namely the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), because of the attainment of the four verified purities through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Second is the prediction concerning joy (*prīti*), which refers to the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*); because one who is about to attain the fundamental dhyāna has already experienced a small degree of joy.

Third is the prediction concerning recollection (*anusmṛti*), which refers to the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*); having already attained the fundamental dhyāna, one currently witnesses various celestial hosts and the Brahma hosts engaging in discourse together, yet one still recollects that the merits of one's own vehicle (*yāna*) as sought have not yet been perfected.
Thus, the determination of the matters concerning the fruits has been explained; the determination of the qualities shall now be explained.
The verse says:
The establishment of all qualities Is due to seventeen types of supremacy.
Those distinctions are limitless, because they counteract the obstacles to be remedied.
The treatise says:
It should be known that these qualities are established by means of seventeen kinds of dominant power.
First, by way of the predominance of compassion for sentient beings, namely the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).

Second, by way of the predominance of the purification of the six obstacles, namely the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
In this context, liberation serves as the means, while fulfillment is achieved through the others.
Regarding the purification of the six obstacles: first, the purification of the obstacle to transformation, by means of the first two liberations;
second, the purification of the obstacle to the supreme dwelling in happiness in the present life, by means of the third liberation, because both the pure and the impure appear as purified.
The purification of the obstacles to the three returns is due to the fourth liberation;
the purification of the obstacles to the noble qualities such as the absence of strife (*araṇā*) is due to the fifth liberation;
and the purification of the obstacles consisting of all outflows (*āsrava*) and existence is due to the sixth and seventh liberations.
The purification of the obstacles to the six most supreme abidings in tranquility should be understood as occurring through the eighth liberation.
Thirdly, by knowing the proper time for proceeding to higher [attainments], namely, the quality of non-contention (*araṇā*).
Fourth, by way of the predominance of the objects of knowledge to be examined, namely, the "knowledge resulting from aspiration" (*praṇidhijñāna*);
fifth, by way of the predominance of verbal instruction, namely, the "unimpeded analytical knowledges" (*pratisaṃvid*);
sixth, by way of the predominance of skill in the six bases, namely, the "six supernormal powers" (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Skillfulness regarding the six sense bases consists of: first, skillfulness in attracting and gathering [disciples];
second, skillfulness in carefully listening to their speech, by means of which skillfulness one uses their own language for debate and refutation in order to preach the True Dharma;
and third, skillfulness in understanding latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Fourth, skill in coming;
fifth, skill in going;
sixth, skill in liberation.
Seventh, by way of the predominance of faith in others, namely the primary and secondary marks;
eighth, by way of the predominance of the purification of the three obstructions, namely the four kinds of universal purity.
The three obstructions are the obstruction of the basis, the obstruction of the object, and the obstruction of the mental faculty.
The nine [powers] are so called because they are predominant in answering all questions.
Tenth, by virtue of the supremacy of crushing all opposing arguments, namely the various forms of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).
Eleventh, by virtue of the supremacy of being without partiality toward the assembly one has gathered, namely the various forms of non-protectiveness (*arakṣa*).
Twelfth, because of the predominance in being able to gather and transform disciples, namely the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Thirteenth, because of the predominance in manifesting the deeds of an omniscient one at all times, namely the permanent eradication of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Fourteenth, due to the predominance of not missing the proper time for those to be converted, namely the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*).
Fifteenth, due to the predominance of observing the world six times during the day and night, namely great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Sixteenth, by way of surpassing the supremacy of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, namely, the unique qualities of a buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma).
Seventeenth, by way of accomplishing the activities of all tathāgatas, namely, the sublime knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).
Furthermore, because these various virtues differ according to their oppositions to the obstacles they counteract, one should know that they possess infinite distinctions.
Moreover, the verse says:
Contemplating meaning, pleasure, and suffering, Mental attention, and abiding.
Hardship and physical appearance, as well as the extraordinary and the non-extraordinary.
The commentary states:
Regarding those various merits, one should contemplate both that which is to be countered and that which serves as the counteragent.
What is reflection?
It refers to whether it is a meaning, or pleasure, or suffering, or mental attention, or abiding, or difficulty, or a characteristic, or something extraordinary or non-extraordinary.
In this context, the meaning of "contemplation" refers to the various phrases subsumed under the meaning of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

There are five kinds of purposes: first, the purpose of engendering reverence for the speaker; second, the purpose of gathering the assembly; third, the purpose of engendering respect for the verbal teaching; fourth, the purpose of recounting the subject matter; and fifth, the purpose of performing much service toward the teaching on the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*).

Furthermore, all phenomena (dharmas) possess three kinds of meanings: namely, the meaning of that which increases, the meaning of that which is increased, and the meaning of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
For example, form (rūpa) has three aspects: that which increases form, that which is increased as form, and the nature of form itself.
This should be understood to apply to all such cases.

Furthermore, there is a principle of the three wheels for proclaiming the teachings on all phenomena: namely, according to the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one proclaims the agent, the instrument, and the action.
As with the giver, the act of giving, and the recipient of the gift— meaning the one capable of practicing giving, the performance of that giving, and the recipient of the gift—
one should understand all such cases in this same way.

Furthermore, there are four kinds of doctrinal teachings on the principles of meaning: first, the teaching on the principle of differentiation; second, the teaching on the principle of establishment; third, the teaching on the principle of non-differentiation; and fourth, the teaching on the principle of non-activity.
Regarding the principle of differentiation herein, it refers to the differentiation of the natures from form up to all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Regarding the principle of establishment, it refers to five types of establishment:

first, the establishment of entry; second, the establishment of instruction; third, the establishment of training; fourth, the establishment of realization; and fifth, the establishment of faults and virtues.
There are six kinds of non-differentiation of principle:
first, the non-differentiation between existence and non-existence, meaning that form and the emptiness of form are non-different; this should be understood to apply to all such cases.
Second, mutual non-differentiation, meaning that the aggregates are mutually non-different when compared to one another; this should be understood to apply to all such cases.
1. There is no difference among the three times; that is, as one observes the future limit within the past limit, so it should be understood for all such cases.
2. There is no difference among the four types of persons (*pudgala*); that is, sentient beings in their mutual relation to one another.
3. There is no difference between obstacles and their remedies; that is, from permanence and impermanence up to saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
The six letters are without difference, namely the name-body (*nāmakāya*) and so forth.

Regarding the principle of the absence of functional activity: this refers to the purity of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍalapariśuddhi*). In accordance with all locations, no agent can be truly found; there is no instrument of action, nor is there any object of action.
There is no person (*pudgala*) who can speak, nor is there any dharma that can be spoken.
There is no person who can train, nor is there any dharma to be trained in.
There is no person who can realize, nor is there any dharma to be realized.
There is no person who can abide in faults or in virtues; furthermore, there is no abiding, no grasping, and no dharma.

All such things further comprise two kinds of immeasurable meanings: first, the immeasurability of initiating questions and discourses; second, the immeasurability of dedicating toward non-apprehension.
Furthermore, in order to counteract three types of bases, it is taught that one should not dwell on the meaning of form, up to and including the meaning of all phenomena.
These three types of bases are: first, the base of attachment; second, the base of conformity; and third, the base of the activity of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding wisdom.

Furthermore, there are three kinds of meaning regarding signlessness (*animitta*): first, signlessness as the absence of intrinsic nature; second, signlessness as the non-existence of that [intrinsic] nature; and third, signlessness as non-manifestation.

Just as it is with signlessness, so too should one understand the cases of the absence of essence (*niḥsvabhāva*), the absence of self-nature (*anātman*), non-arising and non-ceasing, non-attachment, non-action, and non-appropriation to be likewise.

Furthermore, there are three kinds of objects of apprehension: first, the apprehension of an entity; second, the apprehension of the apprehension of an entity; and third, the apprehension of non-apprehension.
Just as there is "attainment," so too should one understand that there is likewise attachment, activity, conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), grasping at views, and clinging to notions;

it is the same for all these. Furthermore, there are three kinds of the sense of attainment: first, attainment of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); second, attainment of non-separation; and third, attainment of non-analysis.

Furthermore, there are three kinds of non-apprehension: first, non-apprehension of intrinsic nature; second, non-apprehension through detachment; and third, non-apprehension through analytical investigation.

Just as there is nothing to be apprehended, so too should one know that it is likewise empty, without attachment, unconditioned, free from conceptual proliferation, without grasping, without views, and without mental construction.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of meanings of non-apprehension: first, non-apprehension of existence; second, non-apprehension of that essence; and third, non-apprehension of manifestation.

Regarding "non-apprehension": when one investigates all phenomena and does not perceive their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is not that nothing whatsoever is apprehended in every respect; rather, at the time when there is non-apprehension of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), one likewise does not observe the dependent characteristic (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*) of those [phenomena].

Furthermore, regarding the scriptural statement that they "correspond to non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*): if there is non-apprehension, does that constitute correspondence? This should be analyzed through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
First, there is the case where there is non-apprehension but no correspondence; this refers, for example, to someone who has absolutely no apprehension regarding a vast matter.
There may be that which is associated with application but not without attainment, namely, the cultivation of various wholesome dharmas by means of the mundane path.
There may be that which is both without attainment and associated with application, namely, the cultivation of various wholesome dharmas by means of the supramundane path.
"Neither non-attainment nor associated" refers to the manifestation of afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena.

Furthermore, there are five kinds of incorrect apprehension of objects (*ayoniśo'rthaparāmarśa*): namely, incorrect apprehension of the person (*pudgala*), incorrect apprehension of phenomena (*dharma*), incorrect apprehension of transformation (*vipariṇāma*), incorrect apprehension of negation (*apavāda*), and incorrect apprehension of differentiation (*viśeṣa*).

Furthermore, there are four types of verbal teachings and meanings: first, speech is fixed while the meaning is not; second, the meaning is fixed while speech is not; third, both speech and meaning are fixed; and fourth, both speech and meaning are not fixed.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of objects to be countered:
first, those countered by the gates of liberation, namely conceptual signs and aspirations;
second, those countered by the perfections (pāramitās), namely stinginess, violation of precepts, anger, laziness, distraction, and wrong wisdom.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of meanings that are the objects countered by emptiness: namely, the manifestation of sixteen types of false conceptions and fourteen types of conceptual fetters.

Furthermore, there are two kinds of meanings regarding the practice of the perfections (pāramitās): namely, mundane practice characterized by apprehension and supramundane practice characterized by non-apprehension.
Furthermore, the practice of reaching the other shore in the world is merely a semblance and not the reality.
Just as it is a semblance, one should know that it is likewise poisonous, obstructed, and devoid of skillful means.
One should know that the supramundane practice of the perfection (pāramitā) is the opposite of this.
Furthermore, if one were to briefly explain the essential meaning of the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā), it should be understood by way of three aspects:
first, the aspect of the basis; second, the aspect of the object; and third, the aspect of the mode of activity.
The characteristic of the basis is the bodhicitta.
The characteristic of the object is phenomena such as form.
There are two kinds of modes of activity: mundane and supramundane.
Mundane practices refer to the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, being like a disease, being like an ulcer, and so forth.
Supramundane practices refer to practices associated with non-apprehension.
Furthermore, there are three meanings of the thorough accumulation and cultivation of the pāramitās:
first, through mental engagement associated with the nature of omniscience, dedicating [the merit] together with all sentient beings toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
second, abiding in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) by means of the various pāramitās.
Third, one does not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "this mind is inconceivable," for what reason is it inconceivable?
This means that by means of this basis and this object, the mind is made to abide; yet both of these are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
If they are devoid of intrinsic nature, they are pure and likewise inconceivable.
This is because this inconceivable [reality], whether it possesses intrinsic nature or lacks intrinsic nature, as well as that mind, are either different in nature or not different in nature.

Furthermore, all modes of conceptual proliferation cause the mind to circulate due to three causes and conditions: first, by way of association; second, by way of the object of focus; and third, by way of establishment.
"By way of proximity" means that at the time of receiving the retribution, one grasps the basis [of existence].
"By way of being the object-condition" means that one experiences various objects and initiates various types of preparatory application.
Regarding "because of establishment," this refers to the habitual perfuming of false conceptualization since beginningless time.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of meanings of discrimination: first, discrimination with [conceptual] content;
second, discrimination without [conceptual] content.
Third, dualistic discrimination; fourth, non-dualistic discrimination.

Furthermore, there are four kinds of meaning regarding non-discrimination: first, non-discrimination of ignorance; second, non-discrimination of insentient things; third, non-discrimination of non-activity; and fourth, non-discrimination of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of verbal teachings and meanings: namely, conventional verbal teachings and ultimate verbal teachings.
Conventional verbal teachings refer to the establishment of two types of principles through differentiation.
Regarding the teaching on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it refers to two principles: being without difference and being without activity.
Furthermore, within the ultimate truth itself, nothing can be expressed; however, within the realm of verbal expression, one should know that there are three characteristics:
first, the characteristic of characteristics; second, the characteristic of affliction (*saṃkleśa*); and third, the characteristic of purification (*vyavadāna*).
Furthermore, one realizes all phenomena through three modes of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
These three modes are: first, provisional designation (*prajñapti*); second, discernment (*vijñapti*); and third, that [discernment] as the sole measure (*tanmātra*).
What do the bodhisattvas take as happiness?
They take the gathering and benefiting of sentient beings as happiness.
What do they take as suffering?
It means that the affliction and harm of sentient beings constitute suffering.
What constitutes the mental orientation (*manasikāra*)?
It means that reflecting upon the welfare of all sentient beings constitutes the mental orientation.
By what does one abide?
It is by means of non-conceptualization that one abides.
Furthermore, there are twelve kinds of difficult matters which a wise bodhisattva-mahāsattva should understand.
First, to either punish or abandon sentient beings who violate the rules and methods is a difficult task for bodhisattvas.
Second, to skillfully engage in acts that cause suffering and distress while guarding one's own mind so that afflictions do not arise is a difficult task for bodhisattvas.
Third, it is a difficult task for these bodhisattvas when immeasurable sentient beings appear before them and demand all their current, improper wealth and possessions.

Fourth, it is a difficult task for these bodhisattvas when they possess only a single body, yet the various affairs of immeasurable sentient beings simultaneously present themselves, requesting them to act as assistants.

Fifth, to dwell in a state of heedlessness—whether it be dwelling in the lovely and wondrous meditative concentrations of the world, or being born in the heavens to bring the mind into a state of pliancy—is a difficult task for these bodhisattvas.
Sixth, constantly seeking to perform deeds that universally benefit sentient beings, yet finding oneself lacking the power and ability to do so—this is a difficult task for bodhisattvas.
Seventh, whether teaching the Dharma to sentient beings who are dull-witted, deceitful, and stubborn, or else abandoning them altogether—this is a difficult task for bodhisattvas.
Eighth, constantly perceiving the great faults within birth and death, yet not abandoning them for the sake of benefiting sentient beings—this is a difficult task for bodhisattvas.
Ninth, failing to realize the superior pure intention (adhyāśaya) and frequently losing mindfulness at the time of death—this is a difficult task for bodhisattvas.
Tenth, when one has not yet realized the superiorly pure intention (*adhyāśaya*), and another comes to request that which is most cherished and supreme, this is a difficult matter for Bodhisattvas.
Eleventh, when sentient beings with various opinions and various inclinations appear before them, whether one instructs or abandons them, this is a difficult task for these bodhisattvas.
Twelfth, to constantly practice the most extreme form of heedfulness while not yet having completely severed all afflictions is a difficult feat for bodhisattvas.

If bodhisattvas encounter such difficult circumstances, they should either contemplate the relative gravity of the situation and establish skillful means accordingly, or discern the individual concerned, or exert effort to provide support in accordance with the shifting conditions.

If one forms a right aspiration, or restrains the mind so that it does not become dissolute, or dwells with the mind in intense observation, one should practice self-patience without giving rise to weariness.
Whether out of compassion they give rise to a mind of relinquishment, or they should arouse fervent diligence, or again reflect upon skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*),

such skillfulness in direct antidotes allows the bodhisattva-mahāsattva to remain free from fear or dread even when such hardships and difficulties are directly present before them, and to be able to liberate themselves.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of true marks of a bodhisattva; by accomplishing these, one enters the ranks of the bodhisattvas.
What are the five? They are:

having compassion for sentient beings, always speaking with endearing words, being courageous and resolute in action, extending the hand in generous giving, and being able to skillfully analyze the profound points of meaning.
Compassion has two types of nature: first, aspiration; second, correct practice.
Aspiration refers to a bodhisattva’s arising of the intention to benefit and the intention to bring peace and happiness toward all sentient beings.

Regarding "right conduct," it refers to bodhisattvas acting toward sentient beings through the physical and verbal actions of gathering and transforming them, according to their inclinations and desires, and in accordance with their own strength and capability.
This is called compassion.
Regarding kind speech: it is to gladden and console others while proclaiming one's own virtues; this is what is meant by a bodhisattva always speaking kind words to all sentient beings.
Regarding "courageous decisiveness in action": this refers to being majestic and fearless, having achieved supreme power; this is called a bodhisattva’s courageous decisiveness in action.
Regarding "generosity with open hands": if bodhisattvas practice vast giving and practice untainted giving, this is called a bodhisattva’s generosity with open hands.

If bodhisattvas are well able to initiate the correct skillful means and wisdom of the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), this is called a bodhisattva’s ability to skillfully analyze the essential nature of the profound nodes of meaning.

Furthermore, there are five kinds of extraordinary and five kinds of non-extraordinary marks of a bodhisattva, as explained previously in the "Chapter on the Compendium of Purified Meanings" (*Śuddhārthasaṃgraha*).
Moreover, regarding the matters of merit, I shall now explain the superior discernment based upon the Mahāyāna.
The verse says:
The spiritual lineage, what the Tathāgata has taught, The many Buddhas and the Single Vehicle,
The five kinds and the ten kinds, And the sixfold and sixfold principles.
The Treatise says:

Regarding the distinctions of spiritual lineages (*gotra*), the Mahāyāna teachings spoken by the Tathāgata, the appearance of many Buddhas in a single period of time, and the nature of the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*), one should understand five types, ten types, six types, and six types of principles, respectively.
Question:
What are the five principles for distinguishing the lineages? Answer:

This is because: (1) all realms can be found to have distinctions; (2) it would be illogical for there to be sentient beings without faculties; (3) it would be illogical for a homogeneous analogy to apply; (4) it would be illogical for a heterogeneous analogy to apply; and (5) it would be illogical for those who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa to exist only in the present life.
Why is it said that "the distinctions among all realms are apprehended"?

This means that the various realms of sentient beings spoken of by the Buddha are manifold and not a single realm of sentient beings; there are inferior and superior realms of sentient beings, and realms of sentient beings with the lineage for parinirvāṇa through the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth, as well as realms of sentient beings without the lineage for parinirvāṇa.
Why is it unreasonable for there to be sentient beings without sense faculties?
That is to say, one cannot claim that, by this same principle, there should also exist sentient beings without sense faculties. Why is this so?
Since those without the lineage are like external objects such as the earth, which are not sentient beings,
how could it be that a similar analogy is illogical? That is to say,

one should not claim that just as the caste of a kṣatriya can change into a non-kṣatriya, or as the destiny of a hell-being can change into a non-hell-being, so too should the spiritual lineage of parinirvāṇa and the non-parinirvāṇa lineage be subject to change.

Why is this? Because the kṣatriyas and others, as well as those in the hells and so forth, possess all varieties of the nature of elements (*dhātu*) and the nature of realms of rebirth (*gati*); thus, the two distinct natures—those destined for parinirvāṇa and those not destined for parinirvāṇa—are mutually contradictory.
If those [beings] were devoid of the nature of the elements (*dhātu*), they would be ultimately incapable of turning back; therefore, the analogy of a similar class is not logical.
Why is it that an analogy of a dissimilar class is also illogical?
That is to say, it cannot be said that in various locations there might first exist certain types of substances—such as gold, silver, copper, iron, or salt—and later cease to exist;
or that what was previously non-existent subsequently comes into existence.
In this way, the lineage (*gotra*) of those destined for parinirvāṇa would likewise have to exist first and then not exist, or not exist first and then exist. Why?
Because if such a principle were true, the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) would be empty and fruitless; therefore, the analogy of different species is also illogical.
Why is it unreasonable to claim that only those in the present life who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa [are excluded]?

It means one should not say that although a person lacks the nature for parinirvāṇa in their current birth, they may later, in a future birth, transform into one who possesses the nature for parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because they lack the dharma of the lineage for parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, if one has already accumulated the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) in this life, why is such a person not said to possess the dharma for parinirvāṇa?
If one has not accumulated at all the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) in this life, how could one attain parinirvāṇa in a future life?
Therefore, there must certainly exist sentient beings who lack the lineage for parinirvāṇa.
Question:
How should one know that the Mahāyāna teachings are the word of the Buddha? Answer:
Due to ten reasons: first, because it was not previously prophesied;
second, because it cannot be known now;
third, because there is much that must be accomplished.
Fourth, because it constitutes an extremely grave obstruction;

fifth, because it is not within the sphere of discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), for if one has not previously heard it, one cannot engage in such conceptualization and deliberation; therefore, to claim that this was spoken by another is unreasonable.
Sixth, because it is the realization of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*); if one who has not yet attained Buddhahood could expound the Buddha’s teachings, it would be unreasonable.
Seventh, because there is no fault of a third vehicle;
eighth, because if this did not exist, there would be no Omniscient One, which would result in the fault [of contradicting reality];
ninth, because by taking this as an object and reflecting upon it according to reason, one counteracts all afflictions.
Tenth, one should not grasp their meaning literally.
Question:
How should one understand that many Tathāgatas appear in the world simultaneously?
Answer:
It is due to six reasons: first, because it is currently observable that immeasurable sentient beings simultaneously give rise to the vow for great enlightenment;
second, because it is currently observable that immeasurable sentient beings collectively cultivate the skillful means and the provisions for awakening.
It is illogical for them to mutually obstruct one another during the third watch;
it is logical that the four accumulations for awakening are simultaneously perfected and together transcend the world;
and it is illogical for them to appear sequentially.
The sixth [point], ultimate non-attainment, is not tenable because it does not accord with reason.
Question:
For what reason did the Tathāgata proclaim the One Vehicle (ekayāna)?
Answer: It is due to six reasons: first, because those various dharmas are explained in terms of their undifferentiated characteristics;
second, because they are explained in terms of their non-conceptual mode of activity.
Third, because of the equality of the selflessness of sentient beings and the selflessness of phenomena;

fourth, because of the equality of liberation—meaning that for those who seek distinctions, the dharmatā, which serves as the object of focus for the antidotes to the afflictions of false conceptualization regarding entities, is not in contradiction [with it];
fifth, because of being well-able to abide in transformations.
Because the six practices have reached their ultimate consummation.
Furthermore, the verse says:
The sublime power of all Buddhas Is the purity of their resultant lands.
Liberation and the Dharma-body are equal, inconceivable, and unsurpassed.
The commentary states:
All Tathāgatas are equal in their functional capacity regarding all deeds to be performed.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the fruits of those capacities—the purification of the Buddha-fields, the liberation-body (*vimukti-kāya*), and the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*)—are all equal, all inconceivable, and all unsurpassed for all Buddhas.
Furthermore, the verse says:
Although no further application of effort is required, It is induced by the power of prior vows;
Arising in reliance upon the unconditioned, The activity performed is devoid of dualistic characteristics.
The Commentary states:

Relying upon the unconditioned *dharmakāya*, although there is no effort of applied cultivation (*prayoga*), all the Buddha-activities performed by the Tathāgatas are spontaneously initiated by the power of the original vows (*pūrvapraṇidhāna*). This is like a practitioner arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Furthermore, one should know that these Buddha-activities which arise possess the characteristic of inexhaustibility; they are neither the characteristic of saṃsāra nor the characteristic of nirvāṇa.
What is the Sūtra-piṭaka?
What is the Vinaya Piṭaka? What is the Mātṛkā Piṭaka?
The verse says:
The proclamation of all phenomena, the analysis of the Prātimokṣa,
and the eleven characteristics of all dharmas— this is the root-piṭaka of Sūtra and Vinaya.
The Commentary says:
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, reveal all phenomena solely by relying on the *saṃgrahavastu* (bases of sympathy); this is called the Sūtra Piṭaka.
Question:
What are the *saṃgrahavastu*?
Answer: It refers to four matters, nine matters, and twenty-nine matters.
What are the four matters?
These refer to the matter of hearing, the matter of taking refuge, the matter of training, and the matter of enlightenment.

As for the nine kinds of matters: first, the matter of the conventionally designated sentient being; second, the matter of what they utilize; third, the matter of their arising; fourth, the matter of their abiding after having arisen; fifth, the matter of their defilement and purification; sixth, the matter of their various distinctions; seventh, the matter of the speaker; eighth, the matter of the Dharma taught; and ninth, the matter of the assembly.

Regarding the twenty-nine types of matters: in the *Sarvābhisamaya-navavastuka-sūtra*, four matters are explained according to the category of affliction (*saṃkleśa*). First, the matter of subsuming all activities; second, the matter of their successive progression therein; third, the matter of establishing the notion of a sentient being therein as the subsequent cause for progression; and fourth, the matter of establishing the notion of phenomena (*dharma*) therein as the subsequent cause for progression.
Furthermore, based on the section on the pure qualities (*śukla-pakṣa*), twenty-five matters are taught: first, the matter of abiding in the object of focus;
second, the matter of exertion therein;
third, the matter of the mind’s abiding.
Fourth, the matter of dwelling in happiness in the present life;
fifth, the matter of the means for taking all suffering as the object of focus;

sixth, the matter of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), which is threefold: namely, thorough knowledge of the basis for inversion; thorough knowledge of the basis for the misconduct of external sentient beings based on the perception of "sentient being"; and thorough knowledge of the internal basis for freedom from overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Seventh, the matter of the basis for cultivation;
eighth, the matter of realization;
ninth, the matter of practice.
10. The matter of its firmness;
11. The matter of its mode of activity;
12. The matter of its object of focus.
Thirteen, skill in discerning what has been abandoned and what has not yet been abandoned through the thirteen contemplations;
fourteen, the matter of that distraction;
fifteen, the matter of that non-distraction.
16. The matter of the basis for non-distraction;
17. The matter of not being separated from the application of tireless cultivation;
18. The matter of the benefits of cultivation.
19. The matter of that firmness;
20. The matter of the chapter on gathering the noble ones (*ārya*);
21. The matter of what is to be avoided in the chapter on gathering the noble ones.
Twenty-two: the matter of penetrating reality;
twenty-three: the matter of realizing nirvana;
twenty-four: the matter of attaining mundane right view within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, which surpasses all external right views.
Twenty-fifth, one does not cultivate these matters that lead to decline.
This is called "decline" because of a lack of cultivation within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, and not due to the fault of wrong views.

Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, taught the Prātimokṣa and the detailed analysis of the teachings associated with the Prātimokṣa for the sake of the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas; this is called the Vinaya Piṭaka.

In this regard, it should be understood that the bodhisattva’s prātimokṣa is briefly subsumed by seven aspects: first, the proclamation of the rules for receiving and maintaining [the vows]; second, the proclamation of matters concerning the *pārājika* offenses; third, the proclamation of matters concerning transgressions; fourth, the proclamation of the nature of transgression; fifth, the proclamation of the nature of non-transgression; sixth, the proclamation of the methods for remedying transgressions; and seventh, the proclamation of the relinquishment of the discipline (*vinaya*).
Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, clearly distinguishes, analyzes, and reveals all phenomena through eleven aspects;
this is called the Mātṛkā-piṭaka. What are these eleven aspects?

1. The characteristic of conventional truth; 2. The characteristic of ultimate truth; 3. The characteristic of the objects of the factors of enlightenment; 4. The characteristic of this mode of activity; 5. The characteristic of this essential nature; 6. The characteristic of attaining this fruit; 7. The characteristic of the manifestation of this experience; 8. The characteristic of these obstructive dharmas; 9. The characteristic of these concordant dharmas; 10. The characteristic of these faults; 11. The characteristic of this praise.

Regarding the characteristics of the conventional, one should know that they consist of the teaching on the *pudgala*, the teaching on the nature of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and the teaching on the characteristics of the functions, actions, and instruments of all phenomena.
Regarding the characteristic of the ultimate truth, one should know that it proclaims the sevenfold aspects of suchness as the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Regarding the characteristic of the object of focus, one should know that it proclaims all types of objects of knowledge.
Regarding these modes of observation, one should know that they proclaim eight types of investigative practice.

What are the eight? First, the investigation of the truths; second, the investigation of establishment; third, the investigation of faults; fourth, the investigation of qualities; fifth, the investigation of the underlying principles; sixth, the investigation of cyclic existence; seventh, the investigation of reasoning; and eighth, the investigation of the detailed and the concise.
"Truth" refers to suchness (*tathatā*).

"Establishment" refers to the establishment of persons (*pudgala*), the establishment of the nature of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the establishment of categorical, analytical, counter-questioning, or setting-aside answers, and the establishment of implicit or explicit explanations.
"Faults" refers to the various and manifold distinct faults among all the defiled phenomena taught by the Buddha.
"Qualities" refers to the various and manifold distinct benefits among all the purified phenomena taught by the Buddha.
Regarding "principles" (naya), there are six kinds of principles as already explained in the Chapter on Compendium of Topics (Vastusaṃgrahaṇī).
Regarding "evolution" (pravṛtti), it refers to the three times, the three characteristics of the conditioned, and the four conditions.
"Reasoning" refers to the four types of reasoning: first, the reasoning of dependence; second, the reasoning of function; third, the reasoning of proof; and fourth, the reasoning of natural law.
If, by means of various causes and conditions, conditioned phenomena arise and are subsequently explained, this is called the principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*).

If, by means of various causes and conditions, dharmas are realized or brought to fulfillment, or if, once arisen, they are able to perform their functional activity (*kāritra*), this is called the principle of efficacy (*kāryakāraṇa-yukti*).

If, by means of various causes and conditions, the meaning established, explained, or set forth is successfully proven and correctly understood, this is called the principle of proof (*upapattisādhanayukti*).
This, in brief, is of two kinds: first, pure; second, impure.
The pure is characterized by five aspects;
the impure is characterized by seven aspects.

The five kinds of characteristics of purity are: first, the characteristic of what is obtained through direct perception; second, the characteristic of that which relies upon what is obtained through direct perception; third, the characteristic of drawing an analogy from within its own class; fourth, the characteristic of establishment; and fifth, the characteristic of well-purified verbal instruction.

Among these, the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the suffering of all conditioned phenomena, and the selflessness of all phenomena (*dharma*) are obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by the world at large.
Such categories as these are called the characteristics obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Whether it be the momentariness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the existence of future lives, or the non-destruction of pure and impure karma—these are obtained through direct perception of coarse impermanence, through direct perception of the various differentiated karmas of sentient beings, and through direct perception of the pure and impure karmas of sentient beings that result in suffering and pleasure.

Because it is obtained through this direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), one infers those phenomena that are not directly perceived; this is called the characteristic of relying on what is obtained through direct perception.

If, within internal and external formations (*saṃskāra*), one adduces the characteristic of arising and ceasing known and attained by all the world, the characteristic of suffering such as arising known and attained by all the world, the characteristic of lack of autonomy known and attained by all the world, and regarding external objects, the characteristic of flourishing and decay known and attained by all the world—such categories as these are called the characteristic of adducing an analogy from its own class.

That is to say, the characteristic obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the characteristic of adducing an analogy of the same class; since these two are invariably certain regarding that which is to be established (*sādhya*), one should know that they are termed the "characteristic of accomplishment" (*siddhilakṣaṇa*).
If various teachings are spoken by the Omniscient One—such as the statement that "nirvāṇa is quiescent" and other similar categories—these are called the characteristics of well-purified teachings.
In this regard, there are five characteristics that can manifest a truly omniscient one. What are these five?
First, if an omniscient one appears in the world, his name and reputation will spread throughout the world as true and authentic.
Second, he is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man;
third, he has accomplished the ten powers to sever all webs of doubt belonging to sentient beings;
fourth, he declares himself to be fully possessed of the four fearlessnesses, such that he cannot be defeated by any opposing arguments and is able to subdue all external doctrines.
Fifth, within his doctrine and discipline, the Noble Eightfold Path and the four fruits of śrāmaṇya are attainable.

Because he thus appears, because he possesses the sublime marks, because he eliminates doubt, because he establishes and refutes, and because of the path and its fruit—by these five characteristics, he is shown to be the true Omniscient One.

Thus, within the principles of proof, by means of direct perception, inference, analogy, logical establishment, and authoritative scripture—through these five characteristics, it is called "purified."

The seven kinds of impure characteristics are: first, the characteristic obtained through partial similarity; second, the characteristic obtained through partial dissimilarity; third, the characteristic obtained through total similarity; fourth, the characteristic obtained through total dissimilarity; fifth, the characteristic of citing a dissimilar analogy; sixth, the characteristic of non-establishment; and seventh, the characteristic of impure verbal instruction.
If all phenomena possess the nature of being cognized by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), this is called the characteristic obtained through the similarity of all [phenomena].

Whether it be their marks, their intrinsic natures, their functions, their phenomena, their causes, or their results—the characteristics of their similarities and differences, or the characteristics of their mutual similarities and differences according to any particular aspect—this is called the characteristic obtained through the similarity and difference of other parts.
Alternatively, when there is a definitive mutual difference in characteristics, this is called the "characteristic obtained from all dissimilar classes.

If there are both remaining partial similarities obtained from similar classes and all dissimilarities obtained from dissimilar classes, because these characteristics do not establish the thesis to be proven with certainty, they are termed "unestablished characteristics" (*asiddha-lakṣaṇa*).

If, together with the simile, there are characteristics obtained from other remaining portions of a different class, as well as all characteristics obtained from the same class, and because these characteristics do not establish the meaning to be proven with certainty, they are also called "unestablished characteristics."
Because it is not accomplished, it is called the "contemplation of impure principles.
Since this contemplation is impure, it should not be cultivated.
Regarding the characteristics of impure verbal teachings, one should know that they refer to those verbal teachings whose intrinsic nature is impure.

The principle of the nature of things (*dharmatā-yukti*) refers to the fact that whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) abide immutably; this is called the principle of the nature of things.
Regarding "concise and extensive": this refers to first stating a single phrase of the Dharma, and subsequently using immeasurable phrases to progressively analyze, clarify, and fully elucidate it.

As for its "essential characteristic," this refers to that which is capable of grasping—whether as activity or as an object—the factors conducive to enlightenment, such as the four foundations of mindfulness; this is called its essential characteristic.

Regarding the characteristics of attaining this fruit: it refers to the fruits of abandoning mundane and supramundane afflictions, as well as the mundane and supramundane virtues they induce; these are called the characteristics of attaining this fruit.

Regarding this characteristic of experiencing and manifesting: it refers to the experience of the characteristics of the fruit attained through the wisdom of liberation, as well as the extensive explanation of those characteristics for others; this is called the characteristic of experiencing and manifesting.

Regarding the characteristics of these obstructive dharmas: they refer to those defiled dharmas that are capable of acting as obstacles when one is cultivating the factors conducive to enlightenment; this is called the characteristic of these obstructive dharmas.

Regarding this characteristic of conformity (*anuloma-lakṣaṇa*): it refers to those factors among the aids to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) that are conducive and perform much service; this is called the characteristic of conformity.
Regarding these characteristics of defects: that which constitutes an obstacle and all such faults is called the characteristic of defects.
Regarding these characteristics of praise: that which accords with the Dharma and all such virtues is called the characteristic of praise.
In whatever context the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, clarify, differentiate, and reveal all phenomena through these eleven aspects, it is called Mātṛkā (Matrix).
Furthermore, the verse says:
"The various characteristics and their cessation, the absence of the means for their destruction,
the two fruits thereof, and their distinctions— this is the summarized meaning of all these sūtras."
The Treatise states:

It should be understood that the meaning of all sūtras, when summarized, consists of five types: first, characteristics; second, cessation and extinction; third, the skillful means of non-destruction; fourth, the fruits of those two; and fifth, the distinctions among characteristics and so forth.
These five are explained in brief as in the *Sujāta-sūtra*.
The Buddha told Sujāta: "Noble son!"
That which possesses two kinds of things both characterized as exquisite is the mark of excellence.
There are two kinds of cessation: namely, the cessation of the grasping for sensual desire and the cessation of the grasping for the basis of existence.
This statement also reveals two kinds of means for non-destruction.

As for the two kinds of means for non-destruction: they refer to [the stages] from shaving off the beard and hair and going forth into homelessness, up to the exhaustion of all outflows and the realization that "birth is exhausted," and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding those two fruits, they refer to the fruit of non-destruction through skillful means (*upāya*).

As for the distinctions in the nature of tranquility (*śāntatā*), there are five kinds of distinctions in tranquility: first, the tranquility of the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*); second, the tranquility of worldly detachment (*laukika-vairāgya*); third, the tranquility of the factors conducive to the lower realm (*avarabhāgīya*); fourth, the tranquility of the factors conducive to the higher realm (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*); and fifth, the tranquility based on the objective basis (*vastu*).
To clarify this, a verse is spoken in that sutra:
“O monks, you are beautiful, Tranquil and free from all outflows;
Free from desire and free from fetters, You have attained nirvana without clinging.”
"Maintaining his final body, he subdues those sent by Māra.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"To summarize the path of yoga: taking as its object the sublime Dharma as it has been heard,"
Calm abiding and insight are accomplished by relying on the mental image.
The commentary says:
If one were to briefly explain the path of yoga, it should be understood as being comprised of extensive learning.
The true Dharma is its object; śamatha and vipaśyanā constitute its essence; and it is accomplished by relying upon images and relying upon the thing-in-itself.
As the Bhagavat said:
"There are five factors that encompass all the yogic stages of every practitioner of yoga: namely, the support, the abiding, the mirror, the transformation, and the reliance."

One should know that hearing the true Dharma is the upholding; the object of focus is the abiding; tranquility and insight are the illumination; the reflected image is the function of the mirror; and accomplishment is the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
*Prakaraṇāryavācāśāstra*, Fascicle Twenty.
